units.la: PAucas istas, & vix fatis, pro materiæ dignitate, elaboratas pagellas tam augusto inscribere nomini erubescerem; Patriæ Patres, Proceres Amplissimi; nisi & seculorum pene omnium consuetudo & malevolorum morositas imbelli huic fœtui patrocinium implorare; pietas vero, quam Civis Reipublicæ debeo, illud ipsum à Vobis potissimum, expectare me juberet. Vestra enim, quod ignorare non potestis, causa agitur. Vestræ Ecclesiæ singulare hoc privilegium est, ut, cum salutaris de Cœna Domini doctrina, Scholasticorum nugis ubiq;, tricis, & tenebris, magno cum totius Christianismi damno, involveretur, per eam non Helvetia modo ; sed universus orbis reformatus lucem veritatis acciperet. Doluit, ante Reformationem, orbis Christianus & ingemuit, in pejus omnia in dies ruere : Magnum & ineffabile Coenae sacrae mysterium, in absurdissimorum dogmatum ossicinam converti: Seddoluit, dico, ingemuit, ultra vix progressus. Authoritatem Ecclesiae Romanae, consuetudinis tyrannidem, Scholasticorum subtilitates plerique adorare, quam adoriri maluerunt. Zuinglius, in his primum oris, postea & alibi, verum & genuinum Verbis institutionis sensum restituit. Restituit, itero, non invenit, aut commentus est. Et cum antea multi quidem animadvertissent, se in avia esse abreptos, modum tamen & cynosuram regiae investigandae viae non repererunt. Primus ausus est Zuinglius interruptam hanc navigationem denuo tentare, fontes obstructos, & obthuratos aperire, adeoque ad Dominicam nos originem revocare. Quid ab eo tempore in Sacramentaria causa, ab Ecclesiae Vestrae Ministris, sit praestitum, jam non enarrabimus : Apologiam hanc, Vestra authoritate, nuper admodum ; cum modestiae & pacis studium nonnulli aliter interpretari vellent; suscep-tam, bonae causae nihil derogaturam confido. Brevis quidem illa est, & succincta; iis tamen classibus instructa, ad quas cætera facilè revocari poterunt argumenta omnia. Ostendimus evidenter Ecclesiam Reformatam, tam in explicatione verborum Cœnæ, quàm in reliqua Sacramenti administratione, Evangelicam sequi authoritatem, Canonémq; Scripturæ; neque subterfugere inferius Patrum consentientiam tribunal, habere sibi faventem fidei analogiam, sobriámque rationem. Ecclesiam contrà, Romanam, ne uno quidem Scripturæ textu posse probare, vel verba Institutionis esse proprie intelligenda, vel calicem laicis auferendum, vel Leitur-
units.tr: I would be ashamed to inscribe these few little pages, hastily worked out and hardly adequate to the dignity of the subject, to so august a name, Fathers of the fatherland, most distinguished nobles; were it not that the custom of nearly every age and the peevishness of ill-wishers bid me seek patronage for this feeble offspring, and the loyalty I owe as a citizen of the republic would order me to look for that above all from you. For, as you cannot be unaware, the cause under discussion is yours. It is a singular privilege of your Church that, while the wholesome doctrine of the Lord's Supper was being wrapped everywhere in the trifles, snares and darkness of the Schoolmen, to the great loss of all Christianity, through your Church not only Helvetia but the whole reformed world received the light of truth. Before the Reformation the Christian world grieved and groaned, as all things daily rushed toward the worse: the great and ineffable mystery of the Holy Supper was being turned into a workshop of the most absurd dogmas. But it grieved, I say, and groaned, scarcely advancing further. Most people chose to adore the authority of the Roman Church, the tyranny of custom and the subtleties of the Schoolmen, rather than to assail them. Zwingli, first here by word of mouth and afterwards also elsewhere, restored the true and genuine sense of the words of institution. He restored it, I say, he did not discover or invent it. And although earlier many had indeed noticed that they had been carried off into wrong paths, they had not found the method or the guiding star for seeking the royal road. Zwingli was the first to dare to try again this interrupted voyage, to open the obstructed and blocked springs, and so to lead us back to the Lord's origin. What has been done in the sacramentarian cause since that time by the ministers of your Church we shall not now recount. This Apology, taken up recently under your authority, when some wished to interpret the zeal for modesty and peace otherwise, I trust will detract nothing from the good cause. It is indeed brief and succinct, yet it is furnished with those main heads to which all the other arguments can easily be referred. We have shown clearly that the Reformed Church, both in the explanation of the words of the Supper and in the rest of the administration of the sacrament, follows the evangelical authority and the canon of Scripture; nor does it shun the tribunal of the consent of the Fathers below that, having the analogy of faith and sober reasoning on its side. The Roman Church, on the contrary, cannot prove from even one text of Scripture either that the words of institution are to be understood properly, or that the cup is to be withheld from the laity, or that the liturgy and consecration are to be performed in Latin, or that the Sacrament of the Supper is to be changed into a proper sacrifice. This we are ready to defend now and hereafter, as far as we are able.

units.la: [The line-final catchword "tur-" is shown here as printed.] turgiam & consecrationem Latine peragendam, vel Sacramentum Cœnæ in proprie dictum Sacrificium permutandum. Id quod & jam, & deinceps, pro virili, defendere sumus parati. Hi carceres nostræ metæ sunto, hi limites, quos extra currere volupe non est. Sive igitur sudantes jam, madentésque chartæ nostræ torqueantur, sive deinceps contradictionis fatum sint experturæ, id unum τὰς ἀντιλέγοντας[?] rogamus, ut ne ad Andabatarum, inutilem pariter atque ingloriam, nos provocent pugnam: Non ingenii hic lusus, non scientiæ tantum exercitium; conscientiæ etiam sacrum certamen est & examen, utrum cibum, vere & mere Spiritualem, panem cœlestem, carnem Filii Dei alio, quàm tanto mysterio convenienti i.e. Spirituali, jubeamur manducare modo? Utrum, præstet unam, eámq; usitatissimam in Sacramentis admittere Metonymiam, quàm, ejus contemtu & repudio, universam sacram Scripturam, totúmque Christianismum præsentissimo exponere periculo? Sed desino præfari. Deumsupplex veneror, ut quod Vobis clementissimè hactenus concessit, Evangelii sui depositum, proporrò conservet, & ad seros nepotes propaget; Rempublicam, Ecclesiam, Scholam Vestram diutiùs esse jubeat affli-ćto{ç}torum asylum, Orthodoxiæ Templum, omnis piæ & solidæ literaturæ Gymnasium, ad sanctissimi sui Nominis gloriam, veritatis conservationem, animarum denique salutem, per & propter Dominum nostrum, Iesum Christum, Amen. Ita vovet Tiguri Cal. Septemb. 1663. Magnificentissimi, Nobilissimi & Amplissimi Nominis Vestri obsequentissimus Joh: Henricus Hottingerus, D.
units.tr: [The line-final catchword "tur-" is shown here as printed.] turgy and consecration... These are the barriers of our course, these the limits beyond which it is not pleasant to run. So whether our paper, now sweating and sodden, is to be racked, or whether hereafter it is to undergo the fate of contradiction, we ask this one thing of our opponents [τὰς ἀντιλέγοντας]: that they do not challenge us to the fight of the Andabatae, useless and equally inglorious. This is no sport of wit, no mere exercise of learning; it is also a sacred contest and examination of conscience, whether we are commanded to eat food that is truly and purely spiritual, the heavenly bread, the flesh of the Son of God in a manner other than what suits so great a mystery, that is, spiritual? Is it better to admit one metonymy in the sacraments, and that a most common one, or, by despising and rejecting it, to expose all of Holy Scripture and the whole of Christianity to the most immediate danger? But I cease to preface. I humbly pray God that what he has most graciously granted you hitherto, the deposit of his Gospel, he may continue to preserve and pass on to remote descendants; that he may will your Republic, Church and School to be for longer the refuge of the afflicted, the temple of orthodoxy, the gymnasium of all pious and solid learning, to the glory of his most holy Name, the preservation of truth and, finally, the salvation of souls, through and for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. So vows, at Zurich, 1 September 1663, your Magnificent, Most Noble and Most Distinguished Lordships' most obedient Johann Heinrich Hottinger, D.

units.la: VOLIM Athenæ, sic vicinum jam nobis Tiberii forum semper aliquid novi! Et instantibus quidem hujus anni nundinis Pentecostalibus illud nobis attulit, quod omnium minime exspectâssemus. Disceptationem brevem de Eucharistia, cum facultate Superiorum, Soloduri, ex Iohannis Iacobi Bernhardi Typographia emissam. Mirabar, notorium Authoris in limine statim omissionis peccatum. Nomen Authoris desiderabam. Id quod, salva constitutione Concilii Tridentini, fieri non poterat. Ita enim sess. 4. statuit sacrosancta Synodus, ut posthac nulli liceat imprimere, vel imprimi facere, quosvis libros de rebus sacris, sine nomine auctoris, propter imminens periculum falsitatis, fraudis aut doli, quod in similibus libris anonymis plerunque latere solet, cum sub incognita facie quælibet liberius audaciúsq; proponantur, ut ex Stephan. Veyms observat Auguft. Barbos. in sess. citatam. Et in Indic librorum prohibitorum, auctoritate Pii IV. & Sixti V. Coloniæ 1597. edito, mandatum ff. 1. de impressione librorum, ita habet: Nullus liber in posterum excudatur, qui non in fronte nomen, cognomen & patriam praeferat Authoris. Mirabar, scriptum privatum, occasione privata, anno 1660. conceptum, jam demum, & quidem post beatam ἐγψδιώκτως Viri doctissimi, & de Ecclesia Reformata praeclare meriti Theologi, ex hac Ecclesia militante in triumphantem translationem; publicae exponi luci. Quasi leoni insultare mortuo illustre atque Heroicum esset facinus! Mirabar insuper, aliud Tigurinis antehac, & initio quidem hujus velitationis literariae, missum esse scriptum, aliud contra Tigurinos jam typis vulgatum. Quantum autem hoc ab illo differat, ex collatione nemini obscurum esse poterit. Mirabar denique, Tigurinos, sine discrimine, ubique vapulare, omnibusque fuisse exedendum, quod unus & alter intrivit. Etsi enim nec causam deserturi fuissent Tigurini, nec patrocinium denegaturi piis defuncti manibus, non consuevit tamen Ecclesia Tigurina inter scripta sua, sive publica, sive symbolica referre, quod non & Amplissimi Magistratus decreto, & totius Ministerii, Ecclesiae saltem repraesentativae calculo sit injunctum, approbatum, & in lucem protractum. Quod quidem cum primis doctissimo Authori (hoc enim nomine, cum suum exstare noluerit, eum, quo cum nobis res est, magno ejus merito, appellare licebit) & tanto diligentius erat observandum, quanto exploratius perspectum ille habet, Ecclesiam Romanam, ne eorum quidem, concontra receptam consuetudinem, fraudi esse permittere authoritatem, quorum tamen scripta, ordinariâ Censorum curâ, probata, elimata & ad prælum destinata sunt. Si mille Bellarminos, Baronios, ne dicam, Espensaos, Marollaos, Montanos, Mutsios, Ecclesiae Romanae vel disensui, vel novitatibus, vel superstitionibus opponamus, unâ expungentur litura omnes; Vnius & alterius judiciis Ecclesiam Romanam nec stare, nec cadere. Cur ergo nobis Talionis legem invideant? Cur salutem Ecclesiae Tigurinae, ejusque, circa Controversiam sacramentariam, sensum à privata hac Monomachia suspendant? Nulli enim, etsi docto, etsi sancto, etsi præclarè merito, unquam hoc dedit Ecclesia Tigurina, ut pro symbolico, totius Ecclesiae scripto recipiendum obtulerit, quod publicae authoritatis & approbationis sigillum non haberet. Quae quidem Ecclesiae nostrae, non vicinis modò, sed remotis etiam adeò nota est Methodus, ut vel monere, Soli sit lucem mutuare. Opportune hoc loco occurrit, quod, in Controversia quoq; sacramentaria, superiori seculo Andrea Fricio, Modrevio, cum Stanislao Orichovio Roxolano, Viro, ut vocat, facundo & erudito, contigit. Magna erat Fricii in Polonia authoritas; ipsi etiam Orichovio, ob eruditionem singularem ille commendatus: Credebat proinde, victoriam, ex prostrato Fricio sibi pulchram & spectabilem, si forte natus esset; ipsâmque adeò
units.tr: ONCE it was Athens; so, too, our neighbouring Forum of Tiberius always has something new! And at the Whitsun fair this year it brought us something we least expected: a short Disputation on the Eucharist, issued at Solothurn with the permission of the superiors, from the press of Johann Jakob Bernhard. I was surprised that the author committed the notorious offence of omission right at the threshold: he gave no name. I wanted his name. Yet, given the decree of the Council of Trent, this could not be done. The holy Synod decreed in session 4 that from now on no one may be allowed to print, or have printed, any books on sacred matters without the name of the author, because of the imminent danger of falsehood, fraud or deceit, which usually lies hidden in anonymous books of this kind, since whatever is put forward under an unknown face is more freely and boldly stated, as Augustinus Barbosa observes, citing Stephan Veyms, in his commentary on that session. And the mandate in the Index of Prohibited Books, published at Cologne in 1597 under the authority of Pius IV and Sixtus V, under the heading on the printing of books, reads: No book shall in future be published unless it bears on its title page the name, surname and country of its author. I was surprised that a private writing, composed for a private occasion in 1660, should only now, and indeed after the blessed departure of that most learned man, a theologian who deserved well of the Reformed Church, from this militant Church into the triumphant one, be brought out into the light of day. It would be a splendid and heroic deed to insult a dead lion! I was surprised, moreover, that one piece was sent to the Zurich men earlier, at the beginning of this literary skirmish, and another, already in print, is now published against the Zurich men. How much the one differs from the other can be clear to no one who compares them. Lastly, I was surprised that the Zurich men are everywhere beaten without distinction and must be devoured by all, because one or two have stumbled. For even if the Zurich men would neither abandon their cause nor deny protection to the departed shade, the Zurich Church has never been accustomed to include among its writings, whether public or confessional, anything that has not been enjoined, approved and brought to light by the decree of the most illustrious magistrate and the vote of the whole ministry, at least of the representative Church. This the most learned author (since he would not have his own name, I may call him by the name of the one with whom we have to deal, with due regard for his merit) should have observed above all, and all the more carefully as he knows very well that the Roman Church, contrary to even the common practice, does not allow the authority of those whose writings, having been approved by the ordinary care of the censors, polished and destined for the press, are yet false. If we set against the Roman Church a thousand Bellarmines, Baronii, not to mention Espencaeus, Marolles, Montanus, Mutsius, as opponents of its dissent, its novelties or its superstitions, all of them would be wiped out with one stroke: the Roman Church neither stands nor falls by the judgements of one or another man. Why, then, do they begrudge us the law of retaliation? Why do they make the welfare of the Zurich Church, and its view on the sacramentarian controversy, depend on this private single combat? For the Zurich Church has never offered, to any man, however learned, however holy, however well deserving, a writing to be received as a confessional statement of the whole Church, if it did not bear the seal of public authority and approval. Indeed, the method of our Church is so well known, not only to neighbours but even to those far away, that to point it out would be like lending light to the sun. Here it is timely to recall what happened in the sacramentarian controversy in the last century, when Andreas Fricius Modrevius had to deal with Stanislaus Orichovius Roxolanus, a man, as he calls him, eloquent and learned. Fricius had great authority in Poland, and Orichovius himself commended him for his singular learning. Orichovius therefore believed that if he had chanced to defeat Fricius, the victory would have been a fine and notable one for him, and the good cause of the Reformed would have received a dangerous wound.

units.la: A 3 bq bonam Reformatorum causam, periculosum accepturam vulnus. Sed magna prudentia & ingenuitate Fricius hunc declinavit ictum, neque unquam voluit per suum latus periclitari Ecclesiam Helveticam, qui ille in doctrina Sacramentaria majorem grato animo acceptam tulit lucem. Confutavit, inquit (Simplic. narrat. & expostulation. cum Stanisl. Orichov. pag. 130.) Orichovius ante annos circiter decem Lutherum, primatum Papæ convellentem. Cur non idem fecit confutandis Helvetiis, qui de Cœna Dominica longe secus docent, quam Papistæ? Non obstitit Orichovius principiis, cum tamen non ignoraret, quid Helvetii docerent. Sciret, dogma illorum in omnes nationes, in Poloniam etiam, abhinc fere decennium profluxisse: hodie in Ecclesiis Reformatis resonare. Dormitabat bonus Orichovius: nunc primum oculos aperuit ad illud confutandum in persona Fricii. Cur ita? An se gloriam ampliorem eo victo relaturum sperabat? Hoc vero perinde est, ac si quis Achille & Hectore omisso, de gregario, milite gloriam reportare velit. Non est operosus labor, vincere inermem, aut certe parum armatum, nec gloriosa victoria, quæ stat sine sanguine & vulnere. Conferenda erant Orichovio manus cum Oecolampadio, cum Zuinglio, cum Bucero, cum Bullingero, cum Calvino, cum Martyre, cumq; aliis antesignanis, ut justum triumphum phum ageret ex hostibus. Fricio enim victo, an causa victa est? Animadvertit doctissimus Vir, quid velim. Neque à proselyto, armis licet à nostris utcunque instructo, arma tamen nostra tractare nondum assueto, exspectandum fuisse ultimum causæ nostræ præsidium; neque Tigurinorum causam ex amicis velitationibus, sed publicis congressibus & symbolicis scriptis æstimandam. Intra arcta privatorum pomœria includi nos non patimur. Zuinglii nostri (ut ne quidem alios commemorem) priùs elidenda fuissent tela, quæ in causa Eucharistica sudit; Petro Martyri argumentorum phalanges, quibus in Anglia, disputationibus publicis triumphans, genuinam de S. Cœna sententiam astruxit, & falsam destruxit, eripiendæ; Arma, quæ Tigurinorum Polyhistor Rodolphus Hospinianus, felicissimè in Adversarios, tam exScriptura, quàm antiquitate, contorsit, extorquenda; antequam ἑπνίκιον non de Tigurinis dicam omnibus, sed uno tantùm, & altero Doctore Tigurino primario, intempestivè caneretur. Hic Rhodus, hic saltus ' Placuit paucis præfari, breviterq; quid in ipso statim Disceptationis vestibulo desideraverimus, monere, non quasi vel vadimonium essemus deserturi, vel doctissimi Viri quicquam in recessu haberent rationes, quod aliquoties jam, & operosè quidem à nostris expensum & confutatum non fuerit; sed ut, tum deTigurinæ Ecclesiæ modestia pacisque studio, quæ privatorum collisionem in publicam contentionis flammam noluit erumpere, constaret; tum e.probaremus, paratos nos esse, quod Petrus flagitat, 1 Ep. 3. 15, ad respondendum cuilibet, petenti rationem ejus spei, quæ in nobis est, cum lenitate & reverentia. Quod posterius Apostoli, disputationum Theologicarum gubernaculum, doctissimo Viro tanto liberalius pollicemur, quanto majorem ipse in sua disceptatione ostendit moderationem. Sed ad rem, & κατὰ πόδα quidem, succinctè, quantum fieri poterit, & dilucidè. Ne verò amica hæc & modesta disputatio nostra tumultuaria sit, vaga, aut incerta, quæextra carceres currat, geminis eam includemus cancellis, κατακοσμήσει, sive assertione sententiæ de Cœna Domini Orthodoxæ, & ἀνακοσμήσει, sive destructione opinionis adversæ. Atque hos limites ipse nobis Vir doctissimus constituit. Primaria enim nuper inter ipsum & nostros in capite de Cœna quæstio erat; Utrum, Ecclesia Romana magis secundum Evangelium sentiret, quam Protestantes, id est, Tigurini? Affirmativam ille tuebatur, fretus scil. verbis, Iohannis Cap. VI. Matthæi, Marci, Lucæ, ac Pauli de institutione Eucharistiæ. Nostri negativam defendebant, tum aliis instructi argumentis, tum vero constanti phrasium sacramentalium usu & consuetudine; quæ asserere nos jubent, Pa-
units.tr: But Fricius, with great prudence and honesty, avoided this blow, and never allowed the Helvetic Church to be endangered through his side; and he accepted with a grateful heart the greater light in sacramentarian doctrine. "Orichovius," he says (A Simple Narrative and Expostulation with Stanislaus Orichovius, p. 130), "refuted about ten years ago Luther, who was overthrowing the primacy of the Pope. Why did he not do the same in refuting the Helvetians, who teach about the Lord's Supper quite differently from the Papists? Orichovius did not resist their principles, although he was not unaware of what the Helvetians taught. He knew that their doctrine had flowed out into all nations, into Poland too, nearly ten years ago, and that today it resounds in the Reformed Churches. The good Orichovius was asleep; only now has he opened his eyes to refute it, in the person of Fricius. Why so? Did he hope to win greater glory by defeating him? But this is just as if someone, leaving aside Achilles and Hector, wanted to win glory from a common soldier. It is no hard labour to conquer an unarmed man, or one only poorly armed, and no glorious victory is one that is won without blood and wounds. Orichovius should have matched his hands against Oecolampadius, Zwingli, Bucer, Bullinger, Calvin, Martyr and the other standard-bearers, to gain a just triumph over the enemy. For if Fricius is defeated, is the cause defeated?"* The most learned man sees what I mean. It must not be expected that our last defence of the cause should come from a convert, however well he may be armed by our people, who is not yet accustomed to handling our weapons; nor is the cause of the Zurich men to be judged by friendly skirmishes, but by public encounters and confessional writings. We do not allow ourselves to be shut within the narrow boundaries of private men. The weapons which our Zwingli hurled in the eucharistic cause (not to mention others) should first have been struck down; the phalanxes of arguments with which Peter Martyr, triumphing in public disputations in England, established the genuine view of the Holy Supper and destroyed the false one, should first have been wrested away; the arms which the Zurich polymath Rudolf Hospinian has so successfully turned against the adversaries, both from Scripture and from antiquity, should be seized, before a premature song is raised, I will not say on behalf of all the Zurich men, but of only one or two of their chief teachers. Here is Rhodes, here is the leap. It has pleased us to say a few words in advance, and to point out briefly what we missed at the very outset of the Disputation; not as though we were going to abandon our bail, or as though the most learned man had any reasons in reserve which had not already been weighed and refuted, more than once, and with labour, by our people; but so that, on the one hand, the modesty of the Zurich Church and its zeal for peace, which did not wish the clash of private men to break out into the public flame of controversy, should be made plain, and on the other hand that we might show that we are ready, as Peter demands, to answer anyone who asks for a reason for the hope that is in us, with gentleness and reverence (1 Pet. 3:15). We promise this, as the Apostle, the rudder of theological disputation, the more freely to the most learned man, as he himself has shown the greater moderation in his disputation. But let us come to the matter, and to it straight away, as briefly as possible and as clearly as we can. Lest our friendly and modest dispute be disorderly, vague or uncertain, running outside the starting gates, we shall enclose it between two barriers: the establishing (katakosmesis), that is the assertion of the orthodox view of the Lord's Supper, and the overturning (anakosmesis), that is the destruction of the opposing opinion. And the most learned man himself has set these limits for us. For the primary question recently between him and our people, in the chapter on the Supper, was this: Whether the Roman Church thinks more in accordance with the Gospel than the Protestants, that is, the Zurich men? He defended the affirmative, relying, namely, on the words of John chapter 6, and of Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul, on the institution of the Eucharist. Our people defended the negative, both with other arguments and with the constant use and custom of sacramental phrases, which bid us assert that the bread

units.la: Panem nem esse corpus Christi, vinum esse sanguinem Christi eodem modo, quo in reliquis Veteris & Novi Testamenti Sacramentis, circumcisio est fœdus, agnus est transitus, baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis. Hæc erat nostra tium thesis five assertio, breviter quidem; sed ita erudite ab iis cum propositta, ut modesto & sedato ingenio satis potuisset facere: sed quando animadverto, scrupulos adhuc superesse cum in explicatione sententiæ nostræ, cum Scripturæ & Antiquitatis quibusdam locis, quæ Vir doctissimus publicæ exposuit luci, totam primariæ controversiæ retexenus telam, ita tamen, ut disceptationis vestigia religiose simus observaturi, ne apicem quidem eorum, quæ ad præsentem rem fecerint, prætereuntes. Altera pars, quæ de fide tantum & sensu quorundam allegatorum agit, adeoque personalis magis est, quàm dogmatica, suo etiam loco & tempore sequetur. Viam hoc prodromo sternimus, vadúmque tentamus; de cæteris Virum doctissimum, quem longiori, tam diu desiderati responsi mora multare inhumanum plane duximus, bene sperare jubemus: quamvis & ex iis, quæ hinc inde ad posteriores partis exceptiones respondemus, absq; negotio idè possit colligere, nihil prorsus habere instantias illas roboris, quod à sententia nos nostra avellere possit aut dimovere. Videbit enim doctissimus Vir, nostram de Cœna Dominica sententiam suffultam esse authoritate Scripturæ, suffragio Antiquitatis, & consensu sanæ Rationis. Eam contrà, à quæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ placet, de Transsubstantiatione, opinionem, & Scripturæ repugnare, & Analogiæ fidei, & Antiquitati, & sobriæ Rationi; doctrinam deniq; incertam, & scandali ita esse plenam, ut nomen Christi, & Christianismi ab infidelibus propterea indignè lacereetur imò, blasphemetur.
units.tr: Bread is the body of Christ, and wine is the blood of Christ, in the same way as in the other sacraments of the Old and New Testament: circumcision is the covenant, the lamb is the passover, baptism is the washing of regeneration. This was our thesis or assertion, briefly stated, but it was set out by them so learnedly that a modest and calm mind could well have been satisfied with it. Yet since I notice that scruples still remain, both about the explanation of our view and about certain passages of Scripture and antiquity, which that most learned man has published, we shall unravel the whole web of the main controversy, while carefully following the traces of the dispute and not passing over even the smallest point that bears on the present matter. The second part, which deals only with faith and with the meaning of some of the authorities cited, and is therefore more personal than doctrinal, will follow in its own place and time. We are laying this preface as a road and testing the ford; as for the rest, we bid the most learned man, whom we thought it cruel to keep waiting so long for a reply he has desired for so long, to take heart. Indeed, from what we answer here and there to the objections to the later part, anyone may readily gather that those objections have no strength to tear us from our view or move us from it. For the most learned man will see that our view of the Lord's Supper is supported by the authority of Scripture, the agreement of antiquity, and the consensus of sound reason. On the other hand, the opinion of the Church of Rome that pleases them, concerning transubstantiation, both contradicts Scripture, and the analogy of faith, and antiquity, and sober reason; and finally it is a doctrine so uncertain and so full of scandal that the name of Christ and of Christianity is thereby unworthily torn and even blasphemed by unbelievers.

units.la: SECTIO II.
units.tr: SECTIO II.

units.la: Occasio disceptationis de Eucharistia Viri doctissimi. ARTICULUS I.
units.tr: Occasion of the disputation about the Eucharist by the most learned man. ARTICLE I.

units.la: DE Monacho, qui (pertæsus illius vitæ, quam reformatam à multis voluisse seculis, scriptores in Ecclesia Romana gravissimos, Vir doctissimus non ignorat) in nostra transire voluit castra; adeóque occasione hujus συζητήσεως, non est quod quidquam laborem. Nobis in eo nec seritur, nec metitur. Ipse Domino suo stat, & cadit, cui etiam suo tempore administratæ villicationis reddet rationem; hoc tamen pia optem solicitudine, ut, missis factiosis, & ipsi Ecclesiæ Romanæ non uno modo fatalibus familiarum Monasticarum nominibus (quod diserte Apostolus, neq; sibi, neque ulli sancto permismissum voluit 1.Cor.3.)omnes pariter Christiani Dei potius imitatores esse studerent, Eph.5.1. quàm hominum. Una omnium Christianorum est Ascetica, vitáque religiosa, ad quam Servator blandissimè nos invitat, Matth.11.verl.28.29. 30. Venite, inquit, ad me omnes, qui fatigati estis, & onerati, & ego faciam ut requiescatis: Tollite jugum meum super vos, & discite à me, quod mitis sum & humilis corde, & invenietis requiem animabus vestris; jugum enim meum facile est, & onus meum leve est. Christi ergò potius crucem veram, quàm humana superstitione fictam aut pictam tollamus, Marc.8.34. Hoc enim Canone, hac regula, qui incedunt, pax super eos, & misericordia, Gal.6.v.16. Qui verò alienũ hic ignem accendunt, qui ore Deo appropinquant, labiis eum honorant, cor autem eorum procul abest, frustra illum colunt, doctrinas docentes, quae sunt mandata hominum; Matth.15. 8.9. Ligant onera gravia difficiliaque portatu, & imponunt in humeros hominum, digito autem suo nolunt eamovere, Matth.23.verl.4. sunt elementa Mundi (Vitæ ratio, omnibus Mundi incolis, Judæis, Gentibus, Turcis, Persis, Indis, Sinensibus obvia) quæ rationem quidem habent sapientiæ in cultu voluntario, & submissione animi, & in eo quòd corpori non parcunt, nec tamen ullius sunt precii, quàm ad ea spectent, quibus farcitur caro, Col. 2. 23. Veram Ascceticam, vitam sanctam, religiosam Reformatas Ecclesias serio urgere, non tamen aliam, quam quae S. Scripturae sequatur cynosuram, publicis illae de Praxi pietatis scriptis, & ordinario Verbi Divini praeconio haud obscure condefaciunt. Sed haec obiter.
units.tr: As for the monk who, weary of that life which many centuries have wished to see reformed (as the most learned man is well aware, serious writers in the Roman Church have said so), wanted to pass over into our camp: there is no reason for me to labour over anything on account of this disputation [συζήτησις]. In that matter we neither sow nor reap. He stands or falls to his own Lord, to whom he will also render an account of his stewardship in due time. Yet I would wish, with pious concern, that, with factious men set aside, and with the names of monastic families (which are fatal in more than one way even to the Roman Church itself; the Apostle expressly would not have them given to himself or to any saint, 1 Cor. 3), all Christians alike should strive to be imitators of God rather than of men, Eph. 5.1. There is one asceticism and one religious life for all Christians, to which the Saviour most kindly invites us: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light," Matt. 11.28-30. Let us therefore take up Christ's true cross, not one feigned or painted by human superstition, Mark 8.34. For "as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy," Gal. 6.16. But those who kindle strange fire here, who "draw near to God with their mouth and honour him with their lips, but their heart is far from him; in vain do they worship him, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men," Matt. 15.8-9; who "bind heavy burdens, grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders, but will not move them with one of their fingers," Matt. 23.4; these are "the elements of the world" (the manner of life familiar to every inhabitant of the world, Jews, Gentiles, Turks, Persians, Indians, Chinese), "which indeed have a show of wisdom in voluntary worship and humility of mind, and in not sparing the body, yet are of no value except to the satisfying of the flesh," Col. 2.23. The Reformed Churches seriously urge a true asceticism, a holy and religious life, yet not one other than that which follows the guiding star of Holy Scripture. Their public writings on the practice of piety, and the ordinary proclamation of the Divine Word, make this plain enough. But these things in passing.

units.la: SECTIO III.
units.tr: SECTIO III.

units.la: De Locutionibus Sacramen- talibus.
units.tr: On Sacramental Locutions.

units.la: I. Sed quid Tigurini per proselytum? Asserunt, panem esse corpus Christi, Vinum esse sanguinem Christi, eodem modo, quo in reliquis Veteris & Novi Testamenti Sacramentis Circumcisio est foedus, Gen. 17. verf. 13. Agnus est Transitus, Exod. 10. verf. 11. & 27. Baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis, ad Tit. cap. 3. v. 5. Cur vero aliter sentiant, aut loquantur, quam Scriptura? Fundi Theologici calamitas est, quod hanc phrasium sacramentalium ἀντιλήψιν Ecclesia Romana non observarit. Neque vero Tigurini tantum, sed caeteri per Germaniam, Galliam, Poloniam, Angliam, Hungariam, Transylvaniam &c. totum quin imo orbem Reformati, constanter docent, in verbis institutionis Coenae Dominicae observari Tropum, Metonymiam, qua, usitatissimo Scripturae stylo, signo tribuitur nomen rei significatæ, tum alibi, tum præsertim in doctrina Sacramentorum.
units.tr: I. But what do the Tigurines mean by a "proselyte"? They assert that the bread is the body of Christ and the wine is the blood of Christ, in the same way as in the other sacraments of the Old and New Testament. Circumcision is the covenant (Gen. 17. verse 13). The Lamb is the Passover (Exod. 10. verse 11 and 27). Baptism is the washing of regeneration (Titus 3. verse 5). Why should they think or speak otherwise than Scripture does? It is a calamity for theology that the Roman Church has not grasped this manner of sacramental speech [ἀντιλήψιν]. Nor do the Tigurines alone teach this constantly, but the other Reformed churches throughout Germany, France, Poland, England, Hungary, Transylvania and, indeed, the whole world. They hold that in the words of the institution of the Lord's Supper there is a trope, a metonymy, by which, in the most common style of Scripture, the name of the thing signified is given to the sign, both elsewhere and especially in the doctrine of the sacraments.

units.la: II. Neque verò nova est hæc Ecclesiarum nostrarum, de locutionibus Sacramentalibus, doctrina, in cerebro nostro heri, aut nudius tertius nata; sed à Christi Ecclesia inde à multis seculis religiosè retenta. Ne Anthropomorphitarum error & altas ageret radices, & præsidium quæreret in iis Scripturæ locis, quæ vel membra, vel affectiones, vel actiones etiam humanas Deo, qui Spiritus est, tribuunt; placuit veteribus generalem suis præscribere Canonem; Talia quidem de Deo dici humano more, intelligi vero modo ei convenienti. Hoc sepimento & vetus Synagoga Judaica, & Ecclesia Christiana curiosa ingenia coërcuit. Eadem ratione, cùm obvia de Sacramentis exempla occurrerent, quæ, absque absurditate, proprie intelligi non poterant, regulas illi extruxerunt generales, quibus, imperitis præsertim, ratio & modus ostenderetur ex mysteriis illis sese extricandi. Unde axiomata generalia Patrum Latinorum & Græcorum, quæ omnino nostra esse volumus, & à quibus ne latum quidem unguem recedimus. Inter Latinos excellit Augustinus, cujus axiomata generalia sunt: Sacramenta sunt signa rerum aliud existentia, & aliud significantia; Cont. Max. lib. 3. c. 22. Suo jam tempore nostram fortiter egit causam: Ex hac autem similitudine (ita ille T. 11.Epist.23. ad Bonifac.) Sacramenta plerumque etiam ipsarum rerum (i. e. symbola rei significatæ) nomina accipiunt. Sicut ergo secundum quendam modum sacramentum corporis Christi, corpus Christi est; sacramentum sanguinis Christi, sanguis Christi est; Ita sacramentum fidei (baptismus) fides est. Idem libro quæstion. in Levitic.cap. 57. Solet res, quæ significat, ejus rei nomine, quam significat, nuncupari. Sicut scriptum est: Septem spicæ, septem anni sunt. Non enim dixit, Septem annos significant: &, Septem boves, septem anni sunt; & multa hujusmodi. Hinc est, quod dictum est; Petra erat Christus. Non enim, dixit, Petra significat Christum, sed tanquam hoc esset, quod utique per substantiam non hoc erat, sed per significationem. Nempe res Sacramenti Veteris & Novi Testamenti est eadem. Delirant, qui putant, signis sacramentisque mutatis, etiam res ipsas esse diversas, quas ritus Propheticus pronuntiavit esse promissas, & quas ritus Evangelicus annunciavit impletas.—Aliis mysteriorum signaculis, passio & resurrectio Christi sutura promissa est, aliis jam facta annunciatur, Ita idem August.lib.19.cont.Faust.cap.16. Hactenus Augustinus. Sed neque Græca Ecclesiæ in universalis regulæ de locutionibus sacramentalibus observatione, suum nobis denegant calculum. Et in specie quidem de Coena Domini, nomine Ecclesiae Orthodoxae Theodoretus docet, Servatorem nostrum nomina commutasse, & corpori quidem id, quod erat symboli, nomen impososuisse: symbolo autem id, quod erat corporis: Ita cum sevitem nominavisset, sanguinem id, quod erat symbolum, appellasse. Symbola qua videntur, appellatione corporis & sanguinis honorasse. Dial. 1. Sed de hoc Theodoreti textu suo loco plenius.
units.tr: II. This doctrine of our churches concerning sacramental locutions is not new, nor has it been born in our brain yesterday or the day before. It has been religiously retained by the Church of Christ from many centuries past. So that the error of the Anthropomorphites should not take deep root and seek support from those passages of Scripture which attribute to God, who is Spirit, members, affections or even human actions, the ancients chose to prescribe a general rule: such things are said of God in a human manner, but are to be understood in a manner fitting to him. By this hedge both the old Jewish synagogue and the Christian Church restrained curious minds. For the same reason, when obvious examples concerning the sacraments occurred which could not be understood literally without absurdity, they constructed general rules by which, especially for the unskilled, the method and manner of extricating themselves from those mysteries might be shown. Hence come the general axioms of the Latin and Greek Fathers, which we want to be wholly our own and from which we do not recede a finger's breadth. Among the Latins Augustine excels, whose general axioms are: sacraments are signs of things existing other than themselves and signifying something other (Contra Maximinum, book 3, chapter 22). In his own time he defended our cause vigorously: From this similarity (thus he writes in Epistle 23 to Boniface) sacraments generally take the names of the things themselves (that is, the symbols of the thing signified). Therefore, just as in a certain manner the sacrament of the body of Christ is the body of Christ, and the sacrament of the blood of Christ is the blood of Christ, so the sacrament of faith (baptism) is faith. The same in the Questions on Leviticus, chapter 57: The thing that signifies is usually named by the name of the thing it signifies. As it is written: seven ears of grain are seven years. For it did not say, they signify seven years; or, seven oxen are seven years; and many things of this kind. Hence it is said: the rock was Christ. For it did not say, the rock signifies Christ, but as if this were that, which indeed was not that in substance, but in signification. Certainly the thing of the sacrament of the Old and New Testament is the same. They rave who think that, with the signs and sacraments changed, the very things are also different, which the prophetic rite declared were promised and which the evangelical rite announced as fulfilled. By other seals of the mysteries the passion and resurrection of Christ were promised as future, by others they are announced as already accomplished. So Augustine again, in book 19 against Faustus, chapter 16. Thus far Augustine. Nor do the Greek churches deny us their vote in the observance of this universal rule concerning sacramental locutions. And in particular concerning the Lord's Supper, in the name of the Orthodox Church, Theodoret teaches that our Saviour exchanged the names, giving to the body the name that belonged to the symbol, and to the symbol the name that belonged to the body; so, having called the bread his body, he called the thing that was the symbol blood. He honoured the symbols which are seen with the name of body and blood (Dialogue 1). But of this text of Theodoret more fully in its place.

units.la: III. Assertionis autem hujus suae fundamentum accerunt Reformati a perpetua Spiritus sancti praxi & consuetudine. Nullius enim Sacramenti Scriptura meminit, in quo haec loquendi formula Metonymica non occurrat, idque b sequentes potissimum rationes. 1. Ob genium Linguae Hebraicae, & Syriacae, quarum utraque Prophetis, Christo & Apostolis erat vernacula. Non amant vel Hebraei, vel Syri significandi verba, quorum loco pronomen demonstrativum frequentissime, rarissime verbum substantivum adhibent, utrumque pro ratione circumstantiarum vel proprie, vel improprie explicandum. Et hoc contra illos monendum, qui ipsi Spiritui sancto leges praescripturi, quaerere audent, cur significandi vox, ad tollendam litem, non fuerit usurpata?
units.tr: III. The Reformed draw the foundation of this their assertion from the constant practice and custom of the Holy Spirit. For Scripture makes mention of no sacrament in which this metonymical form of speech does not occur, and this for the following reasons, chiefly. 1. On account of the genius of the Hebrew and Syriac languages, both of which were the mother tongue of the prophets, Christ and the apostles. Neither the Hebrews nor the Syrians like to use the verb signify; in its place they very frequently use the demonstrative pronoun, and very rarely the substantive verb, and each must be explained either literally or figuratively according to the circumstances. And this must be pointed out against those who presume to prescribe laws to the Holy Spirit himself and dare to ask why the word signify was not used, in order to end the dispute?

units.la: 2. Ut ostenderetur discrimen inter panem cibarium communem, & Sacramentalem. 3. Ut hac nonominum permutatione & Sacramentali locutione ἀναλογία signi & rei signatæ clarius exprimeretur. Si enim Sacramenta non haberent similitudinem quandam earum rerum, quarum sunt Sacramenta, utiq; Sacramenta non essent, ut loquitur Augustin. Epist. cit.ad Bonifac.
units.tr: 2. So that the difference between common food bread and sacramental bread might be shown. 3. So that by this exchange of names and sacramental speech the analogy [ἀναλογία] between the sign and the thing signified might be expressed more clearly. For if sacraments had no certain likeness to those things of which they are sacraments, they would certainly not be sacraments, as Augustine says in the aforementioned Epistle to Boniface.

units.la: 4. Ad denotandam arctam inter signum & rem signatam, in legitimo usu, conjunctionem. Occurrere nempe cœlestis Doctor voluit nostræ infirmitati, ne elementorum externorum abjecta conditione offenli, præceptum Dominicum in Sacramentorum vel administratione, vel participatione negligeremus. Postquam Naaman, ab Elisæo septem vicibus fuisset jussus se lavare, abiit ille iratus, dicens: En cogitabam apud me, egredietur egrediendo, & curabit leprosum. Nonne meliores sunt Amanah, & Parpar fluvii Dammesek omnibus aquis Israelis? Annon si lavero me in illis, mundus ero? Et conversus ibat cum ira, 2. Reg. 5. 11. 12. Idem murmur ab indomita carne facile fuisset metuendum (quæ, verbi gratia, vis abluendi peccata posset inesse aquæ elementari, aut ad nutritionem animæ panis aut vino?) nisi Dei firmissima per usum symbolorum promissio accessisset. Ut Magistratus literis & sigillis, Pater familias clavi, ad rei evidentiam & certitudinem, nomen rei per literas confirmatæ, aut per clavem significatæ, imponit; Hoc est; oblatis literis, jus; illud conconfirmantibus; Ius Civitatis, hoc est feudum, hac est potestas domestica: (clara haec sunt, & quotidiano usu trita, etsi adversariorum cavillis imperite nonnunquam exagitata:) eadem ratione Dominus Dominantium in sacramentis, quae signa sunt & sigilla gratiae Divinae, nomen rei significatae externis tribuere voluit elementis. Nititur igitur Tigurinorum assertio immoto illo fundamento Dialectico, dicto de omni, quod non male regulativum ab aliis, ob insignem ejus usum, vocatur. Quicquid omnibus Veteris & Novi Testamenti convenit Sacramentis, illud utique sacramento Coenae Dominicae non potest abjudicari. Atqui locutiones illae Metonymicae, quibus signo imponitur nomen rei signatae, omnibus communes sunt Sacramentis. E. Cujus quidem argumenti vis haftenus ita stetit immota, ut in reliquis, praesertim V. T., Sacramentis, Tropologiam sacramentalem facile, illi etiam, qui in Coena Dominica literam urgent, admittant; in Coena tantum Domini vocent in dubium. Quod tamen revera aliud nihil est, quam, concessis praemissis, inepte negare conclusionem.
units.tr: 4. To denote the close conjunction between the sign and the thing signified, in lawful use. Indeed the heavenly Teacher wished to meet our weakness, lest, offended by the despised condition of the external elements, we neglect the Lord's command in the administration or the participation of the sacraments. After Naaman had been told by Elisha to wash himself seven times, he went away angry, saying: Behold, I thought within myself, he will certainly come out and heal the leper. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Shall I not, if I wash in them, be clean? And he turned and went away in anger (2 Kings 5. 11, 12). The same murmur would easily have been feared from the untamed flesh (what power, for example, of washing away sins could be in elemental water, or bread or wine for the nourishing of the soul?), unless God's most firm promise through the use of the symbols had been added. As a magistrate imposes the name of the thing confirmed by letters, or signified by a key, upon his seals, and a householder upon his keys, for the sake of the evidence and certainty of the thing: that is, when the letters are presented, the right; and the seals confirming it: the right of citizenship, that is, the fief, that is, domestic power (these things are clear and worn by daily use, although sometimes unskillfully harassed by the cavils of adversaries); by the same reasoning the Lord of lords wished to give the name of the thing signified to the external elements in the sacraments, which are signs and seals of divine grace. The assertion of the Tigurines therefore rests upon that immovable dialectical foundation, the dictum de omni, which by others, on account of its notable use, is not unfittingly called regulative. Whatever belongs to all the sacraments of the Old and New Testament cannot certainly be denied to the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. But those metonymical locutions, by which the name of the thing signified is imposed on the sign, are common to all sacraments. Therefore... The force of this argument has so far stood so unshaken that, in the remaining sacraments, especially of the Old Testament, they readily admit sacramental tropology, even those who insist on the letter in the Lord's Supper; they call it in doubt only in the Lord's Supper. Yet this is really nothing else than, the premises being granted, foolishly to deny the conclusion.

units.la: IV. Sed placet Viro doctissimo ad reliquas primum formulas V. T. Sacramentales quasdam excipere, deinde Elenchum parium ostendere.
units.tr: IV. But the most learned man is pleased first to except certain other sacramental formulas of the Old Testament, and then to show the parallels as refutation.

units.la: Exceptio est: Verba haec; Circumcisio est foedus, Agnus est Transitus, non legiuspiam in Scriptura, sed eo à Tigurinis composita esse, ut sint consimilia his apud Matthæum, Marcum, Lucam, & Paulum; Hoc est Corpus meum; dein sic argumententur, &c. Vix à me impetro ut credam, doctissimum Virum serió agere! Verba, Circumcisio est fœdus; agnus est Transitus in S. Scriptura non extent? Extant tam clarè, & evidenter, quàm clarè bis bina sunt quatuor; & quàm evidenter ex eo, quod Apostolus Ephes. 1. 23. de Ecclesia scribit; quæ est Corpus ipsius (Christi) concludo; Ecclesia est Corpus Christi; non proprio & Grammatico, sed figurato, & mystico sensu. Non putem, doctissimum Virum ad eos nos revocaturum recentiorum quorundam cancellos, qui nullam ex Scriptura argumentationem nostratium ratam habere volunt, quàm quæ totidem exprimitur syllabis. Quasi non alia in S. Scriptura occurrant κατα λέξιν, quoad voces & verba; alia κατα διάνοιαν, & quoad sensum. Majorem de doctissimo Viro mihi polliceor ingenuitatem, quàm à quo infanum illud delirium Methodistarum, quos vocant, nobis sit metuendum; majorem etiam in Ecclesiam Romanam reverentiam, quàm quæ permittat, intempestiva consequentiarum prosciptione, in dubium omnia vocari, pro quibus tamen Scholæ Pontificiæ acerrimè & acerbissimè, tanquam pro aris & focis certant. Tolle enim nim Scholis Pontificiis consequentiarum subsidium, obtorto saepe collo raptum & invitum; & pleraque non Leiturgicae modo, sed & dogmaticae Romanistarum Theologiae capita ruinam minitabuntur. Sit igitur, verba; Circumcisio est foedus; Agnus est transitus, totidem literis & syllabis non extare, probatu tamen proclive fuerit, hunc sensum, hanc mentem esse Spiritus Sancti, ut circumcisio nomen induceret foederis, cum signum tantum fuisset foederis; agnus Paschalis vocaretur transitus, qui tamen signum ejus fuit & figura.
units.tr: The exception is: these words, "Circumcision is the covenant," "The Lamb is the Passover," are nowhere in Scripture, but were composed by the Tigurines so that they might be like those in Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul, "This is my body"; then they argue thus, etc. I can scarcely bring myself to believe that the most learned man is in earnest! The words "Circumcision is the covenant" and "the Lamb is the Passover" are not in Holy Scripture? They are as clearly and evidently there as twice two is four; and as evidently as from the fact that the Apostle writes of the Church in Ephesians 1:23, "which is his body" (of Christ), I conclude: "The Church is the body of Christ," not in a proper and grammatical, but in a figurative and mystical sense. I would not think that the most learned man will call us back to those fences of certain recent writers, who wish no argument from Scripture to be valid unless it is expressed in just so many syllables. As if other things did not occur in Holy Scripture according to the letter [κατα λέξιν], as to words and expressions, and other things according to the sense [κατα διάνοιαν], as to meaning! I promise myself from the most learned man more candour than the insane delirium of the so-called Methodists would fear from us; and more reverence towards the Roman Church than would permit everything to be called into doubt by an ill-timed rejection of consequences, for which the Papist schools fight most fiercely and bitterly, as for altars and hearths. For take away from the Papist schools the aid of consequences, often dragged along with an unwilling neck, and most of the doctrines of the Romanist theology, not only liturgical but also dogmatic, will threaten ruin. Let it be granted, then, that the words "Circumcision is the covenant" and "The Lamb is the transit" are not found in just these letters and syllables; it would nevertheless be easy to prove that this is the sense and mind of the Holy Spirit: that circumcision should take the name of covenant, when it was only the sign of the covenant; and that the Paschal lamb should be called the passover, which was nonetheless its sign and figure.

units.la: IV. A. Ex Spiritus sancti mente & meta Circumcisionem foedus vocari, cum tamen signum tantum fuerit foederis, sequentibus proponitur (Genef. 17. v. 13.) verbis: Erit que foedus meum in carne vestra. Quid, quaeso, illud est, quod foedus suum vocat in carne? Utique aliud nihil, quam Circumcisio in Israelitarum carne conspicua; prout v. 10. Jam praeceßit; Hoc est foedus meum, ut circumcidatur vobis omnis mas. Et verf. 14. de neglectu circumcisionis, Foedus meum irritum fecit. Neq; enim existimo, quicquam aliud vel exterebrari posse. An ergo Circumcisio erat foedus Dei? Negat ipse Deus v. 11. ubi expresse haec ceremonia appellatur signum foederis. Circumcidetis carnem praeputii vestri, & erit in signum foederis inter me & inter vos.
units.tr: IV. A. That, by the mind and purpose of the Holy Spirit, circumcision is called a covenant, although it was only a sign of the covenant, is shown by the following words (Gen. 17:13): And my covenant shall be in your flesh. What, I ask, is that which he calls his covenant in the flesh? Surely nothing other than circumcision, visible in the flesh of the Israelites, as verse 10 had already said: This is my covenant, that every male among you be circumcised. And in verse 14, concerning the neglect of circumcision: He has broken my covenant. For I do not think anything else can be squeezed out of these words. Was circumcision then God's covenant? God himself denies it in verse 11, where this rite is expressly called a sign of the covenant: You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.

units.la: B Ne-
units.tr: B Ne-

units.la: Negat Apostolus Paulus, qui eandem circumcifionem vocat signum & fligillum, Rom.4. 11. Obstat ratio & instrumentum foederis, v.7. expressum, stabilito fœdus, me esse tibi in Deum, & femini tuo post te. Ergòne, Vir Doctissime, Scriptura nusquam vel dicit, vel sentit (de sensu enim quæstio est, non de verbis) Circumcisionem vocari fœdus? Fœdus meum, inquit, erit in carne vestra. Quod autem illud in carne fœdus? Circumcisio utique. Atqui Circumcisio, ipso Judice Spiritu sancto, erat signum tantùm foederis. Alium sensum ne fidiculæ quidem extorserint. Eadem ratio est Pafchatis, Exod. 12. (capite enim decimo, quod allegatur, de inftitutione agni Paschalis, nondum est sermo) v.11.27. ubi Legislator populo Israelitico novum gratiæ suæ μνημόσυνον commendat, Agnum Paschalem. Et postquam rationem standi & comedendi illius agni adverf. 12. exclusive, Israelitis præscripsi fiet, nomen novo ricui imponit; Hoc, inquit, ipsum (ita verba Hebraica sonant) Pascha, i. e. ut Vulgatus vertit, transitus Domini. Quodnam Hoc? Illud ipfum nempe, cujus in immediatè præcedentibus fit mentio; agnus Paschalis. Agnum ergò vocat Transitum; de hoc enim & non alio fermonem esse probatur, 1. Expressis textûs verbis. Hoc ipsum (Hu) quod modò præcessit, & cujus Institutionem Deus populo Israelitico comcommendavit : Huic ipse Deus Transitus imponit nomen, non utique propriè (id enim ne ipse quidem Vir Doctissimus poterat capere, ut postea audiemus) sed Metonymicè. 2. Continua Ecclesiæ Judaicæ praxi, cui usitatissimæ olim erant phrases, facere Pascha, Num. 9. 2. Faciant filii Israëlis Pascha in tempore suo. verf. 4 ut facerent Pascha. v. 5. Fecerunt Pascha, Iof. 5. v. 10. Quid? an Pascha i.e. transitus quotannis faciendus erat Israelitis, quem semel tantum facere debebat Angelus perditor? Non: Agnus Paschalis, transitus μνημόσυνον, uno quoque anno erat mactandus. Unde & Pascha macture dicebantur constanter Judæi, Deut. 16. 5. 6 c. 30. v. 15. c. 35. 1. 6. 11. & alibi. Ne deinceps quidem hæc phraseologia Judæis κυριοκτόνοις, adeóque recentioribus, displicuit. Nihil in scriptis eorum Leiturgicis usitatius, quàm, nomine Paschatis, vel totam intelligere festi illius solennitatem, vel agnum tantum paschalem, utrumque figuratè seu Tropicè. Hinc Pascha primum, ordinarium scilicet & solenne, ex Legis præscripto ad diem 15. Martii celebrandum; & secundum, alias Pascha parvum, quod ex Rabbin. statutis, in mensem rejectum April, unum tantum duravit diem. Nemini profecto in mentem unquam venisset, Paschatis nomine quicquam aliud intelligendum, quàm vel agnum Paschalem; ubi parandi, mactandi, manducandi adhibentur vocabula ; vel integram solennitatem, quorum utrumque μνημόσυνον, symbolum & typus esse debebat, ipso Interprete Spiritu sancto veri. 13. cap. 12. Exod. Accedit 3. optimus verborum Mosaicorum interpres, ipse Dominus noster Jesus Christus in N. T. qui ritus, & notas phrases, parare Pascha, Luc. 22. verf. 8. 12. 13. macтare Pascha verf. 7. Edere Pascha verf. 11. 15. & ipse retinuit, & à discipulis suis retinere voluit. His autem exemplis quid ad probandam Metonymiam sacramentalem clarius, quid difertius? Aliud utique agnus est, aliud transitus. Hic mactari, manducari non poterat; mactari tamen & manducari ubique dicitur, quia Sacramentali locutione ei, ceu rei significatæ, tribuitur, quod signo transitus, Agno nempe, competebat.
units.tr: The Apostle Paul denies it, who calls the same circumcision a sign and seal (Rom. 4:11). The reason and the instrument of the covenant, expressed in verse 7, stand in the way: I will establish the covenant, that I will be God to you, and to your seed after you. Then, most learned sir, does Scripture nowhere either say or mean (for the question concerns the sense, not the words) that circumcision is called a covenant? My covenant, it says, shall be in your flesh. But what covenant in the flesh is that? Circumcision, surely. Yet circumcision, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit himself, was only a sign of the covenant. Not even the rack could wrest another sense from it. The same holds for the Passover (Exod. 12; for the tenth chapter, which is cited, does not yet speak of the institution of the paschal lamb), verses 11 and 27, where the Lawgiver commends to the people of Israel a new memorial [μνημόσυνον] of his grace, the paschal lamb. And after he has prescribed to the Israelites, in verse 12, the manner of standing and eating that lamb, he gives the new rite its name: This, he says, itself (so the Hebrew words sound) Pascha (Hebrew: Hu), that is, as the Vulgate translates it, the passover of the Lord. What is this This? Namely that very thing which is mentioned in the immediately preceding words: the paschal lamb. So he calls the lamb the Passover; for it is proved that the discourse concerns this and not something else, 1. by the express words of the text. This very thing (Hebrew: hu), which has just gone before, and whose institution God committed to the people of Israel: to this very thing God himself gives the name Passover, not properly (for even this learned man could not grasp that, as we shall hear later), but metonymically. 2. By the continuous practice of the Jewish Church, in which the phrases to make the Passover were long in common use (Num. 9:2: Let the children of Israel make the Passover in its season; verse 4: that they should make the Passover; verse 5: they made the Passover; Josh. 5:10). What then? Was the Passover, that is the passover, to be made every year by the Israelites, which the destroying Angel was to make only once? No: the paschal lamb, a memorial of the passing over, had to be slaughtered in every year. Hence the Jews constantly said to slaughter the Passover (Deut. 16:5, 6; 30:15; 35:1, 6, 11) and elsewhere. Nor did this manner of speaking displease the Jews who came later, who were killers of the Lord [κυριοκτόνοις], and so the more recent ones. Nothing is more common in their liturgical writings than to understand by the name Passover either the whole solemnity of that feast, or only the paschal lamb, both figuratively or tropically. Hence the first Passover, that is the ordinary and solemn one, to be celebrated on the fifteenth day of March according to the prescription of the Law; and the second, otherwise called the little Passover, which, according to the rabbinical statutes, was moved to the month of April and lasted only one day. Surely it would never have come into anyone's mind that by the name Passover anything other than either the paschal lamb is to be understood, where the words for preparing, slaughtering and eating are used, or the whole solemnity is meant; and each of these ought to be a memorial [μνημόσυνον], a symbol and a type, as the Holy Spirit himself, the interpreter, has said (Exod. 12:13). Add to this, 3. the best interpreter of the words of Moses, our Lord Jesus Christ himself in the New Testament, who both retained the rite and the familiar phrases, to prepare the Passover (Luke 22:8, 12, 13), to slaughter the Passover (verse 7), to eat the Passover (verses 11, 15), and wished his disciples to retain them too. Now what could prove the sacramental metonymy more clearly or more plainly than these examples? A lamb is one thing, a passover is another. Here the passover could not be slaughtered or eaten; yet it is said everywhere to be slaughtered and eaten, because by sacramental speech that which belonged to the sign of the passover, namely the lamb, is attributed to it as the thing signified.

units.la: SECTIO IV.
units.tr: SECTIO IV.

units.la: De Identitate Phrasium Sacra- mentalium.
units.tr: On the Identity of Sacramental Phrases

units.la: 1. Palàm fecimus, agnoscere Ecclesiam Catholicam Phraseologiam Sacramentalem, qua Sacramenta nomina habent earum rerum, quas significant, ut Cyprianus locutus est, serm. de Chrism. & post eum Augustinus; vel, ut Theodoretus loqui maluit, symbola appellatione cor-poporis & sanguinis honorantur. Gratis ergò singitur, has loquendi formulas eò à Tigurinis compositas, ut consimiles sint his apud Evangelistas & Paulum; Hoc est corpus meum; dum sic argumententur, &c. Sobria est, ipsonteque fluit haec illatio: In Sacramentis V.T. Circumcisione & Agno Paschali, summus Legislator loquendi formulas adhibuit Metonymicas, quibus nomen signi accipit axioma rei significatae, & vice versa. Nihil ergo est absurdi, nihil novi, nulla Tigurinorum maligna compositio, si eandem loquendi rationem in N. T. Sacramentis ostendant. Parium enim par est ratio. Neque, quantum ad stylum & loquendi formulas, ulla hactenus disparitatis umbra ostendi potuit: Imò, contrà, Sacramenta V. & N. T. esse homogenea, & ejusdem planè conditionis, docet Apostolus, 1. Cor. 10. 1. 2. 3.
units.tr: 1. We have made it plain that the Catholic Church acknowledges sacramental phraseology, by which the sacraments take the names of the things they signify, as Cyprian put it in his sermon on chrism, and Augustine after him; or, as Theodoret preferred to say, the symbols are honoured with the name of the body and blood. It is therefore a gratuitous fiction that these forms of speech were devised by the Zurich theologians to resemble those in the Evangelists and Paul, This is my body, when they argue thus, etc. The inference is sober and follows of its own accord: In the Old Testament sacraments, circumcision and the Paschal lamb, the supreme Lawgiver used figurative forms of speech, by which the name of the sign receives what belongs to the thing signified, and vice versa. There is therefore nothing absurd, nothing new, and no malicious invention of the Zurich men, if they show the same manner of speaking in the sacraments of the New Testament. For like is judged by like. Nor, so far as style and forms of speech go, has any shadow of difference yet been shown. Rather, on the contrary, the Apostle teaches that the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments are of one kind and of the same nature (1 Cor. 10:1–3).

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Sed de Circumcisione, pergit vir doctissimus; & Agno clarum est in Scriptura, signa esse foederis & Transitus. Ergo Hoc, seu Eucharistia (quam purum putum panem esse adjunt) nihil aliud item est, quam signum Corporis Christi: Ita ut haec tria loca sic explicari debeant, Circumcisio significat foedus, Agnus significat Transitum, hoc significat corpus meum, utque adeo Verbum EST, in his tribus locis, usurpetur pro SIGNIFICAT. Resp. In Genesi Circumcisionem, in Exodo verò Agnum Paschalem vocari signum fœderis, impense nobis gratulamur. Ita enim novitatis probrum, Reformatoribus nostris odiose impactum, feliciter abstergitur, quando & illi, exemplo & authoritate Scripturæ, loquendi formulas sacramentales improprias in proprias resolverunt. Concedimus ergo 1. Utrumque Sacramentum; Circumcisionem & Agnum Paschalem; signa esse fœderis, non ipsum fœdus. 2. Adeóque & de illis, & de Pane Eucharistico enunciatum verbum substantivum E S T, per significat, exponendum. Ad eandem enim semper paritatis recurrimus legem. 3. Male tamen pronomen Hoc, quod panem notat, cum ipsa Eucharistia confunditur. Illud enim alterum tantum Cœnæ Dominicæ symbolum; hæc integrum notat Sacramentum, signum, & rem signatam; rem terrestrem & cœlestem. 4. Invidiose autem Ecclesiis Reformatis impingitur, quasi Eucharistiam purum putum panem dicerent. De ipsa Eucharistia cum Irenæo libenter loquimur, duabus eam constare rebus, terrena, pane videlicet & vino, & cœlesti, corpore nimirum & sanguine Christi. Adversus Hær. l.4.c.34. Aliud ergo est loqui de significatione particulæ Hoc, in verbis, Hoc est corpus meum; aliud de tota Eucharistia. Illud utique aliud notare nihil potest, quàm panem. Panem enim Christus accepit, panem fregit, panem discipulis dedit, & de eodem, pronomine Hoc indicato, comedere jussit. Hanc vero Reformati constanter negârunt, negant etiamnum eorum Catechismi, Confessiones, scripta Symbolica, & Elenctica, purum esse panem. Cùm Reformatore Zuinglio, Christum verè esse in Cœna docemus, imò non credimus esse cœnam, nisi Christus adsit. Exposit. fid. à se prædicat. Absurditatibus sublatis, quicquid ad exprimendam veram substantialem corporis & sanguinis Dominici communicationem, qua sub sacra Cœna symbolis fidelibus exhibetur, facere potest, libenter cum Calvino recipimus; Instit. lib. 4. cap. 7. §. 19. Num quid aut religiosius, aut devotius, aut tanto mysterio dignius expectari posset, quàm quod publico suo consensu testatæ sunt Ecclesia Tigurina, & Genevensis? Communicari inquiunt, nobis Christi corpus & sanguinem, nullus nostrum negat. Qualis autem sit corporis & sanguinis Domini communicatio, quæritur. Carnalem ipsi palàm & simpliciter asserere quomodo audeant, miror. Spiritualem cum dicimus, fremunt, quasi hac voce realem, ut vulgò loquuntur, tollamus. Nos verò, si reale pro vero accipiant, & fallaci vel imaginario opponant, barbarè loqui mallemus, quàm pugnis materiam præbere. Placidis & moderatis hoc testatum volo, ita secundum nos spiritualem esse communicationis modum, ut re ipsa Christo fruamur. mur ; Ita Calvin.in expofit.Capitum Confeni. cum Tigurin. Et alibi : Dicimus Christum tam externo symbolo, quàm Spiritu suo ad nos descendere, ut veré substantia carnis suæ, & sanguinis fui animas nostras vivificet ; Inftit.lib.4. cap. 17.S.24. Quin imò, Catechumeni nostri figmentum de nudis signis feliciter fatis elidunt. Ita enim, ex Catechesi Tigurina, interrogati, respondere didicerunt: Cuilibet nostrùm in S. Cœna edendum & bibendum exhibetur non tantùm sacer panis & vinum, quod ore corporis edimus & bibimus, sed etiam verum corpus & fusus sanguis Christi, atque adeò Christus Iesus ipse, una cum pretioso suo merito, & omnibus cœlestibus thesauris, quos nobis vi N.T. acquisivit, & quibus fide, ore videlicet anima, vivimus & fruimur advitam æternam. Num hæc, absurdam de puro, pane, adeóque vacuis & inanibus symbolis facramentalibus, Ecclesiis Reformatis tributam opinionem, non fatis diluunt ? Spero, Virum Doctissimum, pro candore suo, aliter de nobis in posterum sensurum, scriptisq; symbolicis majorem, quàm putidis aliorum calumniis, fidem adhibiturum. Nullam enim, ingenuè fatemur, ægriùs Ecclesiæ noftræ ferunt injuriam, quàm qua purus putus panis Sacro-sanctæ Domini Cœnæ ab iis administratæ relinquitur. Rogamus ergo, ut ne deinceps hanc nobis insulsam reponant Crambem, quicunque de Eucharistia nobilcum agere volunt. 4. Quòd Vir Doctissimus subjungit; Pronomen Hoc, & quippe allere Eucharistia, ambiguum est. Si de pane Eucharistico, Vir Doctissimus, illud intelligat, res erit in vado, & sic, quod volumus, Hoc notabit panem. Si verò ipsum intelligat corpus Christi, cum aliis fidei suae confecraneis transfigat, qui hoc illi dare non possunt, nisi & simul concedant, panem, ante consecrationem, esse transsubstantiatum. Quod quàm non placeat pluribus Ecclesiae Romanae Doctoribus, Vir Doctissimus ignorare non potest. Nos illam jam Camarinam non movebimus, quàm nihil certi habeat Ecclesia Romana, in pronominis hujus sensu, & quàm longis à se invicem Scholastici in explicatione ejus abeant pallibus. Dilfenfum Theologorum hoc loco obiter monere, quàm multas de eo, quòd facile nobis esset, & ab aliis jam operose est demonstratum, implere chartas, consultius duximus. Satis sit, Pronomine Hoc, Eucharistiam, i.e. Corpus Christi jam transsubstantiatum, salvo Ecclesiae Romanae judicio, notari non posse; solàque de Pronomine Hoc Scholasticorum disceptationes adeò violentas esse, caliginosas, tortuosas, perplexas & lubricas, ut Doctissimi Viri Conscientiae relinquam, an in tanto sententiarum divortio, vel sibi, vel aliis hactenus potuerit satisfacere. Quâ de re postea.
units.tr: But the most learned man goes on to say that it is clear from Scripture that circumcision and the passover lamb are signs of the covenant and of the passing over. Therefore This, that is the Eucharist (which they add is plain bare bread), is likewise nothing other than a sign of Christ's body. So that these three passages must be explained thus: circumcision signifies the covenant, the lamb signifies the passing over, this signifies my body; and the word IS in these three places is to be taken as SIGNIFIES. Reply: we gladly congratulate ourselves that in Genesis circumcision, and in Exodus the Paschal lamb, is called a sign of the covenant. For in this way the reproach of novelty, invidiously fixed on our Reformers, is happily wiped away, since they too, by the example and authority of Scripture, resolved the improper sacramental forms of speech into proper ones. We therefore concede: 1. Both sacraments, circumcision and the Paschal lamb, are signs of the covenant, not the covenant itself. 2. Consequently, the substantive verb IS spoken of them, and of the Eucharistic bread, must be expounded as signifies. For we always return to the same law of parity. 3. Yet it is wrongly done when the pronoun This, which denotes the bread, is confused with the Eucharist itself. For that denotes only the one symbol of the Lord's Supper, but this denotes the whole sacrament, sign and thing signified, the earthly and the heavenly thing. 4. Moreover, it is spitefully charged against the Reformed Churches that they call the Eucharist plain bare bread. About the Eucharist itself we gladly speak with Irenaeus, that it consists of two things, the earthly, namely bread and wine, and the heavenly, namely the body and blood of Christ (Adv. Haer. 4.34). It is one thing, then, to speak of the signification of the particle This in the words This is my body, and another to speak of the whole Eucharist. That word can surely denote nothing other than the bread. For Christ took bread, broke bread, gave bread to the disciples, and bade them eat of it, the thing indicated by the pronoun This. But the Reformed have constantly denied that this is bare bread, and their catechisms, confessions, symbolical and polemical writings still deny it. With the Reformer Zwingli we teach that Christ is truly present in the Supper, indeed we do not believe there is a Supper unless Christ is present (Exposition of the faith, which he himself published). Absurdities removed, whatever can help to express the true substantial communication of the body and blood of the Lord, which is offered to the faithful under the symbols of the sacred Supper, we gladly receive with Calvin (Institutes 4.7.19). Could anything more devout, more religious, or more worthy of so great a mystery be looked for than what the Churches of Zurich and Geneva have attested by their public agreement? They say: That the body and blood of Christ are communicated to us, no one among us denies. But what kind of communication of the body and blood of the Lord it is, is the question. I wonder that they dare to assert plainly and simply that it is carnal. When we say spiritual, they rage, as if by this word we were removing the real, as they commonly speak. But we would rather speak barbarously than give material for fights, if they take real for true and set it against the fallacious or imaginary. To the calm and moderate I wish this to be witnessed: that the mode of communication is spiritual with us, in such a way that we actually enjoy Christ. So Calvin, in the exposition of the articles agreed with the Zurich men. And elsewhere: We say that Christ descends to us both by the outward symbol and by his Spirit, so that by the true substance of his flesh and blood he quickens our souls (Institutes 4.17.24). Indeed, our catechumens have happily refuted the fiction of bare signs, well enough. For, questioned from the Zurich Catechism, they have learned to answer thus: To each of us in the holy Supper is offered to eat and drink not only the sacred bread and wine, which we eat and drink with the mouth of the body, but also the true body and shed blood of Christ, and indeed Jesus Christ himself, together with his precious merit and all the heavenly treasures which he has won for us by the power of the New Testament, and by which we live and enjoy eternal life, by faith, that is, with the mouth of the soul. Do these not sufficiently refute the absurd opinion ascribed to the Reformed Churches, that the sacramental symbols are mere bread and therefore empty and void? I hope that the most learned man, in his candour, will judge otherwise of us in future, and will give more credit to the symbolical writings than to the foul calumnies of others. For, to be frank, our Churches bear no injury more grievously than that by which plain bare bread is left in the holy Supper of the Lord as administered by them. We ask therefore that from now on they no longer set before us this insipid gruel, whoever wishes to deal with us about the Eucharist. 4. As for what the most learned man adds: The pronoun This, and indeed the Eucharist to which it refers, is ambiguous. If he understands the Eucharistic bread, the matter will be on firm ground, and then what we want, that This will denote the bread. But if he understands the body of Christ itself, he goes over with the other fellow-believers of his faith, who cannot grant this to him unless they also concede that the bread, before consecration, was transubstantiated. How little this pleases many teachers of the Church of Rome, the most learned man cannot be ignorant. We will not now move that chamber-pot, how little certainty the Church of Rome has about the meaning of this pronoun, and how far the Schoolmen stray from one another in its explanation. We judged it better briefly to warn of the disagreement of theologians on this point, which we could easily fill pages with, and which others have already laboriously demonstrated. It is enough that by the pronoun This the Eucharist, that is the body of Christ already transubstantiated, cannot be denoted, saving the judgement of the Church of Rome; and that the disputations of the Schoolmen about the pronoun This alone are so violent, obscure, tortuous, perplexed and slippery, that I leave to the conscience of the most learned man whether, in such a divorce of opinions, he has been able hitherto to satisfy either himself or others. More on this matter later.

units.la: III. Sed duo, Vir Doctissimus, in hac argumentatione & Comparatione nostra desiderat.
units.tr: III. But the most learned man, in this argument and comparison of ours, desiders two things.

units.la: 1. Necessum esse, hæc verba, Circumcisio est fœdus, Agnus est Transitus, reperiri in Scriptura, sicut illa, Hoc est corpus meum, ter in Evangelio, & semel apud Paulum legantur. Atqui supra jam demonstravimus, utrumque asserere Spiritum sanctum, &, Circumcisionem esse fœdus; & agnum esse transitum, idque iisdem plane formulis, eadem Metonymia, quibus ab Evangelistis & Paulo panis vocatur corpus. ꟼNT Zoth, Hoc, hic ritus, ceremonia (nempe ut circumcidatur vobis omnis masculus, uno verbo, circumcisio) fœdus meum, Genes. 17. vers. 10. ꟼNT PDS Pesach hu, Hoc ipsum (agnus nempe mastandus, &, juxta præscriptos ritus, manducandus) est Transitus. Judicet, quisquis exercitatos, quos à Christiano Paulus requirit, habet sensus, an quicquam clarius proponi possit, tum ad evincendum, Scripturam Circumcisionem vocare fœdus, agnum Transitum, tum etiam, ad phraseologiæ demonstrandam Identitatem & æquipollentiam? Adeo ut mirari subeat, illud in Controversiam verti, quod vel communis hic dictat sensus, & mediocris Tropologiæ notitia sine negotio expedit. Qui in totam Theologiam pariter & Philosophiam, Gratiam & Naturam arietare malunt, quàm unius ejusque usitatissimi Tropi concessione diuturnæ & periculosæ liti colophonem imponere, oftendunt, nondum se didicisse spiritualia spiritualibus, similia similibus aptare, 1. Cor. 2.13.2.
units.tr: 1. He says it is necessary that these words, Circumcision is the covenant, the lamb is the passing over, be found in Scripture, just as those, This is my body, are read three times in the Gospels and once in Paul. Yet we have already demonstrated above that Scripture asserts both, that circumcision is the covenant and the lamb is the passing over, and that in exactly the same forms and by the same metonymy by which the bread is called the body by the Evangelists and Paul. Zoth [זאת], This, this rite, this ceremony (namely, that every male among you be circumcised; in a word, circumcision), my covenant, Gen. 17:10. Pesach hu [פסח הוא], This very thing (namely the lamb to be slain and, according to the prescribed rites, eaten) is the passing over. Let whoever has, as Paul requires of the Christian, trained senses judge whether anything clearer can be put forward, both to prove that Scripture calls circumcision the covenant and the lamb the passing over, and also to demonstrate the identity and equivalence of the phraseology. So that one is moved to wonder that this should be turned into a controversy, which even common sense and a moderate knowledge of tropes settles without trouble. Those who prefer to wrestle over all theology and philosophy, over grace and nature, rather than put an end to a long and dangerous quarrel by conceding one very common trope, show that they have not yet learned to fit spiritual things to spiritual, like to like (1 Cor. 2:13).

units.la: IV.
