Sed oporteret, ut in eadem Scriptura, aut Evangelio (inquit Vir Doctissimus) de Eucharistia, quam habebat Christus prae manibus, postquam dixit, Hoc est corpus meum, diceretur, id esse signum Corporis ejus, quod & non dicitur uspiam, in S. Scriptura aut Evangelio, quemadmodum de Circumcisione & Agno, haec esse signa foederis & Transitus. Resp.
units.tr: IV. "But," says the most learned man, "it would be necessary that in the same Scripture, or Gospel, concerning the Eucharist, which Christ had before his hands after he said, This is my body, it should be said that it is a sign of his body. This is nowhere said in Holy Scripture or the Gospel, just as concerning circumcision and the lamb, these are called signs of the covenant and of the Passover." Reply.

units.la: 1. Aliam Eucharistiam prae manibus Christum habuisse, cum diceret; Hoc est corpus meum, quam panem consecratum, neque ex Scriptura, neque ex Evangelio agnoscimus. Panem vocant omnes Evangelistae. Panem Apostolus Paulus, tam ante quam post consecrationem. Panis, inquit, quem frangimus, est communio Corporis Christi, 1. Cor. 10.16. Omnes sumus unus panis & unum corpus, qui de uno pane participamus, v. 17. Quotiescunque manducabitis hunc panem, 1. Cor. 11.26. Quicunque manducaverit hunc panem, & biberit hoc poculum, 27. Probet seipsum homo, & ita de pane illo edat, & de poculo bibat, v. 28. Magna & constans Interpretis Apostolici fides! Ne vel infideles crassa, adeoque Capernaitica manducatione Carnis Christi offenderentur, vel fideles etiam, literae morosius insistentes, in verbis instilituationis hærerent, Apostolus unius propositionis improprie & Metonymicæ sensum verum & genuinum quinque distinctis vicibus proprie proponit.
units.tr: 1. We do not acknowledge, from Scripture or the Gospel, that Christ had before him another Eucharist when he said This is my body, apart from the consecrated bread. All the Evangelists call it bread. The Apostle Paul calls it bread, both before and after consecration. The bread which we break, is the communion of the body of Christ, 1 Cor. 10.16. We are one bread and one body, since we all partake of the one bread, v. 17. As often as you eat this bread, 1 Cor. 11.26. Whoever eats this bread and drinks this cup, 27. Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup, v. 28. Great and constant faith of the Apostolic interpreter! So that neither unbelievers should be offended by a crude, Capernaite eating of Christ's flesh, nor believers, dwelling too literally on the words of institution, should be stuck there, the Apostle sets out the true and genuine sense of a single proposition, which is improper and metonymic, five separate times, plainly.

units.la: V. Nuspiam tamen, inquit, Vir Doctissimus propositio, Hoc est Corpus, per æquipollentem, Hoc est signum Corporis mei, exprimitur? Resp. 1. Non erat necesse. Sexcentæ in sacris literis sunt parabolæ, & figuratæ locutiones, quæ in proprias nunquam leguntur resolutæ; de his tamen nullum periculum, cur ergo hoc loco Spiritui sancto figamus legem? Quid, quod ipsa experientia ejusmodi interpretis beneficium respuit? In re nummaria nihil notius est, quàm, sine æquipollenti explicatione, Adrianum, Trajanum, Constantinum, appellare numismata, quæ Imperatores modo memoratos referunt, aut repræsentant. Ne rustici quidem vel Galli, vel Helvetii, cum Ludovici, qui vulgò vocantur, sive aurei sive argentei oftenduntur, œdipo habent opus, non ipsum esse Christianissimum Galliarum Regem, sed imaginem tantum ejus. Ulu didicerunt de ejusmodi judicare loquendi formulis, absque Interprete. Ita in re sacramentaria formulæ apud judæos, usitatæ æquipollentiam nullam exigebant. Sacramentum ergo Christus cum instituerit; Sacramentalem etiam loquutionem retinere commodè potuit, quam discipuli, sine difficultate, aut scrupulo (qui proinde eximendus non erat) intellexerunt. Scholæ Judaicæ trita & obvia erat phrasis, qua agnum Paschalem גופו של פסח gupho schal pasach, corpus Paschatis, i.e. Translitus, appellárunt; Sacramentaliter & Metonymicè, pro corpore agni, qui Paschatis fuit μνημόσυνον, seu memoraculum. Hac Judæorum phrasi nemo, adeóque neque discipuli Christi offendebantur: Et tamen extra controversiam omnes ponebant, Agni corpus, non Transitus corpus esse; sed signum Transitus. 2. Lingua Syriaca rarissimè signi vel significandi verbum, in iis propositionibus, ubi Prædicatum de Subjecto improprie enuntiatur, adhibet, ne in promiscuo quidem loquendi usu, sed vel verbum substantivum אית Ith, Est vel Pronomen הנא Honau, hoc ipsum: Quid ergo necesse erat, in re Sacramentaria; ubi ex Judæorum consuetudine, Tropologia fuit trita; lumen adhiberi vel æquipollentiæ, vel explicationis? 3. Omnino sacra Scriptura satis indicat manifeste, phrasin, Hoc est corpus meum, alteri, Hoc est signum corporis mei, æquipollere, tum 1. quia ipse Spiritus sanctus alibi, imò fere ubique; ubi videlicet de Sacramentis loquitur; phrasin impropriam per propriam explicat. Exempla de circumcisione, Paschate supra à nobis sunt allata. Parium autem par nobis semper manebit ratio; Tum 2. quia constanter Christus stus panem vocat corpus : Atqui Panis, proprie nunquam est Corpus. Panis & Corpus sunt disparata, quæ de se invicem affirmativè non possunt enuntiari : Aut ergo falsa erit Propositio, quod impium & blasphemum est; aut Tropica; quod & verum, & in Sacramentis cumprimis usitatum : Tum 3. quia Paulus panem communionem vocat corporis Christi. Jam verò aliud est corpus ipsum, aliud communio corporis. Nihil enim sui ipsius communio esse potest, ut nullum relatum suum ipsius est correlatum. Etsi ergo, non totidem apicibus, panis vocetur signum corporis Christi, necessaria tamen & inevitabili consequentia, aut panis ipsum erit Corpus; quod τὸ ῥητὸν exigeret, naturæ autem rei repugnat, & schési, in qua de se prædicantur disparata; aut signum tantùm ejus, quod Sacramenti conditio flagitat.
units.tr: V. "Nowhere, however," says the most learned man, "is the proposition This is the body expressed through an equivalent, This is the sign of my body?" Reply. 1. There was no need. The sacred letters contain countless parables and figurative expressions which are never found resolved into plain terms; yet there is no danger from these. Why then should we fix a law for the Holy Spirit in this place? What is more, experience itself rejects the benefit of such an interpreter. In monetary matters nothing is better known than that, without any equivalent explanation, we call coins Hadrian, Trajan, Constantine, which bear or represent the emperors just named. Not even country folk, whether French or Swiss, when shown the gold or silver pieces commonly called Louis, need an Oedipus to tell that it is not the most Christian King of France himself but only his image. By use they have learned to judge such forms of speech without an interpreter. So in sacramental matters the formulas used among the Jews required no equivalence. Since Christ instituted a sacrament, he could fittingly retain sacramental speech, which the disciples understood without difficulty or scruple (and so there was no need to remove any scruple). A phrase common and familiar in the Jewish schools was that by which they called the Passover lamb gupho schal pasach [גופו של פסח], the body of the Passover, that is, of the crossing; sacramentally and metonymically, for the body of the lamb, which was the memorial of the Passover. By this Jewish phrase no one, and so not even the disciples of Christ, was offended. And yet everyone agreed beyond dispute that it was the lamb's body, not the body of the crossing, but the sign of the crossing. 2. The Syriac language very rarely uses a word for sign or to signify in propositions where the predicate is said improperly of the subject, not even in ordinary common usage; it uses either the substantive verb Ith, Est, or the pronoun Honau, this very. What necessity, then, was there in a sacramental matter, where the trope was familiar from Jewish custom, to bring in a light of equivalence or explanation? 3. Certainly Holy Scripture indicates clearly enough that the phrase This is my body is equivalent to the other, This is the sign of my body, both 1. because the Holy Spirit himself, elsewhere, indeed almost everywhere, where he speaks of the sacraments, explains the improper phrase by a proper one. Examples concerning circumcision and the Passover have been given above by us, and the same reasoning will always hold for like cases. Then 2. because Christ constantly calls the bread body. But bread is never properly body. Bread and body are disparate things, which cannot be affirmed of each other; therefore either the proposition will be false, which is impious and blasphemous, or it is tropical, which is both true and especially customary in sacraments. Then 3. because Paul calls the bread communion of the body of Christ. Now the body itself is one thing, and the communion of the body another. For nothing can be the communion of itself, just as nothing is its own correlate. Therefore, even if bread is not called sign of the body of Christ in so many words, by a necessary and inevitable consequence either the bread itself will be the body, which the literal sense [τὸ ῥητὸν] would demand but the nature of the thing opposes, since disparate things are predicated of each other in a relation [σχέσει]; or it will be only the sign of it, which the condition of the sacrament requires.

units.la: SECTIO V.
units.tr: SECTION V.

units.la: Non est Zuinglii Commentum, Est, poni, pro significat.
units.tr: That "Is" Standing for "Signifies" Is Not a Fiction of Zwingli's

units.la: 1. Non ergo, quando Zuinglius ve ba Christi, Hoc est corpus meum, Tropicè; Est, per significat, explicuit; commentum fuit, quo Tigurinos ab Ecclesia sententia de Eucharistia abduxit. Hoc doctissimo Viro, quod cum cæteris ris fidei sociis commune habere placuit convitium, libenter donabimus, modò justæ & moderatæ Apologiæ locum heic cedat. Eandem enim Zuinglium cum vetustissimis Ecclesiæ Græcæ & Latinæ Patribus defendisse sententiam, ipse jam, cum superstiti idem objiceretur novitatis pruritus, prolixè asseruit. Commendamus, brevitatis causa, Viro Doctissimo Zuinglii subsidium, sive Coronidem de Eucharistia; Planam & brevem Institutionem de Cœna Domini, quæ remotione falsarum & positione veræ sententiæ constat; Epistolas item quasdam & scripta Polemica contra Lutherum, quæ omnia Oper. T. II. ordine exhibentur. Videbit ut spero, non illotis ad hæc sacra manibus, nec imparatum Zuinglium accessisse. Præmeditata omnia suis Scripturæ authoritate munita, & veterum etiam exemplo confirmata.
units.tr: 1. Therefore, when Zwingli explained the words of Christ, This is my body, as a trope, rendering is as signifies, it was not a fiction by which he drew the Tigurines away from the Church's view of the Eucharist. We will gladly grant this most learned man the reproach that he shares with the other founders of the faith, provided that it leaves room here for a fair and moderate apology. Zwingli himself, when the same charge of novelty was brought against him while he was still alive, argued at length that he had defended the same view as the most ancient Fathers of the Greek and Latin Church. For the sake of brevity, we commend to the learned reader Zwingli's Subsidy, or Coronis, on the Eucharist; his plain and short Instruction on the Lord's Supper, which consists in removing false views and setting out the true one; and also certain letters and polemical writings against Luther, all of which are given in order in the second volume of his works. He will see, I hope, that Zwingli came to these matters with clean hands and not unprepared. Everything he wrote was carefully considered, fortified by the authority of Scripture, and confirmed by the example of the ancients.

units.la: Illud tamen dissimulare nolumus, Zuinglium in sententia sua, masculè jam antea defensa, multum fuisse confirmatum, postquam ex collatione locorum parallelorum, animadverti sīt, nihil plane suæ explicationi repugnare, ne phrases quidem Sacramentales Testamenti Veteris. Agnum vocari transitum, cum signum esset translatus; nullum ergo novitatis probrum extimescendum, si & ipse de similibus similiter judicaret. Ita sensit Zuinglius, ita ante eum, ita post eum Viri de Ecclesia Christi præclarè memeriti. Consensum Phraseologiæ, quæ toties Zuinglio tanquam nova & confista exprobata erat, non denegat vetustissima Ecclesia Latina. Ita enim Tertullianus: Christus acceptum panem & distributum discipulis corpus suum illum fecit, hoc est, corpus meum dicendo, id est, figura corporis mei. Advers. Marc. l. 4. cap. 40. Ambrosius: Vera utique caro Christi, quæ crucifixa est, quæ sepulta est, vera ergo carnis illius Sacramentum est. Ipse clamat Dominus Iesus; Hoc est corpus meum. Ante benedictionem Verborum Cœlestium alia species nominatur, post consecrationem corpus Christi significatur. Lib. de initiand. c. 9. Et alibi; Dicit, inquit, Sacerdos, fac nobis hanc oblationem adscriptam rationabilem, acceptabilem: quod sit in figuram corporis & sanguinis Domini nostri Iesu Christi: Lib. 4. de Sacram. cap. 5. Augustinus agmen claudat inter Latinos (neque enim de numero heic soliciti sumus) cujus verba sunt diserta: Non enim Dominus dubitavit dicere, Hoc est Corpus meum, cum signum daret corporis sui. Cont. Adim. cap. 12. Et iterum: Iudam adhibuit ad convivium, in quo corporis & sanguinis sui figuram discipulis commendavit & tradidit. Argum. seu Præfat. in Psalm. 3. Sed & assentsum præbet Græca Ecclesia. Eusebius, Cæsariensis Episcopus, totus noster est; Modò enim ait, Christum usum pane, ne, tanquam symbolo proprii corporis, modò symbola Divinæ dispensationis discipulis suis tradidisse, imaginem proprii fui corporis facere jussisse : Modò memoriam nobis tradidisse loco sacrificii, Deo jugiter offerendam: Opponit memoriam sacrificio. Inspiciatur Demonstrat. Evangel.l.8.c.1.& lib.1.c.ult. Gregorius Nazianzenus, etiam post consecrationem elementa, panem & vinum, semel atque iterum vocat ἀντίτυπα ; videat. Oration. 1. Apologet. & orat. 2. quam fecit funebrem in laudem defunctæ sororis suæ Gorgoniæ. Chryfoftomus Homil. 82. in Matth. Homil. 17. in Epist. ad Hebr. voces τύπος, συμβόλων, ἀναμνήσεως frequenter adhibet. Ubi notandum, veteres inter τύπον & ἀντίτυπον discrimen nullum agnoscere; neque etiam agnosci ullum posse, nisi quòd τύπῳ fit rei futuræ pariter & præteritæ, ἀντίτυπον ferè præteritæ. Ita aqua diluvii recte vocari potest Baptismi τύπῳ, ut Baptismus aquæ ἀντίτυπον, 1. Pet. 3.21. Ita & symbolum nunquam usurpatur nisi de signo rei, quæ est aut fuit, non futuræ. Theodoretus citra ambages nomine Ecclesiæ Orthodoxæ profitetur; In mysteriorum traditione Dominum panem appellasse corpus, & sanguinem id, quod in calice infusum, & commixtum erat. Item, symbola quæ videntur, appellatione corporis & sanguinis honorasse. Sacramentum Eucharistia esse imaginem, corpus
units.tr: We do not, however, wish to hide that Zwingli, though he had already defended his view vigorously, was much strengthened in it after he noticed, from comparing parallel passages, that nothing in his explanation clashed even with the sacramental phrases of the Old Testament, such as the lamb being called the passover, when it was the sign that had been transferred. So there is no disgrace of novelty to fear if he judged similar expressions in a similar way. So Zwingli thought, and so before him and after him men who have deserved well of the Church of Christ. The most ancient Latin Church does not deny agreement with the phraseology which was so often objected to Zwingli as new and strange. Thus Tertullian: "Christ, taking the bread and distributing it to the disciples, made it his body, that is, by saying, 'This is my body,' that is, the figure of my body." Against Marcion, book 4, chapter 40. Ambrose: "Surely the flesh of Christ, which was crucified and which was buried, is the true sacrament of that flesh. The Lord Jesus himself cries out, This is my body. Before the blessing of the heavenly words another species is named; after consecration the body of Christ is signified." On the Initiation, chapter 9. And elsewhere: "The priest says, 'Make for us this oblation enrolled, reasonable, acceptable, which is to be the figure of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.'" Book 4 on the Sacraments, chapter 5. Augustine closes the line among the Latins (for we are not anxious here about their number), and his words are plain: "For the Lord did not hesitate to say, This is my body, when he gave the sign of his body." Against Adimantus, chapter 12. And again: "He admitted Judas to the banquet, in which he committed and handed over to the disciples the figure of his body and blood." Argument or preface on Psalm 3. But the Greek Church also lends its assent. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, is entirely on our side. For at one point he says that Christ used bread, not as a symbol of his own body, nor that he handed to his disciples symbols of the divine dispensation, nor that he bade them make an image of his own body; at another point he says that he handed down to us a memorial, to be offered continually to God in place of a sacrifice. He sets memorial against sacrifice. See the Demonstration of the Gospel, book 8, chapter 1, and book 1, the last chapter. Gregory Nazianzen, even after consecration, calls the elements, bread and wine, once and again antitypes [ἀντίτυπα]; see his first Apologetic Oration and his second oration, which he made as a funeral eulogy for his dead sister Gorgonia. Chrysostom, in Homily 82 on Matthew and Homily 17 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, frequently uses the words type, symbols, remembrance [τύπος, συμβόλων, ἀναμνήσεως]. Here it must be noted that the ancients recognised no distinction between type [τύπον] and antitype [ἀντίτυπον], nor can any be recognised, except that the type [τύπῳ] refers equally to a thing future and past, while the antitype [ἀντίτυπον] refers almost always to a thing past. Thus the water of the flood can rightly be called the type [τύπῳ] of baptism, as baptism by water is the antitype [ἀντίτυπον]; 1 Peter 3:21. So too symbol is never used except of the sign of a thing which is or was, not of a thing future. Theodoret professes this without ambiguity in the name of the Orthodox Church: "In the handing down of the mysteries the Lord called the bread his body, and the blood the thing poured and mixed into the cup." Likewise he honoured the symbols which are seen with the name of the body and blood, and calls the sacrament of the Eucharist an image, the body and blood of the Lord [of this image, antitype].

units.la: C autem & sanguinem Domini imaginis huius ἀντιτύπου Dial. 1. & 2. Zuinglii ergo commentum fuerit, quod Veterum adeo pleno confirmari potest suffragio?
units.tr: But is Zwingli's invention then, which can be confirmed by such full support of the Fathers, something to be wondered at? (The stray "C" at the start of this unit is a printing artifact and is not translated.) Dialogues 1 and 2.

units.la: II. Mirum igitur merito videatur, Virum doctissimum adduci non posse ut credat, in locis ex Genesi & Exodo adductis, sententiam Scripturæ esse, Circumcisionem esse fœdus, aut agnum esse transitum &c. cum nullus, quod confidenter dicimus, alius erui possit sensus, qui vel scopo dicentis, vel materiæ subjectæ, vel Patrum explicationi rectius conveniat. Hanc observo lucem ex Pontificiis Commentatoribus non paucos, nec sine causa, metuisse. Certe Cornelius à lapide, Emanuel Sa, Johannes Mariana, silentio ea omnia, quæ in Genesi & Exodo de locutionibus istis Sacramentalibus habentur, maluerunt involvere, quàm perspicuum & sponte fluentem sensum in controversiam vocare, adeóque notoria ἀμετρία ἀνθολογίας, quam Veteres appellant, peccare. Sed quia de his in sequentibus plenior differendi patebit campus, pedem ad illa paulatim moveamus.
units.tr: II. It may therefore seem a matter of wonder that so learned a man cannot be brought to believe that, in the passages cited from Genesis and Exodus, the sense of Scripture is that circumcision is the covenant, or that the lamb is the passover, and so on. For no other sense can be drawn from them, as we confidently say, which agrees more correctly either with the purpose of the speaker, or with the subject matter, or with the explanation of the Fathers. I observe that not a few of the Papist commentators feared this light, and not without reason. Certainly Cornelius a Lapide, Emmanuel Sa, and John Mariana preferred to wrap up in silence everything in Genesis and Exodus concerning these sacramental expressions, rather than call into dispute a clear and naturally flowing sense; and so they sinned by the well-known excess of collecting quotations [ἀμετρία ἀνθολογίας], as the Ancients called it. But since a fuller field for discussion of these matters will open in what follows, let us move our steps gradually towards them.

units.la: III. Eccur Verbum Est pro significat adhiberi, vel nos fluctuemus, vel vobis, Vir Doctissime, adversarij videamur? Quomodo, quæso, septem spicæ sunt septem anni, Genes. 41.27. Septem capita, septem montes, Apoc. 17.17. Decem cornua, decem reges v.12. nisi
units.tr: III. Why the verb Is should be used for signifies, either we waver, or, most learned sir, we may seem to your opponents to be waverers? How, I ask, are seven ears of grain seven years, Genesis 41:27; seven heads, seven mountains, Revelation 17:17; ten horns, ten kings, verse 12; unless

units.la: significative? Addantur Deut. 22.15. Ezech. 37. 11. Dan. 2.38. & 4. 20.22. cap. 7.17.24. c. 8.20. 21.22. Matth. 13. verf. 37.38.39. Luc. 8.11. Joh. 10.7. & 11. 1. Gal. 4. verf. 24. In illis praesertim locutionibus, quae typicae sunt, Sacramentales &c. ut jam monuimus, nihil frequentius. Ita sacrificia vocantur peccata, Hos. 4. 8. coll. 2. Cor. 5.21. Sanguis vitulorum & Hircorum sanguis foederis, Heb. 6.20. Exod. 24.8. Baptismus mors & sepultura, Rom. 6.4. Coloss. 2.12. de reliquis supra jam est actum.
units.tr: figuratively? Add Deuteronomy 22:15; Ezekiel 37:11; Daniel 2:38, and 4:20, 22, chapter 7:17, 24, chapter 8:20, 21, 22; Matthew 13:37, 38, 39; Luke 8:11; John 10:7, and 11:1; Galatians 4:24. Especially in those expressions which are typical, sacramental, and so on, as we have already noted, nothing is more frequent. So sacrifices are called sins, Hosea 4:8, compared with 2 Corinthians 5:21. The blood of calves and goats is the blood of the covenant, Hebrews 9:20; Exodus 24:8. Baptism is death and burial, Romans 6:4; Colossians 2:12. Of the rest we have already treated above.

units.la: Unde igitur Adversariorum nomen in tam amico, quem exspectamus, consensu? Haec, plurraque alia, pro nobis, exempla omnia militant. Universa Scripturae Phraseologia Sacramentalis nostra est. Unico contra, quod serio rogamus, Vir doctissimus Scripturae probet documento, verbum Est, copulative sive conjunctive sumtum, idem significare, quod Transsubstantiari, in aliam mutari substantiam, & ita quidem, ut destructo subjecto remaneant Accidentia? Non dissimulabo; ut de integritate causae nostrae constet; esse, non Adversarios tantum (prout memini, Araufioni aliquando Capucinum Linguae Hebraeae non mediocriter peritum, multum sibi fuisse blanditum in locis, quae mox exprimemus) sed & ex nostris Theologis reperiri, qui ad textum Exod. 3. v. 3.4. cap. 7.9. 10.12.15. & cap. 8.16. notet, Esse ibi. ibi poni pro converti,quod tamen nos nunquam dabimus,neque propter manifestum Elenchum parium, dare possumus. Ne unicus quidem citatorum locorum est, in quo substantivum Est ponatur absolutè; sed cum particula inseparabili Lamed; quæ significationis aliam prorsus induit naturam. Unde non dicitur Virga fuit serpens,sed in serpentem; pulvis in pediculos &c. quod quantum differat ab altera phrasi controversa, Hoc est corpus meum,illi non ignorant, qui vel inter apia Hebraismi versantur. Eadem planè ratio est reliquorum locorum in quibus Est pro fieri vel effici, poni, etiam ex nostratibus nonnulli observant, ut Gen. 17. 16. Exod. 9. 9. Num. 33. 55. Iud. 11. 8. Psalm. 31. 3. Psalm. 71. 3. Ies. 7. 23. Ierem. 47. vers. 2. Matth. 19. 6. Luc. 3. 5. In quibus omnibus locis, semper phrasis Hebraica esse in gentem, in pulverem, in spinas &c. vel successionem, vel statum & conditionem, vel transsubstantiationem notat, sed adeò diversa loquendi formula, ut tutò postulatum meum repetere liceat, ne unicum, Virum Doctissimum, monstraturum locum ubi Esse, absolutè positum idem significet, quod fieri vel mutari. Quid autem sit in retam sublimi, mysteriíque plena à recepta Scripturæ phrasi & sententia recedere, novam, eámque violentam, multisque absurdiditatibus involutam cudere,id vero Doctissimi Viri religioso conscientiae examini relinquo.
units.tr: Whence then the name of Adversaries in so friendly a consensus, which we look for? These, and very many other examples, all fight on our side. The whole Sacramental phraseology of Scripture is ours. Against this, most learned sir, we seriously ask you to prove by a single document of Scripture that the word Is, taken copulatively or conjunctively, means the same as to be transubstantiated, to be changed into another substance, and that in such a way that, with the subject destroyed, the accidents remain. I will not conceal that, so that the integrity of our cause may be clear, there are found not only Adversaries (as I recall, a Capuchin at Orange, once no mean expert in the Hebrew language, flattered himself much on the passages which we shall shortly set out), but also some among our own theologians who, on the text Exodus 3:3, 4; chapters 7:9; 10:12, 15; and chapter 8:16, note that to be there stands for to be turned; which we shall never grant, nor, on account of the manifest refutation of equal cases, can we grant it. Not even one of the passages cited is one in which the substantive Is is put absolutely; but it is joined with the inseparable particle Lamed, which takes on an entirely different nature of meaning. Hence one does not say the staff was a serpent, but into a serpent; dust into lice, and so on. Those who are versed even in the rudiments of Hebraism know how far this differs from the other disputed phrase, This is my body. The same reasoning applies to the remaining passages in which Is is put for to become or to be made, as some of our own people also observe: Genesis 17:16; Exodus 9:9; Numbers 33:55; Judges 11:8; Psalm 31:3; Psalm 71:3; Isaiah 7:23; Jeremiah 47:2; Matthew 19:6; Luke 3:5. In all these places the Hebrew phrase to be into a nation, into dust, into thorns and so on denotes either succession, or state and condition, or transubstantiation; but the form of speech is so different that I may safely repeat my demand: that the most learned man should not show me a single place where Is, put absolutely, means the same as to become or to be changed. But what it is to depart, in a matter so lofty and full of mystery, from the received phrase and sense of Scripture, and to coin a new and violent sense, entangled in many absurdities, that I leave to the religious examination of the conscience of the most learned man.

units.la: IV. Loci Apostolici 1. Cor. cap. 10. vers. 4.
units.tr: IV. Apostolic passage, 1 Cor. 10, verse 4.

units.la: Petra autem erat Christus, Vir Doctissimus priori suo ad Tigurinos responso non meminit; jam demum hac Editione accessit, sed sine magno Auctoris commodo. Nec dum Tigurinos poenitet, indicâsse, verbum Erat hoc loco usurpari pro significabat; adeoque cum verbis institutionis contulisse. Apostolus enim (Corinthiis suis probaturus, etiam Patres in Veteri Testamento Spiritualem habuisse escam & potum, adeoque medullam & nucleum Sacramentorum,) utriusque meminit Sacramenti, Baptismi & Eucharistiae. De Eucharistia loquitur v. 3. & primo quidem de pane; omnes eandem escam spiritualem edisse, Christum videlicet, per Manna sacramentaliter praefiguratum; postea etiam v. 4 de potu: Et omnes eundem potum spiritualem bibisse, bibisse enim ex sequenti spirituali Petra, quae Petra fuerit Christus. Quomodo Christus erat Petra? Utique non proprie; sed sacramentaliter, & significative, ut ipse explicat Augustinus contra Adversarium Legis lib. 2. cap. 6. & Epist. 102. Et lib. 4. de doctrina Christiana cap. 21. expresse scribit, Petram illam typum habuisse corporis Christi. Expressissime lib. Quaestion. in Levit. c. 57. quem supra jam citavimus.
units.tr: The rock was Christ. The most learned man did not mention this in his earlier reply to the Zurich ministers. It has now been added in this edition, but not to the author's advantage. The Zurich ministers still do not regret having pointed out that the word was here is used for signified, and so compared it with the words of institution. The Apostle, meaning to prove to the Corinthians that the Fathers in the Old Testament also had spiritual food and drink, and so the marrow and kernel of the sacraments, mentions both sacraments, Baptism and the Eucharist. He speaks of the Eucharist in verse 3, first of the bread: all ate the same spiritual food, namely Christ, prefigured sacramentally by the manna. Then in verse 4 he speaks of the drink: all drank the same spiritual drink, for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ. How was Christ the rock? Certainly not properly, but sacramentally and significatively, as Augustine himself explains against the Adversary of the Law, book 2, chapter 6, and in Epistle 102. In book 4 of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 21, he writes expressly that that rock had the type of the body of Christ. Most expressly in the Questions on Leviticus, chapter 57, which we have already cited above.

units.la: V. Sed Petra, quam percussit Moses in deserto, significavit, non fuit Christus; pergit vir doctissimus. Non contradicimus, quod Augustini modò authoritate stabilivimus. De hac autem non dixit Apostolus: Petra autem erat Christus, sed de Petra spirituali, consequente Israelitas, quæ verè erat Christus. Inanis cavillatio, ex Bellarmino mutuata lib. 1. de Eucharistia cap. 9. ff. Iam quod attinet. Bibebant Israelitæ ex Petra, ut legere, est, Exod. 17.6. Num. 20.10. & 21.16. hanc (quod satis est manifestum, tum ex articulo Græco ἡ δὲ πέτρα, hæc autem, cujus modò meminerat, Petra; tum ex eo, quòd omnes de ea dicuntur bibisse, v. 4. de Christo autem, Spirituali Petra, non omnes biberunt; tum denique, quòd Christus Israelitas non fuit secutus ut comes itineris; sed præcessit ut dux viæ; Exod. 23.20,23.) Apostolus vocat Spiritualem, non per substantiam, ut Augustinus loquitur, sed per significationem, quia ausum habuit Sacramentalem: Typus enim erat venturi Messiæ, ut ex Augustino didicimus, qui Messias vera erat Petra, imò aqua illa viva, de qua ipse Servator, Joh. c. 4. 14. Sit ergo, quò ad iem & subsantiam, ut revera est, alia hæc Petra Christus, ab illa Mosaica, sit Christus Petra Spiritualis, ut vocatur ab Apostolo; semper tamen manebit, Christū propriè Petram appellari non posse. Aliud enim Petra est sive lapis, aliud Christus Θεάνθρωπος. Verum proinde est, quod ex Hieronymo subjungit vir doctissimus, Christum postmodum secuturum aut nascituram, sed & hoc verum, ex eodem Hieronymo; ejus figuram Petram à Mose percussam gessisse: Petram proinde spiritualem Christum vocari non proprie; sed, tum Metonymicè, tum Metaphoricè, adeóque; id quod probandum nobis erat; figuratè. Miror, Doctissimum Virum, nodum etiam nectere, ubi plana omnia sunt & perspicua. Israëlitæ dicuntur bibisse ex Petra spirituali, quæ, ut immediatè subjicitur, erat Christus. Ut igitur nulla proprie dicta Petra spiritualis (lapis enim & Spiritus affirmatè de se enuntiata implicant) dari potest; ita nec Christus Petra, proprie, ullo modo appellari. Non quæritur de re ipsa, an Christus sit Petra, de quo nullus inter nos dissensus, sed de modo loquendi, proprius ne sit an improprius. Proprius esse non potest, non magis, quàm si in V. Testamento Deus Petra appellatur: Impropria ergò & Metaphorica hæc est denominatio, quod vel Scholasticis, in Tropologia utcunque versatis, notum esse existimem.
units.tr: V. But the rock which Moses struck in the desert signified, but was not, Christ, the most learned man goes on. We do not contradict this, which we have just established by Augustine's authority. But the Apostle did not say of this rock, "The rock was Christ," but of the spiritual rock that followed the Israelites, which truly was Christ. This is an empty quibble, borrowed from Bellarmine, On the Eucharist, book 1, chapter 9. As for what is said: the Israelites drank from the rock, as is read in Exodus 17:6, Numbers 20:10 and 21:16. This rock (which is clear enough, both from the Greek article ἡ δὲ πέτρα, "but the rock", of which he had just spoken, and from the fact that all are said to have drunk from it in verse 4, whereas not all drank from Christ the spiritual rock; and finally because Christ did not follow the Israelites as a companion on the journey, but went before them as the guide of the way; Exodus 23:20, 23) the Apostle calls spiritual, not by substance, as Augustine speaks, but by signification, because it had the sacramental character. For it was a type of the coming Messiah, as we have learned from Augustine, and the Messiah was the true rock, indeed that living water of which the Saviour himself speaks, John 4:14. So let this other rock, Christ, be different in nature and substance from that Mosaic rock, as it truly is; let Christ be the spiritual rock, as the Apostle calls him. Still it will always remain that Christ cannot be properly called a rock. For a rock is one thing, Christ the God-man is another. It is true, as the most learned man adds from Jerome, that Christ was to follow or be born afterwards; but this too is true, from the same Jerome, that the rock struck by Moses bore his figure. Therefore Christ is not properly called a spiritual rock, but is so called by metonymy and by metaphor, and so, which was what we had to prove, figuratively. I am surprised that the most learned man ties knots where everything is plain and clear. The Israelites are said to have drunk from the spiritual rock, which, as is immediately added, was Christ. So, just as no spiritual rock can be properly so called (for a stone and spirit, predicated affirmatively of themselves, contradict each other), so Christ cannot in any way be properly called a rock. The question is not about the thing itself, whether Christ is the rock, on which there is no disagreement between us, but about the manner of speaking: whether it is proper or improper. It cannot be proper, no more than if in the Old Testament God is called a rock. This denomination is therefore improper and metaphorical, which I think is known even to the Scholastics, who have some acquaintance with tropology.

units.la: VI. Verba Genes. 17. verf. 13. Eritque pactum meum in carne vestra, alium sensum, quàm sequentia ejusdem capitis v. 1. 20. Circumcidetis carnem præputii vestri, ut sit in signum fœderis inter me & vos, non habere; vi-
units.tr: VI. The words of Gen. 17:13, "And my covenant shall be in your flesh," should not be given a different sense from the following verses of the same chapter, vv. 1 and 20: "You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you." The learned man

units.la: C 4 10 ro doctissimo utraque largimur manu ; nisi quòd prior loquendi formula impropria sit & Rhetorica;posterior propria & Grammatica. Sed annon ita Adversarii nostri, nostri judices? Deut. 32. verf. 31. Annon eadem ratione & nos, cum ex Scriptura dicimus, verba Hoc est corpus meum, eundem habere sensum cum verbis Pauli ; Hoc (panis quem frangimus) est communio, testera communionis, symbolum corporis Christi; praeeuntem habemus ipsum Deum interpretem? Cur ergo moras nectamus, aut sequi tergiversemur? Non dabit vir doctissimus, & recte quidem, ipsam circumcisionem esse pactum in carne Israelitarum, proprie : Et tamen Deus ita diserte vocat; Pactum meum erit in carne vestra, id est, ut ipse explicat, signum pacti mei sive foederis. Cur igitur nobis, exemplo & authoritate Spiritus S. phrases Sacramentales improprias resolvere non liceat in proprias? Aut quodnam inter explicationem ipsius Dei : Erit circumcisio pactum meum, i. e. signum pacti mei, & Reformatorum in materia plane homogenea; Hoc (panis) est corpus meum, i.e. signum corporis mei, discrimen? Captus es, vir doctissime, ut cum Theodoreto Dial. 2. loquamur, retibus quae ipse texuisti. Nam, quia mystica symbola propriam naturam post sanctificationem non amittunt; sed in priori manent substantia, & figura specie,& videri,tangique possunt, qualia etiam prius erant ; impropriæ ejusmodi locutiones perproprias necessariò sunt reddendæ.
units.tr: ...grants both readings with both hands, except that the former form of speech is improper and rhetorical, the latter proper and grammatical. But are not our opponents, our judges, so? (Deut. 32:31.) Do we not likewise, when from Scripture we say that the words This is my body have the same sense as Paul's words, This (the bread which we break) is the communion, the token of the communion, the symbol of Christ's body, have God himself going before us as interpreter? Why then do we delay, or shrink from following him? The learned man will not deny, and rightly so, that circumcision itself is properly the covenant in the flesh of the Israelites. Yet God so plainly calls it: My covenant shall be in your flesh, that is, as he himself explains, a sign of my covenant. Why then may we not, by the example and authority of the Holy Spirit, resolve the improper sacramental phrases into proper ones? Or what difference is there between God's own explanation, Circumcision shall be my covenant, that is, a sign of my covenant, and that of the Reformed in a matter quite similar: This (bread) is my body, that is, a sign of my body? You have been caught, most learned sir, in the nets you yourself have woven, when we speak with Theodoret, Dialogue 2. For since mystical symbols do not lose their proper nature after consecration, but the substance remains as before, and they can be seen and touched in species and figure, just as they were before, such improper expressions must necessarily be rendered as entirely proper.

units.la: VII. Exodi XII. agnum dici Transitum
units.tr: VII. Exodus 12. That the lamb is called the Transit

units.la: Domini, supra satis manifeste, ut ipero,evicimus; quod Vir doctissimus illud non videt, dolemus equidem. Dolemus, adeò tortam eum, novam, & absurdam facile videre verborum Institutionis explicationem; non videre planam, perspicuam, toties in S. Scriptura utriusque Testamenti expositam, ut non possit de alio quàm de agno, vox Paschatis, intelligi. Non satis capere Virum doctissimum, quomodo hoc dici potuit, cum transitus sit motus euntis de loco ad locum, per quoddam spatium medium, quod de agno illic dici nequit; non miramur: Neque nos capimus, nec capere vel debemus vel possumus, neque etiam capere jubemur, quomodo agnus, proprie, sit Transitus. Improprie tamen agnum vocari Transitum, cujus signum erat, quid prohibeat? Hinc vero iterum evidenter colligimus, cum utrumque sit verum, & agnus vocetur Transitus, & tamen Transitus non potuit esse proprie agnus; quòd necessario propositio sit Tropica. Ita etiam capiendum, cum Christus dicitur Petra, spiritualis: cum enim omninò aliud sit Petra aliud Christus, quæ de se invicem affirmari proprie non possunt, ad eam Scripturæ necessario confugiendum explicationem, quæ neq; naturam rei evertat, neque Spiritus sancti verba in Controversiam quoquomodo vocet, adeoq; analogicam & symbolicam, non verò propria & Grammaticam sequatur significationem.
units.tr: That the Lord's Passover has already been shown above, quite plainly as I think, the most learned man does not see, and I grieve for it. I grieve that he so easily sees a twisted, novel and absurd explanation of the words of the Institution, but does not see the plain and clear explanation which is set out so often in Holy Scripture of both Testaments, namely that the word Passover can be understood of nothing but the lamb. That the most learned man does not sufficiently grasp how this could be said, since a transit is the motion of one going from place to place through some intervening space, and this cannot be said there of a lamb: we are not surprised. Nor do we grasp it, nor ought we or can we grasp it, nor are we even commanded to grasp how a lamb can properly be a Transit. But what prevents the lamb, of which it was the sign, from being called the Transit in a figurative sense? From this we again clearly conclude that, although both are true, that the lamb is called the Transit and yet the Transit could not properly be the lamb, the proposition must be tropical. So too must it be understood when Christ is called a spiritual Rock: since the Rock is altogether other than Christ, and things which cannot properly be predicated of one another, we must necessarily take refuge in that explanation of Scripture which neither overturns the nature of the thing nor in any way calls the words of the Holy Spirit into controversy, and so follows the analogical and symbolic, not the proper and grammatical, meaning.

units.la: VIII. Instat Vir doctissim°; At verba Domini; Est enim Phase, i.e. Transitus Domini, non dicuntur de agno, quasi agnus sit Transitus; sed, postquam Deus iussit Israelitas immolare agnum, obtinere postes ejus sanguine &c. Addit hujus rei rationem; Est enim, inquit, Phase, i. e. Transitus Domini, quod nihil aliud significat, quam adest Transitus Domini, id indicant sequentia verba: Et transibo per terram Ægypti nocte illa; & paulo post: Erit autem sanguis vobis in signum in ædibus, in quibus eritis, & videbo sanguinem, & transibo vos. Resp. 1. Imò verò verba; Hoc est Phase, Hic est Transitus; de agno dicuntur. Pronomen enim demonstrativum Hu, Hoc, ad suum antecedens, (ιṇɴ Otho) illum v. 11. agnum nempe perfectum, ut v. 5. appellatur necessario referendum, five Grammaticam respiciamus, pronominis cum substantivo masculino convenientiam: sive Logicam connexionem, ubi oratio infinitiva ante verbum finitum, sive expressum, sive sub intellectum naturali constructione ponitur pro nominativo & pro subjecto: ut de circumcisione, Gen. 17. verf. 10. & 11. Imò, planè ut, cùm Christus de pane dixit; Accipite, edite, confestim subjecit; Hoc est corpus meum.
units.tr: VIII. The most learned man objects: But the words of the Lord: "It is the Passover, that is, the Transit of the Lord," are not said of the lamb, as if the lamb were the Transit; but after God commanded the Israelites to slaughter the lamb and to smear its blood on the posts, and so on. He adds the reason for this: "It is the Passover," he says, that is, the Transit of the Lord, which signifies nothing other than that the Transit of the Lord is present; the following words show this: "And I will pass through the land of Egypt that night"; and a little later: "The blood shall be a sign to you on the houses in which you are, and I will see the blood and will pass over you." Reply, first: on the contrary, the words "This is the Passover, this is the Transit" are said of the lamb. For the demonstrative pronoun this (Hebrew ôthô [אותו]) must necessarily refer to its antecedent, him, namely the perfect lamb, which in v. 5 is so named, whether we look to the grammatical agreement of the pronoun with the masculine noun, or to the logical connection, where an infinitive clause is placed before a finite verb, whether expressed or understood by natural construction, in the place of the nominative and of the subject, as in the case of circumcision, Gen. 17 vv. 10 and 11. Indeed, just as when Christ spoke of the bread, "Take, eat," he immediately added "This is my body."

units.la: 2. Vir doctissimus infirma nititur hypothesi, quasi in textu ipso particula Est occurreret, pro Adest. Nuspiam illa apparet, in Originali contextu, sed ab Interpretibus, explicationis ergò, est addita. 3. Et quid si versiculus hic unicus ; quod tamen non largimur; aliquam haberet difficultatem, ut Pronomen Hoc, vel ad Historiam, vel totins festi solennitatem referretur, num propterea improprietas phraseos, Agnus est Transitus: & Transitus est agnus, erit controversa ? Nihil hic periculi. Manet adhuc semper, &, ex supra allatis exemplis, manebit incomcussum, nihil Spiritui sancto in utroque Testamento, Judaicæ etiam Ecclesiæ fuisse usitatius, quàm agnum, eo tempore mactandum, Paschatis sive Transitus nomine intelligere. Ut stupendum profecto potius, quàm mirandum videatur, in hoc etiam scirpo nodum quæri, aut iis scotomata offundi, quæ luce meridiana clariora sunt. Transitum mactare, edere, parare, &c. Scripturæ phrases sunt, obviæ & usitatæ, adeóque veræ, quas tamen si capere velit Vir doctissimus, Tropologiæ usitatæ luce illustrare debet. 4. Αἰτιολογία, Viri doctissimi, subjecta, plane inconveniens est; quasi Deus diceret, adesse transitum Domini. a Particula enim ne quidem in textu occurrit. b Illa demum sequitur v. 12. c Sacrorum Annalium scriptor,initio capitis,mandat Israelitis, ut, antequam exirent Ægypto, Sacramentum agni Paschalis celebrarent. Agni eligendi, maftandi, coquendi, manducandi oftendit modum & rationem ad v. 12. Et ut ne existimarent Judæi, hoc convivium profanum esse aut commune, nomen ei imponit sub finem v. 11. Hoc, inquit, quod vos manducare jussi, est Pascha, est Transitus. Ne vero ignorarent, cur hoc potissimum ei nomen Dominus impositum voluisset, v. 12. Ego enim, inquit, transibo per terram Ægypti &c. Non ergo abrupta hic est oratio; sed Errymi tantum subnexa ratio, cur nempe Deus agnum illum Transitus nomine insignierit. Mansit deinceps constanter huic agno, totiq; ritui nomen Transitus, addita tamen iterum ea explicatione, quàm in N. Testamenti Sacramentis retinuerunt Reformatores. Ita v. g. v. 13. additur; Erit sanguis in signum; & v. 14. Et erit dies iste vobis in memoriam, εἰς ἀνάμνησιν liberationis ex Ægypto & potestate Pharaonis, plane ut Christus cœnam instituit, in fui memoriam, gratam recordationem mortis pro nobis, nofiráque liberatione ex potestate Satanæ, oppetitæ. Hæc sobria, vera, & genuina textus præfentis est explicatio, ipsis fontibus sponte innata, non vero violenter illata, aut falsis suppositionibus, quasi vel particula Enim, vel subsubstantivum Est, pro Adest in textu occurreret, suffulta.
units.tr: 2. The most learned man rests on a weak hypothesis, as if the particle is occurred in the text itself in the sense of is present. It appears nowhere in the original text, but has been added by the translators for the sake of explanation. 3. And what if this single verse, which however we do not concede, had some difficulty, such that the pronoun this referred either to the history or to the solemnity of the whole festival: would the impropriety of the phrase The lamb is the Transit, and the Transit is the lamb then be open to dispute? There is no danger here. It remains always, and from the examples cited above it will remain unshaken, that nothing was more usual to the Holy Spirit in both Testaments, or even in the Jewish Church, than to understand by the name Passover or Transit the lamb to be slaughtered at that time. So it seems truly more astonishing than wonderful that a knot should be sought in this reed too, or that mists should be cast before the eyes of those things which are clearer than the midday sun. To slaughter, eat, prepare the Transit, and so on, are phrases of Scripture, common and customary, and therefore true; yet if the most learned man wishes to grasp them, he must illustrate them by the light of the customary tropology. 4. The causal clause [αἰτιολογία] of the most learned man is wholly unsuitable, as if God were saying the Transit of the Lord is present. (a) The particle for does not even occur in the text. (b) It follows only at v. 12. (c) The writer of the sacred annals, at the beginning of the chapter, orders the Israelites to celebrate the sacrament of the Paschal lamb before they left Egypt. He shows the manner and the reason of choosing, slaughtering, roasting and eating the lamb in v. 12. And so that the Jews might not think this feast was profane or common, he gives it a name at the end of v. 11: This, he says, which I have commanded you to eat, is the Passover, is the Transit. And lest they should not know why the Lord wished this name to be given to it in particular, he says in v. 12: For I, he says, will pass through the land of Egypt, and so on. The discourse is therefore not abrupt here, but only the reason is added why God marked that lamb with the name of Transit. Thereafter this lamb, and the whole rite, constantly kept the name Transit, though with the further explanation which the Reformers retained in the sacraments of the New Testament. Thus, for instance, in v. 13 it is added: The blood shall be a sign; and in v. 14: And this day shall be to you for a memorial [εἰς ἀνάμνησιν] of the liberation from Egypt and from the power of Pharaoh, just as Christ instituted the supper for a memorial of himself, a grateful remembrance of his death for us and of our liberation from the power of Satan, which was suffered. This is the sober, true and genuine explanation of the present text, arising naturally from the sources themselves, not forced upon them violently, nor supported by false suppositions, as if either the particle for or the verb is in the sense of is present occurred in the text.

units.la: IX. Quòd versus 27. solicitatur, id verò doctissimo Viro, multis nominibus minus est dignum; & vellem equidem, Homerum non ita periculosè hic dormitâsse. De Genitivo ne quidem sum solicitus. Quamvis dilutum nimis est Argumentum ab Accentu, casuum distinctivo, petitum. Non credo, Veteres hoc ita vel legisse vel observâsse. Editio Coloniensis 1529. 1530 Lugdunensis 1527. aliæque, Vulgatæ illa etiam, quæ cum Nicolai Lyrani glossis prodiit, imò & elegantissima Antvverpiensis 1624. Διάχεσιν Genitivi Transitus, quam clarâ em esse in textu Latino Vir doctissimus monuit, plane ignorant. Neque etiam hoc sensu verba: Agnus est victima Transitus Domini; Veteres intellexisse, non obscurè hinc patet, quòd Vulgato cum LXX. Interpretibus ut plurimum bene conveniat. At LXX. expresse habent nominativum τὸ πάσχα, hoc Pascha, plane ut v, 11. Quanquam nostra prorsus nihil referat, si vel Genitivum maximè admittamus, quem etiam, quod non neganus, Syrus & Arabs retinent: Plura sunt loca, eaque ἀναυλίππηκα, quæ nullum plane alium funduнt sensum, quàm quo Pasach, Phase, Transitus, pro agno, sumitur, non utique proprie, quod neque nos cum Viro doctissimo capimus; sed figuratè. Repeti possunt, quæ supra de hac Phraseologia diximus
units.tr: IX. That v. 27 is disturbed, this is far less worthy of so learned a man in many respects; and I would have wished that Homer had not nodded so dangerously here. I am not even concerned about the genitive. Although the argument drawn from the accent, the distinguishing mark of the cases, is far too weak. I do not believe the Ancients either read or observed it so. The Cologne edition of 1529, the Lyons edition of 1527, and others, the Vulgate too, which appeared with the glosses of Nicolas of Lyra, and indeed the very elegant Antwerp edition of 1624, plainly do not know the construction of the genitive of the Transit, which the most learned man said is clear in the Latin text. Nor is it obscure that the Ancients understood the words The lamb is the sacrifice of the Lord's Transit in this sense either, since the Vulgate agrees well for the most part with the Seventy translators. But the Seventy expressly have the nominative τὸ πάσχα, the Passover, just as in v. 11. Yet our argument hardly matters, even if we admit the genitive altogether, which the Syrians and Arabs too, as we do not deny, retain. There are several passages, and these of a kind [ἀναυλίππηκα] which yield no other sense than that in which Pasach, Phase, Transit is taken for the lamb; not, of course, properly, which neither we nor the most learned man grasp, but figuratively. What we have said above about this phraseology may be repeated.

units.la: X. Sed Gordium sibi, Vir doctissimus, nectit nodum; videamus an solvere eum commodè possimus. Certum est, inquit Sensum Scripturæ non esse Agnum esse Translatum, quod nemo intelligere possit, &c. Ita est: Nemo intelligere potest, qui rigidius literæ inhærens, Agnum proprie esse Translatum; obtinere veller. Cur autem intelligere non possimus, si cum, & ex Scriptura, Ecclesiæ praxi & consuetudine loquamur, Agnus est Translatus; figuratè, id est, signum translatus; non est translatus, proprie? Quæ, quæso, in ejusmodi explicationibus Tropicis, (quas nisi admittamus, absurdissimarum in Theologia inferemus opinionum iliadem,) vel difficultas vel absurditas? Cur frustra crucem nobis figamus? Tota ut utique Scriptura sacra locutionibus ejusmodi scatet. Non improbo, hunc de agno Paschali locum ægrè sibi Virum doctissimum eripi passum esse; ereptum autem jam, spero planam & expeditam structuram viam, ad legem ὁμοογενείας diligentius in aliis observandam.
units.tr: X. But the most learned man ties himself a Gordian knot; let us see whether we can conveniently loosen it. It is certain, he says, that the sense of Scripture is not that the lamb is the Transit, which no one can understand, and so on. So it is: no one can understand it who, clinging too rigidly to the letter, wishes to maintain that the lamb is properly the Transit. But why could we not understand, if we speak with Scripture, with the practice and custom of the Church, that the lamb is the Transit, figuratively, that is, the sign of the Transit, and is not the Transit, properly? What difficulty or absurdity, I ask, is there in such tropical explanations, which, unless we admit them, we shall bring upon ourselves a whole iliad of most absurd opinions in theology? Why do we fix our cross in vain? For all of Holy Scripture is indeed full of expressions of this kind. I do not disapprove that the most learned man has been unwilling to see this passage about the Paschal lamb taken from him with difficulty; but now that it has been taken, I hope the way is open and clear for a more careful observance of the law of homogeneity [ὁμογενείας] in other passages.

units.la: XI. Illud, quicquid sit in Hebræo textu, Viro doctissimo vellem nunquam excidisse. Scio, multos esse in Ecclesia Romana, qui decretum Synodi Tridentinæ de Editione authentica, ita explicant, ut Latinam omnibus Editionibus, Hebraicis etiam & Græcis præferant; non puto tamen Virum doctissimum latere, Celeberrimos Sorbonæ Doctores, aliósque, eruditione, integritate cæteris multis parasangis superiores, nunquam voluisse permittere, ut sontibus præferrentur rivuli, Textui authentico qualescunque Translationes. Nota sunt publica scripta & judicia Virorum solide Doctorum, Simeonis de Muis, Flavigni, aliorumque, quibus nimia pro Vulgata Latina superstitio nunquam placuit. Cardinalis Cajetanus dicere solebat: Intelligere textum Latinum, non esse intelligere verbum Dei. Verbum Dei errare non posse; sed vocem interpretis errori esse obnoxiam. Nemini vel ignotum vel obscurum esse potest, Regum & Principum diplomata non ex versionibus vel translationibus, sed authenticis tabulis, & prototypis indicanda esse atque judicanda: Sed hæc obiter.
units.tr: XI. I wish whatever the Hebrew text may say had never slipped from our most learned man. I know that many in the Roman Church explain the decree of the Council of Trent on the authentic edition so as to prefer the Latin to all editions, Hebrew and Greek included. Yet I do not think our most learned man is unaware that the most celebrated teachers of the Sorbonne, and others far superior to many in learning and integrity, never wished to allow that streams should be preferred to their source, or that any translations whatever should be placed before the authentic text. The published writings and judgments of solidly learned men, Simon de Muis, Flavigny, and others, who never favoured excessive superstition towards the Latin Vulgate, are well known. Cardinal Cajetan used to say: To understand the Latin text is not to understand the word of God. The word of God cannot err; but the voice of the interpreter is liable to error. No one can fail to know that the diplomas of kings and princes are not to be indicated and judged from versions or translations, but from authentic records and originals. But these things in passing.

units.la: XII. Verba, Baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis, totidem syllabis ad Tit. 3. v. 5. non ostendimus: Agi autem illo Pauli loco de Baptismo, quis Theologorum, ut de scopo dicentis, & locorum parallelismo nihil dicamus, salva Veterum authoritate, negare sustineat? Quid enim usitatius illis est, quàm Baptismum appellare λουτρὸν σωτήριον, ἁγιον λουτρὸν, Lavacrum sanctum, Lavacrum pœnitentiæ; Lavacrum cœleste, ut vocat Lactantius. An vero Ba-
units.tr: XII. We have not shown, in as many syllables, the words Baptism is the washing of regeneration at Titus 3:5. But who among theologians, to say nothing of the purpose of the speaker and the parallelism of the passages, would dare to deny, saving the authority of the Ancients, that Paul's passage there concerns Baptism? For what is more common with them than to call Baptism "saving washing" [λουτρὸν σωτήριον], "holy washing" [ἁγιον λουτρὸν], "washing of repentance", or "heavenly washing", as Lactantius calls it? Or indeed whether Bap-

units.la: Baptismus, id est, immersio, vel alperfio aquæ, proprie est lavacrum regenerationis? An insita quadam virtute, externum hoc elementum a peccatis, internis animæ sordibus, nos purget? Non profecto. Nisi velimus, omnes, qui externa aquæ baptismatis unda sunt abluti, regenerationem ipso actu, per eam, ceu vehiculum, consequi: Cui tamen quotidiana reclamat praxis; repugnant exempla eorum, qui Baptisma quidem fluminis acceperunt, Flaminis non item. Solus nos Christi sanguis purgat a peccatis, 1. Joh. 1. 7. cujus, aqua Baptismi, proprerea typus est, sive figura, quia convenientissimam nobis offendit analogiam. Quemadmodum enim aquâ macula eluitur, sordes expurgantur, ita & sanguine Christi, ejusque aspersione maculæ animæ, peccata abluuntur & expiantur. Neque verò video, cur Vir doctissimus Comparationem seu Identitatem propositionum impropriarum concedat in verbis, Aqua, aut lavacrum, seu Baptismus est Spiritus sanctus; & Hoc est corpus meum; in sequentibus vero Apostoli verbis; Salvos nos fecit per lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis Spiritus sancti, non item. Cur, amabo, Baptismus exterior, qui fit ablutione aquæ, magis proprie vocari possit lavacrum regenerationis (quam enim externum Elementum aquæ habeat Virtutem in animam, ejusque facultates, in regenerationem, quæ, ut actio est intrinseca, totáque spiritualis, ita etiam spiritualiter debet intelligi, judice Servatore Ioh. cap. 3.) quàm, Baptismus est Spiritus sanctus, nondum oftendit. Utrobique disparatorum est enunciatio, sive dicam, Baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis, cujus signum tantùm est & sigillum; sive, Aqua vel Baptismus est Spiritus sanctus, quo sensu aquæ vocabulum Theologi accipi volunt Ioh. 3.v.5. Utraque proinde impropria sive Tropica.
units.tr: tism, that is, immersion or sprinkling with water, is properly the washing of regeneration? Does this external element, by some inherent power, cleanse us from sins, the inner filth of the soul? Certainly not. Unless we are willing to hold that all who have been washed with the outward water of baptism thereby obtain regeneration by that very act, as through a vehicle. Yet daily practice cries out against this, and the examples of those who received the baptism of the river but not of the Spirit refute it. Only the blood of Christ cleanses us from sins, 1 John 1:7; and the water of baptism is accordingly a type or figure of it, because it presents us with a most fitting analogy. For just as a stain is washed away by water and filth is cleansed, so also by the blood of Christ and its sprinkling the stains of the soul and sins are washed away and atoned for. Nor indeed do I see why our most learned man should grant a comparison or identity of improper propositions in the words, Water, or washing, or Baptism is the Holy Spirit, and This is my body, but not in the following words of the Apostle, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, not likewise. Why, pray, can the outward Baptism, which is effected by the washing of water, be more properly called the washing of regeneration? (For what virtue the outward element of water has upon the soul and its faculties for regeneration, which as an action is intrinsic and wholly spiritual, and so must be understood spiritually, the Saviour judging in John chapter 3, has not yet been shown.) Why not rather Baptism is the Holy Spirit? In both cases the statement joins things that differ: whether I say Baptism is the washing of regeneration, of which it is only the sign and seal, or Water or Baptism is the Holy Spirit, in which sense the theologians wish the word water to be taken in John 3:5. Both expressions are therefore improper or figurative.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Atque sic spero, Virum doctissimum visurum, quo pacto dicere possint Tigurini, se credere, panem esse corpus Christi, quemadmodum in Genesi, Exodo, Epistola ad Titum, Circumcisio est fœdus, Agnus est Transitus, Baptismus est lavacrum regenerationis; quia & formulæ istæ in Genesi, Exodo, Epistola ad Titum, extant, & plane sunt similes verbis Institutionis: utrobique enim de Sacramentis sermo est, utrobique loquutiones adhibentur Sacramentales, utrobique ergo eadem verba illa explicandi ineunda est via. Neque diffitemur, necesse omnino esse dicere cum Christo, Panem esse Corpus Christi, Vinum esse sanguinem Christi: Quis enim de eo ambigat, quod, qui ipsa est veritas, protulit? Aut quid nos offendat tam plana & perspicua, etsi Tropica locutio, ut non dictam aut defensam eam velimus? De veritate verborum non est controversia; sed de ratione & modo veritatem investigandi, sit ne immediatus, verbis propriis, an mediatus, Tropicis, enuntiatus? Christus se Leonem, viam, vitem, &c. appellat; nemo hoc in dubium vocat: Proprie tamen Christum esse Leonem, viam, vitem (etsi vera nuncupetur) non dabunt Adversarii. Non vero propterea inconstantia nobis aut levitas exprobranda, cum iterum dicimus, esse signa corporis & sanguinis Christi, quod idem est, ac si diceremus, panem & vinum esse & non esse corpus & sanguinem Christi: Sunt enim omnino, panis & vinum, Elementa, symbola, figuræ, typi, antitypa, ut appellari solent ab Ecclesiæ Patribus; salsissimum tamen, & jam supra à nobis confutatum est, nihil aliud esse, quàm nuda & vacua signa. Sunt, ut mentem nostram apertius declaremus, signa i significantia, quæ fractione nobis panis, effusione vini Christum pro peccatis nostris passum, corpus ejus fractum, sanguinem effusum ob oculos ponunt, & depingunt; Matth. 22.28. Gal. 3.
units.tr: And so I hope the learned man will see how the Tigurines can say that they believe bread to be the body of Christ, just as in Genesis, Exodus, and the Epistle to Titus we have Circumcision is the covenant, The lamb is the Passover, Baptism is the washing of regeneration. For these formulas are found in Genesis, Exodus, and the Epistle to Titus, and are plainly similar to the words of institution. In each case the discourse concerns sacraments, and in each case sacramental expressions are used, so in each case the same way of explaining those words must be entered upon. Nor do we deny that one must necessarily say with Christ that bread is the body of Christ and wine is the blood of Christ. For who could doubt what he who is the truth himself has declared? Or what could offend us in so plain and clear a locution, even if it is figurative, so that we would not wish it to be uttered or defended? There is no controversy about the truth of the words, but about the method and manner of seeking the truth: is it stated immediately in proper words, or mediately in figurative ones? Christ calls himself a lion, the way, the vine, etc.; nobody calls this into doubt. Yet the adversaries will not grant that Christ is properly a lion, the way, or the vine, though he is rightly named so. Nor therefore should inconstancy or levity be charged against us when we again say that they are signs of the body and blood of Christ, which is the same as if we said that bread and wine are and are not the body and blood of Christ. For bread and wine are indeed elements, symbols, figures, types, antitypes, as they are commonly called by the Fathers of the Church. Yet it has been refuted by us above as most absurd that they are nothing other than bare and empty signs. To declare our mind more plainly, they are signifying signs, which by the breaking of bread and the pouring out of wine set before our eyes and depict for us Christ suffering for our sins, his body broken and his blood poured out; Matthew 26:28; Galatians 3.

units.la: 1. Sunt signa 2. exhibentia, quæ verè & realiter, Christum nobis ejusque meritum exhibent & offerunt, non per inclufionem, neque per Transsubstantiationem, sed per spiritualem, (prout omnis nostra in & cum Christo communio spiritualis est) veram tamen & realem in legitimo usu participationem, adeò ut elementa, Panis & vinum, accedente, per Ministrum, verbo, virtute & ordinatione Divina fiant Sacramentum; quo corpus & sanguinem Christi, ad vitam spiritualem edimus & bibimus. Per hanc manducationem cum Christo ita arcte unimur, ut fiamus caro de carne ejus, & os de ossibus ejus, per quam etiam conservamur ad vitam aeternam. Quia igitur & cibus spiritualis est, & vita, ad quam nos nutrit spiritualis, ipsum quoque os spirituale esse oportet. Mysterium enim est, quod animam reficit, sensus non afficit, nec ad vitam corporalem quicquam confert. Sunt denique signa confirmantia, obsignantia & applicantia, adeo ut quaecunque verbum audibile Evangelii omnibus promittit credentibus in genere, illa ipsa, verbum hoc visibile, Sacramentum, unicuique confirmet, obsignet & applicet in specie. Quemadmodum enim Abraham accepit Circumcisionem, signum, quod obsignaret justitiam fidei, Rom. 4. vet. 11. ita etiam cuilibet fideli, usu elementorum Dominicorum, tanquam per arrhas, annulos, sigilla, obsignatur, confirmatur & applicatur, quicquid Christus suo merito illi acquisivit. Et prout Paschalis festum in V. T. in gratam Exitus gloriosi populi Israelitici ex Aegypto recordationem; institutum fuit, atque ab uno quoque Israelita celebratum; ita & in memoriam liberationis a peccato, & Diabolo, Christus Coenae suae repetitionem nobis commendavit: Idque eo potissimum, ut promissionibus suis sigillum adderet, nostraeque adeo succsuccurreret infirmitati. Procul ergo à sacris illis abstinet profani! Illotis manibus ad illa nemo accedat: Probet se quisque, juxta Pauli monitum, 1. Cor. 11. & tum demum de pane illo edat, & de poculo illo bibat. Hæc autem, digne communicaturi, pia esse possunt jacula & vota: Eja! adsum o Domine, facturus voluntatem tuam, grata mente memoriam, in confirmationem fidei, mortis tuæ celebraturus. Gratiam mihi fac, ut non panem tantum accipiam Domini, sed & panem Dominum; non elementa tantum & signum, sed & rem significatam, medullam & nucleum, corpus & sanguinem Christi, quorum participatione Ille sit in me, & ego in Ipso, crescam in virum perfectum ad mensuram staturæ adulti Christi, Ephes. 4. verf. 13. Hunc usum habent signa Sacramentalia, in legitimo usu, qui longè plus pollicetur, quàm carnalis illa Verborum de carne & sanguine Christi explicatio, quemque universa primitiva Ecclesia & religiose observavit, &, ut postea audiemus, assiduè inculcavit. Absurdum proinde non est, si, diverso respectu panem & vinum dicimus esse corpus Metonymicè & Sacramentaliter; panem & vinum non esse corpus, proprie & literaliter: Utrumque enim asserit Scriptura. Christus panem vocat corpus suum, & vinum sanguinem suum. Negat, panem esse corpus, & vinum sanguinem suum, quandoquidem fieri non potest, ut panis sit corpus Christi, fructus vitis sit fructus ventris, vinum sit sanguis, nisi improprie, & usitato Tropo. Et, si Viro doctissimo certum fuit visum, sensum Scriptura non esse, agnum esse translatum; si capere non potuit (ubi tamen nulla nisi sponte accersita difficultas) quomodo hoc dici possit, cum translitus sit motus euntis de loco ad locum per quoddam spatium medium; quomodo alios capere existimet, Panem proprie esse Corpus Christi, cum ille ex multis constet granis, mixtura sit aquae & farinae, hoc vero virtute Spiritus sancti in utero Beatae Mariae Virginis ex substantia ejus conceptum & natum. Iterum ergo, quod jam in antecedentibus a nobis observatum est, monemus, propositionem; Panis est corpus Christi, vel esse falsam, (quod vel cogitatu nefas) vel tropicam.
units.tr: (1) They are signs, first, signifying. (2) They are signs exhibiting, which truly and really exhibit and offer to us Christ and his merit, not by enclosure, nor by transubstantiation, but by a spiritual participation (as all our communion in and with Christ is spiritual), yet a true and real participation in lawful use, so that the elements, bread and wine, when the word is added by the minister, through the divine power and ordinance, become a sacrament, by which we eat and drink the body and blood of Christ unto spiritual life. Through this eating we are so closely united with Christ that we become flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, and by it we are also preserved unto eternal life. Therefore, since the food is spiritual and so is the life to which it nourishes us, the mouth itself must also be spiritual. For it is a mystery which refreshes the soul, does not affect the senses, and contributes nothing to bodily life. Lastly, they are signs confirming, sealing and applying, so that whatever the audible word of the Gospel promises to all believers in general, this same visible word, the Sacrament, confirms, seals and applies to each one in particular. For just as Abraham received circumcision, a sign which sealed the righteousness of faith (Romans 4, Old Testament, verse 11), so too to every believer, by the use of the Lord's elements, as through earnests, rings and seals, is sealed, confirmed and applied whatever Christ has acquired for him by his merit. And just as the Passover feast in the Old Testament was instituted in grateful remembrance of the glorious exodus of the Israelite people from Egypt, and was celebrated by every Israelite, so also Christ commended the repetition of his supper to us in remembrance of our deliverance from sin and the Devil, and especially so that he might add a seal to his promises and so come to the aid of our weakness. Let the profane therefore keep far from those holy things! Let no one approach them with unwashed hands. Let each one prove himself, according to Paul's warning, 1 Corinthians 11, and only then let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. These may be pious ejaculations and prayers for those who are to communicate worthily: Come! Here I am, O Lord, about to do your will, with a grateful mind, about to celebrate the memory of your death for the confirmation of faith. Grant me that I may receive not only the bread of the Lord, but the Lord who is the bread; not only the elements and the sign, but the thing signified, the marrow and kernel, the body and blood of Christ, by whose participation he may be in me and I in him, and I may grow into a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, Ephesians 4, verse 13. Sacramental signs have this use when lawfully used, which promises far more than that carnal explanation of the words about the flesh and blood of Christ, and which the whole primitive Church observed religiously and, as we shall hear later, constantly impressed. It is therefore not absurd, if in different respects we say that bread and wine are the body metonymically and sacramentally, but that bread and wine are not the body properly and literally. For Scripture asserts both. Christ calls the bread his body, and the wine his blood. He denies that bread is the body and wine his blood, since it cannot happen that bread should be the body of Christ, the fruit of the vine the fruit of the womb, or wine be blood, except improperly and by a customary trope. And if the learned man thought it certain that the sense of Scripture is not that the lamb is translated; if he could not grasp (where there is no difficulty except one invited by himself) how it could be said that it is translated, since passing over is the motion of one going from place to place through some intervening space; how does he think others can grasp that bread is properly the body of Christ, since the one consists of many grains, is a mixture of water and flour, while the other was conceived and born by the power of the Holy Spirit from the substance of the blessed Virgin Mary in her womb? So again, as we have observed above, we warn that the proposition Bread is the body of Christ is either false (which is an impiety even to think) or figurative.

units.la: SECTIO VI. De sensu verborum; Hoc est Corpus meum, Tropico seu figurato.
units.tr: SECTION VI. On the sense of the words "This is my body": tropical or figurative.

units.la: I. Atque sic, ut opinor, manifestum satis est;
units.tr: I. And so, as I think, it is sufficiently clear:

units.la: 1. ex Spiritus sancti mente & intentione ritum circumcisionis appellari foedus, cum signum tantum foederis fuerit; Translitum, agnum, idque per Metonymiam Sacramentalem.
units.tr: 1. From the mind and intention of the Holy Spirit, the rite of circumcision is called a covenant, though it was only the sign of the covenant; and the Passover lamb is called the Passover, this by sacramental metonymy.

units.la: 2. Hujus Metonymiae Interpretem esse ipsum Spiritum sanctum, & ad eundem plane modum, quem hodie retinet Ecclesia Tigurina. Ecclesiam primitivam has loquendi formulas inter prima Theologiæ suæ capita retulisse.
units.tr: 2. The interpreter of this metonymy is the Holy Spirit himself, and in exactly the same way as the Tigurine Church holds it today. The primitive Church counted these forms of speech among the first heads of its theology.

units.la: 4. Ac proinde non Tigurinorum fuisse compositionem, quòd totidem verbis & in Scriptura reperiunt, & in Antiquitate. 5. Zuinglium, quo ad phraseologiæ Sacramentalis expositionem, novitatis argui non posse, nisi Græci patriter & Latinæ Ecclesiæ eodem involvantur reatu. Sufficere hæc possent in causæ primariæ subsidium.
units.tr: 4. Therefore the composition was not the Tigurines', since they find the same words both in Scripture and in antiquity. 5. Zwingli, as regards the explanation of sacramental phraseology, cannot be charged with novelty, unless the Greek Fathers and the Latin Church are involved in the same guilt. These points may suffice as support for the primary cause.

units.la: Quia verò observo, totius Controversiæ nostræ Cardinem in hoc versari, utrum verba Institutionis ; Hoc est corpus meum, Tropice an proprie sint intelligenda? paululum nobis subsistendum erit. Est enim trabalis clavus, qui infirmiorum aut præ posteré de nobis sentientium animos gravissimè vulnerat.
units.tr: But since I observe that the hinge of our whole controversy lies in this, whether the words of institution, "This is my body," are to be understood tropically or literally, we must pause here a little. For this is a great nail of a beam, which grievously wounds the minds of the weaker, or of those who judge us unfairly.

units.la: Afferto verò & evicto, Tropica esse institutionis verba, cætera sponte vel stabunt, vel cadent. Hoc scrupulo exemto, nihil in hac disceptatione superesse, quod magni sit momenti, animadverto. Reliqua enim omnia, quæ Vir doctissimus in sequentibus proponit, facti potius sunt & authoritatis Ecclesiasticæ, quàm solidæ rationis & juris Divini. Experiamur ergo causæ nostræ robur.
units.tr: But once it is asserted and proved that the words of institution are tropical, the rest will stand or fall of its own accord. With this scruple removed, I observe that nothing of great moment remains in this dispute. For all the rest that the most learned man sets forth in what follows belongs rather to fact and ecclesiastical authority than to solid reason and divine right. Let us, then, test the strength of our cause.

units.la: Quæritur: Utrum verba; Hoc est Corpus meum; Hic est sanguis meus (hæc enim duo quia Scriptura conjungit, divelli a nobis non debent, præsertim cum posterius prioris sit ἐξηγητικὸν) proprie an Tropice sint intelligenda? Si de facto quæstio sit, utrum vel Reformati, vel Lutherani, vel Pontificii verba proprie intelligant, an Tropice? aperte fateor, Tropum omnibus reipsa placere, etsi verbis a Pontificiis & Lutheranis ille rejiciatur. Pontificii verba: Hoc est corpus meum, explicant: Hoc fit, mutetur, vel mutatum est in corpus, & ita quidem, ut sublato Subjecto mera supersint Accidentia. Hoccine est retinere τὸ ῥητὸν, literam, verba? Quàm longis hic currITur ambagibus? An uspiam Est; & mutari in aliquid, æquipollent? Imò toto cœlo differunt & illud ὑπαρξιν dicit seu Existentiam, adeóque statum præsentem; hoc, intercedente privatione, γένναν, generationem seu productionem futuram. Sed & Lutheranorum explicatio, Hoc est Corpus meum, per Synecdochen; quam etiam concedunt; In, cum, & sub pane est corpus meum, reddunt. De Reformatis conclamatum est! Scilicet, non Tropum tantùm, sed & commodam Tropi sedem indicant. Utut ergo Pontificii & Lutherani aversum à Tropo ostendant animum, sententiam tamen, absque Tropologia suam, nullo colore vel afferere, vel defendere possunt. Iterum ergo Viro doctissimo judicandum relinquo, qua fronte Scholastici, in verbis; Hoc est corpus meum, æquipollentiam extorqueant verborum; Hoc fit; fiat, mutetur in corpus meum. Esse & Transubstantiari nullam prorsus inter se habent affinitatem, neq; Grammaticam, neque Theologicam, neque Physicam.
units.tr: The question is: whether the words "This is my body" and "This is my blood" (for since Scripture joins these two, they ought not to be separated by us, especially since the latter is an explanation [ἐξηγητικὸν] of the former) are to be understood literally or tropically. If the question concerns fact, namely whether the Reformed, the Lutherans, or the Papists understand the words literally or tropically, I frankly confess that in reality a trope pleases everyone, although the Papists and Lutherans reject it in words. The Papists explain the words "This is my body" as "This becomes, is changed, or has been changed into the body," and so that, the subject being removed, only accidents remain. Is this to keep the literal sense [τὸ ῥητὸν], the letter, the words? How long are the detours run here! Or are "is" and "is changed into something" anywhere equivalent? Indeed they differ entirely, for the one signifies existence [ὑπαρξιν], that is the present state, while the other, with a privation intervening, signifies generation [γένεσιν], that is, a future production. Again, the Lutheran explanation of "This is my body" by synecdoche, which they also concede, they render as "In, with, and under the bread is my body." Against the Reformed they have cried out! Clearly they indicate not only a trope but also a convenient seat for the trope. Therefore, however much the Papists and Lutherans show their minds turned away from a trope, they can neither assert nor defend their opinion in any plausible way without tropology. Again I leave it to the most learned man to judge with what face the Scholastics extort an equivalence of words from "This is my body" and "Let this become, let it be changed into my body."
