"To be" and "to be transubstantiated" have absolutely no affinity with each other, neither grammatical, nor theological, nor physical.

units.la: II. Sed nolumus de facto contendere, jure quid fieri expediat examinaturi, Tropicè, Institutionis verba explicanda esse, breviter & dilucidè ita probamus. 1. Vsus est Christus locutione Sacramentali, E. Tropica. Antecedens in confesso est. Conseq. tum ex fundamento dicti de omni procedit; tum ipsa etiam exemplorum inductione, omnium nempe ordinariorum, utriusque Testamenti, Sacramentorum, manifestum est; id quod ex superioribus repeti hoc loco debet. Debet haec regula Patrum in Ecclesia non minus esse universalis & recepta, quàm altera illa, cujus meminimus, de anthropopathiis. Haec enim per εἰκόνας, τύπους, ςυμβόλα operationes nobis divinas proponit; illa contrà symbolis, & typis nomen rerum caelestium, & beneficiorum divinorum imponit. Haec meta est, ad quam qui non attendunt, de Sacramentis nunquam sobrie differunt; & à qua divelli nos possumus.
units.tr: II. But we do not wish to contend about fact; wanting to examine what it is right to do, we prove briefly and clearly that the words of institution are to be explained tropically. 1. Christ used sacramental language; therefore it is tropical. The antecedent is granted. The consequence follows both from the foundation of the dictum concerning all [de omni], and from the induction of examples, namely all ordinary ones, of both Testaments and of the sacraments, which is manifest; and this must be repeated here from what has gone before. This rule of the Fathers ought to be no less universal and received in the Church than that other rule we mentioned, concerning anthropopathies. For the latter sets before us divine operations through images, types, and symbols [εἰκόνας, τύπους, σύμβολα]; the former, on the contrary, gives the names of heavenly things and divine benefits to symbols and types. This is the goal: whoever do not attend to it never speak soberly about the sacraments, and from it we must not let ourselves be torn away.

units.la: 2. Verba, de altero Elemento, Vino nempe, sunt Tropica, E. & de pane. Antecedens proba-tur textibus Scripturæ. Luc. 22. 20. Hoc poculum, est novum illud Testamentum, per sanguinem meum, qui pro vobis effunditur. 1. Cor. 11, 25. Hoc poculum est novum illud Testamentum in sanguine meo. Utut in omnes se adversarii vertant partes, eluctari tamen non poterunt, quo minus Tropum in his verbis admittere debeant. Quomodo enim poculum proprie esse queat Novum Testamentum? Quod si haec Tropica sint, quae institutionis Coenae alteram constituunt partem, cur in priori membro, cum parium par sit ratio, locum relinquere Tropo tergiversentur? Hunc hactenus nemo, quod sciam, solvere, secare multi conati sunt nodum: Sed irrito omnia tentata successu. Quod enim nonnulli, Testamentum vocari, quia Christus nobis Testamento legavit sanguinem suum, excipiunt, impertinens plane est. Nam ne sic quidem verba Tropica esse desinunt, imo Tropum clarius ostendunt. Ratio enim tantum, exceptione illa, redditur, cur Christus poculum vocarit Novum Testamentum; quod poculum Testamentum proprie dicatur, non ostenditur. Quanquam, Testamentum in sanguine, non potest esse sanguis. Nemo enim unquam sic loquutus est, ut rem Testamento legatam, vocet Testamentum in re, quod hoc loco fit. Sed & ipsa Tropi explicatio non satis Theologica est. Ideo enim, secundum Scripturam, Christus poculum vocat Testamentum, quia signum erat sanguinis, quo N. T. fuit ratum, Heb. 7. verf. 22. Gal. 3. 14.
units.tr: 2. The words about the other element, namely the wine, are tropical; therefore so are those about the bread. The antecedent is proved by the texts of Scripture. Luke 22:20: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." 1 Cor. 11:25: "This cup is the new testament in my blood." However much the adversaries turn themselves in every direction, they will not be able to struggle free of admitting a trope in these words. For how can a cup properly be the New Testament? But if these are tropical, which make up the second part of the institution of the Supper, why do they hesitate to leave room for a trope in the first member, since the reasoning ought to be the same for like cases? So far, as far as I know, no one has solved this knot; many have tried to cut it, but all attempts have had no success. For what some take exception to, that the cup is called "testament" because Christ bequeathed his blood to us by testament, is quite beside the point. For even so the words do not cease to be tropical; indeed they show the trope more clearly. That explanation gives only the reason why Christ called the cup the New Testament; it does not show that the cup is properly called a testament. Moreover, "testament in blood" cannot be blood, for no one has ever spoken in such a way as to call the thing bequeathed by a testament a testament in the thing, which is what happens here. But the very explanation of the trope is also not theological enough. For according to Scripture, Christ calls the cup a testament because it was a sign of the blood by which the New Testament was ratified: Heb. 7:22; Gal. 3:14.

units.la: 3. Verba Christi sunt Testamentaria, E. Tropica. Hoc argumentum, ex adversariorum antithesi profectum, studioque iis, qui exceptionem in Testamentis quaerunt, oppositum, innititur perpetuae Praxi sanctorum, Veteris &
units.tr: 3. Christ's words are testamentary; therefore they are tropical. This argument, proceeding from the antithesis of the adversaries and directed against those who seek an exception in wills, rests on the constant practice of the saints of the Old and

units.la: D 5 N. N. Testamenti, quorum verba Testamentaria & legatoria, ut plurimum, imo omnia sunt Tropica, Isaaci, Gen. 27. Jacobi, Gen. 49. Mosis, Deut. 33. Davidis, 2. Sam. 23. Pauli 2. Timoth. 4.6.
units.tr: New Testaments, whose words of testament and bequest are for the most part, indeed all of them, tropical: of Isaac, Gen. 27; of Jacob, Gen. 49; of Moses, Deut. 33; of David, 2 Sam. 23; of Paul, 2 Tim. 4:6.

units.la: 4. Ferè omnia reliqua Institutionis Coenæ verba impropria sunt; Nihil ergo absurdi, si hic quoque Tropo relinquamus locum; aut danda nobis est ratio disparitatis. Geminus Tropus latet in verbis: Poculum est N. Testamentum. Tropica sunt; quod pro vobis frangitur, quod pro vobis effunditur, in remissionem peccatorum. Corpus tum proprie non erat fractum, nec sanguis in remissionem peccatorum, quod fieri debebat in ara crucis, effusus. Tropica sunt; Non bibam ab hoc tempore ex hoc fructu vitis, usquedum bibam vobiscum novum in regno Patris. Hæc etiam verba Christi sunt, an vero propterea ita morose Hagellanda, ut cœlum Muhammedicum, Perediam & Perbibefiam hinc fingamus?
units.tr: 4. Almost all the remaining words of the institution of the Supper are improper. There is nothing absurd, then, if here too we leave room for a trope; otherwise we must be given a reason for the difference. A double trope lies hidden in the words: "The cup is the New Testament." Tropical are: "which is broken for you," "which is poured out for you, for the remission of sins." The body was not then broken properly, nor was blood poured out for the remission of sins, which had to happen when it was shed on the altar of the cross. Tropical are: "I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine, until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of the Father." These too are Christ's words. Or are we therefore to whip them so pedantically that we invent from them a Muhammadan heaven, Perediam and Perbibefiam?

units.la: 5. Eo modo Christus in Cœna panem corpus suum vocat, quo Judæi in celebratione Paschatis, corpus agni appellarunt corpus Paschatis. Hoc factum Tropicè ꝟ. & illud. Ratio consequentiæ, quia Christus agno Paschali Cœnam suam substituturus, eadem retinere voluit elementa, easdem fere phrases & ceremonias, quibus discipuli assueverunt, ut hoc eos Pædagogo facilius doctrinæ suæ ritibus imbueret. Quod arargumentum alia occasione prolixius poterit tractari, ejusque momentum ita dilucide proponi, ut nemini dubium esse queat, hanc, inter utrumque Sacramentum, analogiam, ad componendum difficilium Sacramentarium magnum afferre momentum. Certè, quando Apostolus, ipsum Christum pro nobis immolatum, Pascha sive transitum appellat, (Pascha nostrum pro nobis sacrificatum est, Christus, scribit 1. Cor. 5.7.) haud obscurè innuit, alterum peralterum commodè explicandum.
units.tr: 5. In the same way Christ in the Supper calls the bread his body, as the Jews in the celebration of the Passover called the body of the lamb the body of the Passover. The former is a trope, and so is the latter. The reason for the consequence is this: Christ, about to substitute his Supper for the Paschal lamb, wished to keep the same elements, almost the same phrases and ceremonies to which the disciples were accustomed, so that by this tutor-like method he might more easily imbue them with his teaching through the rites. This argument can be treated more fully on another occasion, and its weight set forth so clearly that no one can doubt that this analogy between the two sacraments brings great weight to the settling of the difficult sacramentarian controversy. Certainly, when the Apostle calls Christ himself, sacrificed for us, our Passover (for he writes, "Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us," 1 Cor. 5:7), he quite plainly hints that the one may conveniently be explained by the other.

units.la: 6. Ita verba Coenæ nobis sunt explicanda, prout explicuisse ea videmus Apostolos. At Apostoli ea Tropicè explicuerunt. Paulus quinquies corpus Christi vocat panem, etiam post consecrationem. Atqui nec panis proprie est corpus, nec corpus panis. E Tropicè, per Metonymiam signi. Idem 1. Cor. 10. vers. 16. panem quem frangimus, vocat communionem corporis Christi. E non ipsum corpus. Aliud enim est communio rei, aliud res ipsa. Ubi tamen communionis vocabulum, pro signo communionis est accipiendum: Id quod ex scopo Apostoli satis evidenter patet. Ut enim Idolothyta κοινωνία vocantur, sive communio Dæmoniorum, & velcentes Idolothytis κοινωνοί, consortes dæmoniorum, quia sacrificia illa signum & tessera erant, qua Collegium seu corpus constituebatur eorum, qui Dæmoniis cultum, obsequium & homagium præstiterunt; Ita vice versa, qui de papane & vino Dominico participant, publico communionis signo testantur, ad quem coetum seu gregem pertineant, Dominicum nempe, teste Apostolo: Panis, quem frangimus, nonne est communio corporis Christi; tum veri & naturalis, tum mystici, id est, Ecclesiae, 1.Cor. 10. 16. 17. collat.
units.tr: 6. The words of the Supper must be explained as we see the Apostles explained them. But the Apostles explained them figuratively. Paul calls the body of Christ bread five times, even after the consecration. But bread is not properly the body, nor the body bread. Therefore the expression is figurative, by metonymy of the sign. The same Paul, at 1 Cor. 10:16, calls the bread which we break the communion of the body of Christ, not the body itself. For communion is one thing, the thing itself another. Yet the word communion here must be taken for the sign of communion, as is clear enough from the Apostle's purpose. Just as things offered to idols are called koinōnia [κοινωνία], that is, the communion of demons, and those who eat them are called koinōnoi [κοινωνοί], partners of demons, because those sacrifices were a sign and token by which the company or body of those was constituted who paid worship, service and homage to demons, so, conversely, those who partake of the Lord's bread and wine bear public witness by this sign of communion to which company or flock they belong, namely the Lord's. This is the Apostle's testimony: Is not the bread which we break the communion of the body of Christ? (compare 1 Cor. 10:16, 17), both of the true and natural body and of the mystical body, that is, the Church.

units.la: 7. Accedit suffragium antiquitatis; Ut enim Copulam Est, per significare, repraesentare, memorare Patres interpretantur; Ita panem & vinum corporis & sanguinis Christi vocant signa, Sacramenta, figuras, symbola, typos, Antitypos, mysteria, exemplaria, similitudine, imagines, memorias; id quod prolixe & solide non demonstratum modo, sed & vindicatum est a Theologis Reformatis.
units.tr: 7. Add to this the witness of antiquity. For just as the Fathers interpret the copula is as signifies, represents, commemorates, so they call the bread and wine of the body and blood of Christ signs, sacraments, figures, symbols, types, antitypes, mysteries, examples, likenesses, images, memorials. This has been demonstrated at length and solidly, and moreover defended, by the Reformed theologians.

units.la: 8. Propositio, Hoc est corpus meum, habet notas & characteres, veras & essentiales, Propositionis Tropicae; E. Tropica est. Utriusque veritatem vidit Augustinus lib. 3. de doctrina Christiana cap. 16. Si praeceptiva locutio est, aut flagitium aut facinus vetans, aut utilitatem aut beneficentiam jubens, non est figurata: si autem flagitium aut facinus videtur jubere, aut utilitatem aut beneficentiam vetare, figurata est. Nisi manducaveritis carnem filii hominis, & biberitis sanguinem ejus, non habebitis vitam in vobis, facinus vel flagitium videtur jubere, figura est, praecipiens, passioni Domini esse communicandum, & suaviter atque utiliter recondendum in memoria, quod pro nobis caro ejus crucifixa & vulnerata. Quid in rem nostram clarius dici posset ab Augustino? Negemus, propriam propositionem hoc loco facinus jubere aut flagitium? Contradicentem habemus & Augustinum & experientiam. Sed de hac re postea.
units.tr: 8. The proposition This is my body has the marks and true and essential characteristics of a figurative proposition; therefore it is figurative. Augustine saw the truth of both points in On Christian Doctrine, book 3, chapter 16: If the language is directive, forbidding a crime or vice, or commanding usefulness or kindness, it is not figurative; but if it seems to command a crime or vice, or to forbid usefulness or kindness, it is figurative. Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you: since this seems to command a crime or vice, it is a figure, enjoining that we share in the Lord's passion and store up sweetly and usefully in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us. What could be said more clearly in our cause than this by Augustine? Shall we deny that the proposition, taken literally, here commands a crime or vice? We have both Augustine and experience against us. But more on this matter later.

units.la: 9. Hæc verba aut sunt intelligenda per usitatam Metonymiam Sacramentalem, aut panis mutabitur in corpus Christi, per Transsubstantiationem, aut in, cum & sub pane erit corpus Christi per consubstantiationem. At non per consubstantiationem, quod ipse Bellarminus concedit, (agnoscit enim Christi verba nonnisi geminum admittere sensum, vel, ut corpus Christi realiter sit præsens, quod per Transsubstantiationem sieri vult; vel, ut panis sit corporis Christi signum: Lutheranorum sententiam ipse rejecit Cardinalis) nec per Transsubstantiationem. E. per Metonymiam Sacramentalem.
units.tr: 9. These words must be understood either by the customary sacramental metonymy, or the bread will be changed into the body of Christ by transubstantiation, or the body of Christ will be in, with and under the bread by consubstantiation. But not by consubstantiation, which Bellarmine himself concedes (for he admits that the words of Christ allow only a twofold sense: either that the body of Christ is really present, which he wants to happen by transubstantiation, or that the bread is a sign of the body of Christ; the cardinal himself rejected the view of the Lutherans). Nor by transubstantiation. Therefore by sacramental metonymy.

units.la: SECTIO VII.
units.tr: SECTION VII.

units.la: Transsubstantiationi nec Scriptura patrocinatur, nec Ratio, nec Antiquitas.
units.tr: Transubstantiation is supported neither by Scripture, nor by reason, nor by antiquity.

units.la: 1. Dignum est ultimum superioris sectionis argumentum, quod paulò pressius à nobis urgeatur. Id ut fiat negativè primò, palàm faciemus,
units.tr: 1. The last argument of the previous section deserves to be pressed somewhat more closely. To do this, first negatively, we will show plainly

units.la: Transsubstantiationem nec verborum Institutionis, nec ullius omnino Scripturæ habere assensum; sanæ & sobriæ (imò illuminatæ, quæ res plane ut sunt in natura sua, & ex ordine authoris Naturæ consideratur) Rationis, & Antiquitatis negatum consensum paucis attingemus; cum positive contra Transsubstantiationis tam novitatem, quàm absurditatem militare Scripturam, Fidei analogiam; quam Transsubstantiatio totam erit; Antiquitatem, & sobriam rationem, etiam indicabimus.
units.tr: that transubstantiation has the assent neither of the words of institution nor of any Scripture at all, nor of sound and sober reason (indeed of enlightened reason, which considers things plainly as they are in their own nature and in the order established by the author of Nature), nor of antiquity. We will briefly touch on this denied consent. Then, positively, we will also show that Scripture and the analogy of faith stand against transubstantiation, against its novelty as much as its absurdity, and that the whole of transubstantiation is entirely contrary to them. We will also point out antiquity and sober reason.

units.la: II. A negatione assensus facturi initium, ita procedimus. Transsubstantiatio neque fundamentum habet in Scriptura, neque in Antiquitate, neque sana ratione E. Non in Scriptura. Confidenter enim iterum pronuntiamus, nusquam in sacra Scriptura vel vocem Transsubstantiationis occurrere, vel phrasin. Esse corpus, multò minus, esse panem, idem valere, quod mutari, converti in corpus; vel rem, phrasi expressam, ita panem in Christi corpus mutari, ut, destructo Subjecto, sola supersint Accidentia.
units.tr: II. Beginning with the denial of assent, we proceed thus. Transubstantiation has no foundation in Scripture, nor in antiquity, nor in sound reason. Therefore, first, not in Scripture. For we confidently declare again that nowhere in Holy Scripture does either the word transubstantiation or the phrase occur. That to be is the body, much less that to be is bread, means the same as to be changed or converted into the body; or that a thing expressed by the phrase, namely that bread is changed into the body of Christ so that, the subject being destroyed, only the accidents remain.

units.la: Ostendatur vel illius, vel istius, vel hujus apex, volaveltigium! Satis, ut puto, hoc stringit argumentum, ab enumeratione partium absolutum. De voce, quæ vel sola barbarie novitatem prodit, nolumus esse soliciti; repetimus, de re ipsa, nullo Scripturæ loco probari posse, vel in thesi, Esse æquipollere verbo Transsubstantiari, vel in hypothesi, panem Transsubstantiari in corpus Christi. Dogma vero tam absurdum, prodigiosum & portentosum extra & contra Scripturam obtrudere, nimiae est temeritatis, dicam an audaciae?
units.tr: Let anyone show the summit or even the trace of that or this or the other! This argument, I think, is sufficiently settled, complete in its enumeration of parts. We do not wish to be anxious about the word, which by itself betrays its novelty through its barbarism. We repeat that about the thing itself no passage of Scripture can be shown to prove, either in theory, that is is equivalent to the verb to be transubstantiated, or in the case at hand, that bread is transubstantiated into the body of Christ. But to thrust forward a dogma so absurd, monstrous and portentous, outside of and against Scripture, is excessive rashness; shall I say audacity?

units.la: III. Quod verba Institutionis; Hoc est corpus meum, identidem occinunt, id vero ad rem prorsus nihil facit. Nam i. haec verba sunt, τὸ κρινόμενον. Quaeritur, utrum haec Transsubstantiationis propria sit fides? Et utrum nihil prorsus a tot difficultatibus, absurditatibus, contentionibus, ambiguitatibus, scrupulis, quibus doctrina Transsubstantiationis est intricata, nos liberet; aliumque, faciliorem & commodiorem, qui cum Scriptura pariter & Natura conciliari queat, fundat sensum? An praestet unius propositionis nodum solvere, quam sexcentos nectere.
units.tr: III. As to the words of institution, This is my body, which they keep repeating again and again, this has nothing at all to do with the matter. For, first, these words are the very point in question [τὸ κρινόμενον]. The question is whether this is the proper faith of transubstantiation. And whether nothing frees us from the many difficulties, absurdities, disputes, ambiguities and scruples with which the doctrine of transubstantiation is entangled, and whether it does not establish another sense, easier and more convenient, which can be reconciled equally with Scripture and with nature. Or is it better to untie the knot of one proposition than to tie six hundred?

units.la: Et mirari quidem satis non possumus, malle adversarios omnia prorsus pessundari, in ipsa Theologiae & Naturae principia impingi, quam sobriam hoc loco, Est, pro significat admittere, Metonymiam; qua tamen usitatius nihil est vel in Scriptura, vel in Antiquitate, vel in profanis authoribus. Unam negant Metonymiam, & infinitas fingunt exceptiones, limitationes, &c. Num quid luculentius (Scripturae enim exempla jam supra a nobis sunt allata) verbis Justini Martyris: Ἡν γὰρ τὸ πάσχα ὁ Χριστὸς, ὁ τυ-θεὶς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν. Erat enim Pascha (agnus Paschalis) Christus, qui postea immolatus est, Dial. cum Tryph. Num aliter Christus Pascha vocatur, quàm per significationem? Plane ut Augustinus: Aries Christus erat i.e. significabat, Germanus, Episcopus Constantino politanus; ἐν τῇ νομικῇ τεταγμένῃ ἦν τὸ μάννα, ὅ ἐστι Χριστός, in Legali mensa erat manna, quod est Christus. Idem loquendi genus profanis etiam placuit authoribus. Ælian. Hist. variar. lib. 10. cap. 10. Cùm ars pictoria primùm inciperet, adeò ruditer depinxerunt animantia, ut pictores adscriberent: τοῦτο (ἐστὶ) βοῦς, ἐκεῖνο (ἐστὶ) ἵππος, τοῦτο (ἐστὶ) δένδρον. Hoc bos est, illud equus, illud arbor, i.e. signum, figura, typus bovis, equi &c. 2. Diximus, & intrepidè repetimus (quod satis expendere velemus Adversarios) toto coelo differre, Esse corpus, & mutari in corpus: neque enim Grammaticè, nec Physicè, nec Theologicè æquipollent. Illud Christus dixit, hoc non. Imò, verbum Est, ubi copulandi (quod hic fit) vim habet, mutandi vel permutandi significatum nunquam alciscit. 3. Magnæ igitur fuerit præsumptionis, illud pro concesso sumere, quod nullo prorsus exemplo poterit probari. 4. Verba Institutionis vel seorsim, vel conjunctim sumta Transsubstantiationi patrocinantur. At nec seorsim, nec conjunctim sumta verba, eam juvant. E. Non seorsim. Neque enim particula Hoc, vim illam Transsubstantiandi, adeóque creandi habet, tum quia ipsi nescint Pontifici, quid sit illud aut significet (individuum vagum plerique hic intelligunt) tum quia revera ipsum Panem;
units.tr: Indeed we cannot sufficiently wonder that our opponents prefer to have everything utterly overthrown and driven against the very principles of theology and nature, rather than admit here the sober trope, namely that is means signifies. Yet nothing is more common than this, whether in Scripture, in antiquity, or in profane authors. They deny the one metonymy, and invent endless exceptions, limitations and so on. Could anything be clearer than the words of Justin Martyr (for examples of Scripture have already been cited by us above): "For Christ was the Passover, who was slain for us" [Ἡν γὰρ τὸ πάσχα ὁ Χριστὸς, ὁ τυθεὶς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν]. "For the Passover (the paschal lamb) was Christ, who was afterwards sacrificed," Dial. cum Tryph. Is Christ called the Passover in any other way than by signification? Just as Augustine says: "The ram was Christ," that is, signified Christ. Germanus, Bishop of Constantinople: "In the legal table there was manna, which is Christ" [ἐν τῇ νομικῇ τεταγμένῃ ἦν τὸ μάννα, ὅ ἐστι Χριστός]. The same way of speaking has also pleased profane authors. Aelian, Varia Historia, book 10, chapter 10: When the art of painting first began, they painted animals so crudely that the painters wrote beneath them: "This is (is) an ox, that is (is) a horse, this is (is) a tree" [τοῦτο (ἐστὶ) βοῦς, ἐκεῖνο (ἐστὶ) ἵππος, τοῦτο (ἐστὶ) δένδρον]. That is, "this is an ox, that a horse, that a tree," that is, the sign, figure or type of an ox, a horse, etc. 2. We have said, and boldly repeat (which we would have our opponents weigh well), that to be the body and to be changed into the body differ by the whole heavens. For they are not equivalent grammatically, physically or theologically. Christ said the one, not the other. Indeed, the verb is, where it has the force of joining (as it does here), never takes on the meaning of changing or exchanging. 3. It would therefore be great presumption to take for granted what can be proved by no example at all. 4. The words of institution, whether taken separately or together, support transubstantiation. But the words, whether taken separately or together, do not help it. Therefore, first, not separately. For the particle this does not have that power of transubstantiating, and so of creating, both because the Papists themselves do not know what it is or what it signifies (most of them understand here a vague individual), and because it really denotes the bread itself

units.la: Transcription of the Greek is approximate; see notes. Panem ; vel, ut Pontificii nonnulli loquuntur, speciem panis; denotat, quem Christus modò antea accepit, fregit, dedit. Panis ergo est; panis manet, prout panem Apostolus etiam post consecrationem vocat; panem Patres appellant.
units.tr: bread, or, as some Papists speak, the appearance of bread, which Christ had just taken, broken and given. Therefore it is bread; it remains bread, just as the Apostle also calls it bread after the consecration, and the Fathers call it bread.

units.la: II. Absurdissimum est vulgi χρηστοφύγετον: Panem dici, non quod sit, sed quia videatur. Belluli homines' Credi sibi voluntate corpus, cujus nullum videtur vestigium, esse realiter praesens; panem, qui realiter praesens est, tantum videri. Nonne hoc est aliud Evangelium annunciare? Aut, unum oStendant locum, in quo ita Apostolus explicet mentem. Panis est, (inquit Augustinus apud Bedam 1. Cor. 10.) quod videtur in altari, quod etiam oculi renuntiant. Quod autem fidem postulat, panis est corpus Christi, & calix sanguis. Non dicit; quod in altari est, panem videri; sed quod videtur, id est, conspicitur, panem esse. Profecto, si haec licentia Scripturam explicandi fuerit admissa, praecipua religionis Christianae dogmata periclitabuntur. Ostende Marcioni carnem & ossa Christi, ut veritatem corporis ejus probes: Negabit tuis verbis sequelam. Apparere carnem, apparere ossa, vera eadem non esse. Objice Muhammedano ipsius Pilati de Christo verba: Ecce homo! Negabit Christum esse; videri tantum, sensuum judicium fallere. Non Christum; sed Judam proditorem loco ejus cruci esse affixum. Ita ad-
units.tr: II. It is a most absurd notion of the common people, a most mischievous one: that it is called bread not because it is, but because it appears to be. Foolish men! They believe by their will that the body, of which no trace is seen, is really present, while the bread, which is really present, only appears. Is this not to proclaim another gospel? Or let them show one place in which the Apostle explains his meaning in this way. Bread is (says Augustine, cited by Bede on 1 Cor. 10) what is seen on the altar, which the eyes also report. But what requires faith is that the bread is the body of Christ, and the cup the blood. He does not say that what is on the altar appears to be bread, but that what is seen, that is, what is looked upon, is bread. Surely, if this licence of explaining Scripture is admitted, the principal dogmas of the Christian religion will be imperilled. Show Marcion the flesh and bones of Christ, to prove the reality of his body: he will deny your inference. That flesh appears, that bones appear, does not mean they are real. Object to a Muslim the words of Pilate about Christ: "Behold the man!" He will deny that this is Christ; it only seemed so, the judgment of the senses deceives. It was not Christ but Judas the traitor who was fixed to the cross in his place. Thus we supply arms to our opponents, where, without any scratch [ἀτερ χαράξης], that is without Scripture, we indulge in our own smooth words.

units.la: E versariis arma subministramus, ubi ἀτερ χαράξης absq; Scriptura, nostris indulgemus suaviloquiis.
units.tr: From our opponents we supply ourselves with weapons, where, without a stake [ἀτερ χαράξης] and without Scripture, we indulge our own smooth words.

units.la: III. In particula Est, proram & puppim disputationis suæ constituunt Adversarii: Sed frustra a. Attendendum enim, ante omnia, ad Linguam, qua Christus usus est, Syriacam, quæ, ut significandi verbis non delectatur, itain vulgari usu verbum substantivum Est raro admittit: Ejus vero loco, more Hebræorum, Demonstrativum הוא Hu, vel הנה Honau, adhibet. Unde & antiquissima Translatio Syriaca, quam Marco Evangelistæ nonnulli, alii Ecclesiæ primitivæ Doctoribus, Apostolorum discipulis, tribuunt, loco verborum: Hoc est corpus meum, usitato Syriasmo, ponit; הנה Honau ipsum, Matth. 26. 26. Marc. 14. 24. Luc. 22. 19. (ubi verbum Est nuspiam apparet) corpus meum. Quemadmodum vero Exod. 12. 27. verba Hebræa Pasach hu, hoc ipsum Pascha, (ubi vocula Est in fontibus etiam desideratur) LXX. reddiderunt: Est hoc Pascha; Ita Syriasmum, Græca Lingua donaturi Evangelistæ, verbum Est; etiam Syris minus usitatum, Græciæ autem solenne; libere substituerunt: utrobique tamen significandi notione legentis judicio relicta. Vt peritis loquor, inquit Apostolus, judicate vos, quod ajo, 1. Cor. 10. 15. Cum judicio igitur ad istorum locorum examen accedendum est: Phrasium, rituum, ceremoniarum, diligens collatio; quæ in hujusmodi disputatio tionibus plus habet præsidii, quàm subtilissimarum distinctionum plaustra; instituenda. Cuius enim aliunde genuinum verborum sensum tuatius exspectemus, quàm ex ea, qua propositae illa sunt, Lingua? Obiter hæc moneo, ut videant Adversarii, quàm incertum illud, quod in toties nobis inculcata vocula Est quærunt, sit subsidium: cùm, vernaculâ suâ linguâ Christum formaliter eam adhibuisse, nondum satis sit probatum. b. Argumentum procedit à particulari. Christus in hac propositione utitur verbo substantivo, Est; E. proprie illa sumenda. Quis hujus propositionis universalitatem sustineat? Verba Christi sunt: Ego sum vitis illa vera, (anne & propria? imò Metaphorica) & Pater meus est vinitor, Johannis 14. 6. Ego sum Ostium, Joh. 10. 9. Cujus vel mentem subeat, hæc morosius secundum literam esse urgenda? At sunt hæc ἀναγραφισμοί, quia non agunt de Sacramentis; alia ratio est Sacramentorum & Testamentorum, quæ proprias amant loquutiones. Est omnino Sacramentorum ratio alia, hæc nempe, ut, cùm alibi impropriæ ejusmodi loquutiones obseruentur rarius, utrisque, & Sacramentis & Testamentis, illæ penè sint propriæ, & domesticæ. Unde & κατ' ἐξοχὴν Sacramentales appellantur. Ostendimus nuper, nullum esse Sacramentum, quod hujus loquendi formulæ non præbeat exemplum. Eadem ratio est Testamentorum. Unde hoc ipsum jam supra invertimus arargumentum; ostendere etiamnum parati iumus, Linguæ sanctæ; quæ in improprietate termonis elegantiam quærit; factum idiotisimo, ut nullæ facile dari possint populi Israelitici Testamentorum formulæ, quæ hoc testellatum dicendi genus non ament. Hoc qui nesciunt, morem genii & ingenii Hebraici, omniumque feré Orientalium ignorant. Rogati igitur exempla impropriæ loquutionis in Testamentis & Sacramentis; vicissim intrepidè rogamus, vel unicam sive Testamenti, sive Sacramenti sedem, ubi ejusmodi Tropi ordinarium locum non habeant. c. Si particula Hoc, quod vult Vir doctissimus, ipsam notat Eucharistiam, tum vocula Est, non erit operativa, aut Transsubstantiativa, quod tamen volunt Pontificii; sed factæ jam tantum mutationis ostensiva, aut declarativa. Hoc non dabunt Pontificii. Ita enim aliud aliquod verbum operatorium & Transsubstantiativum verba, Hoc est corpus meum, præcedere fuerit necesse, cujus virtute panis esse desierit, & corpus Christi esse cœperit, quod tamen nec agnoscent illi, nec demonstrabunt.
units.tr: III. Our opponents set up the prow and stern of their dispute on the particle is, but in vain. For attention must be paid, above all, to the language Christ used, Syriac, which, since it does not delight in words for signifying, also rarely admits the substantive verb is in common usage. In its place, after the manner of the Hebrews, it uses the demonstrative הוא Hu, or הנה Honau. Hence the very ancient Syriac Translation, which some attribute to the Evangelist Mark, others to the teachers of the early Church and disciples of the Apostles, in place of the words This is my body, uses the common Syriacism הנה Honau ipsum, Matt. 26. 26; Mark 14. 24; Luke 22. 19 (where the verb is nowhere appears), my body. And just as in Exod. 12. 27 the Hebrew words Pasach hu [פסח הוא], this itself the Passover (where the little word is is also lacking in the sources), the Seventy rendered as It is this Passover, so the Evangelists, about to give the Syriacism to the Greek language, freely substituted the verb is, less usual for the Syrians but customary for the Greeks; in both places, however, the sense of signifying was left to the judgment of the reader. I speak as to wise men, says the Apostle, judge for yourselves what I say, 1 Cor. 10. 15. Therefore one must approach the examination of these passages with judgment: a careful comparison of phrases, rites and ceremonies must be undertaken, which in disputes of this kind has more help than carts full of the subtlest distinctions. For from what other source should we more surely expect the genuine sense of the words than from the language in which they were spoken? I note this in passing, so that our opponents may see how uncertain is the help they seek in the little word is, which they keep pressing on us, since it has not yet been sufficiently proved that Christ used it formally in his own vernacular. b. The argument proceeds from the particular to the general. Christ uses the substantive verb is in this proposition; therefore it must be taken properly. Who could uphold the universal application of this proposition? Christ's words are: "I am the true vine" (is that proper too? No, it is metaphorical), "and my Father is the vinedresser," John 15. 1; "I am the door," John 10. 9. Who would think these must be pressed literally? But these, it will be said, are tropes because they do not treat of the sacraments; the sacraments and testaments have another reason, since they love proper expressions. Indeed the reason for the sacraments is different, namely that, while such improper expressions are rarely observed elsewhere, in both sacraments and testaments they are almost proper and familiar. Hence they are called sacramental par excellence. We have shown recently that there is no sacrament which does not supply an example of this form of speech. The same reasoning applies to the testaments. Hence we have already turned this very argument back above; we are prepared to show again that the Holy Tongue, which seeks elegance in the impropriety of expression, has made it so that no formulas of the testaments of the Israelite people can easily be found which do not love this kind of speech, adorned with figures. Those who do not know this are ignorant of the manner and character of the Hebrew mind and of nearly all Orientals. Therefore, having been asked for examples of improper speech in the Testaments and Sacraments, we in turn boldly ask for a single seat in Testament or Sacrament where such tropes do not have their ordinary place. c. If the particle this, as the most learned man maintains, denotes the Eucharist itself, then the word is will not be operative or transubstantiating, as the Papists nonetheless want, but only indicative or declarative of a change already made. The Papists will not grant this. For then some other operative and transubstantiating verb would have to precede the words This is my body, by whose power the bread would have ceased to be and the body of Christ begun to be. Yet neither they admit this, nor will they demonstrate it.

units.la: IV. Vox Corporis non potest esse operativa per se, tum quod opus potiùs, ut ita loquar, sit operatum, juxta Pontificios, quàm operans; tum etiam, quòd non panis tantùm, sed & Ecclesia, Christi corpus vocatur, Ephes. 1. 23. Coloss. 1. 18. non utique per Transsubstantiationem, sed per analogiam & similitudem; tum denique, quia aliud corpus Christus intellexit, aliud singunt Sacerdotes. Illius fragile erat, mortale, πρω- τὸν, ut plenius postea audiemus; hoc gloriosum, &, ut Gabriel Biel Lect.4. vocat, impassibile. Etsi, inquit, Coeli Regina, & Mundi Domina (ita B. Virginem appellat) in gratia plenitudine reliquas creaturas supergrediatur universas; Hierarchis tamen cedit Ecclesia, in commissi mysterii executione. Illa nempe prolatis octo verbulis: Ecce ancilla Domini, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum; semel concepit Dei filium, & Mundi Redemptorem. Isti a Domino consecrati, quinque verbis contextam consecrationis formam, cum debita intentione proferentes, eundem Dei Virginisque Filium advocant quotidie corporaliter in sacrificium, in criminum purgationem. Illa, perpetua virginitate servata, summum coeli Principem de se incarnatum, mortalem atq; passibilem mundo edidit Salvatorem. Isti, consecratione divina eundem coeli terraeq; Principem, in Sacramento veritissime contentum, impassibilem, gloriosumque contrectant, victorem mortis & bathri destructorem.
units.tr: IV. The word Body cannot be operative in itself, first because, according to the Papists, it is the thing operated on rather than the thing that operates, so to speak. Second, the Church as well as the bread is called the body of Christ (Ephes. 1. 23. Coloss. 1. 18.), and not by transubstantiation but by analogy and likeness. Third, Christ's body is one thing and the priests imagine another. His was frail and mortal, [πρῶτον] as we shall hear more fully later; this one is glorious and, as Gabriel Biel calls it in Lect. 4, impassible. Although, he says, the Queen of Heaven and Lady of the World (this is how he styles the Blessed Virgin) surpasses all other creatures in the fullness of grace, the Church yields to the hierarchs in the execution of the mystery committed to them. She, of course, after speaking eight words, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to your word," conceived once the Son of God and Redeemer of the world. The priests, consecrated by the Lord, pronounce the form of consecration, woven from five words, with due intention, and summon daily, bodily, that same Son of God and the Virgin to be a sacrifice and an atonement for sins. She, keeping her perpetual virginity, brought forth from herself the highest Prince of heaven, made flesh, and gave the world a mortal and passible Saviour. They, by divine consecration, handle that same Prince of heaven and earth, most truly contained in the Sacrament, impassible and glorious, the conqueror of death and destroyer of the grave.

units.la: V. Conjunctim consecrationis verba Transsubstantiationi non velificantur. 1. Tota actione Christus instituit Sacramentum. E. nullus hic Transsubstantiationi locus. Antecedens sua luce clarer. Consequentia robur dependet a. ab inductione omnium Sacramentorum. In nullo Sacramento vel V. vel N Testamenti datur, aut dari potest Transsubstantiatio, neque in Circumcisione, neque agno Paschali, nec Baptismo; E. neque in Cœna Domini. De Circumcisione dicitur, quòd sit fœdus in carne Israëlitarum, Gen. 17 : de agno, quòd sit transitus. Neutrum tamen per hanc formulam transsubstantiatur. Baptismus vocatur lavacrum regenerationis, neque in sanguinem Christi, quo solo à peccatis abluimur, transsubstantiatur. b. A natura Sacramentorum, de qua Augustinus in Johannem: Accedit verbum ad elementum, & fit Sacramentum. Ponit, non tollit elementum Augustinus in Sacramento, quod tamen per Transsubstantiationem fieri necesse est. 2. Si hac consecratione Sacramentali fiet Transsubstantiatio, incurret illa in sensus. At non incurrit in sensus. Ratio consequentia, quia nullius Transsubstantiationis Adversarii dabunt exemplum, quod ab hac regula excipiatur. Cum aqua mutata esset in vinum, Joh. 2. gustu illam mutationem architriclinus probavit, v. 9. Pulvis conversus fuit in pediculos per totam terram Ægyptiorum, Exod. 8. vers. 16. & extitit pediculorum copia in hominibus & jumentis, vers. 7. Voluit Deus, ut converterentur aquæ in sanguinem, cap. 7. vers. 22. & conversæ sunt omnes aquæ, quæ erant in uno quoque rivo in sanguinem, &c. Hæc ratio Transsubstantiationis est, quam Spiritus sanctus propterea con-stanstanter observare voluit, ut Divinæ potentiæ Majestas, quæ in illa maxime lucet, omnibus tam fidelibus, quàm infidelibus redderetur manifestior. 2. Si verba Institutionis conjunctim sumta panem commutant in Corpus, mutatio illa aut erit naturalis, aut magica, aut miraculosa. Si Naturalis, dent rationem, cur soli Sacerdotes, & non quilibet alii hoc Transsubstantiandi habeant beneficium. Magicam dicent? Blasphemiæ reatum non declinabunt; quamvis valde dura, & tanto mysterio indigna sint verba Gabriel.Biel, Can.Miss.Lect.4.p.8. Breviter annotandum, quid in Missa celebratione Sacerdos sua virtute efficiat; circa quod advertendum, quod aliquid ab alio effici, vel fieri, tripliciter potest accipi. Nam aliquid dicitur ab alio fieri vel naturali potestate, vel meritoria operatione, vel assistente Virtute &c. Tertio modo (quo postea probat Transsubstantiatio nem fieri) aliquid dicitur ab aliquo fieri aliqua Virtute occulta, non insistente ei, a quo talefieri dicitur, sed assistente, secundum quem modum malefici & incantatores quosdam effectus producere dicuntur, & extrahere lac vaccarum de sedibus, seu manubriis securium, quod fit non virtute naturali maleficorum, neque ex eorum merito, sed Virtute occulta, sive bona sive mala assistente. Sed miraculosam relinquamus. Atque sic Transsubstantiatio, quæ fit ordinarie, miraculum erit. Miraculum autem esse non poteft. 1. Miraculum in spectatoribus vel evidentem (propter manifestam rei mutationem, quâ, ex gratia extraordinariæ providentiæ Divinæ gubernatione illa, fiat, quod natura & ordinario cursu esse non poterat) excitat admirationem, vel notorium, & in sensus incurrens affert commodum. At neutrum præstant symbola Sacramentalia, opinione Transsubstantiata. E. Antecedens ex Augustino mutuabimus. 'Miraculum, inquit, de utilit. credend. ad Honorat. c. 16. voco, quicquid arduum, aut insolitum, supra spem, vel facultatem mirantis apparet. In quo genere nihil est populis aptius, & omnino stultis hominibus, quàm id, quod sensibus admovetur. Sed rursus hæc in duo dividuntur. Quædam enim sunt, quæ solam faciunt admirationem, quædam verò magnam etiam gratiam benevolentiámque conciliant. Nam si quis volantem hominem cernat, cùm ea res nihil spectatori afferat commodi; præter ipsum spectaculum; miratur tantummodo. Si quis autem gravi & desperato morbo affectus, mox, ut jussum fuerit, convalescat, admiratione sanitatis suæ, sanantis etiam charitate superabit. Talia facta sunt illo tempore, quo Deus in vero homine, quantum sat erat, hominibus apparebat. Sanati languidi, mundati leprosi, incessus claudis, cæcis visus, surdis auditus est redditus. Homines illius temporis aquam in vinum conversam, saturata quinque millia quinque panibus, transita pedibus maria, mortuos resurgentes viderunt: Ita quædam corpori manifestiori beneficio, quædam vero menti occultiore signo, & omnia hominibus majestatis testimonio consulebant, sic in se tunc animas errantes mortalium divina commovebat auctoritas. Cur, inquis, ista modò non fiunt? Quia non moverent, nisi mira essent? At, si solita essent, mira non essent. Nam diei & noctis vices, & constantissimum ordinem rerum cælestium, annorum quadrifariam conversionem, decedentes redeunt efq; frondes arboribus, infinitam vim seminum, pulchritudinem lucis, colorum, sonorum, odorum, saporumq; varietates da, qui primum videat atq; sentiat, cum quo tamen loqui possimus, hebescit obruiturq; miraculis: Nos vero hæc omnia mon cognoscendi facilitate, (quid enim causis illis obscurius?) sed certè sentiendi assiduitate contemnimus. 2. Miraculorum ergò donum ordinarium sublatum est. Chrysost. in Psalm. 142. Quando notitia Dei nondum erat diffusa, miracula fiebant, nunc ea docendi forma amplius non est opus. Et in Joh. homil. 24. Cur non hodieque fiunt miracula? Si tu fidelis es, ut par est te esse, & Christum amas, ut amare debes, miraculis non indiges, nam hæc infidelibus dantur. Eucherius Lugdunensis, in verba Evangelii Matth. 18.v.1. Nobis signa & miracula nunc necessaria non sunt, quibus ea, quæ facta sunt, solummodo legere & audire sufficit. Credimus enim Evangelio, credimus & Scripturis ista narrantibus. 3. Miraculosam corcorporisChristi praesentiam ab ordinaria Transsubstantiatione Adversarii distinguunt; ceu pater ex illis Scriptoribus, qui nobis modo puerulos incarnatos, modo languinem madentem, labia & manus squalentia &c. modo ad Pastorum consecrationem offas carnis ostendunt; adeóq; veritatem Transsubstantiationis probaturi, damnatas illas, & impie Veteribus Christianis impactas ἀνθρωπείων σαρκῶν βοῤῥῆς, carnium humanarum comestur as revocant. Carnem & languinem humanum; quem & fundere, & edere Deus adeo severe in V.T. prohibuerat; in dulcissimo Servatore licitum imo religiosum censeamus? Tetra absurditatum lerna & sententia, a quibus mens pia, & Christianismi sancta mysteria plane abhorrent! Quanquam ne sic quidem quicquam habeant certi, & ejusmodi miracula Idololatriae aeque apertae, ac devotionis praetextui possint inservire. Unde Auct. Tract. Corp. Christi: Quaero, An si appareat caro, vel puer, debeat adorari, ut corpus Christi? Dic, quod non simpliciter, sed sub conditione poterit, quod saepe Angelus Sathanas se transfert in lucis Angelum, & per talem modum illudit hominibus. Neque vero hic metus vanus est, aut inanis. Quid superiori seculo in inclyta Berna, occasione Tragoediae Dominicanorum contigerit, aetatis illius Scriptores dubitare nos non sinunt. Ut apparitionem Barbarae mancipio suo Monachi probarent, literas eidem oftendunt, fido Servatoris cruore, ut author Pontificius loquitur, obsignatas. Sed & Iohannes, Monachus Vitoduranus in Annalibus suis p. m. 58. refert, suo tempore excitatam contra Iudaeos procellam, propter (ipsa recito authoris verba) quendam Sacerdotem inopia pressum, qui hostiam sanguine aspersit, & a se projectam juxta Iudaeos, eos suspectos reddidit, & graviter infamavit; qua (hostia) cum reverentia maxima ad Ecclesiam praedicti malefici Presbyteri delata & deducta esset, & ibi collocata, a populo totius terra circumposita frequentabatur, Sacrificiisque oblationibus devotissime venerabatur, quos Presbyter recipiens multis diebus notabiliter locupletatus est. Qui postquam populum Christianum diu delusisset, sub specie simplicis panis, praetendentis verum corpus Christi & consecratum, tandem nutu Dei proditus fuit, eo mediante, cujus adminiculo id flagitium finxit & perpetravit, in sua anima, & innumerabilium animarum perditionem.
units.tr: V. The words of consecration taken together do not favour transubstantiation. 1. Christ instituted the Sacrament by the whole action. Therefore there is no place here for transubstantiation. The antecedent is clear in its own light. The strength of the consequence depends on induction from all the Sacraments. In no Sacrament of the Old or New Testament is transubstantiation given or can it be given: not in Circumcision, not in the Passover lamb, not in Baptism; therefore not in the Lord's Supper either. Of Circumcision it is said that it is a covenant in the flesh of the Israelites (Gen. 17); of the lamb, that it is a passover. Yet neither is transubstantiated by this formula. Baptism is called the washing of regeneration, and it is not transubstantiated into the blood of Christ, by which alone we are washed from sins. b. From the nature of the Sacraments, of which Augustine says on John: The word comes to the element, and it becomes a Sacrament. Augustine says that the element is kept, not taken away, in the Sacrament, whereas by transubstantiation it would necessarily cease to be. 2. If transubstantiation were brought about by this sacramental consecration, it would fall under the senses. But it does not fall under the senses. The reason for this consequence is that the opponents of transubstantiation will give no example of any transubstantiation excepted from this rule. When water was changed into wine (John 2.), the master of the feast tested that change by taste (v. 9). Dust was turned into lice throughout all the land of Egypt (Exod. 8. v. 16), and there was an abundance of lice on men and beasts (v. 17). God willed that the waters be turned into blood (ch. 7. v. 22), and all the waters that were in every river were turned into blood, etc. This is the manner of transubstantiation, which the Holy Spirit therefore wished to observe constantly, so that the majesty of divine power, which shines most brightly in it, might be made more manifest to all, faithful and unfaithful alike. 2. If the words of institution taken together change the bread into the body, that change will be either natural, or magical, or miraculous. If natural, let them give a reason why only priests, and not any others, have this benefit of transubstantiating. Will they call it magical? They will not escape the guilt of blasphemy, although the words of Gabriel Biel (Can. Miss. Lect. 4, p. 8) are very harsh and unworthy of so great a mystery. It should be briefly noted what the priest effects by his own power in the celebration of the Mass; in regard to which it must be observed that something can be said to be effected or made by another in three ways. For something is said to be made by another either by natural power, or by meritorious action, or by an assisting power, etc. In the third way (by which he afterwards proves that transubstantiation is made) something is said to be made by someone through some hidden power, not residing in him by whom it is said to be so made, but assisting him; in this manner, sorcerers and enchanters are said to produce certain effects, and to draw milk from cows out of the seats or handles of axes, which is done not by the natural power of sorcerers, nor by their merit, but by a hidden power, whether good or evil, that assists. But let us leave the miraculous aside. And so transubstantiation, which happens in the ordinary way, would be a miracle. But a miracle it cannot be. 1. A miracle either excites admiration in spectators, as something evident (on account of the manifest change of the thing, which by the grace of God's extraordinary providential governance comes about in a way that could not occur by nature or in the ordinary course), or, being well known and falling under the senses, brings some benefit. But the sacramental symbols, supposing them transubstantiated, do neither. Therefore the antecedent we shall borrow from Augustine. 'I call a miracle,' he says (On the Profit of Believing, to Honoratus, ch. 16), 'whatever appears arduous or unusual, beyond the hope or ability of the one who wonders. In this category nothing is more suited to peoples, and altogether to foolish men, than what is presented to the senses. But again these are divided into two. For some things merely produce admiration, while others also win great favour and goodwill. For if someone sees a man flying, since that thing brings the spectator no benefit beyond the spectacle itself, he only wonders. But if someone afflicted with a grave and desperate illness recovers at once when commanded, he will be overcome by admiration at his health and by love for the one who heals him. Such deeds were done at that time when God appeared to men in a true man, as far as was enough. The sick were healed, the lepers cleansed, the lame made to walk, the blind given sight, the deaf given hearing. The people of that time saw water turned into wine, five thousand fed with five loaves, the sea crossed on foot, the dead rising. Thus some things served the body by a more manifest benefit, and others the mind by a more hidden sign, and all bore witness to majesty for men; so the divine authority then moved the wandering souls of mortals.' Why, you ask, are these things not done now? Because they would not move us unless they were wonderful? But if they were customary, they would not be wonderful. For the alternation of day and night, and the most constant order of heavenly things, the fourfold turning of the years, the leaves that fall and return to the trees, the infinite power of seeds, the beauty of light, and the variety of colours, sounds, odours and flavours: give someone who sees and feels these for the first time, and with whom we can still talk, he is dazed and overwhelmed by miracles. But we despise all these things, not because they are easy to know (for what is more obscure than their causes?), but surely because we feel them every day.' 2. The ordinary gift of miracles has therefore ceased. Chrysostom on Psalm 142: When the knowledge of God was not yet spread abroad, miracles were done; now there is no more need for that form of teaching. And on John, homily 24: Why are miracles not done even today? If you are faithful, as you ought to be, and love Christ, as you ought to love him, you do not need miracles, for these are given to unbelievers. Eucherius of Lyons, on the words of the Gospel, Matt. 18. v. 1: We do not now need signs and miracles, for it is enough to read and hear only of those things that were done. For we believe the Gospel, and we believe the Scriptures that relate these things. 3. The opponents distinguish the miraculous presence of the body of Christ from the ordinary transubstantiation, as is clear from those writers who now show us little children made flesh, now blood dripping, lips and hands defiled, etc., now morsels of flesh at the consecration by ministers; and so, wishing to prove the truth of transubstantiation, they revive that condemned practice, impiously imposed on the early Christians, of eating human flesh [ἀνθρωπείων σαρκῶν βορά]. Shall we think that flesh and blood of man, which God so severely forbade in the Old Testament to be shed and eaten, is lawful and even religious in our most sweet Saviour? A foul hydra of absurdities and an opinion from which a pious mind and the holy mysteries of Christianity utterly shrink! Yet even so they have nothing certain, and such miracles could serve as idolatry no less plainly than as a pretext of devotion. Hence the author of the Tract on the Body of Christ: I ask, if flesh or a boy appears, ought it to be adored as the body of Christ? Answer: not simply, but on a condition it may be, since Satan often transforms himself into an angel of light and in this manner deceives men. Nor is this fear vain or empty. What happened in the famous city of Bern in the last century, on the occasion of the tragedy of the Dominicans, the writers of that age do not let us doubt. To prove the appearance of Barbara to their servant, the monks showed him letters, sealed, as the Papist author puts it, with the faithful blood of the Saviour. But also John, the monk of Vitoduranum, in his Annals, p. 58, reports that in his time a storm was stirred up against the Jews because of (I quote the author's own words) a certain priest, pressed by poverty, who sprinkled a host with blood and threw it away near the Jews, making them suspect and gravely defaming them; and this host, carried and brought with the greatest reverence to the church of the aforesaid evil presbyter and placed there, was frequented by the people from all around the land, and was most devoutly venerated with sacrifices and offerings; the presbyter, receiving them, was notably enriched for many days. But after he had long deceived the Christian people under the appearance of plain bread, pretending it was the true and consecrated body of Christ, at last by the will of God he was betrayed, through the very means by which he had devised and perpetrated that crime, to the destruction of his own soul and of countless souls.

units.la: Nam more Ieroboam gentem peccare fecit, dum superstitionis & Idololatriae causam scienter, motus avaritia, qua est Idolorum servitus, dedisset. Nam homines panem pro Eucharistia, quamvis ignoranter, adorabant, ipso procurante. Atque haec quidem ad fundamentum Transubstantiationis, quod ex Scriptura ostendere conantur Adversarii, in verbis Institutionis. Paulum, ut spero, nisi tortum, suum non fafacient, qui, ut supra monuimus, noster totus est. Rationis patrocinium Pontificii exspectare non audent. Quin potius usum ejus, in examine hujus mysterii, totum proscribunt; quam etiam ancoram, ut suo loco audiemus, Vir doctissimus, sed minus feliciter arripuit. Antiquitatis consensum postea nos urgebimus. Eum Ecclesiae Romanae ingenue satis abjudicat Scoti sententia, qua, teste Bellarmino lib. 3. de Eucharistia cap. 23. asseruit, Transsubstantiationem demum in Lateranensi Concilio a. Ch. 1215. inter fidei dogmata esse relatam; cui Gabriel Biel accedit, apud Suarez. Tom. 3. disput. 50. sf.
units.tr: For in the manner of Jeroboam he made the nation sin, when, knowingly and moved by greed (which is the slavery of idols), he gave the cause of superstition and idolatry. For men adored bread in place of the Eucharist, though they did so ignorantly, with him contriving it. Indeed, this is the foundation of Transubstantiation, which the Adversaries try to show from Scripture, in the words of institution. I hope they will not make Paul their own, unless twisted, since he is, as we noted above, wholly ours. The Papists do not dare to look for the support of reason. Rather, they reject its use altogether in examining this mystery. The very learned man also grasped at this as an anchor, as we shall hear in its place, but not very happily. Later we shall press the consensus of antiquity. The opinion of Scotus frankly strips the Roman Church of this consensus. According to Bellarmine (book 3 on the Eucharist, chapter 23), he asserted that Transubstantiation was only later placed among the dogmas of faith at the Lateran Council in the year 1215. Gabriel Biel agrees with him, according to Suárez, vol. 3, disp. 50, sect. 1 and following.

units.la: 1. Quin imo Thomas Mortonus (ex Widdringtono Pontificio) annotavit, cum nihil plane ad doctrinam Ecclesiasticam spectans in Concilio Lateranensi, ex communi Patrum assensu, decretum fuerit, posse, ut falsum, impugnari articulum de Transsubstantiatione; de Eucharist. Part. 2. Clas. 2. Cap. 2. ff. 2. Quod vocabula transmutationis in Cyrillo Hierosolymitano, mutationis, & commutationis in Ambrosio, immutationis in Chrysostomo, Vir doctissimus, Transsubstantiationi patrocinari existimat; fallitur. Neque enim substantialem, sed accidentalem, non φύσεως, sed χρήσεως καὶ χρέσεως, inferre mutationem, ipse etiam Suarez observavit; Tom. 3. disp. 50. S. 1. Habent veteres Graeci voces μεταβολῆς, μετατυπώσεως, μεταρρυθμίσεως, & μεταχοιχειώσεως; Latini mutationis, nis, transmutationis, &c. Sed nihil ad rem facere, non de substantiali, sed accidentali ea agere mutatione, non μεταβολὴν φύσεως, sed χρήσεως ; non ἐλαττώσεια κτήσας, sed συνθέσεως χαράτος, ut loquuntur Patres, & quidem eodem plane modo, quo in hominis regeneratione, pridem a nostris est observatum. Ipsum certe μεταςυνχεῶσις vocabulum (quod Transelementationem tamen proprie notat, non Transsubstantiatione) ab antiquis fuit usurpatum Patribus, ad eas mutationes exprimendas spirituales, quae nihil minus sonant, quam substantiarum & formarum inter se transmutationes. Gregorius Nyss in Epist. Canon. meminit τῶν ἐκ πακλιγγενέσεως μετασυνχειρισμένων, transelementatorum per regenerationem; an & μετασιωμένων Transsubstantiatorum? Negat Clemens Alexrandrinus, negat Irenaeus, negat tota Ecclesia. Et Clementis quidem verba sunt: Καὶ γὰρ διδαχὴ μεταρρυθμίζει τὸν ἄνθρωπον· μεταρρυθμισμὸς ἡ φύσιον ποιεῖ· καὶ διὰ γενήσεως ὑδέν, ἡ φύσεως ἀναλογίας ἐδαφιζομένη ὅτι δὲ ἡ χρόνῳ, καὶ μαθήσει μεταλυπωθήναι. Ἀμφὼ ἡ ὁ Κύριος παρέ-σχηκε τὸ μὲν κατὰ τὴν δημιουργίαν· τὸ δὲ κατὰ τὴν ἐκ τῆς διαθήκης ἀνάκλισιν τε καὶ ἀνανέωσιν. Doctrina enim hominem refingit, (iisdem etiam verbis Graeci Patres, ad exponendam μεταβολὴν Sacramentalem, utuntur) & transfigurat. Vbi autem sic transfiguravit, in alteram quasi naturam eum convertit. Non enim differt, natura formatus fuerit talis, an tempore, & doctrina
units.tr: 1. Indeed, Thomas Morton (following the Papist Widdrington) noted that, since nothing at all bearing on ecclesiastical doctrine was decreed at the Lateran Council, it was by the common agreement of the Fathers that the article on Transubstantiation may be attacked as false; On the Eucharist, Part 2, Class 2, Chapter 2, ff. 2. The most learned man thinks the words "transmutation" in Cyril of Jerusalem, "change" and "alteration" in Ambrose, and "immutation" in Chrysostom favour Transubstantiation; he is mistaken. For Suarez himself also observed that these words bring in not a substantial change but an accidental one: not a change of nature (φύσεως) but of use (χρήσεως καὶ χρέσεως), and so on. The ancient Greeks have the words μεταβολῆς, μετατυπώσεως, μεταρρυθμίσεως and μεταχοιχειώσεως; the Latins have mutatio, transmutatio, and so on. But none of this matters to the question: they are not speaking of a substantial change but of an accidental one, not a change of nature (μεταβολὴν φύσεως) but of use (χρήσεως); not a gaining of a different substance but a composition of matter (συνθέσεως χαράτος), as the Fathers put it, and in exactly the same way that our people have long since observed in the regeneration of a man. The word μεταςυνχεῶσις itself (which properly signifies transelementation, not transubstantiation) was used by the ancient Fathers to express spiritual changes, which mean anything but transmutations of substances and forms into one another. Gregory of Nyssa, in his canonical epistle, mentions those who have been transelemented [μετασυνχειρισμένων] through regeneration; but does he also mention the transsubstantiated [μετασιωμένων]? Clement of Alexandria denies it, Irenaeus denies it, the whole Church denies it. Clement's words are these (Greek: "For teaching reshapes the man; the reshaping makes him of another nature, and is changed by a kind of generation or analogy of nature, which is accomplished in time and by learning to be transformed. The Lord has given both: the one in creation, the other in the restoration and renewal of the covenant"). For teaching reshapes man (the Greek Fathers too use the same words to explain the sacramental change) and transfigures him. But when he has thus been transfigured, he is converted, as it were, into another nature. For it makes no difference whether a man was formed such by nature, or was transformed by time and teaching.

units.la: CtriEtrina transformatus. Utrumque præstat Dominus, alterum per creationem, alterum per regenerationem ac renovationem ex Testamento. Stromat. lib. 4. Irenæus vero adversus Hæreses lib. 5. Quemadmodum oleaster inserta, subsistantiam quidem ligni non amittit, qualitatem autem fructus immutat, & aliud percipit vocabulum, jam non oleaster; sed fructifica olea existens, & dicitur: Sic & homo per fidem insertus, & assumens Spiritum Dei, subsistantiam quidem carnis non amittit, qualitatem autem fructus operum immutat, & aliud accipit vocabulum, significans illam, quæ in melius est transmutationem, jam non caro & sanguis, sed homo spiritualis existens & dicitur. p. 453. Tale, non aliam, veteres voluisse mutationem, quis dubitet, cum constet, eos alteram per alteram mutationem probâsse? Ambros. Ergo, ut tibi respondeam, non erat corpus Christi ante consecrationem, sed post consecrationem; dico tibi, quod jam corpus est Christi. Ipse dixit & factum est; ipse mandavit, & creatum est. Tu ipse eras, sed eras vetus creatura, posteaquam consecratus es, nova creatura esse cœpisti. Accipe ergo, quemadmodum termo Christi creaturam omnem mutare consueverit, & mutat, quando vult, instituta Naturæ. De sacram. l. 4. c. 4. Ita Eusebius Emissen. vel potius Eucherius Lugdun. Homil. de corpore & sanguine Christi. Quanta, inquit, & quam celebranda vis divinæ benedictionis operetur,& quomodo tibi novum & impossibile videri non debeat,quod in Christi substantiam terrena & mortalia commutantur; te ipsum,qui jam Christo es regeneratus,interroga. Sed & de Baptismi aqua Cyrillus, aliique veteres dicebant,eam μετασυνχεισθαι in virtutem quandam divinam. An per transubstantiationem? Negat Ephremus apud Phot.in Bibl.c. 229. Baptismus, etsi totus sit spiritualis factus, & unus tantum existat,proprietatem tamen substantiae visibilis, aquae nimirum, servat, & id quod fuit,esse non definit. Haec ille.
units.tr: transformed by teaching. The Lord bestows both: the one through creation, the other through regeneration and renewal from the covenant. (Stromata, book 4.) Irenaeus, moreover, in Against Heresies, book 5: "As a wild olive, when a graft is inserted, does not lose the substance of the wood but changes the quality of its fruit, and takes another name, no longer a wild olive but a fruitful olive: so also a man, grafted by faith and receiving the Spirit of God, does not lose the substance of his flesh but changes the quality of his fruit in works, and takes another name, signifying that change which is into something better, and is called no longer flesh and blood but a spiritual man." (p. 453.) Who could doubt that the ancients meant such a change, and not another, since it is evident that they proved the one by the other? Ambrose: "Therefore, to answer you: the body of Christ was not there before consecration, but after consecration I tell you it is now the body of Christ. He spoke and it was done; he commanded and it was created. You yourself were, but you were an old creature; after you were consecrated, you began to be a new creature. Learn therefore how the word of Christ is accustomed to change every creature, and does change the ordinances of nature whenever he wills." (On the Sacraments, book 4, chapter 4.) So too Eucherius of Lyons (rather than Eucherius of Emesa), in his homily on the body and blood of Christ: "How great, he says, and how worthy of celebration is the power of the divine blessing that works, and why should it not seem to you new and impossible that earthly and mortal things are changed into the substance of Christ? Ask yourself, who have already been regenerated in Christ." But Cyril and other ancient writers also said that the water of baptism is changed [μετασυνχεισθαι] into a certain divine power. Is this through transubstantiation? Ephrem denies it, as reported by Photius in the Bibliotheca, chapter 229: "Baptism, though it has been made wholly spiritual and exists as one only, nevertheless keeps the property of the visible substance, namely water, and does not cease to be what it was. So he says."

units.la: SECTIO VIII.
units.tr: SECTIO VIII.

units.la: Transsubstantiatio aperte contradi- cit Scripturae.
units.tr: Transubstantiation openly contradicts Scripture.

units.la: I. Haec de negatione Alfensus. Rejectio Transubstantiationis ceu novi dogmatis, traditur iterum diversis Scripturae verbis, Fidei Analogia, Antiquitatis suffragio, & sobriae rationis consensu. Scripturae authoritas hoc commentum tum alibi evertit, tum in eo maxime loco, ubi Sacramenti hujus institutio traditur: id quod ex antithesi manifestius emerg et. 1. Christus, in Coena, accepit panem, integram masssam, & eam quidem,quae frangi potuit, & distribui inter discipulos. At Transubstantiationis commentum, superstitionem etiam numu-lalariorum panum invexit. 2. In Coena Christus jussit edere, quod accepit, consecravit, distribuit, id est, panem, veram & solidam substantiam. Transsubstantiatio tantum porrigit accidentia, sive speciem panis. 3. Christus dicit, Hoc est Corpus meum, non effective panem mutando in corpus, sed indicative tantum. Dicit, quid sit, quod porrexit, non quid futurum esset. 4. Datur exemplum, verbo copulativo Est, ubique in tota Scriptura, virtutem tribui effectivam, vel operativam. Novum ergo, peregrinum, inusitatum in Transsubstantiatione verba induunt significatum. 5. In Coena Domini illud corpus manducatur, quod ex Beata Maria Virgine natum, discipulis ita tradebatur, ut tamen paulo post frangi potuerit & crucifigi. At Transsubstantiatio novum quotidie, ex pane creatum, format corpus, neque fractioni, neque ulli passioni amplius obnoxium. 6. Illud ipsum numero corpus manducandum nobis in Coena praebetur, quod suis praebuit discipulis Christus: Id ipsum enim Apostoli tradiderunt, quod a Domino acceperunt, 1. Cor. 11. 23. At corpus illud, quod visibiliter, substantialiter & realiter fractum pro nobis est, sanguis, qui visibiliter, realiter effusus est; frangi & fundi proprie eadem numero amplius non possunt. Corpus Christi pati amplius non potest : sanguis vero ejus in terram effusus non servatus est, nec postea in corpus rediit; sed more aliorum hominum sanguinis exaniexaruit. 7. Illud discipulis manducandum erat corpus, & ille bibendus sanguis; de quo in praesenti enuntiavit Christus: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur; Hic est sanguis meus, qui pro vobis effunditur. Atqui accumbentis tum corpus nec proprie frangebatur, nec sanguis effundebatur: utrumque paulo post fieri debuit. 8. Tale corpus in verbis institutionis intelligitur, quale Christus dedit discipulis. At proprium & essentiale corpus, vere & realiter manducandum non dedit. Nam a. Illud accubuit mensae. b. Edisset suum ipsius corpus, & bibisset suum ipsius sanguinem, & quidem in remissionem peccatorum, Illud absurdum; hoc plasphemum est. Vide Marc. 14. 25 coll. Luc. 24. 15. 18. c. Mortuus, discerptus, laceratus, destructus, (nulla enim manducatio oralis salvo Subjecto dari poterat) Christus fuisset ante mortem, i. e. ante divinitus destinatum crucis maledictae supplicium, quum tamen S. Scriptura de una morte expiatoria ubique, praesertim in Epistola ad Hebraeos, loquatur. d. Habuisset duo corpora, alterum transubstantiatum ex pane, alterum transubstantians consecratione; vel si unum velint tantum, simul gestans & gestatum, agens & patiens, quod eodem tempore & respectu fieri non poterat. 9. Illius corporis Christus dedit Sacramentum discipulis, quod frangendum postea demum & lacerandum militum erat manibus. Cyprian. lib. de unctione Christi
units.tr: I. These are the arguments for the denial. The rejection of Transubstantiation, as a new dogma, is again refuted by various words of Scripture, by the analogy of faith, by the testimony of antiquity, and by the agreement of sound reason. The authority of Scripture overturns this fiction both elsewhere and especially in the passage where the institution of this sacrament is related, as becomes clearer from the contrast: (1) In the Supper Christ took bread, a whole mass, and one that could be broken and distributed among the disciples. But the fiction of Transubstantiation has introduced the superstition of wafers stamped with a design. (2) In the Supper Christ bade them eat what he had taken, consecrated and distributed, that is, bread, a true and solid substance. Transubstantiation leaves only the accidents, or the appearance of bread. (3) Christ says, This is my body, not effecting a change of the bread into body, but only indicating. He says what the thing he handed over is, not what it would become. (4) There is an example, in the whole of Scripture, of the copula is everywhere being given an effective or operative force. Transubstantiation therefore gives the words a new, foreign and unusual meaning. (5) In the Lord's Supper that body is eaten which was born of the blessed Virgin Mary and was so delivered to the disciples that, a little afterwards, it could be broken and crucified. But Transubstantiation daily forms a new body, created from bread, no longer liable to breaking or to any suffering. (6) The very same body to be eaten by us in the Supper is offered as Christ offered it to his disciples: For the Apostles handed on what they had received from the Lord, 1 Cor. 11.23. But that body which was visibly, substantially and really broken for us, and that blood which was visibly and really poured out, cannot properly be broken and poured out again in the same numerical body. The body of Christ can no longer suffer; and his blood, poured out on the earth, was not kept, nor did it afterwards return to a body, but like the blood of other men it dried up. (7) The disciples were to eat that body and drink that blood, of which Christ said in the present tense: This is my body, which is broken for you; this is my blood, which is poured out for you. Yet at that time the body was not properly broken, nor the blood poured out, while he sat at table; both had to happen a little later. (8) In the words of institution, the body is understood to be such as Christ gave to the disciples. But he did not give them his own proper and essential body, to be eaten truly and really. For: (a) that body was reclining at the table; (b) he would have eaten his own body and drunk his own blood, and that for the remission of sins. The former is absurd, the latter blasphemous. See Mark 14.25 with Luke 24.15, 18. (c) Christ would have been dead, torn, lacerated and destroyed before his death, that is, before the punishment of the accursed cross, which God had appointed, whereas Holy Scripture everywhere speaks of one expiatory death, especially in the Epistle to the Hebrews. (d) He would have had two bodies, one transubstantiated from bread and the other transubstantiating by consecration; or if they want only one, it would be at once bearing and borne, acting and suffering, which could not happen at the same time and in the same respect. (9) Christ gave the sacrament of that body to the disciples, which afterwards had to be broken and torn by the hands of soldiers. Cyprian, book on the anointing of Christ

units.la: F mat. Dedit itaque Dominus noster in mensa, in qua ultimum cum Apostolis participavit convivium,propriis manibus panem & vinum, in cruce vero manibus militum corpus tradidit vulnerandum,ut in Apostolis secretius impressa sincera veritas,& vera sinceritas exponeret Gentibus,quomodo vinum & panis caro esset & sanguis, & quibus rationibus causa effectibus convenirent,& diversa nomina vel species ad unam reducerentur essentiam, & significantia & significata iisdem censerentur vocabulis. Panem & vinum revera dedisse in Coena Apostolis, dicit; corpus vero militibus in cruce vulnerandum. 10. Christus in Coena Sacramentum instituit corporis sui veri, circumscripti, mortalis, imo, per figuram fracti panis, pro peccatis nostri mortui. Unde Evangelistae Graecam vocem σῶμα adhibent, quae de exanimi proprie dicitur corpore & exanimi. Hinc Graecorum Philologi: Σῶμα πᾶν τὸ πνευματικὸς πτῶσις ... ψυχὴ ... Hac vox σῶμα apud antiquos de omni exanimi dicitur; νεκρὸς de vivente, quod colligatur cum anima. Hoc sensu sumitur in T. N. Matth. 14. 12. Luc. 17.37. Ita Latine Corpora defunctorum. LXX. hinc inde pro voce גויה usurpant, quod vocabulum in manducatione agni Paschalis veteres judaei, ut supra p.29. monuimus, etiam adhibebant. Sed & Syriaca vocula ܓܘܫܝܐ, quam retinent Evangelistae. liftæ, propria & nativa significatione corpus exanime significat, idque ex usu primitivi Hebraici, de quo Hebræorum doctissimus, R. D. Kimchius: הפגר הוא הגוף בלא רוח Pægæt corpus denotat inanime; Lib.radic. Tale nobis Christus in Cœna sua commendat corpus: at in Transsubstantiatione gloriosum, omnisque passionis, expers cœlo eliciunt, dum, ut Patres loquuntur Tridentini, statim post consecrationem, verum Christi corpus, verumque ejus sanguinem, sub panis & vini specie, una cum ipsius anima & divinitate concipiunt. 11. Christus S. Cœnæ Sacramentum instituit voluit in sui ἀνάμνησιν, recordationem, Luc. 22. 19. E. noluit fieri Transsubstantiationem. Absentium enim, non præsentium memoriam habendam, ipse clara antithesi docet Christus, Matth. 26. 11. Marc. 14. 17. quam Augustinus, in præsenti etiam materia urget. Quod de præsentium recordatione confingunt adversarii, in thesi satis est infirmum; in hypothesi vero salsum. Ad animum enim revocare deberent, hanc propterea formulam εἰς ἀνάμνησιν in memoriam, recordationem; ordinariam esse Sacramentorum appendicem, ut constaret nobis, instituta ea esse ad celebrandam beneficiorum Dei in nos collatorum memoriam. Indignum valde est, disputare de novo, insolito, absurdo vocis usu, ubi, Veteris & recepti, Auctorem & Interpretem habemus ipsum Spiritum sanctum. 12. Sanguis vocatur Novum Testamentum, non Transubstantiatione, sed significatione, E. & panis, corpus Christi est, significatione. Cujus argumenti vim non videmus ullo posse modo eludi, infirmari aut infringi. Cur enim alio sensu panis dicatur corpus, quàm sanguis Novum Testamentum, cùm evidentissima utrobique sit Tropologiae ratio, non in eodem tantùm capite, sed in eadem plane materia? 13. Transubstantiatio fingit & comminiscitur concomitantiam. Ea verò institutioni Dominicae repugnat. Duo enim Christus adhibuit elementa, panem & vinum. Duo etiam nobis commendavit, duo Apostoli tradiderunt, duo Ecclesia primitiva per aliquot secula constanter retinuit.
units.tr: Our Lord therefore gave, at the table at which he shared his last supper with the Apostles, bread and wine with his own hands, but on the cross he handed over his body to the soldiers' hands to be wounded, so that the sincere truth, impressed more secretly upon the Apostles, might set forth to the Gentiles how wine and bread are flesh and blood, by what reasons cause and effects agree, how diverse names or species are reduced to one essence, and how signifying things and things signified are reckoned under the same words. He says that Christ gave bread and wine to the Apostles at the Supper, but his body to be wounded by the soldiers on the cross. (10) In the Supper Christ instituted the sacrament of his true body, circumscribed, mortal, indeed, by way of a figure, of broken bread, dead for our sins. Hence the Evangelists use the Greek word sōma [σῶμα], which is properly said of a lifeless body and a corpse. Hence the Greek philologists: Soma [Σῶμα] is everything that has fallen away from the spirit ... soul ... This word soma was used by the ancients of any lifeless body; nekros [νεκρὸς] of a living thing, as it is joined with a soul. It is taken in this sense in the New Testament, Matt. 14.12; Luke 17.37. So in Latin, corpora defunctorum, bodies of the dead. The Septuagint use it in place of the Hebrew word gewiyah [גויה], which the ancient Jews also used in the eating of the Passover lamb, as we noted above on p. 29. But also the Syriac word gushya, which the Evangelists retain, by its proper and native meaning signifies a lifeless body, and this from the usage of the primitive Hebrew, of which the most learned of the Hebrews, R. D. Kimchi, says: pegher [הפגר הוא הגוף בלא רוח] denotes an inanimate body, Lib. Radic. Such is the body Christ commends to us in his Supper; but in Transubstantiation they devise a glorious body, free from all suffering, to be in heaven, while, as the Tridentine Fathers say, immediately after the consecration the true body of Christ, and his true blood, under the species of bread and wine, together with his soul and divinity are believed to be present.
