(11) Christ willed that the Supper of his sacrament be instituted in remembrance [anamnēsin ἀνάμνησιν], recollection, Luke 22.19. Therefore he did not will Transubstantiation to take place. For Christ himself teaches with a clear contrast that one must have a memory of the absent, not of the present, Matt. 26.11; Mark 14.7, which Augustine also presses in this very matter. What the opponents fabricate about the recollection of the present is weak enough in theory, and false in practice. For they ought to recall that this formula eis anamnēsin [εἰς ἀνάμνησιν], into remembrance, is the usual appendix to the sacraments, so that it would be plain to us that they were instituted to celebrate the memory of the benefits of God bestowed upon us. It is most unworthy to dispute about a new, unusual and absurd use of a word when we have as its old and accepted author and interpreter the Holy Spirit himself. (12) The blood is called the New Testament, not by Transubstantiation but by signification; therefore also bread is the body of Christ by signification. We do not see that the force of this argument can in any way be evaded, weakened or overturned. For why is bread called body in a different sense from that in which blood is called the New Testament, when the reason for the trope is most evident in both, and not only in the same chapter but in the very same matter? (13) Transubstantiation feigns and invents a concomitance. But this is contrary to the Lord's institution. For Christ used two elements, bread and wine. He also commended two to us; the Apostles handed on two; and the primitive Church kept two constantly for some centuries.

units.la: II. Haec, ex Verbis Institutionis depromta, argumenta in Praxi Apostolica redeunt omnia, Pauli praesertim repetitione, instituta, 1. Cor.XI. ubi, postquam Christi verba institutiva, Apostolus semel tepetiisset, nunquam deinceps amplius impropriae illius propositionis, Hoc est corpus meum, meminit; sed semper, & quidem quinquies, etiam post consecrationem, panem nobis introducit, non communem, ut rectè distinguit Iren. lib. 4. advers. haeres. cap. 34. non λιτὸν, ut Cyrill. Hierosol. Catechesi Myst. 5. loquitur; sed Sacramentalem. Et ut clarius mentem suam, Gentium Apostolus exprimeret, à contrariis mensis, Christi & Belialis, Do- Domini & Dæmoniorum argumentum suum accersit. Ab Idolothytis enim Corinthios suos capite præcedenti Paulus dehortaturus, Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, ait, esse communionem sanguinis Christi; an per Transsubstantiationem? Non, sed per communicationem, participationem, concelebrationem, prout Idolothyta communio vocantur Dæmoniorum.
units.tr: II. All these arguments, drawn from the words of institution, return in the apostolic practice, especially in Paul's repetition of them, 1 Cor. 11, where, after the Apostle had once touched upon Christ's words of institution, he never afterwards mentioned that improper proposition, This is my body; but always, and indeed five times, even after the consecration, he presents to us bread, not common bread, as Irenaeus rightly distinguishes, book 4 against heresies, chapter 34, nor leitos [λιτὸν], as Cyril of Jerusalem speaks in his Mystagogical Catechesis 5, but sacramental bread. And so that the Gentiles' Apostle might express his meaning more clearly, he draws his argument from the contrary tables, of Christ and of Belial, of the Lord and of demons. For Paul, about to dissuade his Corinthians from idol-offerings in the preceding chapter, says that the cup of blessing which we bless is the communion of the blood of Christ; is this through Transubstantiation? No, but through communication, participation, joint celebration, just as idol-offerings are called the communion of demons.

units.la: III. Miror equidem, adeo sibi adversarios multum de præsenti Pauli textu, voce præsertim communionis, polliceri, cum, si scopum & intentionem, adeoque Pauli argumentationem spectemus, vix in Scriptura locus figuratam loquendi rationem verborum; Hoc est corpus meum, solidius stabiliat. Apostoli mens & sententia est: Ἀσύγχυτος esse, & una fede morari non posse, Christi esse, & Belialis communionem habere cum mensa Domini & Dæmoniorum; sacris interesse Christianis, & simul litare Idolis: quem Samaritanismum quidam ex Corinthiis introducere voluisse videbantur. Per legitimum Cœnæ Dominicæ usum, tanquam notam, testeram, symbolum, communionem alios habere cum Ecclesia, quæ Christi corpus est; per Idolothytorum vero participationem, alios membra fieri Synagogæ Diaboli. Mixturam ex duobus, salvo Christianismo, ne quidem tentandam, sequenti, eaque manifesta Paulus probat argumentatione: Qui unus sunt panis, unum corpus, illi etiam in una communione cum Christo, communionisque publica conteßeratione, quæ fit per consecratum poculum & fractum panem debent acquiescere, cum aliis se non miscere, verf. 16.17. At vos (Corinthii) unus estis panis, unum corpus, quia omnes ex uno pane participatis, verf 17. Quod iterum confirmat assumtum, 1. Cor. 12. 13. Per unum Spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus sumus baptizati, & una omnes potione potionati sumus in unum Spiritum. Quid igitur absurdius fuerit, & à scopo Pauli alienius quàm dicere, communionem corporis Christi, ipsum transsubstantiatum esse corpus, cum corpus & communio differant, ut absolutum & relatum; & ipse panis fractus, seu fractio panis, eo sensu, sit corporis Christi communio, quo participatio Idolothytorum, communio est Dæmoniorum, nempe symbolice, & Characteristice? Ut ergo alibi legimus, fideles habere κοινωνίαν seu communionem cum Patre & Filio ejus Jesu Christo, 1. Joh. 1. verf. 3. dicuntur vocati ad communionem Jesu Christi, 1. Cor. 1.9. ita quando Paulus hoc loco scribit, panem, quem frangunt Christiani, esse communionem corporis Christi, aliud nihil intendit, quàm, eos communionem habere cum Cœtu Dominico, cujus symbolum sit fractio panis.
units.tr: III. I am indeed surprised that our opponents promise themselves so much from the present text of Paul, especially from the word communion, when, if we look at the aim and intention of the passage and so at Paul's argument, there is scarcely any place in Scripture where a figurative way of speaking, This is my body, is more firmly established. The Apostle's mind and meaning is that [Ἀσύγχυτος] is incompatible, that one cannot remain in both at once: that those who have communion with the table of the Lord, which is Christ's, cannot also have communion with the table of demons; that one cannot attend the Christian sacred rites and at the same time sacrifice to idols. Some seem to have wished to introduce this Samaritan-style mixing among the Corinthians. Through the lawful use of the Lord's Supper, as a mark, a token and a sign, the faithful have communion with the Church, which is the body of Christ; but through partaking of idol sacrifices, others become members of the synagogue of the Devil. Paul proves by the following argument, and a plain one, that a mixture of the two, which must not even be attempted if Christianity is to stand, is not allowed: Those who are one bread, one body, must also in one communion with Christ, and in the public witness of communion which takes place through the consecrated cup and the broken bread, rest content and not mix themselves with others, verse 16, 17. But you (Corinthians) are one bread, one body, because you all partake of one bread, verse 17. This he confirms again from the premise, 1 Cor. 12. 13: By one Spirit we are all baptized into one body, and we have all been given to drink of one cup into one Spirit. What then could be more absurd, and more foreign to Paul's aim, than to say that the communion of the body of Christ is the body of Christ itself transubstantiated, since body and communion differ as absolute and relative, and the bread itself, when broken, or the breaking of the bread, is a communion of the body of Christ in the same sense in which the partaking of idol sacrifices is a communion of demons, namely symbolically and characteristically? So, as we read elsewhere that the faithful have koinonia, that is communion, with the Father and his Son Jesus Christ, 1 John 1. verse 3, and are said to be called to the communion of Jesus Christ, 1 Cor. 1.9, so when Paul in this place writes that the bread which Christians break is the communion of the body of Christ, he intends nothing else than that they have communion with the Lord's assembly, of which the breaking of the bread is the symbol.

units.la: SECTIO
units.tr: SECTION

units.la: SECTIO IX.
units.tr: SECTION IX.

units.la: De vero Scopo Concionis Dominica Joh. C. VI. eámque Transsubstantia- tioni non favere, ne quidem áv. 48.
units.tr: On the true purpose of the Lord's sermon in John 6, and that it does not favour transubstantiation, not even at verse 48.

units.la: I. Atque hæc de Praxi Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ: Superest insignis Christi concio, Joh. C. VI. præsertim à v. 48. (de præcedentibus enim nobis magnam litem adversarii non movent) in qua Vir doctissimus causæ suæ primarium oftendit præsidium, sed frustra, uti audiemus. Ut autem de loci hujus genuino nobis constet sensu, notandum, 1. Dari manducationem mysticam & spiritualem, quæ fidei tantum sit, eámque veram & realem. 2. Illam à Sacramentali manducatione differre. 3. Hoc loco non agi de Sacramentali, sed mystica manducatione, quod ex Pontificiis Doctoribus gravissimi quique afferunt, & iis quidem innixi rationibus, quibus & nos haud gravatim subscribere possumus, quæ & quæ à cæteris, secus sentientibus, nec satis sunt expensa, nec solide refutata. 4. Pontificios, qui de manducatione Sacramentali locum intelligunt, Transsubstantiationem suam praesentissimo exponere periculo. 5. Magnam tamen hunc locum afferre lucem explicanda doTrina de manducatione Sacramentali, adeóque ingens nostra assertioni afferre pondus.
units.tr: I. So much for the practice of the apostolic Church. There remains the notable sermon of Christ in John 6, especially from verse 48 onward. (Our opponents do not raise a great dispute over what precedes it.) In this sermon the most learned man shows his chief defence of his cause, but in vain, as we shall hear. To be sure of the genuine sense of this passage, the following should be noted: (1) There is a mystical and spiritual eating, which belongs to faith alone, and it is true and real. (2) It differs from sacramental eating. (3) In this place the subject is not sacramental but mystical eating. The most serious of the Papist teachers themselves maintain this, relying on reasons with which we too can readily agree, and which others who think otherwise have neither weighed adequately nor refuted soundly. (4) Those Papists who understand the passage of sacramental eating expose their own transubstantiation to the greatest danger. (5) Nevertheless, this passage casts great light on the doctrine of sacramental eating that is to be explained, and so lends great weight to our assertion.

units.la: II. A. Duo sunt primæ observationis nostræ lemmata, alterum, dari manducationem mysticam sive Spiritualem, quæ fidei tantum sit; alterum, veram illam esse, non fictitiam, aut imaginariam, ut probrose nobis objiciunt, qui nullam realitatem agnoscunt, nisi quæ præsentiam præsupponat corporalem, essentialem, locale.
units.tr: II. A. There are two premises of our first observation: the first, that there is a mystical or spiritual eating, which belongs to faith alone; the second, that this eating is true and not fictitious or imaginary, as those who acknowledge no reality except what presupposes a bodily, essential, and local presence shamefully object to us.

units.la: Manducationem dari Spiritualem, Christiani tam non debent dubitare, quàm persuasum habere possunt, dari vitam Spiritualem, generationem Spiritualem, incrementa Spiritualia. Hæc si tibi in hac vita ademeris, alteram, cælestem, æternam nunquam possidebis. Sed quia etiamnum Sadducæorum quædam superest propago, quæ si Angelos & Spiritus physicè non tollat, Theologicè tamen, quid Spiritualis vel vita vel manducatio sit, ignorat, eam sceptice cavillatur, impiè sugillat, exosæ novitatis larvam ei induit, antiquitatem solicitare, & quàm nostris nihil hastenus vel quoad phrasin, vel quo ad rem, exciderit, quod primitivæ Ecclesiæ calculo receptum non fuerit, Doctorum antiquissimorum experiri lubet evidentissimis verbis.
units.tr: Christians ought no more to doubt that there is spiritual eating than they can be persuaded that there is spiritual life, spiritual generation, and spiritual growth. If you were to take these away from you in this life, you would never possess the other, heavenly and eternal life. But since a certain remnant of the Sadducees' brood still survives, which, if it does not deny angels and spirits in the physical sense, nevertheless in the theological sense does not know what spiritual life or spiritual eating is, and which sceptically scoffs at it, impiously disparages it, and puts on it the mask of a hated novelty, while it seeks to disturb antiquity, I am pleased to test, in the clearest words of the most ancient teachers, whether anything in our teaching, either in its phrasing or in its substance, has so far departed from what was received by the reckoning of the primitive Church.

units.la: Primò ergò cum Ecclesia primitiva loquimur, quando Manducare idem nobis est, quod credere. Ita Christus ipse explicat Joh.6.v.35. coll. cum 64. Ita Patres, August. T. IX. Tractat. 25. in Joh. Dixerunt ergò ad eum: Quid faciemus, ut operemur opera Dei ? Dixerat enim illis: Operamini escam,non quæ perit,sed quæ permanet in vitam æternam. Quid faciemus,inquiunt ? Quid observando hoc,præceptum implere poterimus ? Respondit Iesus,& dixit eis: Hoc est opus Dei,ut credatis in eum,quem misit ille. Hoc est ergo manducare cibum,non qui perit; sed qui permanet in vitam æternam. Ut quid paras dentes & ventrem? Crede & manducâsti. Ipse hic locus citatur de Consecrat. Dist. 2. cap. Vt quid &c. Ex quo colligimus 1. ex mente Augustini, credere & manducare esse æquipollentia. Atque hoc ipsum est,quod urgemus. 2. Manducationem Spiritualem,naturali per dentes,opponi. Reprehensio enim tacita est: Vt quid paras dentes & ventrem? 3. Cibum hunc cœlestem, quem daturus est Christus,v. 27. eundem esse cum pane cœlesti v. 31. carne & sanguine Christi vers. 54. 4. Adeóque credere, vers. 29. & 35. operari in cibo,qui non perit, v. 27. edere panem vitæ, v. 35. plane idem esse. 5. Non ergo Judæis tantum,sed & omnibus,qui de cibo hoc cœlesti non recte sententiunt,dictum voluit Augustinus,ut quid paras dentes ? &c. Alter itidem Augustini locus nobis impendio favet,ex initio Tractat. 26. Daturus ergo Dominus Spiritum sanctum dixit,se panem,qui de cœlo descendit,hortans,ut credamus in eum. Credere enim in eum,hoc est manducare panem vivum. Qui credit in eum,manducat ; invisibiliter saginatur, quia invisibiliter renascitur. Infans intus est, novus intus est, ubi novellatur, ibi satiatur. Nihil hactenus opponi potuit aut oppositum est, quod nostram infringat thesin. Clara apud Augustinum extant verba, edere Christi carnem, & credere in eum, esse æquipollentia. Quæ enim ad præsentem locum vir doctissimus excepit, ad circumstantiarum potius varietatem pertinent, quàm ipsius substantiæ veritatem. 2. Spiritualem hanc manducationem Spirituali respondere generationi, i.e. regenerationi. Clem. Alexand. Paed. lib. 1. cap. 6. Quemadmodum autem regeneratio convenienter, ita etiam (corpus Christi) cibus hominï factus Spiritualis. 3. Cibus hic totus est Spiritualis. Athanas. Orat. in illud: Quicunque dixerit verbum &c. Propterea (Joh. 6, vers. 62.) Filii hominis in cœlos ascensionis mentionem fecit, ut a corporali eos cogitatione abstraheret, ac deinde carnem suam, de qua loquutus erat, cibum e supernis cœlestem & Spiritualem alimoniam ab ipso datam intelligerent. Quæ enim loquutus sum vobis, inquit, Spiritus sunt & vita sunt, quod perinde est ac si diceret: Quod ostenditur & datur, pro mundo, in cibum dabitur, ut Spiritualiter unicuique tribuatur, & singulis munimentum ad resurrectionem vitæ æternæ fiat. 4. Gustus Spiritualis. Basil. in Psalm. 33. Quandoquidem vero verus panis Dominus noster, & caro ejus verus cibus, necesse est, est, ut voluptas laetitia panis per gustum Spiritualem in nobis gignatur. 5. Os spirituale. Idem ibid: Est os quoddam Spirituale hominis interni, quo nutritur, dum particeps fit verbi vita, quod est panis, qui de coelo descendit Cyrill. Alexand. Anathemat. Apoll. XI. Concil. c. 1. part. 2. Nostrum itaque Sacramentum non docet hominum escam, nefariè edentium, mentem ad evanidas cogitationes adigens, & ratiocinationibus humanis ea subjicere cogitans, quae sola & indiscussa, seu indubitata fide accipiuntur. 6. Effectus Spirituales, ut sunt, a: Spiritualis nutritio. Cibo Spirituali, seu Eucharistia sanguis carnésquae nostrae, secundum mutationem (non Physicam substantiae, sed moralem usus & significationis) aluntur; Justin. Martyr. Apol. 2. b. Est unctio (quam conviviis Veteres adhibere solebant) Spiritualis. Duplex, inquit Clem. Alexand. Paedag. lib. 2. cap. 2. est sanguis Domini, alter quidem carnalis, quo redemti sumus ab interitu; alter vero Spiritualis, quo scilicet unctii sumus. Et hoc est bibere sanguinem Jesu, Dominica immortalitatis participem fieri. c. Communio ejusdem sum Christo naturae. Cyrill. Hierosol. Myst 4. Divinorum mysteriorum participes, corporis & sanguinis Christi compotes sacti estis. d. Coalitio in unum Corpus. Chrysost. Homil. 24.
units.tr: First, then, we speak with the primitive Church when to eat is for us the same as to believe. Christ himself explains it so in John 6:35, compared with verse 64. So too the Fathers, Augustine, Tractate 25 on John, vol. IX: "They said therefore to him: What shall we do, that we may work the works of God? For he had said to them: Labour for the food that perishes not, but that remains unto eternal life. What shall we do, they say? What can we accomplish by observing this precept? Jesus answered and said to them: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. This, then, is to eat the food that perishes not, but remains unto eternal life. Why do you prepare teeth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten." This very passage is cited in De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter "Ut quid" etc. From this we gather: (1) According to Augustine's mind, to believe and to eat are equivalent. And this is exactly what we press. (2) Spiritual eating is set over against eating by the teeth in the natural way; for the rebuke is implicit: Why do you prepare teeth and belly? (3) The heavenly food that Christ will give (v. 27) is the same as the heavenly bread (v. 31), the flesh and blood of Christ (v. 54). (4) Therefore to believe (vv. 29 and 35), to labour for the food that does not perish (v. 27), and to eat the bread of life (v. 35) are plainly the same. (5) Augustine therefore meant Why do you prepare teeth? and so on not only for the Jews but for all who think wrongly about this heavenly food. Another passage of Augustine, from the beginning of Tractate 26, also greatly favours us: "The Lord, therefore, about to give the Holy Spirit, said that he was the bread that came down from heaven, urging us to believe in him. For to believe in him is to eat the living bread. He who believes in him eats; he is invisibly fed, because he is invisibly reborn. The infant is within, the new one is within; where he is nourished, there he is satisfied." Nothing so far has been or could be advanced that overturns our thesis. In Augustine there stand clear words that to eat the flesh of Christ and to believe in him are equivalent. What the most learned man has taken up in the present passage pertains rather to the variety of circumstances than to the truth of the substance itself. (2) This spiritual eating corresponds to spiritual generation, that is, regeneration. Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus I, chapter 6: "But just as regeneration is fitting, so also the body of Christ, made food for man, is spiritual." (3) This whole food is spiritual. Athanasius, Oration on the words: "Whoever shall say the word, etc." "Therefore" (John 6:62) "he spoke of the ascension of the Son of Man into heaven, that he might draw them away from bodily thought, and then that they might understand his flesh, of which he had spoken, as the heavenly and spiritual nourishment given by him from above. For the words that I have spoken to you, he says, are spirit and are life, which is just as if he said: What is shown and given for the world will be given as food, so that it may be bestowed spiritually on each, and become a safeguard to each for the resurrection of eternal life." (4) Spiritual taste. Basil, on Psalm 33: "Since indeed our Lord is the true bread, and his flesh the true food, it is necessary that the pleasure and joy of the bread be begotten in us through spiritual taste." (5) A spiritual mouth. The same, in the same place: "There is a certain spiritual mouth of the inner man, by which he is nourished, while he becomes a partaker of the word of life, which is the bread that came down from heaven." Cyril of Alexandria, Anathematism 11 of the Council, chapter 1, part 2: "Our sacrament, therefore, does not teach that the food of men is eaten wickedly, driving the mind to empty thoughts, and thinking to subject these things to human reasonings, which are received only and without examination, or indubitably, by faith." (6) Spiritual effects, as they are: spiritual nourishment. By spiritual food, or the Eucharist, our flesh and blood are nourished, according to a change (not a physical change of substance but a moral change of use and signification). Justin Martyr, Apology 2, b: "There is an anointing (which the ancients used to apply at their feasts), spiritual. There is a double blood of the Lord," says Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus II, chapter 2, "the one indeed fleshly, by which we were redeemed from destruction; the other spiritual, by which we are anointed. And this is to drink the blood of Jesus, to become a partaker of the Lord's immortality." (c) Communion of the same nature with Christ. Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catechesis 4: "You have become partakers of the divine mysteries, and have been made sharers in the body and blood of Christ." (d) Coalition into one body. Chrysostom, Homily 24

units.la: in 1. Corinth. T. 3. Sumus illud ipsum corpus. Quid enim est panis? Corpus Christi. Quid autem fiunt, quid sumunt? Corpus Christi. Quemadmodum enim panis ex multis granis compositus, unitus est, ut nusquam appareant grana, sed sint quidem ipsa, non autem manifesta sit eorum differentia, propter conjunctionem, ita etiam inter nos, & cum Christo conjungimur. Et Hom. 81. in Matth. Re ipsa nos corpus suum facit. Item: Nos facti sumus corpus Christi & una. Gregor. Nyssen. Homil. 8. in Eccles. Propterea nobis seipsum esculentum proponit is, qui semper est, ut cum ipsum in nos ipsos recepérimus, illud fiamus, quod ipse est. 7. Haec vero nec per contactum fit, nec per Transsubstantiationem, aut quamlibet praesentiam localem; sed fidei apprehensionem. Nostra (ita Cyprianus serm. de Coen. Dom.) & ipsius conjunctio nec miscet personas, nec unit substantias, sed affectus consociat, & confoederat voluntates. Augustt. tract. 50. in Joh. Quomodo absentem tenebo? Quomodo in coelum manum mittam ut ibi sedentem teneam? Eodem mitte & tenuisti. Item: Secundum praesentiam carnis recte dictum est discipulis; Me autem non semper habebitis. Idem in 1. Joh. Epist. Dominum jam in coelo sedentem manu contrectare non possumus, sed fide contingere. Quemadmodum Christus in nobis hic, ita nos ibi in illo sumus. Placuit haec distincte Patrum verbis pro-poponere,ut,quid & qualis ista sit manducatio corporis Christi Spiritualis, de qua ipse Seruator diserte Johannis Cap. 6.agit, illi qui litem hic nobis & controuersiam mouent, intelligant: simúlque Reformatis ejusmodi manducationem, velut sigmentum cerebri humani, & ridiculum commentum, obiicere desinant.
units.tr: on 1 Corinthians, vol. III: "We are that very body. For what is the bread? The body of Christ. And what do they become, what do they receive? The body of Christ. For just as bread, made of many grains, is united, so that the grains nowhere appear, yet they are indeed themselves, though their difference is not manifest because of the joining, so also we are joined among ourselves and with Christ." And Homily 81 on Matthew: "In fact, he makes us his body." Likewise: "We have been made the body of Christ and one." Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 8 on Ecclesiastes: "For this reason he who always is sets himself before us as food, so that, when we have received him into ourselves, we may become what he himself is." (7) Yet this does not happen through contact, nor through transubstantiation, or any local presence whatever, but through the apprehension of faith. Cyprian, in his sermon on the Lord's Supper: "Our union with him neither mixes persons nor unites substances, but joins affections and binds wills together by agreement." Augustine, Tractate 50 on John: "How shall I hold one who is absent? How shall I send my hand into heaven to hold him who sits there? Send there by faith, and you have held." Likewise: "It was rightly said to the disciples according to the presence of the flesh: You will not always have me." The same, on 1 John: "We cannot touch the Lord, who now sits in heaven, with the hand, but we touch him by faith. As Christ is in us here, so we are in him there." It has seemed good to set these things forth distinctly in the words of the Fathers, so that those who here raise this dispute and controversy against us may understand what, and of what kind, this spiritual eating of the body of Christ is, of which the Saviour himself speaks expressly in John chapter 6; and at the same time that they may cease to object to the Reformed such an eating, as if it were a figment of the human brain and a ridiculous invention.

units.la: III. Neque enim, ut de veritate manducationis spiritualis aliquid adhuc addamus, corpus & sanguis Christi, vera percepta fide, minùs sunt verus cibus, & verus potus animæ, quàm panis & vinum, utriusque symbola; sunt alimenta corporis sustentationi destinata. Non sunt imaginariæ aut phantasticæ operationes fidei, sed, ut ita loquar, realissimæ. Fides est illud, quo extant, quæ sperantur, & quæ demonstrat, quæ non videntur; Heb. 11. vers. 1. Fide Spiritualiter vivimus, Rom. 7. 17. Gal. 2. 20. & 3. 11. Heb. 10. 38. Fides est oculus, quo Christum pro nobis crucifixum, sanguinemque ejus pro peccatis susum; etiam remotissimum, siue loco, siue tempore; & quidem tanquam depictum Joh. 8. v. 56. Gal. 3. v. 1. intuemur. Fides est manus, qua sola Christum, ejusque meritum fidelis amplectitur, & per quam solam justificatur; Rom. 3. v. 28. Gal. 2. 16. Fides est os, quo anima famelica Christum, cœlestem panem, accipit, & ad sufficientem, salutarésque alimoniam, magna aviditate, comedit; Joh. 6. Fides sacram carnis & sanguinis Domini communicationem ita celebrat. brat, realemque agnoscit, quasi in offa & me dulas penetraret. Unde eximii praeterea fructus, ex arctissima cum Christo per fidem unione emergentes. Est ventilabrum illud, quo nostra purgantur corda. Act. 15. 9. Est sanctissimum illud philtrum, quod Deo nos placere facit, Heb. 11. 6. nostrisque ei opera grata reddit Gen. 4. 5. coll. Heb. 11. 4. Haec denique nobis vitam confert aeternam, Joh. 3. 15. 16. cap. 6. v 35. 40. 47. cap. 10. 9. Fidei igitur πίστεως, fidei substantia, & realissima realitas, fundamentum est verae & realis manducationis Spiritualis, quam Servator noster tam prolixe nobis praesenti Johannis loco commendat.
units.tr: III. For, to add something more about the truth of spiritual eating, the body and blood of Christ, when faith has truly received them, are no less true food and true drink of the soul than bread and wine, their symbols, are. They are nourishment designed to sustain the body. They are not imaginary or fanciful operations of faith but, so to speak, most real ones. Faith is that by which things hoped for are present, and which demonstrates things not seen; Heb. 11. vers. 1. We live spiritually by faith, Rom. 7. 17; Gal. 2. 20 and 3. 11; Heb. 10. 38. Faith is the eye by which we look upon Christ crucified for us and his blood shed for sins, even the most remote, whether in place or in time, and indeed as if it were painted before us: John 8. v. 56; Gal. 3. v. 1. Faith is the hand by which the faithful alone embraces Christ and his merit, and through which alone he is justified: Rom. 3. v. 28; Gal. 2. 16. Faith is the mouth by which the hungry soul receives Christ, the heavenly bread, and eats him with great eagerness as sufficient and saving nourishment: John 6. Faith celebrates the sacred communion of the flesh and blood of the Lord in this way, and acknowledges it as real, as if it penetrated to the bones and marrow. Hence there also arise outstanding fruits from the most intimate union with Christ through faith. It is that winnowing fan by which our hearts are cleansed: Acts 15. 9. It is that most holy love-charm which makes us please God, Heb. 11. 6, and makes our works pleasing to him, Gen. 4. 5, compared with Heb. 11. 4. Finally, it confers eternal life on us: John 3. 15, 16; ch. 6. vers. 35, 40, 47; ch. 10. 9. Faith, therefore, the πίστις [πίστεως], the substance of faith and its most real reality, is the foundation of the true and real spiritual eating, which our Saviour so fully commends to us in the present passage of John.

units.la: IV. B. Neque tamen manducationem Spiritualem cum Sacramentali prorsus esse eandem, ex institutA utriusque collatione, manifestum erit. Differunt enim I. Ratione materiae externae sive symbolorum: Sacramentalis enim, ut videmus, symbola sua habet, panem & vinum, Matth. 26. Mystica vero symbolis caret: imo ut in illa symbolum nomen rei significatae, ita in hac res significata symboli nomen obtinet. Carnem enim suam Christus panem vocat, verf. 51. II. Ratione formae externa tam substantialis, quam Accidentalis. In Sacramentali manducatione verba praeceptiva, determinativa & explicantia: actio etiam fractionis, distributionis observantur &c. In mystica hi actus distincti non requiruntur: imo, præmissa externorum symbolorum seu elementorum rejectione (occasio enim desumta est a miraculosa tum Mannæ, tum exigui panum commeatus virtute, quibus cibum efficaciorem longè, panem nempe cœlestem, seipsum, opponit) rem Spiritualem ejusque participationem, manducandi, bibendi; credendi, veniendi verbis Christus exprimit. III. Ratione finis partialis, qui in Cœna est, ἀναμνήσεως, recordatio mortis Christi. Luc. 21. 19. 1. Cor. 11. 15. In manducatione Spirituali est mystica illa unio de qua vers. 56. Qui edit carnem meam, bibit sanguinem meum, ille manet in me, & ego in ipso. In Cœna Domini οὐχ ἐπὶ non tantùm observatur inter Christum & fideles, sed & fidelium inter se 1. Cor. 11. At, ex mystica manducatione Christi tantùm & fidelium unio colligitur.
units.tr: IV. B. Nor, however, will it be plain from a comparison of the institution of each that spiritual eating is altogether the same as sacramental eating. For they differ, first, by reason of the external matter, or symbols. The sacramental eating, as we see, has its symbols, bread and wine: Matt. 26. The mystical eating lacks symbols. Indeed, just as in the former the symbol bears the name of the thing signified, so in the latter the thing signified bears the name of the symbol, for Christ calls his flesh bread: vers. 51. Second, by reason of the external form, both substantial and accidental. In sacramental eating the preceptive, determinative and explanatory words are observed, as are the actions of breaking and distributing, and so on. In the mystical eating these distinct acts are not required. Indeed, the external symbols or elements being set aside beforehand (the occasion being taken from the miraculous power of both the manna and the small supply of loaves, to which Christ opposes a far more efficacious food, namely the heavenly bread, himself), Christ expresses the spiritual thing and its participation in the words of eating, drinking, believing and coming. Third, by reason of the partial end, which in the Supper is the remembrance [ἀναμνήσεως] of the death of Christ: Luc. 21. 19; 1 Cor. 11. 15. In spiritual eating there is that mystical union of which v. 56 speaks: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. In the Lord's Supper the bond is observed not only [οὐχ ἐπὶ] between Christ and the faithful, but also among the faithful themselves: 1 Cor. 11. But from the mystical eating only the union of Christ and the faithful is inferred.

units.la: IV. Ratione effectorum. Participationis Sacramentalis effecta alia per se sunt, alia per accidens. Neque enim, malitia communicantium, suum semper illa assequitur fructum; Spiritualis verò manducatio fine suo nunquam frustratur. Unde Servator causam cum effectu indivulso nexu conjungit. Vide v. 51. 55. 56. 57. Vitam æternam, resurrectionem ad vitam, mutuam ἀξιοῦχον pollicetur omni, Spiritualiter se manducanti, id est, ut v. 44. explicatur, ad se venienti, & vers. 47. credenti. Hæc enim omnia esse συνώνυμα, ex locorum circumstantiis apparet. Atqui hæc cum Sacramentali manducatiocatione, omnium respectu subiectorum, reciprocari non possunt. Neque enim qui panem Domini, sed qui panem Dominum edunt, eximiorum illorum fructuum participes sunt. Unde Augustinus de verbis Domini in Evangelio, secundum Matthaeum ferm. II. Multi denique qui vel corde fidelo carnem illam manducant, & sanguinem bibunt, vel cum manducaverint & biberint, apostata fiunt. Numquid manent in Christo, aut Christus in eis? Sed profecto est quidam modus manducandi illam carnem, & bibendi illum sanguinem, quo modo qui manduca-verit & biberit, in Christo manet, & Christus in eo. Non ergo quocunque modo quisquam manducaverit carnem Christi, & biberit sanguinem Christi, manet in Christo, & in illo Christus, sed certo quodam modo, quem modum ipse utique videbat, quando ista dicebat. Ibid. Qui manducat carnem meam, & bibit sanguinem meum, in me manet & ego in illo, quomodo intelle-cturi sumus? Numquid etiam illos hic poterimus accipere, de quibus dicit Apostolus, quod judicium sibi manducent & bibant, cum ipsam carnem manducent & sanguinem bibant? Numquid & Judas, Magistri venditor & traditor impius, quamvis primum ipsum manibus ejus confectum Sacramentum, carnis & sanguinis ejus cum cateris discipulis, sicut ap-ertius Lucas Evangelista declarat, manducaret & biberet, mansit in Christo & Christus in eo. Et alibi: Qui manducat carnem meam, & bibit sanguinem meum, in me manet, & ego in eo. Ostendit, quidsit, non Sacramento tenus, sed revera corpus Christi manducare, & ejus sanguinem bibere, hoc est enim in Christo manere, ut in illo maneat & Christus. Sic enim hoc dixit, tanquam diceret: Qui non in me manet, & in quo ego non maneo, non se dicat aut existimet manducare corpus meum, aut bibere sanguinem meum. De Civit. Dei lib. 21. cap. 25. V. Sacramentalis manducatio vocatur συνάξις, congregatio, quòd in loco congregationis esset instituenda, vid. 1. Cor. 11. In mystica verò, ipse qui manducat, templum Christi est, & Spiritùs sancti. Ad nullum sive publicum illa restringiturlocum, sive privatum; sed, prout (ita Ioh. 4. 23. legimus) cœtus Christianorum Proseuchæ sunt, ubicunque Deus in Spiritu & Veritate adoratur: Ita & manducatio Spiritualis, ab omni locorum descriptione libera est. Unde universalitas: Quisquis ederit; Quisquis crediderit &c. VI. Subjecti etiam ratione manducatio per Johannem descripta, à Sacramentali differt. Illius Subjectum sunt veri fideles tantùm, illi nempe, qui describuntur vers. 51. 56. 57. Hujus verò vocati, quamdiu publicis scandalis & impietate vitæ, his se sacris ipsi non arcent. Unde vocatio ad Convivium Sacramentale, conditionata est, officium jubens; ad mysticam manducationem invitans, stipulatoria beneficii, absoluta.
units.tr: IV. By reason of effects. The effects of sacramental participation are partly essential and partly incidental. For it does not always attain its fruit, because of the wickedness of the communicants; spiritual eating, however, is never frustrated of its end. Hence the Saviour joins cause and effect in an unbroken bond. See vv. 51, 55, 56, 57. He promises eternal life, resurrection to life, and mutual [ἀξιοῦχον] to everyone who eats him spiritually, that is, as v. 44 explains, who comes to him, and v. 47 adds, who believes. That all these are synonymous appears from the circumstances of the passages. But these cannot be reciprocated with sacramental eating, with respect to all subjects. For it is not those who eat the bread of the Lord, but those who eat the Lord's bread, who are partakers of those outstanding fruits. Hence Augustine, on the words of the Lord in the Gospel according to Matthew, sermon II: Finally, many who eat that flesh and drink that blood with a faithful heart, or who, after they have eaten and drunk, become apostates... do they abide in Christ, or Christ in them? But certainly there is a certain manner of eating that flesh and drinking that blood, by which he who eats and drinks abides in Christ, and Christ in him. Therefore it is not in whatever manner anyone eats the flesh of Christ and drinks the blood of Christ that he abides in Christ and Christ in him, but in a certain manner, which manner he surely had in view when he said these things. Ibid. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him: in what way are we to understand this? Can we perhaps take here also those of whom the Apostle says that they eat and drink judgment to themselves, although they eat the very flesh and drink the blood? And Judas, the betrayer of the Master and impious traitor, although he first ate and drank the sacrament made by his own hands, of his flesh and blood with the other disciples, as the Evangelist Luke declares more plainly, did he abide in Christ and Christ in him? And elsewhere: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. He shows what it is to eat the body of Christ and drink his blood, not merely sacramentally but in reality: for this is to abide in Christ, that Christ also abide in him. For he spoke as if to say: he who does not abide in me, and in whom I do not abide, let him not say or think that he eats my body or drinks my blood. Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 21, ch. 25. V. Sacramental eating is called synaxis [συνάξις], a gathering, because it was to be instituted in a place of assembly: see 1 Cor. 11. In the mystical eating, however, he who eats is himself a temple of Christ and of the Holy Spirit. It is restricted to no place, whether public or private; but, as we read in John 4. 23, the assemblies of Christians are houses of prayer wherever God is worshipped in Spirit and truth. So too spiritual eating is free from every description of place. Hence its universality: Whoever shall eat; whoever shall believe, etc. VI. The eating described by John also differs from the sacramental in respect of its subjects. The subjects of the former are only true believers, namely those who are described in vv. 51, 56, 57. Of the latter, those who are called do not keep themselves away from these sacred rites, so long as they are not kept away by public scandals and impiety of life. Hence the invitation to the sacramental feast is conditional, a command of duty; while the invitation to mystical eating is stipulatory of a benefit, absolute.

units.la: G
units.tr: G

units.la: VII. Adjunctorum etiam respectu differunt. 1. Temporis; Manducatio Sacramentalis, vel singulis diebus, vel diebus Dominicis, vel diebus festis in Ecclesia primitiva celebrari consueverat: manducatio haec vel singulis momentis, domi, foris, belli, ruri, locum habere poterit inter ultimos agonizantium halitus. 2. Necessitatis. Manducatio Spiritualis ad salutem simpliciter in adultis necessaria: Sacramentalis non item. 3. Amplitudinis. Amplior est usus, respectu Subjecti, manducationis Sacramentalis, quam Spiritualis.
units.tr: VII. They also differ in respect of their adjuncts. 1. Of time: sacramental eating was customarily celebrated in the primitive Church either every day, or on the Lord's days, or on feast days. Spiritual eating may take place at every moment, at home, abroad, in war, in the country, even among the last breaths of the dying. 2. Of necessity: spiritual eating is simply necessary to salvation in adults; sacramental eating is not so. 3. Of extent: with respect to subjects, the use of sacramental eating is wider than that of spiritual eating.

units.la: IV. C. Satis, ut caetera mittamus; quae diximus, probant Johannis Cap. VI. non de Coena agi proprie, sed de manducatione mystica & Spirituali, quae ab illa tot respectibus differt: Eadem & a Patribus, ut postea audiemus, recepta est sententia, & in quam Adversarii nonnulli, viri gravissimi, manibus pedibusque concedunt; adeo, ut audax nimis Coffetaei Pontificii effatum sit: Constanter opinari omnes Catholicos (Papistas sic appellat) in hoc sexto capite peculiariter de Eucharistia sermonem esse. Errat bonus vir, non modo aliter, & nobiscum quidem, sentiunt Gabriel Biel in Canonem Lect. 84. p, m. 251. b. Nicolaus Cusanus, Epist. 7. ad Bohemos; Cajetanus Part. 3. quaest. 80. art. 8. Johannes Hefelius, lib. de communione sub utraque specie. Iansenius cap. 59. Concord. Evangel. Ruardus Tapperus, Artic. 15. Waldensis, T. 2. de Sacramentis. cap. 91. Johannes de de Ragusio, de Communione sub utraque. Armacanus, lib. 9. c. 8. Sed & Johannes Ferus in c. 6. Johannis, & Aeneas Silvius, Epist. 130. circa medium. Qui quidem non modo agnoscunt, hoc caput de Sacramentali manducatione non agere, sed & rationes luculentas assertioni suae addunt; incommoda, quae ad Ecclesiam Romanam inde redundant, deteguntque; objectionesque fidei domesticorum refutant. Nos, quia tam manifestus consensus causae nostrae non uno expedit nomine, unum tantum & alterum audiemus, disertissime de hac manducatione, ex mente & ore Reformatorum, quo ad praesentem Controversiam, loquentes. Gabrielis Biel verba sunt: Ad Joh. 6. Nisi manducaveritis &c. dicitur; quod in toto illo capite Dominus loquitur de manducatione & bibitione Spirituali, quae non distinguuntur: quia, qui manducat Spiritualiter, bibit Spiritualiter, & e converso; & non carnali neque Sacramentali: sicut carnaliter verba Christi intelligentes abierunt retrorsum. Unde Christus sua verba manentibus discipulis exponens, dixit: Spiritus est qui vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam, scilicet sine Spiritu: Verba, quae ego loquutus sum vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt. Sic & Sacramentalis communio non est simpliciter necessaria, sed Spiritualis.
units.tr: IV. C. To pass over the rest, what I have said proves that John 6 is not properly about the Supper, but about the mystical and spiritual eating, which differs from it in so many respects. This is also the view received by the Fathers, as we shall hear later, and some of our opponents, very weighty men, concede it hands and feet. So the bold claim of the Papist Coffetaeus is wrong: "All Catholics (as he calls the Papists) hold consistently that the sermon in this sixth chapter is particularly about the Eucharist." The good man is mistaken. Not only do these men think otherwise, and with us: Gabriel Biel on the Canon, Lect. 84, p. 251, b; Nicolaus Cusanus, Epistle 7 to the Bohemians; Cajetan, Part 3, question 80, article 8; Johannes Hefelius, the book on communion under both kinds; Jansenius, chapter 59 of the Concord of the Gospels; Ruardus Tapper, Article 15; Waldensis, vol. 2, On the Sacraments, chapter 91; Johannes de Ragusio, On Communion under Both Kinds; Armachanus, book 9, chapter 8. Also Johannes Ferus on John 6, and Aeneas Silvius, Epistle 130, near the middle. These men not only acknowledge that this chapter is not about sacramental eating, but also add clear reasons for their assertion. They expose the inconveniences that flow from this into the Roman Church, and they refute the objections of their own people. Since so clear an agreement in our cause does not need one name, we shall hear only one or two, speaking most clearly about this eating, from the mind and mouth of the Reformed, as far as the present controversy goes. The words of Gabriel Biel are these: "On John 6, 'Unless you eat,' etc.: in that whole chapter the Lord speaks of spiritual eating and drinking, and these are not distinguished, because whoever eats spiritually drinks spiritually, and conversely; and it is not carnal or sacramental eating. Just as those who understood Christ's words carnally went away backwards. Hence Christ, explaining his words to the disciples who remained, said: 'It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing,' that is, without the Spirit. 'The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.' So too sacramental communion is not simply necessary, but spiritual."

units.la: Æneas Silvii Epist. 130. verba sunt: Negat Iohannes, ut ait, imo negat apud Iohannem, Dominus vitam esse cuipiam, nisi carnem suam comederit. Quibus verbis non minus utriusque speciei communionem, quàm baptismatis undam mandatam censes. Vetus hæc Armenorum insania fuit, qui natos, ut in lucem veniebant, mox baptisatos, mox altaris Sacramento reficiebant, quod & vos ajunt facere, qui dementes atque infantes ad Eucharistia libamenta vocatis, inhonorantes divinissimum Sacramentum, communionemque Pauli despicientes, quando ad Corinthios scribens ait : Probet seipsum homo, & sic de pane illo edat, & de calice bibat. Quomodo se parvuli & dementes probare possunt, quibus nec certus, nec verus rationis est usus. Sed non est in Evangelio Iohannis quem ibi sensus ascribitis. Non bibitio Sacramentalis illic præcipitur; sed Spiritualis insinuatur. Nam sanguis Christi triplicem potum, Alberti Magni sententia, tradidit, in eo sermone quem de Christi corpore, non minus subtiliter quàm veraciter edidit. Est enim potus Sacramentalis, quem soli Sacerdotes accipiunt. Est intellectualis, qui plebibus Christianis sub specie panis ministratur. Et est Spiritualis, quo salvandi omnes utuntur, incarnationem passionemque Domini pia & assidua meditatione recolentes. Et de hac bibitione Dominus apud Iohanne præcipit, sicut verborum Evangelista series lucu lenter ostendit. Nam, cum dixisset Dominus: Caro mea verè est cibus, & sanguis meus verè est potus; qui manducat meam carnem, & bibit meum sanguinem, in me manet & ego in eo.
units.tr: The words of Aeneas Silvius, Epistle 130, are these: "John says, or rather says in John, that the Lord is life to no one unless he eats his flesh. By these words you would think the communion of both kinds is commanded no less than the washing of baptism. This was the old madness of the Armenians, who as soon as children were born baptized them and at once fed them with the sacrament of the altar. You are said to do this too, who call madmen and infants to the tastings of the Eucharist, dishonouring the most divine sacrament and despising the communion of Paul, when he writes to the Corinthians: 'Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup.' How can little children and madmen examine themselves, when they have no certain or true use of reason? But the sense you read into the Gospel of John is not there. No sacramental drinking is commanded there, but spiritual drinking is hinted at. For the blood of Christ, according to Albert the Great's view, gave a threefold drink, in that sermon on the body of Christ which he published no less subtly than truly. There is a sacramental drink, which only the priests receive. There is an intellectual drink, which is given to Christian people under the form of bread. And there is a spiritual drink, which all who are to be saved use, recalling the incarnation and passion of the Lord by pious and constant meditation. It is of this drinking that the Lord commands in John, as the sequence of the evangelist's words plainly shows. For when the Lord had said: 'My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink; he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.'"

units.la: Multi audientes ex discipulis ejus dixerunt: Durus est hic sermo, quis potest eum audire? Sciens autem Jesus apud semetipsum, quare murmuraverant de hoc discipuli ejus, dixit eis; Hoc vos scandalizat; si ergo videritis filium hominis ascendentem ubi erat prius. Spiritus est qui vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam. Verba, quae ego loquutus sum vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt. Sed sunt ex vobis, qui non credunt. Declarat Dominus his verbis, non carnalis esus aut potus illic, sed Spiritualis arcana mysterii contineri, dum ait, Spiritus est, qui vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam. Et iterum: Verba quae loquutus sum vobis, Spiritus & vita sunt. Vis aperte cognoscere, quomodo de Spirituali manducatione, qua fit per fidem, loquatur Evangelista, adverte qua dicit Dominus: Qui manducat & bibit, instantis non futuri temporis sunt verba. Erant igitur, dum sic loqueretur Dominus, qui manducabant, & qui bibebant eum. Nondum passus Dominus erat, nec adhuc institutum fuit Sacramentum. Quomodo ergo manducabant bibebantque Christum, nisi spiritualiter per fidem & charitatem, credentes in eum & facientes opera ejus. Nam & prius dixerat: Ego sum panis vitae, qui venit ad me, non esuriet, & qui credit in me, non sitiet unquam. Qui credebant in eum, & opera sectabantur ejus, hi carnem edebant ejus, hi potabant sanguinem. Atqui hic verior est Evangelii sensus, quia aliter edi caro, aut bibi Christi sanguis non poterat. Fuit enim figurata loquutio Domini; sicut & Samaritanæ, & in cruce sitire se dixit, quia fidem illius, & nostram salutem sitiebat. Sic glossator intelligit hoc Evangelium; sic magnus Augustinus, doctrina & verecundia justa nobilis, cujus tanta gloria est, ut nullius laudibus crescat, vituperatione minuatur; quo posito, si quis Vicleffum Rochezanamque sequitur, luci tenebras, veritati mendacium praefert. Quid plura? Nonne Dominus in textu Evangelii dicit: Ego sum panis vitæ, qui venit ad me, non esuriet, & qui credit in me non sitiet unquam. E'ccum tibi panem, cibus & potus est! qui esuriem tollit & sitim. Cui tollit & quomodo? Credenti tollit, per charitatem tollit. Nam qui fidem rectam habet, & opera facit digna fide, hic est, qui carnem Domini manducat, & sanguinem bibit, & acquirit vitam æternam: mundo mortuus Christo vives. Sic quod de Iohanne vobis assumitis, nostra sententia, non vestra confert.
units.tr: "Many of his disciples who heard said, 'This is a hard saying; who can hear it?' But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples murmured at this, said to them, 'Does this offend you? If then you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before.' It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." The Lord declares by these words that there is contained here not carnal eating or drinking, but the hidden mystery of the Spirit, when he says, "It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing." And again: "The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life." If you want to know clearly how the evangelist speaks of spiritual eating, which takes place through faith, note what the Lord says: "He who eats and drinks"; these are words of the present and not of the future time. So those who ate him and drank him were there while the Lord spoke thus. The Lord had not yet suffered, nor had the sacrament yet been instituted. How then did they eat and drink Christ, except spiritually, through faith and love, believing in him and doing his works? For he had said before: "I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst." Those who believed in him and followed his works, these ate his flesh and drank his blood. Yet this is the truer sense of the Gospel, because otherwise his flesh could not be eaten or his blood drunk. For the Lord's words were figurative, just as when he said to the Samaritan woman, and on the cross, that he thirsted, because he thirsted for her faith and our salvation. So the glossator understands this Gospel; so great Augustine, a noble man of learning and of proper modesty, whose glory is so great that it is not increased by praise nor diminished by blame. If anyone, once this is laid down, follows Wycliffe and Rokycana, he prefers darkness to light and falsehood to truth. What more? Does not the Lord say in the text of the Gospel: "I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst"? Here is bread for you; food and drink, which takes away hunger and thirst. To whom does it take them away, and how? It takes them away from the believer, it takes them away through love. For he who has true faith and does works worthy of faith, this is the one who eats the flesh of the Lord and drinks his blood, and obtains eternal life: dead to the world, you will live to Christ. So what you take from John for yourselves supports our opinion, not yours.

units.la: Johannis Feri in Johan.Cap.6. superest suffragium, dignum, quod hoc etiam loco infertur. Atqui vere ardua sunt, quæ Christus hic dicit, nempe nedum possibile, sed & necessarium esse, ut manducemus carnem ejus. Hoc autem verbum palàm arguit, Christum in hoc capite deSpirituali manducatione etiam loqui. Fides enim in Christum pro nobis mortuum adeò necessaria est, ut sine ipsa neque salus, neque vita cuiquam contingere possit. Qui enim non credit, jam judicatus est. Dicere autem, quod sine corporali perceptione Sacramenti nulli possit contingere vita, admodum durum, imò temerarium & falsum est. Hinc enim sequeretur, quod Patres Veteris Testamenti, imò & Iohannes Baptista non haberent vitam. Deinde etiam sequeretur, quod pueri etiam baptizati, ante annos discretionis morientes, non possent salvari, eò quod non accepissent Sacramentum. Sequeretur item, quod pueris etiam dandum esset hoc Sacramentum, alioquin non victuros: quemadmodum & quidam faciunt contra expressum Pauli verbum, qui vult, ut sumturus Sacramentum prius probet seipsum, quod pueri non possunt. Praterea sequeretur, quod qui articulo temporis, vel alia quadam necessitate constringuntur (sicut nonnulli Confessores, quos nec baptizari aqua, persequutionis & mortis instantia permisit) non possent sanari, quantumvis Sacramentum desiderarent. Demum, si Christus hic de sumtione Sacramenti loqueretur, sequeretur, quod omnes, qui Sacramentum sumunt, salvarentur, cum Christus expresse dicat: Qui manducat meam carnem &c. habet vitam æternam. Atqui etiam Iudas Sacramentum sumsit, nec tamen vitam habuit. Imò Paulus manifestè di-cit, oit, aliquos Sacramentum hoc sumere in judicium, & condemnationem. Unde clarum est, quod Christus de spirituali manducatione, qua fit per fidem, non de Sacramentali loquitur.
units.tr: There remains the testimony of John Ferus on John 6, worth inserting here too. "Yet what Christ says here is truly hard: that it is not only possible but necessary that we eat his flesh." This word plainly shows that Christ in this chapter also speaks of spiritual eating. For faith in Christ who died for us is so necessary that without it neither salvation nor life can come to anyone. For he who does not believe is already judged. But to say that life cannot come to anyone without the bodily reception of the sacrament is very harsh, indeed rash and false. For it would follow that the fathers of the Old Testament, and even John the Baptist, would not have life. Further, it would follow that children who have been baptized and die before the age of discretion could not be saved, because they had not received the sacrament. It would follow also that this sacrament would have to be given to children too, otherwise they would not live; as some indeed do, against the express word of Paul, who wills that one who is about to receive the sacrament first examine himself, which children cannot do. Besides, it would follow that those who are bound by the moment of death or some other necessity (as some confessors were, whom the pressing danger of persecution and death did not allow to be baptized with water) could not be healed, however much they desired the sacrament. Lastly, if Christ were speaking here about receiving the sacrament, it would follow that all who receive the sacrament are saved, since Christ expressly says: "He who eats my flesh, etc., has eternal life." Yet Judas also received the sacrament, and yet did not have life. Indeed Paul plainly says that some receive this sacrament to judgement and condemnation. Hence it is clear that Christ speaks of spiritual eating, which takes place through faith, and not of sacramental eating.

units.la: Pergit deinceps Ferus, & instantias superioribus argumentis oppositas solvit.
units.tr: Ferus goes on to answer the objections raised against the earlier arguments.

units.la: V. Exscripsi haec, tum quod citati authores, obvii omnibus non sint, tum etiam, quod ipse quoque vir doctissimus existimet, Aeneam Silvium, cum aliis recentioribus, manducationem Spiritualem Joh. cap. 6. intellexisse, propterea tantum, sive quod multum, sive maxime adversari crederent communioni laicorum, sub sola specie panis: Alias illos urgere rationes, solidas, praegnantes, attenta & seria nos locorum inspectio docebit. Non omnes Doctores Pontificii, qui de Spirituali manducatione textum explicant, communionis vel sub una, vel duabus Speciebus meminerunt; caeteris occasio tantum est, non argumentum, cur locum sibi ad evincendam communionem sub utraque specie, metuendum non existiment. Non propterea, quod utramque speciem Christus flagitaret in administratione Coenae, praesenti capite, Aeneas Silvius, Biel, Ferus, ad manducationem illud retulerunt Spiritualem; sed quia de Spirituali manducatione agere Servatorem certissimis collegerunt argumentis, Sacramentalem non obtrudendam prudenter suis suaserunt, ne, praeter necessitatem, novis intricarentur difficul-tatatibus. Hoc consilium Iansenii erat, Gandavensis Episcopi, Reflat, inquit, totum hunc locum convenientissime intelligi de manducatione Spirituali, quae est per fidem, in carnem traditam in cruce, & in sanguinem effusum pro nobis, quomodo ut intelligatur, & praecedentia & sequentia satis exigunt, & sic cessant omnes difficultates, quae oriuntur, si de Sacramentali manducatione accipitur : Harm. Evangel. cap. 59.
units.tr: I have copied these passages both because the authors cited are not easy for everyone to find, and because the learned man himself thinks that Aeneas Silvius, along with other more recent writers, understood the spiritual eating in John 6 only because they believed it strongly opposed the communion of the laity under one kind alone. A careful and serious examination of the places will show that they had other reasons, which are sound and weighty. Not all the Papist teachers who explain the text of spiritual eating mention communion under one kind or under both kinds. For the others it is merely an occasion, not a reason, for thinking they must fear that this passage will be used to prove communion under both kinds. Aeneas Silvius, Biel and Ferus did not refer this chapter to eating in spirit because Christ demanded both kinds in the administration of the Supper. They did so because they gathered from very certain arguments that the Saviour is speaking of spiritual eating, and they wisely advised that sacramental eating should not be forced on the text, lest, beyond necessity, they become entangled in new difficulties. This was also the view of Jansenius, the Bishop of Ghent. "I think," he says, "that this whole passage is most suitably understood of the spiritual eating which takes place through faith, in the flesh delivered on the cross and the blood shed for us. That it should be understood in this way, both what goes before and what follows sufficiently require, and so all the difficulties which arise, if it is taken of sacramental eating, cease." Harmony of the Gospels, chapter 59.

units.la: VI. Et certe, magno Ecclesiae Romanae incommodo Caput 6. Iohannis a verf. 48. de manducatione Sacramentali intelligi, miror Virum doctissimum non praevidere. Primo enim, Transsubstantiatio Romana, veram, realem, substantialem, corporalem in Coena carnis Christi tam praesentiam urget, quam manducationem. Christus vero ex professo eam refutat. Etenim inter manducationem crassam, id est, naturalem (neque enim ulla dari potest manducatio naturalis, quam sic voco ratione objecti sensibilis seu naturalis, corporis nempe Physici, quae non sit crassa, id est, quae non fiat per contactum, comminutionem, abligurit ionem;) & mysticam, Christus hoc loco manifestum instituit discrimen. Illam cum Judaei ex superioribus verbis male & imperite collegissent, Christus verf. 52. tollit, & ita quidem, ut suam, ante omnia, ponat & confirmet sententiam, verf. 53. Omnino suam carnem esse connedendam, & sanguinem bibendum; carnem suam vere esse cibum & sanguinem vere potum. Umbras cessàsse, iplum jam adesse corpus. Mannam sui, tanquam panis coelestis, typum tantum gessisse. Cum vero vidisset, discipulos etiam suos hac offendi assertione v. 60. 61. explicuit deinceps, quomodo caro sua sit verus cibus, & sanguis verus potus. Caro cibus est, κατὰ πνεῦμα Spiritualiter, accepta: proinde & percepta per veram fidem. Fides enim est os illud, quo cibum coelestem admittimus, & per quam manemus in Christo, ille vero in nobis verf. 56. Fides est, quae vivere nos facit per Christum, v. 57. Qualis autem vita, talis nutritio. At vita in Christo Spiritualis. Ergo & cibus: Ergo & ὀρτανον ἐκτικόν, quae omnia inter se sunt relata. Atque hoc est, quod Christus murmurantibus objicit Apostolis: Spiritus est, qui vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam. Verba quae ego loquor vobis, Spiritus sunt, & vita sunt, verf. 63. Quasi dicat: Quid in istis haeretis? Cur hac mea loquendi ratione offendimini? Et vos ignoratis, Spiritualiter esse intelligenda, non carnaliter, quae de carnis meae loquutus sum manducatione? Non enim de corporis alimento, adeoque de carne, corporis mei parte, hoc loco sermo erat; sed de nutritione Spirituali, eamque sequente conjunctione vestri, ceu membrorum, mecum, capite v. 63. de vita vestra per me, quae temporalis non est, sed aeterna, 57. ad quam vos suscitaturus sum ultimo die, verf. 54. Ita Spiritus, id est, sensus spiritualiter sumtus, verbaque recte intellecta vivificant : caro vero ; verba carnaliter & crasse accepta nihil prosunt. Cum ergo verba mea Spiritus sint, de Spiritualibus agant ; cum de vita, non temporali, sed aeterna, nutritioneq; mystica, qua in unum coalescimus corpus, ego loquar, cur crassum & carnalem mihi affingatis sensum? Justissima igitur haec Servatoris fuit ἐπιστολὴ, qui, postquam operose Judaeis monstrasset, vere carnem suam cibum esse, mox manducandi modum addit Spiritualem, carnali, i. e. naturali remoto. ὁ λέγει τοῦτο ἐχι πνευματικῶς δεῖ (ἀ πνεῦ ἐμὲ ἀκούειν. ὁ δὲ σαρκικῶς ἀκούσας, οὐδὲν ὠφελεῖται, οὐδὲ τῇ κεφαλῇ ἀπολαύσει. Quod dicit, ejusmodi est : Spiritualiter mea verba intelligenda sunt. Nam qui corporaliter accipit, nihil proficit, nec ullum inde emolumentum percipit ; ita Graeci enarratores Christi verba interpretantur. Et Maldonatus Jesuita: Verum cibum, & verum potum vocat, quia vere animum nutrit, & vitam aeternam illis praebet. Sicut v. 32. vocavit se panem verum, non utique natura; nec enim vere & proprie, si naturam spectes, panis est ; sed effectu, quia vere praestat, quod panis praestare solet, cum ad id fiat, ut vere homines vivant ; & cap. 25. verf. 1. vocat se vitem veram, non quod vera sit vitis, sed quod id, quod vitis facit, ut sarmenta sua nutriat atque sustentet, multo ipse verius facit ; in Joh. 6. verf. 55.
units.tr: VI. Indeed, I am surprised that so learned a man does not foresee that John chapter 6, from verse 48, to be understood of sacramental eating, is a great embarrassment to the Roman Church. For, first, Roman transubstantiation insists on a true, real, substantial and bodily presence of Christ's flesh in the Supper, just as it insists on eating it. But Christ expressly refutes this. Between crass eating, that is, natural eating (for no natural eating can be given, which I call natural from the nature of the sensible or natural object, namely a physical body, that is not crass, that is, that does not happen by contact, comminution or licking up), and mystical eating, Christ here makes a clear distinction. When the Jews had wrongly and unskilfully gathered the former from the preceding words, Christ, in verse 52, removes it, and does so in such a way that he first sets down and confirms his own opinion in verse 53: that his flesh must indeed be eaten and his blood drunk; that his flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink. The shadows have ceased, and the body itself is now present. The manna was only a type of himself, as the heavenly bread. But when he saw that his own disciples were offended by this assertion (v. 60, 61), he then explained how his flesh is true food and his blood true drink. The flesh is food, spiritually understood [κατὰ πνεῦμα], and so it is received and taken in through true faith. For faith is that mouth by which we admit the heavenly food, and through which we remain in Christ, and he in us (v. 56). Faith is what makes us live through Christ (v. 57). But what kind of life, such is the nourishment. Yet the life in Christ is spiritual. Therefore the food is also spiritual. Therefore it is also an organ of nourishment [ὄργανον ἑκτικόν]; all these things are related to one another. And this is what Christ says to the murmuring Apostles: It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit and are life (v. 63). As if he said: What are you finding in these things? Why are you offended by my manner of speaking? Do you not know that what I have said about the eating of my flesh is to be understood spiritually, not carnally? For the discourse here was not about bodily food, and so not about flesh, a part of my body, but about spiritual nourishment; and the conjunction that follows, of you as members with me as head (v. 63), concerns your life through me, which is not temporal but eternal (v. 57), and to which I shall raise you up on the last day (v. 54). Thus the Spirit, that is, the sense taken spiritually and the words rightly understood, give life; but the flesh, that is, words taken carnally and crassly, profit nothing. Since then my words are spirit, and deal with spiritual things, and since I am speaking of a life that is not temporal but eternal, and of a mystical nourishment by which we grow together into one body, why do you fasten on me a crass and carnal sense? Therefore this reply of the Saviour was most just. Having laboriously shown the Jews that his flesh is truly food, he at once adds the mode of eating as spiritual, removing the carnal, that is, the natural. [ὁ λέγει τοῦτο ἐστι πνευματικῶς δεῖ ἀκούειν·] "What he says, that is, that it is to be heard spiritually. For whoever hears carnally profits nothing and gains no advantage from it," so the Greek expositors interpret Christ's words. And the Jesuit Maldonatus: "He calls it true food and true drink, because it truly nourishes the soul and gives them eternal life. Just as in v. 32 he called himself the true bread, not in nature (for if you look at nature, it is not truly and properly bread), but in effect, because it truly does what bread usually does, namely makes men truly live; and in chapter 15, verse 1, he calls himself the true vine, not because he is a true vine, but because he does much more truly what the vine does, namely nourishes and sustains its branches." On John 6, verse 55.

units.la: II. Verba : Nisi manducaveritis carnem filii hominis, & biberitis sanguinem ejus, non habebitis vitam in vobis, Tropicè debent intelligi. Ergo & verba Institutionis. Antecedens supra, totidem Augustini verbis propositum. Consequens fluit ex hypothesi & æquipollentia, quam larga nobis manu Adversarii largiuntur. Et hoc argumentum non obscurè pro causa bona militat.
units.tr: II. The words, "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you," must be understood figuratively. Therefore so must the words of institution. The antecedent is set out above, in the very words of Augustine. The consequent follows from the hypothesis and the equivalence which our opponents grant us with a generous hand. And this argument clearly fights on behalf of a good cause.

units.la: III. Christus Joh. VI. omnem tollit sive sensualem, sive corporalem præsentiam atque manducationem. E. & Pontificiam.
units.tr: III. Christ in John 6 removes every presence and every eating, whether sensual or bodily. Therefore also the Papist presence and eating.

units.la: IV. Christus Capernaiticam damnat anthropophagiam: Ergo & Romanam αυτοφαγίαν. Nullum enim inter illam & hanc vel fingi potest discrimen. Ajunt, quòd illi aperta conceperint manducationem, hi tectam: illi crassam, hi subtilem; illi frustillatim discerptam; hi integram proponant carnem. Hoc verò est à scopo aberrare. Neq; enim disputat Servator contra rem, contra carnem suam, ejusque participationem, quæ omnino tota nostra fieri debet; sed contra modum rei, cujus distinctæ duæ sunt species, carnalis, localis, seu corporalis (sive frustillatim fiat discerpendo, sive in totum abliguriendo, & in stomachum recondendo) quam simpliciter removet omnem, verf. 63. & Spiritualis, per fidem, quam ponit ibidem.
units.tr: IV. Christ condemns the Capernaite man-eating. Therefore also the Roman self-eating [αὐτοφαγία]. For no distinction can be imagined between that and this. They say that the former conceived an open eating, the latter a hidden one; the former crass, the latter subtle; the former proposes the flesh cut into pieces, the latter the flesh whole. But this is to wander from the point. For the Saviour does not dispute against the thing, against his flesh and its participation, which altogether ought to become wholly ours; he disputes against the manner of the thing, which has two distinct kinds, carnal and local, or bodily (whether it is done by tearing it in pieces, or by licking it all up and storing it in the stomach). He removes this altogether, simply, in verse 63, and sets up the spiritual manner, by faith, which he likewise posits there.

units.la: Imò, verisimile sit, sive Capernaitas, sive discipulos tam crassis de manducatione Corporis Christi dedisse locum cogitationibus, quàm absurdis quidem decretis, papalinodiis, Ecclesia Romana Transsubstantiationem exprimi voluit? Credamus, Capernaitarum fuisse mentem, carnem Christi adesse sensualiter, non solum Sacramento, sed in veritate manibus Sacerdotum tractari, frangi, & fidelium dentibus atteri? Est & Adversariorum; ut ex Berengarii manifestum est Palinodia, à Nicolao Papa dictata; de Consec. dist. 2. Can. Berengarius. Crediderint Capernaitae, sed plane Creatores futuros sui Creatoris, ut veram Christi carnem comederent, & realitatem praesentiae carnalis defenderent? Credunt & Adversarii. Unde Stella Clericorum: Quid ergo retribuam Domino pro omnibus, qua retribuit mihi? Ille qui creavit me, dedit mihi creare se: qui creavit me sine me, creatur mediante me. Crediderint (quod credidisse tamen ego non credo) Christum etiam à brutis posse devorari? Credunt & Adversarii. Communis haec est Scholae sententia: Brutum comedens Sacramentum, verum Christi corpus devorare, ut habet Iosephus Anglus, qui flores Scholasticorum colligit, Quaest. de suscip. Euchar. Artic. 3. Unde Alexander Alensis; Part. 4. q. 45. m. 1. Si canis vel porcus deglutiret hostiam consecratam integram, non video, quare corpus Domini, non simul trajiceretur in ventrem canis vel porci. Antonini, Archiepiscopi Florentini, addere placet tanto Mysta & mysterio dignam observationem ex 3. Par. de defect. Missae cap. 6. l. 3. Si mus, inquit, aut aliud animal per negligentiam tiam species Sacramenti comederit, ille per cujus negligentiam hoc accidit, debet 40. diebus pœnitere: Et debet mus capi, si potest, & comburi: & cinis juxta altare reponi. Sed Petrus de Palude dicit, quod mus exenterari debet, & mus quidem comburi, & cinis in piscinam conjici; pars autem hostiæ, si eam horret homo sumere, debet in tabernaculo reverenter poni, & tamdiu ibi dimitti, quousque naturaliter consumetur. Ipsa autem hostia nequaquam debet in piscinam projici, sicut fecit quidam Sacerdos de musca reperta post consecrationem in calice. Et si quidem homo esset tanti fervoris, quod hujusmodi non horreret, sed sumeret, commendandus esset, si tamen esset jejunus. Sic B. Hugo Cluniacensis commendavit Goderanum, sumendo portiunculas hostiæ, quas leprosus cum vilissimo sputo evomuerat; dicens cra ticulam Laurentii fuisse tolerabiliorem. Quid? quod Creatorem hunc a Creatura creatum indignissimis quibusvis modis tractari, abjici in latrinam, evomi, a muribus corrodi, ita mordicus defendunt, ut secus sentientibus dicam hæreseos pridem impegerint. Accidit enim hoc Andreæ Bonagetæ, Minoritæ Anno Christi 1371. Statuit hic (quod tamen sub excommunicationis pœna prædicari erat vetitum) quod si hostia consecrata cadat aut projiciatur in cloacam, lutum, seu aliquem turpem locum, quod, Speciebus remanentibus, sub eis esse desinat Corpus Christi: & redeat subsubstantia panis. Quòd si hostia consecrata à mure corrodatur, seu à bruto sumatur, quòd, remanentibus dictis specie[bus], sub eis esse desinat corpus Christi, & redeat substantia panis. Quòd si hostia consecrata à iusto, vel à peccatore sumatur, quòd, dum species dentibus teritur, Christus ad cœlum rapitur, & in ventrem hominis non trajicitur. Sed nimis hic verecundus & modestus erat Theologus. Cæteris, ut cum auctore Tract. Corp. Christi loquamur; non est absurdum, quòd descendat ad stomachum hominis aut animalis, cum etiam in fœtida pyxide vel latrina possit poni, vel etiam in cacabo pleno aqua bullienti, sicut fecit quidam Iudæus Parisinus. Creditne doctissimus Vir, hæc talia vel Capernaitas, vel discipulos hic Christi, per febrim cogitâsse? Et tamen, si cogitâssent, si credidissent, si decretis sanxissent, in Scholis docuissent, Ecclesiæ Romanæ per omnia convenirent. Quodnam igitur, amabò, discrimen vel fingi speciosè hic queat? Imò, quis non animadvertat, longè absurdiorem de reali præsentia Christi opinionem, publicè ab Ecclesia Romana receptam, quàm Capernaitæ vel cogitationibus ausi fuissent consequi? Illi non crediderunt, vel per Dei voluntatem, & tot diserta præcepta de non edendo sanguine; vel per conditionem carnis Christi fieri posse, ut verè & realiter manducandus Christus proponeretur: quæsiverunt igitur, quomodo fieri illud posset? AdAdversarii nec quaerunt, nec in Christi responsionibus acquiescunt, sed praesentiae modum a Christo simpliciter refutatum mordicus defendunt.
units.tr: Or is it rather probable that the Roman Church wished to express transubstantiation through palinodes, decrees as absurd as they are, which gave the Capernaites, or the disciples, such crude thoughts about eating the Body of Christ? Shall we believe that the mind of the Capernaites was that the flesh of Christ is present sensually, not only in the sacrament, but in truth is handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful? This is also the opinion of our adversaries, as is clear from the palinode of Berengar dictated by Pope Nicholas (De Consecratione, dist. 2, can. Berengarius). Did the Capernaites believe, but plainly that they would become the creators of their Creator, so that they might eat the true flesh of Christ and defend the reality of his carnal presence? Our adversaries believe this too. Hence the Stella Clericorum: What then shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? He who created me gave me the power to create him; he who created me without me is created through me. Did they believe (though I do not believe that they did) that Christ can even be devoured by beasts? Our adversaries believe this too. This is the common opinion of the Schools: a beast that eats the sacrament devours the true body of Christ, as Joseph the Englishman has it, who gathers the flowers of the Scholastics, in his Quaestio de suscipiendo Eucharistiam, Article 3. Hence Alexander of Hales (Part 4, q. 45, m. 1): If a dog or a pig should swallow the consecrated host whole, I do not see why the body of the Lord would not at the same time be carried into the belly of the dog or pig. It pleases Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, to add an observation worthy of such a mystic and mystery, from the Third Part, on the defects of the Mass, chapter 6, book 3: If a mouse or another animal eats the species of the sacrament through negligence, the one through whose negligence this happens ought to do penance for forty days. The mouse should be caught, if possible, and burned, and the ashes placed near the altar. But Peter de Palude says that the mouse ought to be disembowelled, and indeed the mouse burned, and the ashes cast into the piscina; but if a person shrinks from taking the part of the host that remains, it ought to be placed reverently in the tabernacle and left there until it is consumed naturally. The host itself must by no means be thrown into the piscina, as a certain priest did with a fly found in the chalice after the consecration. And if a person were of such fervour that he did not shrink from such things, but took them, he would deserve commendation, provided he were fasting. So Blessed Hugh of Cluny commended Goderanus, who took up the little pieces of the host which a leper had vomited up with a most vile spittle, saying that the gridiron of Lawrence had been more bearable. What of it, that they defend so stubbornly that this Creator, created by a creature, may be treated in the most unworthy ways whatsoever, cast into the latrine, vomited up, gnawed by mice, that those who think otherwise have long since been charged with heresy? For this happened to Andrew Bonaged, a Minorite, in the year of Christ 1371. He decreed (which nevertheless it was forbidden to preach under pain of excommunication) that if a consecrated host falls or is thrown into a sewer, mud, or some foul place, the body of Christ ceases to be under the species, which remain, and the substance of bread returns. But if a consecrated host is gnawed by a mouse, or taken by a beast, the body of Christ ceases to be under the said species, and the substance of bread returns. And if a consecrated host is taken by a just man or by a sinner, then, while the species are ground by the teeth, Christ is caught up to heaven and is not carried into the belly of a man. But this theologian was too modest and restrained. To speak with the author of the Tractatus de Corpore Christi for the rest: it is not absurd that it should descend into the stomach of a man or an animal, since it can even be placed in a stinking pyx or a latrine, or even in a cauldron full of boiling water, as a certain Parisian Jew did. Does the most learned man believe that the Capernaites, or the disciples here, thought up such things in a fever? And yet, if they had thought them, believed them, sanctioned them by decrees, taught them in the Schools, they would agree in every respect with the Roman Church. What difference, then, dear sir, could be speciously feigned here? Indeed, who does not see that the opinion on the real presence of Christ, publicly received by the Roman Church, is far more absurd than the Capernaites would have dared to pursue even in thought?
