They did not believe, either through the will of God and so many plain precepts about not eating blood, or through the condition of Christ's flesh, that Christ could be set forth to be truly and really eaten; they therefore asked how that could come about. The adversaries neither ask, nor do they rest in Christ's answers, but stubbornly defend a manner of presence which Christ simply refuted.

units.la: IV. Si hoc Capite de Sacramento Eucha- ristiae postea instituendo agitur, necessario illud sub utraque specie est administrandum.
units.tr: IV. If this chapter is discussing the Sacrament of the Eucharist, to be instituted later, then it must necessarily be administered under both kinds.

units.la: Ratio consequentiae, quia verf. 55. Caro & sanguis indivulso nexu, distincte tamen, cohaerent: Caro mea vere est cibus, & sanguis meus vere est potus. At negant hanc necessitatem, imo contrarii assertionem falsam, erroneam proclamant adversarii. Unde, quod modo ostensum, ex illis, nec pauci, nec postremi negant, hoc capite de manducatione agi Sacramentali, ne ad has necessitatis, utriusque speciei, leges compellerentur.
units.tr: The reason for the consequence is that in verse 55 flesh and blood hold together in an unbroken bond, yet distinctly: my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. But the opponents deny this necessity, and indeed loudly proclaim the contrary assertion false and erroneous. Hence what has just been shown is denied by not a few, and not the least of them, namely that this chapter speaks of sacramental eating, lest they be forced under these laws of necessity for both kinds.

units.la: V. Christus se vocat panem vitae, panem qui de caelo descendit verf. 48. 50. 51. An ergo Christus ex farinacea massa panis est? an in panem mutatus? an proprie dictus panis caelestis est? Quis Tropum hic non agnoscit? Ipsum supra consentientem dedimus Maldonatum. Cur ergo metuamus figuram agnoscere, ubi, inversa Propositione, Christus panem, suum vocat corpus? Annon tot penè fulmina contra Transubstantiationem, quot quidem hic sunt verba?
units.tr: V. Christ calls himself the bread of life, the bread which came down from heaven (verses 48, 50, 51). Is Christ then bread made of a floury mass? Has he been changed into bread? Is he properly called heavenly bread? Who does not recognise a trope here? We have already cited Maldonatus as agreeing with us. Why then should we fear to recognise a figure where, with the proposition reversed, Christ calls the bread his body? Are there not almost as many thunderbolts against transubstantiation as there are words here?

units.la: VI. Optimus Interpres verborum quisque suorum. Cur igitur Christo, qui edere, & bibere, provenire ad se verf. 44. & 65. & credere in se, exp-licat, fidem non adhibeamus, & in simpulo fluctus excitemus? Postquam Servator, occasione quinquinque panum, de manna primùm, postea etiam de semet ipso, pane cœlesti, disserere cœpisset, & Judæi sibi quoque panem illum dari petiissent, ad fidem eos rejecit & accepsum. Ego, inquit, sum panis ille vitæ, qui veniet ad me, nequaquam sitiet, & qui credit in me, sitiet nunquam. Plane ut cap. IV. v. 34. escam suam vocat executionem voluntatis ejus, qui misit ipsum, & consummationem operis ejus; ita hoc loco seipsum, vera fide apprehensum, nostrum appellat cibum & potum. Et quemadmodum vers. 25. capitis IV. cùm mulier aquam sibi, de qua si quis biberet, non sitiret in æternum, dari petiisset, adventum ad se, id est, sui cognitionem, quòd verus esset Mundi Messias, intellexit, ut ex sequentibus manifestum est; ita, quando hoc loco sanguinis & carnis suæ, ceu veri cibi & potûs meminit, ipse Servator, de solida, & salutari sui notitia, adeóque accessione, & meriti sui per fidem apprehensione, ea explicat. Utenim nasci spiritualiter, est regenerari per Spiritum sanctum; ita pasci spiritualiter, est passionis & meritorum Christi per fidem fieri participem. VII. Si de Sacramentali hoc loco agitur manducatione, ejusque absoluta necessitate; etiam infantibus erit communicandum. At hoc posterius damnavit Ecclesia Romana. E. Est hoc argumentum non modò Ecclesiæ Veteris Græcæ, de qua Lyran. Joh. 6. vers. 53. sed etiam August. lib. 1. de peccat. Merit. & Remiss. Cap.
units.tr: VI. Each man is the best interpreter of his own words. Why then, when Christ explains to eat and to drink, to come to him (verses 44 and 65) and to believe in him, do we not apply faith, and stir up a tempest in a teacup? When the Saviour, on the occasion of the five loaves, had begun to speak first of the manna and then also of himself as the heavenly bread, and the Jews had asked that this bread be given to them too, he sent them back to faith and acceptance. I am, he said, the bread of life; whoever comes to me will by no means hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst. Just as in chapter IV, verse 34, he calls his food the doing of the will of him who sent him, and the completing of his work, so in this place he calls himself, grasped by true faith, our food and drink. And just as in verse 25 of chapter IV, when the woman asked for water, of which whoever drinks will never thirst for ever, he understood coming to him as knowing him, that he was the true Messiah of the world, as is clear from what follows; so when in this place he speaks of his flesh and blood as true food and drink, the Saviour himself explains this as a sound and saving knowledge of himself, and so as coming to him and grasping his merit by faith. For as to be born spiritually is to be regenerated by the Holy Spirit, so to be fed spiritually is to become a partaker of the passion and merits of Christ through faith. VII. If this place is speaking of sacramental eating and its absolute necessity, then infants too must be communicated. But the Roman Church has condemned this latter. Therefore this argument is found not only in the ancient Greek Church, of which Lyra speaks on John 6:53, but also in Augustine, On Sins, Merits and Forgiveness, book 1, chap.

units.la: H 20. & 24. Quod & supra celebrem illum Moguntinum concionatorem, Iohannem Ferum praefiit. VIII. Non agi Joh. C. VI. vel de Transsubstantiatione, vel Sacramento Coenae; sed Spirituali carnis Christi manducatione, Patres magno docent numero. Tertull. de Resur. carnis: Quia durum & intolerabilem existimaverunt sermonem ejus, quasi vere carnem suam illis edendam determinasset, ut in Spiritum disponeret statum salutis, pramisit: Spiritus est, qui vivificat; atque ita subjunxit: Caro nihil prodest, ad vivificandum scilicet. Exequitur etiam quid velit intelligi Spiritum: Verba, quae locutus sum vobis, Spiritus sunt, & vita sunt, sicut & supra:Qui audit sermones meos, & credit in eum, qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam, & in judicium non veniet, sed transibit de morte ad vitam. Itaque sermonem constituens vivificatorem, quia Spiritus & vita sermo, eundem etiam carnem suam dixit; quia & sermo caro erat factus; proinde in causam vitae appetendus, & devorandus auditu, & ruminandus intellectu, & fide digerendus. Aperta Tertulliani verba, quae removent manducationem carnalem; Spiritualem contra ponunt, & eam quidem, quae consistit partim in salutari auditu verbi Dei, partim in vera fide in Christum, quem auditu devorandum, ruminandum intellectu, & fide dicit digerendum. Sed & Hieronymus textum de Scripturis sacris explicat in Psalm. 147. Legimus sanctas ScriScripturas: Ego corpus Iesu Evangelium puto, sanctas Scripturas puto doctrinā ejus: Et quando dicit: Qui non comederit carnem meam, & biberit sanguinem meum, licet in mysterio hoc possit intelligi, tamen verius corpus Christi & sanguis ejus sermo Scripturarum, doctrina divina est: Si quando imus ad mysterium (qui fideli est, intelligit) si in maculam ceciderit, periclitatur; si quando audimus sermonem Dei, & sermo Dei, & caro Christi, & sanguis ejus in auribus nostris funditur, & nos aliud cogitamus, in quantum periculum incurrimus? Hoc Hieronymi habent praemissae. Ex iis vero colligere & concludere, Christum Johannis sexto Transsubstantiationis dogma stabilire; est argumentari a baculo in angulo ad pluviam. Summa, in confesso est, de qualibet alia manducatione, de quolibet alio corpore priscos Doctores, quam Transsubstantiato, locum intelligere maluisse. Unde & Augustinus de Verbis Apostoli serm. 2. Hoc vos scandalizat: Si ergo videritis filium hominis ascendentem ubi erat prius. Quid sibi vult, hoc vos scandalizat? Putas, quia de hoc corpore, quod videtis, partes facturus sum, & membra mea conscisurus, & vobis daturus? Quid si ergo filium hominis videritis ascendentem ubi erat prius? Certe, qui integer ascendere potuit, consumi non potuit? Ergo & de corpore ac de sanguine suo dedit nobis salubrem refectionem, & tam magnam breviter solvit de sua integritate quæstionem. Manducent ergo, qui manducant, & bibant qui bibunt, esuriant & sitient, vitam manducent, & vitam bibant. Illud manducare refici est, sed sic reficeris, ut non deficiat, unde reficeris. Illud bibere, quid est nisi vivere? Manduca vitam, bibe vitam, habebis vitam, & integra est vita. Tunc autem hoc erit, id est, vita unicuique erit corpus & sanguis Christi, si, quod in Sacramento visibiliter sumitur, in ipsa veritate Spiritualiter manducetur, Spiritualiter bibatur. Audivimus enim Dominum dicentem, Spiritus est, qui vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam: Verba quæ loquutus sum, Spiritus & vita sunt. Quid, quòd, ut Ferus in Joh. p. 165. b. monet, Augustinus cum aliis, de corpore mystico, Ecclesia, non Sacramentali, multò minus naturali, textum exposuit? Eusebius Eccles. Theol. lib. 3. cap. 12. Ne enim existimetis, me dicere, carnem, qua circumdatus sum, edendam esse; neque putetis me præcipere, sanguinem sensibus expositum & corporalem bibendum esse: probè enim nostis, verba mea, quæ loquutus sum vobis. Spiritum esse & vitam: unde ipsa verba & sermones ejus caro & sanguis sunt, quibus qui participat, semper, ut ita dicam, cœlesti pane nutritus, cœlestis vitæ particeps futurus est. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechet. Mystag. 4. Christus olim cum Judæis differens, dicebat: Nisi manducaveritis carnem meam, & biberitis sanguinem meum, non habebitis vitam. bitis vitam in vobis. Illi vero non audientes Spiritualiter ea, quæ dicebantur, offensi, abierunt retro, quòd exi\-stimarent Christum eos ad humanarum carnium esum incitare. Erant in Veteri quoque Testamento panes Propositionis; sed illi ad vetus pertinentes, finem consequuti sunt: in Novo verò Testamento, panis cœlestis, & poculum salutare, quæ corpus & animam sanctificant: sicut panis corpori, ita verbum animæ convenit: ne ergo tanquam nudis attendas, pani & vino. Chrysostomus Homil. 47. in Joh. Carnale erat dubitare, quomodo nobis posset carnem dare manducandam? Hæc omnia carnalia, quæ mysticè & Spiritualiter intelligere oportebat. Item. Verba quæ ego loquutus sum vobis, divina & Spiritualia sunt, nihil carnale habent. Et rursus: Illi quidem (qui offendebantur) carnaliter & secundum humanam rationem audiverunt; hi verò (Apostoli) Spiritualiter, fidei omnia permittentes.
units.tr: H 20. & 24. This, too, the famous Mainz preacher John Ferus has anticipated above. VIII. The Fathers teach in great numbers that John 6 speaks neither of transubstantiation nor of the Sacrament of the Supper, but of the spiritual eating of Christ's flesh. Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh: Because they thought his word hard and intolerable, as though he had determined to give them his flesh to eat in reality, he first said, in order to set them in a state of salvation through the Spirit: It is the Spirit that gives life; and then added: the flesh profits nothing, namely for giving life. He also explains what he wishes the Spirit to be understood as: The words that I have spoken to you are spirit, and they are life, as also above: He who hears my words and believes in him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but passes from death to life. Therefore, in establishing the word as the giver of life, because the word is spirit and life, he also called it his flesh, because the word too had become flesh; accordingly it is to be sought as the cause of life, and devoured by hearing, chewed over by understanding, and digested by faith. Tertullian's words are plain: they remove carnal eating and set spiritual eating in its place, which consists partly in the saving hearing of God's word and partly in true faith in Christ, whom he says is to be devoured by hearing, chewed over by understanding, and digested by faith. Jerome, too, explains the text of the holy Scriptures in Psalm 147: We read the holy Scriptures: I think the body of Jesus is the Gospel, I think the holy Scriptures are his teaching. And when he says: Whoever does not eat my flesh and drink my blood, although in this mystery it may be understood, yet more truly the body of Christ and his blood is the word of the Scriptures, the divine teaching. If at any time we come to the mystery (he who is faithful understands), if it falls into a stain, it is in peril; if when we hear the word of God, the word of God and the flesh of Christ and his blood are poured into our ears, and we think of other things, into how great a danger do we run? The preceding words of Jerome say this. To gather from them and conclude that Christ in John 6 establishes the dogma of transubstantiation is to argue from a stick in the corner to rain. In sum, it is agreed that the ancient teachers preferred to understand the passage of any other eating and any other body than the transubstantiated one. Hence also Augustine, in sermon 2 on the words of the Apostle: This scandalizes you: If then you see the Son of man ascending where he was before. What does it mean, this scandalizes you? Do you think that I am going to make parts of this body which you see, and cut my limbs apart, and give them to you? What if then you see the Son of man ascending where he was before? Surely he who could ascend whole cannot be consumed? So he also gave us from his body and blood a wholesome refreshment, and briefly resolved the question of his integrity, which is so great. Let those who eat, eat, and those who drink, drink; let them hunger and thirst; let them eat life, let them drink life; they will have life, and life is whole. To eat this is to be refreshed, but you are refreshed in such a way that what you are refreshed from does not fail. To drink this, what is it but to live? Eat life, drink life, you will have life, and life is whole. This will be so, however, when life is for each one the body and blood of Christ, if what is taken visibly in the sacrament is eaten spiritually and drunk spiritually in the very truth. For we have heard the Lord saying: It is the Spirit that gives life, the flesh profits nothing; the words which I have spoken are spirit and life. What of the fact that, as Ferus observes on John, p. 165 b, Augustine together with others expounded the text of the mystical body, the Church, not the sacramental body, much less the natural one? Eusebius, Ecclesiastical Theology book 3, chap. 12: For do not think that I say the flesh with which I am clothed is to be eaten, nor suppose that I command the blood, exposed to the senses and bodily, to be drunk: for you know well that my words, which I have spoken to you, are spirit and life; so these very words and sayings of his are flesh and blood, and whoever partakes of them, always, so to speak, nourished with heavenly bread, will be a sharer of heavenly life. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis Mystagogica 4: Christ once, disputing with the Jews, said: Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in you. But they, not hearing spiritually what was said, were offended and went away backwards, because they thought Christ was urging them to eat human flesh. There were also the showbreads in the Old Testament, but those, belonging to the old covenant, have reached their end; in the New Testament, however, there is the heavenly bread and the saving cup, which sanctify body and soul. As bread suits the body, so the word suits the soul; do not therefore look at the bread and wine as bare things. Chrysostom, Homily 47 on John: Was it carnal to doubt how he could give us his flesh to eat? All these things are carnal, which one ought to understand mystically and spiritually. Likewise: The words that I have spoken to you are divine and spiritual; they have nothing carnal. And again: Those indeed who were offended heard carnally and according to human reasoning; but these, the Apostles, heard spiritually, entrusting everything to faith.

units.la: VI. E. Magnam denique, hunc locum, lucem explicandæ doctrinæ, de manducatione afferre, libenter concedimus.
units.tr: VI. E. Finally, we gladly grant that this passage brings a great light to the explanation of the doctrine of eating.

units.la: 1. Ostendit Servator, unum sui manducandi modum, Spiritualem nempe, per fidem, vers. 47. 2. Tollit omnem præsentiæ modum, qui locali ejus incœlum ascensioni repugnat, vers. 62. 3. Identitatem Objecti indicat; tam in Spirituali, quàm in Sacramentali manducatione; Carnem, seu Corpus, & sanguinem suum: nisi quòd, inversa propositione, in illa se appellet panem; carnem suam, cibum; in hac vero panem, suum corpus. Etsi enim cum Petro Martyre, caeterisque Theologis nostris recte sentiamus, sermonem hoc loco de Sacramento Coenae non institui; asserimus tamen, cum eodem: Sexto capite Iohannis traditam esse Spiritualem manducationem carnis Christi per fidem, & Christum in ultima illa sua Coena, symbola ad eam, & certa quaedam verba adhibite, nec ullam concedimus veram carnis Christi manducationem nisi Spiritualem, quam ita distinguimus, quod externa symbola interdum adjuncta habeat, interdum non habeat. Hujus vero manducationis Spiritualis ratio & modus nusquam plenius exponitur, quam praesenti loco. Verbo, Caput sextum plana est & dilucida explicatio omnium eorum, quae in institutione Eucharistiae ambigua videri queunt, adeo ut Spiritus sancti tam eximium beneficium & gratiam, non grato satis agnoscant animo, qui vel alium exspectant Doctorem, vel in aperta deinceps caecutire malitiose pergunt luce.
units.tr: 1. The Saviour shows one mode of eating him, namely the spiritual mode, through faith, ver. 47. 2. He removes every mode of presence that conflicts with his local ascension into heaven, ver. 62. 3. He indicates the identity of the object, both in spiritual and in sacramental eating: his flesh, or body, and blood. Except that, with the order of the statement reversed, in the former he calls himself bread, his flesh, food; but in the latter, bread, his body. For although we rightly agree with Peter Martyr and our other theologians that the discourse in this place is not about the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, we nevertheless assert, with him: In the sixth chapter of John the spiritual eating of Christ's flesh through faith is delivered, and in his last Supper Christ, using symbols for it and certain set words, and we allow no true eating of Christ's flesh except the spiritual, which we distinguish in this way: that it sometimes has the external symbols added, sometimes not. But the reason and mode of this spiritual eating is nowhere set out more fully than in the present place. In a word, the sixth chapter is a plain and clear explanation of all those things in the institution of the Eucharist that may seem ambiguous, so that those who either await another teacher, or who maliciously persist in blindness in the open light, do not acknowledge with a grateful mind so outstanding a benefit and grace of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VII. Feliciores ac cordatiores hac in re Patres erant, qui, ad decidendam Sacramentariam Controversiam, praesentem hunc Johannis textum prae aliis in subsidium vocarunt, manducationemque in Coena Domini salutarem, Spiritualem fidei, esse voluerunt. Ita Augustinus de verbis Apostoli serm. 2. quem locum supra jam citavimus. Et de doctr. Christian. lib. 3. Cap. 5. &
units.tr: VII. The Fathers were more fortunate and more discerning in this matter, who, in order to settle the Sacramentarian controversy, called upon this text of John in preference to others as their support, and wished the eating in the Lord's Supper to be salutary and spiritual through faith. Thus Augustine on the words of the Apostle, sermon 2, which passage we have already cited above; and in On Christian Doctrine, book 3, chapter 5 and

units.la: & 16. Item in Psalm. 98. Spiritualiter intelligite, quod loquutus sum. Non hoc corpus, quod videtis, manducaturi estis, & bibituri sanguinem illum, quem fusuri sunt, qui crucifigent. Sacramentum aliquod commendavi vobis, Spiritualiter intelleQum vivificabit vos. Clemens Alexandrinus, Paedag. lib. 2. cap. 2. Basilius Epist. 141. quae est ad Caesarienses; Chrysostomus de Sacerdotio lib. 3. c. 6.
units.tr: and 16. Likewise on Psalm 98: "Understand spiritually what I have said. You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor to drink that blood which those who will crucify me are going to shed. I have commended to you a sacrament; understand it spiritually, and it will give you life." Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 2, chapter 2. Basil, Epistle 141, which is to the Caesareans. Chrysostom, On the Priesthood, book 3, chapter 6.

units.la: SECTIO X.
units.tr: SECTIO X.

units.la: Transsubstantiatio repugnat Ana- logia fidei.
units.tr: Transubstantiation contradicts the analogy of faith.

units.la: VULt Apostolus nostram Prophetiam, id est, solidam & sobriam Scripturæ explicationem, fieri secundum analogiam sive proportionem fidei, Rom. 12. vers. 6. Neque verò absre. Quis enim inficias eat, in profundo S. Scripturæ Oceano, ab imperitis nautis ad scopulos nonnunquam allidi, & variarum sententiarum vortices? Cynosura proinde opus est, ad quam quisque cursum suum tutò dirigat. Ea autem est analogia fidei, quo nomine veteres Theologi, Irenæus, Augustinus, Ambrosius Symbolum intellexerunt Apostolicum: alii prima & indubitata religionis capita; alii perspicua & manifesta Scripturæ loca, quibus obscuriora illustrantur. Utrum quædam sigillatim, an omnia simul, nomine hoc debeant intelligi, jam non disputabimus. Sit analogia fidei Symbolum, sint primaria Christianismi capita, utrinque repugnantem habemus; in explicatione verborum, Hoc est Corpus meum, per Transubstantiationem; fidei analogiam. Nam 1. Credimus, Christum, ex Beata Maria Virgine, verum assumsisse corpus, adeoque extensione sua quantum, suis partibus distinctum, locale, visibile, etiam post Resurrectionem, secundum Scripturam, Luc. 24. 39. Joh. 20. 20. 27. cap. 21. 5. Transubstantiatum vero corpus multiplex est, ἀπὸ τοῦ ... ἀόρατον, ἀόρι- στον &c. adeoque nullum. Et tamen audent suam Transubstantiatores creaturam, B. Virginis sanctissimæ præferre proli, ut ex Gabriel Biel Lect. 4. pag. 8. supra audivimus.
units.tr: The Apostle wishes our prophecy, that is, the solid and sober explanation of Scripture, to be made according to the analogy or proportion of faith (Rom. 12:6). Nor is this without reason. For who denies that in the deep ocean of Holy Scripture unskilled sailors are sometimes dashed against rocks and swept into whirlpools of conflicting opinions? A cynosure is therefore needed, by which each may safely direct his course. This is the analogy of faith, a name by which the ancient theologians, Irenaeus, Augustine, Ambrose, understood the Apostles' Creed. Others understood it as the first and undoubted heads of religion, others as the plain and manifest passages of Scripture by which the obscure ones are illuminated. Whether these things should be understood individually or all together under this name, we shall not now dispute. Let the analogy of faith be the Creed, let it be the primary heads of Christianity: we have it opposed on both sides to the explanation of the words This is my Body by Transubstantiation. For (1) we believe that Christ took true body from the Blessed Virgin Mary, and so a body with its extension, distinct in its parts, local, visible, even after the Resurrection, according to Scripture (Luke 24:39; John 20:20, 27; John 21:5). But the transubstantiated body is manifold, [ἀπὸ τοῦ ... ἀόρατον, ἀόριστον], that is, invisible, indefinite, and so on, and therefore is nothing. And yet the Transubstantiators dare to set their creature above the most holy offspring of the Blessed Virgin, as we heard above from Gabriel Biel, Lect. 4, p. 8.

units.la: II. Credimus, corpus Christi semel crucifixum & mortuum, ita definiente aliquoties Scriptura, Rom. 6. 10. Heb. 9. 28. c. 10. 10. At in Transubstantiatione toties illud, quoties hæc fit, crucifigi ac mori necesse est, si panis fractus, proprie & literaliter, est Corpus Christi fractum pro nobis; Vinum item effusum, proprie ac literaliter sanguis Christi pro nobis effusus. III. Credimus, Christum ita ascendisse in cœlum, ut terram reliquerit, Luc. 24. v. 50. Act. 1. v. 9. 10. proinde in terra localiter non amplius esse cum corpore suo præsentem, ut ipse futurum prædixit, Marc. 14. 7. Atque hujus argumenti vim Veteres diligenter pressam, localis præsentiæ commento opposuerunt. Eusebius Emisenus, ut est in iure Canon. de Confec. distinct. 2. c. 35. Ambrosius lib. 10. in Luc. cap. 24. August Tract. 2. in Johan. & Epist. 57. ad Dardanum. Imo, ipso hoc argumento Servator Capernaitas refutavit, Joh. 6. 62. At per Transsubstantiationem Christus quotidie revocatur in terram. Nive frigidius est Rhætica, quòd modo tantum quodam Christum corpore suo absentem voluntate, humili, abjecto, paupere. Aperte & absque parabolis Christus fuit locutus, cùm diceret, se relicturum mundum, Joh. 16, vers. 29. Nullam hic conditionis admittit restrictionem Augustinus in Johan. Tract. 50. Pauperes semper habebitis vobiscum, me autem non semper habebitis. Accipiant & hoc boni; sed non sunt soliciti: Loquebatur enim de præsentia corporis sui. Nam secundum majestatem suam, secundum providentiam, secundum ineffabilem & invisibilem gratiam, impletur quod ab eo dictum est: Ecce vobiscum sum, omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi: Secundum carnem verò, quam verbum assumsit, secundum id, quod de virgine natus est, secundum id, quod à Judæis comprehensus est, quod ligno confixus, quod de cruce depositus, quod linteis, quod in sepulchro conditus, quod in resurrectione manifestatus, non semper habebitis me vobiscum. Quare? quoniam conversatus est secundum corporis præsentiam quadraginta diebus cum discipulis suis, & eis deducentibus videndo, non sequendo ascenditin cœlum, & non est hic: Ibi enim sedet ad dexteram Patris, & hic est. IV. Credimus, semel tantum Christum rediturum, & visibiliter quidem, eo modo quo abiit, Act. 1. verf. 11. ad ultimum judicium, Act. 3, 21. At per Transubstantiationem quotidie, & plurimis quidem in locis, simul redit invisibiliter. Hujus verò adventus corporalis spem nobis non modò dulcissimus Servator nullam facit; sed & graviter serioque dehortatur, ne talem confingentibus adhibeamus fidem, Matth. 24. verf. 23. V. Eam credimus Veteris & N. Testamenti sanctorum communionem, quâ utrisque idem cibus Spiritualis, & potus Spiritualis tribuitur, secundum Paulum, 1, Cor. 10.3. At Transubstantiationis, Veteris Testamenti fideles, capaces esse non poterant, quando Christus nondum fuit natus E. necessario Spiritualis admittenda. Nexum & veritatem hujus argumenti; ex Paulo & Augustino petiti; suprà etiam agnovit Johannes Ferus. VI. Credimus, remissionem peccatorum, per Corpus Christi, pro nobis fractum, & sanguinem effusum, Matth. 20. verf. 28. At, si panis proprie est Corpus Christi, pro nobis traditum; vinum proprie est sanguis Christi, pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum effusus, reconciliatio cum Deo, & remissio peccatorum a Deo petenda (adeóque etiam credenda) erit propropter id, quod latet sub speciebus, quod manibus gestatur, quod ore comeditur ac bibitur. Id quod ab Idololatriae suspicione liberari nequit. Atque hoc argumentum, ab Analogia fidei petitum, Augustino persuasit, ut suis etiam Auditoribus suaderet, verba; Hoc est corpus meum; improprie esse intelligenda. Ita enim gravissimus author, Sermone ad Infant. ad altar. de Sacramento : Hoc, quod videtis in altari Dei, etiam transacta nocte vidistis; sed quid esset, quid sibi velit, quam magna rei Sacramentum contineret, nondum audistis. Quod autem fides vestra postulat instruenda, panis est corpus Christi, calix est sanguis. Breviter quidem hoc dictum est, quod fidei fortasse sufficiat; sed fides instructionem desiderat, dicit enim Propheta: Nisi enim credideritis, non intelligetis. Potestis ergo modo dicere mihi, praecepisti ut credamus, expone ut intelligamus. Potest enim in animo cujuspiam cogitatio talis oriri: Dominus noster Iesus Christus novimus unde acceperit carnem, de virgine Maria lactatus est, nutritus est, crevit, ad juvenilem aetatem perductus est, a Judaeis persecutionem passus est, ligno suspensus est, in ligno interfectus est, sepultus est, tertio die resurrexit, quo die voluit in coelum ascendit; illuc levavit corpus suum unde est venturus, ut judicet vivos et mortuos, ibi est modo sedens ad dextram Patris: Quomodo est ergo panis corpus ejus? Et calix, vel quod habet bet calix, quomodo est sanguis ejus? Ista, fratres, ideo dicuntur Sacramenta, quia in eis aliud videtur, aliud intelligitur. Quod videtur, speciem habet corporalem, quod intelligitur fructum habet Spiritualem. Εὑρηκα, exclamabit Transsubstantiator! Quod videtur, inquit Augustinus, speciem habet corporalem, quod intelligitur fructum Spiritualem. Perge, & ipsum, ex Augustino, Augustinum admitte Interpretem. De corpore mystico, de Ecclesia locum explicat, hanc Christi corpus & poni, t& prolixè, ex Apostolo, exponit. An per Transsubstantiationem? Hoc Vir doctissimus nec capiet, nec dabit. Ita nempe durissimæ Patrum locutiones ubi accuratè examinantur, nostræ favent causæ.
units.tr: (II) We believe that the body of Christ was crucified and died once, as Scripture repeatedly declares (Rom. 6:10; Heb. 9:28; Heb. 10:10). But in Transubstantiation it must be crucified and die as often as this is done, if the bread broken is, properly and literally, the broken body of Christ given for us, and likewise the wine poured out is, properly and literally, the blood of Christ poured out for us. (III) We believe that Christ so ascended into heaven that he left the earth (Luke 24:50; Acts 1:9-10), and therefore that he is no longer present on earth locally with his body, as he himself foretold (Mark 14:7). And the Fathers pressed the force of this argument carefully against the invention of local presence: Eusebius of Emesa, as is in the canon law, de Consecratione, distinction 2, chapter 35; Ambrose, book 10 on Luke, chapter 24; Augustine, Tractate 2 on John, and Letter 57 to Dardanus. Indeed, the Saviour himself refuted the Capernaites with this very argument (John 6:62). But through Transubstantiation Christ is daily brought back down to earth. It is colder than ice, the Rhaetian claim that Christ is absent in his body, present only in a certain manner, by his will, in a humble, abject and poor way. Christ spoke openly and without parables when he said that he would leave the world (John 16:29). Augustine, on John, Tractate 50, admits no restriction of this condition here: "You will always have the poor with you, but me you will not always have." Let good people take this too, but let them not be anxious: for he was speaking of the presence of his body. For according to his majesty, according to his providence, according to his ineffable and invisible grace, what he said is fulfilled: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." But according to the flesh, which the Word assumed, according to that which was born of the virgin, according to that which was seized by the Jews, that which was fastened to the wood, that which was taken down from the cross, that which was wrapped in linen cloths, that which was laid in the sepulchre, that which was manifested in the resurrection, you will not always have me with you. Why? Because he dwelt with his disciples in the bodily presence for forty days, and, while they watched and did not follow, he ascended into heaven, and is not here: for there he sits at the right hand of the Father, and here he is. (IV) We believe that Christ will return only once, and visibly indeed, in the same way as he went away (Acts 1:11), at the last judgment (Acts 3:21). But through Transubstantiation he returns daily, and in very many places at once, invisibly. Our most sweet Saviour not only gives us no hope of such a bodily coming, but also earnestly and seriously warns us not to give faith to those who invent such things (Matt. 24:23). (V) We believe in that communion of the saints of the Old and New Testaments, by which the same spiritual food and the same spiritual drink are given to both, according to Paul (1 Cor. 10:3). But the believers of the Old Testament could not be partakers of Transubstantiation, since Christ had not yet been born; therefore a spiritual reception must be admitted. The connection and truth of this argument, drawn from Paul and Augustine, John Ferus also recognised above. (VI) We believe in the forgiveness of sins through the body of Christ broken for us and the blood poured out (Matt. 20:28). But if the bread is properly the body of Christ given for us, and the wine is properly the blood of Christ poured out for the remission of sins, then reconciliation with God and the remission of sins must be sought from God (and therefore also believed) because of that which lies hidden under the appearances, which is carried in the hands and eaten and drunk by the mouth. This cannot be freed from the suspicion of idolatry. And this argument, drawn from the analogy of faith, persuaded Augustine to tell his hearers too that the words This is my body must be understood improperly. For so that most weighty author says in his sermon to the newly baptised at the altar, on the Sacrament: "What you see on the altar of God, you saw also on the night that has passed; but what it is, what it means, how great a mystery of the thing it contains, you have not yet heard. What your faith requires to be taught is that the bread is the body of Christ, the cup is the blood. This has been said briefly, which perhaps suffices for faith; but faith desires instruction, for the Prophet says: 'Unless you have believed, you will not understand.' So you may now say to me: you have commanded us to believe, explain so that we may understand. For such a thought may arise in someone's mind: our Lord Jesus Christ, we know whence he took flesh, was nursed from the virgin Mary, was nourished, grew, was brought to youthful age, suffered persecution from the Jews, was hanged on the wood, was killed on the wood, was buried, rose on the third day, and on that day wished to ascend into heaven; he lifted his body thither whence he is to come to judge the living and the dead, and there he now sits at the right hand of the Father. How, then, is the bread his body? And the cup, or what the cup holds, how is it his blood? These things, brethren, are called sacraments for this reason, that in them one thing is seen, another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit." Eureka! the Transubstantiator will cry out [Εὕρηκα]! "What is seen," says Augustine, "has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit." Go on, and admit Augustine himself, from Augustine, as your interpreter. He explains the place about the mystical body, about the Church, and at length, from the Apostle, expounds the phrase this is the body. But through Transubstantiation? This most learned man will neither grasp nor grant it. Thus indeed the harshest-sounding expressions of the Fathers, when they are carefully examined, favour our cause.

units.la: SECTIO XI.
units.tr: SECTION XI.

units.la: Transsubstantiationem Antiquitas destruit.
units.tr: Antiquity destroys transubstantiation.

units.la: I. Ad Antiquitatem accedimus, cui Pontificiæ Transsubstantiationis figmentum fuisse ignotum, densa testium nube, magnóque veterum numero posset probari. Sed quando ad portum paulatim tendimus, paucis defungemur. Etsi enim Patres, ut in aliis, sic hoc etiam dogmate, tot nondum ortis novitatibus, quæstionumque absurditatibus; modò securius, modò incautius, modò incommodius, hinc inde, suo tempore videantur locuti, eos tamen non metuimus. Et quamquam, quando ille, qui fuit ante omnes, unicus Doctor & Magister Iesus Christus, noster est, de sequioris ætatis Scriptoribus non multum debeamus esse solliciti; ne tamen Antiquitatis indicium (judicium enim solius Spiritus Sancti est, per Prophetas, Evangelistas & Apostolos in Scriptura loquentis) declinare videamur, unum primò & alterum; ut ne exceptioni viri doctissimi, loca afferri ex Patribus, aut obscura per se, aut dubia, à reliquo quippe textu avulsa &c. pateat rima; afferemus, qui ex professo nostræ sententiæ patrocinium suscipiunt, qui nobiscum & sentiunt & loquuntur, non præcipitanter, sed præmeditatè; non popularï, Homilico, libero; sed agnostico, Elenctico, eóque accurato stylo: certas deinde ex antiquitate instruemus argumentorum classes, cum quibus Transsubstantiatio subsistere non poterit.
units.tr: I. We now come to Antiquity, where the fiction of the Papists' transubstantiation could be shown to have been unknown, by a dense cloud of witnesses and a great number of the ancients. But since we are making gradually for harbour, we shall be brief. For although the Fathers, as in other matters, so also in this doctrine, before so many novelties and absurd questions had arisen, seem to have spoken at their time now more securely, now more carelessly, now less suitably, here and there, we do not fear them. And although, since he who was before all, the one Teacher and Master, Jesus Christ, is ours, we need not be greatly concerned about writers of a later age, nevertheless, lest we seem to shun the testimony of Antiquity (for judgment belongs to the Holy Spirit alone, who speaks in Scripture through the Prophets, Evangelists and Apostles), we shall first set out one or two passages. This is so that no crack be open to the objection of the most learned man, that passages from the Fathers are brought forward which are either obscure in themselves or doubtful, torn of course from the rest of the text, and so on. We shall cite those who expressly take up the defence of our opinion, who both think and speak with us, not hastily but deliberately, not in a popular, homiletic and free style, but in an investigative, elenctic and therefore careful style. Then, from Antiquity, we shall set out certain classes of arguments with which transubstantiation cannot stand.

units.la: II. Ex Græcis; ut à consensu Ecclesiæ Græcæ cum Reformatis auspicemur; in prima merito collocandus acie antiquus pariter, & dif- fusa eruditione clarus Cyri Episcopus, Theodo- retus.
units.tr: II. From the Greeks. To begin with the agreement of the Greek Church with the Reformed, the first place in the line is deservedly given to the ancient Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, equally famous for his wide learning.

units.la: Scripsit hic, præter cætera, Dialogos tres, quorum primus ἀτρέπτῳ, certamen pro immutabili unigeniti Deitate suscipit; secundus ἀσυγχύτῳ, unionem Deitatis & humanitatis Christi, absque alteratione atque confusione factam, demonstrat; Tertius ἀπαθῶς, Servatoris Deitatem omnis passicnis expertem condocefacit. Romae & alibi hi Dialogi sunt impressi. Et in primi quidem Dial. cap. 8. duo Episcopus proponit. Analysin primo & rationem locutionum Sacramentalium explicat; veritatem deinde corporis & sanguinis Christi, ita ex iis probat, ut neget Sermonem in carnem mutatum. Sacramentalium locutionum duo genera constituit, quorum alterum nomen seu appellationem signi, hoc est, rei terrestris & visibilis tribuit rei significatae, coelesti & invisibili, quo sensu Christus corpus suum panem appellavit; alterum, signis seu Sacramentis externis nomen rei significatae seu coelestis imponit, ut, cum Christus panem corpus vocat, vinum sanguinem. Dialogo II. cap. 24. ex mysticis symbolis, corporis & sanguinis Christi, probat veritatem. Sunt autem tres capitis illius partes. In prima, ex relatione symbolorum ad rem significatam, veritatem corporis Christi Orthodoxus hoc demonstrat argumento: Si divina mysteria sunt corporis revera existentis symbola; tum sequitur, corpus etiam num esse Domini corpus, non indivinitatis Naturam mutatum; sed divina gloria repletum. Prius est verum. E. & posterius. Secunda capitis parte Eraniste argumentum a symbolis mysticis sumtum in Orthodoxum contorsus, eoque suam opinionem stabiliturus, ex partium collatione, ita argumentatur: Quod symbolis Dominici corporis & sanguinis, post ininvocationem Sacerdotis, accidit, idem corpori Christi, post assumtionem usu venit. At symbola corporis & sanguinis Christi alia sunt, & aliter nominantur ante invocationem sacerdotis, & alia fiunt post eam. E. & corpus Dominicum post assumtionem in aliam Naturam, nempe divinam, est mutatum. Mox vero tertia capitis parte per retorsionem argumenti Orthodoxus assumtionem negat, atque ex Natura Relatorum & Parium ita adversarium constringit: Typus respondeat necesse est veritati. At mystica symbola, typi, figura corporis Christi, post sanctificationem a propria essentia non recedunt. E. nec ipsum corpus assumtum a Deitate, a propria Essentia recedit. Assumtionem confirmat partim ab Adjunctis symbolorum, partim ab eorundem fine & officio. Manent enim in priori Essentia, specie, figura; visibilia sunt, & tactui obnoxia, ut antea erant; mente autem intelliguntur, creduntur, honorantur tanquam essent ea, qua creduntur, hoc est, res coelestes. Ita, Ecclesiae orthodoxae nomine, Theodoretus, Cyri Episcopus, cui & Synodus Calcedon. hoc perhibuit testimonium: Dignus est Theodoretus sede Ecclesia: Orthodoxum Ecclesia pastorem recipiat: Orthodoxum Ecclesia Doctorem recipiat. Et Leo: Benedictus Deus nostler, cujus invincibilis veritas ab OMNI hareseos macula mundum te secundum sedis Apostolica judicia demonstravit. Sed merentur a-cucutissimi disputatoris v[?] inserantur, ne quid illi praesidium caulae nostrae [?] Ita ergo locus ex Dial. I[?]
units.tr: Among other works, he wrote three Dialogues, of which the first, Immutable [ἀτρέπτῳ], undertakes the defence of the unchangeable Deity of the only-begotten; the second, Unconfused [ἀσυγχύτῳ], demonstrates the union of the Deity and humanity of Christ, effected without alteration or confusion; the third, Impassible [ἀπαθῶς], teaches that the Deity of the Saviour is free from all suffering. These Dialogues have been printed at Rome and elsewhere. In the first Dialogue, chapter 8, the Bishop puts forward two points. First he explains the analysis and reasoning of sacramental expressions; then he proves from them the truth of the body and blood of Christ, while denying that the Word was changed into flesh. He establishes two kinds of sacramental expressions. The one kind gives the name or appellation of the sign, that is, of the earthly and visible thing, to the thing signified, which is heavenly and invisible; in this sense Christ called bread his body. The other kind imposes on the external signs or sacraments the name of the thing signified or heavenly; thus, when Christ calls the bread his body, he calls the wine his blood. In Dialogue II, chapter 24, he proves the truth of the body and blood of Christ from the mystical symbols. That chapter has three parts. In the first, from the relation of the symbols to the thing signified, the Orthodox man demonstrates the truth of the body of Christ by this argument: If the divine mysteries are symbols of a body really existing, then it follows that the body is still the Lord's body, not changed into the nature of the Deity, but filled with divine glory. The first is true. Therefore the second also. In the second part of the chapter, Eranistes twists the argument taken from the mystical symbols against the Orthodox man, and, wishing to establish his own opinion, argues from the comparison of the parts thus: What happens to the symbols of the Lord's body and blood after the invocation of the priest, happens to the body of Christ after the assumption. But the symbols of the body and blood of Christ are different and are named differently before the invocation of the priest, and become different after it. Therefore the Lord's body, after the assumption, has been changed into another nature, namely the divine. Then, in the third part of the chapter, by turning the argument back, the Orthodox man denies the assumption and, from the nature of correlatives and of things alike, presses his opponent thus: A type must correspond to the truth. But the mystical symbols, types and figures of the body of Christ, after sanctification do not depart from their own essence. Therefore neither does the body itself, assumed by the Deity, depart from its own essence. He confirms the assumption partly from the accidents of the symbols, partly from their end and office: For they remain in their former essence, species and figure; they are visible and subject to touch, as they were before; but they are understood by the mind, believed in, and honoured as being those things which are believed, that is, heavenly things. Thus Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, speaking in the name of the Orthodox Church, to whom the Council of Chalcedon also gave this testimony: Theodoret is worthy of his see. Let the Orthodox Church receive him as an Orthodox minister; let the Orthodox Church receive him as an Orthodox teacher. And Leo: Blessed be our God, whose invincible truth, free from every stain of heresy, has shown you to the world according to the judgments of the Apostolic See. But the most acute disputant's [?] must be inserted, lest that defence of our cause [?] be a source of help to him. Thus, then, the passage from Dialogue I [?]

units.la: OPΘΟ. ...
units.tr: ORTH. ...

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. οἶδα ὅτι ἀρ-τὸν ὁ Θεὸς, τὸ οἰκεῖον σῶμα·
units.tr: ORTH. I know that God called the bread his own body [οἶδα ὅτι ἄρτον ὁ Θεὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον σῶμα ἐκάλεσεν].

units.la: ΕΡΑ. οἶδα.
units.tr: ERA. I know.

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. καὶ ἐπρώτησ̈ ὃ τὴν σάρκα, σὴν ὀνόμα-σεν.
units.tr: ORTH. And elsewhere he called the flesh wheat [καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ τὴν σάρκα σῖτον ὠνόμασεν].

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Οἶδα καὶ τῶν. ἠκουσα γὰρ αὐτὸς λέγον-τος, ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα, ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου· καὶ ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος τοῦ σί-του πεσὼν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἀποθάνῃ, μόνος μένει· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, πολλὸν καρπὸν φέρει.
units.tr: ERA. I know that too. For I heard him say, "The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified; and unless the grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" [ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα, ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου· καὶ ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος τοῦ σίτου πεσὼν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἀποθάνῃ, μόνος μένει· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, πολλὸν καρπὸν φέρει].

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. ἐν δὲ γε τῇ μυστηρίων παραδόσει σῶμα τὸν ἄρτον ἐκάλεσε, καὶ αἷμα τὸ ποτήριον. erba, quæ ipsa hoc loco affinxisse, aut ficulneum æ quæsiviisse videamur. habet.
units.tr: ORTH. But in the handing down of the mysteries he called the bread body, and the cup blood [ἐν δὲ γε τῇ μυστηρίων παραδόσει σῶμα τὸν ἄρτον ἐκάλεσε, καὶ αἷμα τὸ ποτήριον]. (Words which we seem to have supplied here ourselves, or to have sought out as a fig-leaf, he has.)

units.la: ORTH. Scis, quòd panem Deus proprium appellârit corpus.
units.tr: ORTH. You know that God called the bread his own body.

units.la: ERA. Scio.
units.tr: ERA. I know.

units.la: ORTHO. Alibi verò carnem triticum nominavit.
units.tr: ORTH. Elsewhere, however, he named the flesh wheat.

units.la: ERA. Scio & hoc. Audivi enim ipsum dicentem (Joh. 12.) Venit hora, ut glorificetur filius hominis. Et nisi granum tritici in terram cadens mortuum fuerit, solum manet; si verò mortuum fuerit, copiosum fructum gignit.
units.tr: ERA. I know that too. For I heard him say (John 12) "The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified. Unless the grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit."

units.la: ORTH. In mysteriorum verò institutione panem appellavit corpus, & id quod mixtum est, sanguinem.
units.tr: ORTH. But in the institution of the mysteries he called the bread body, and what is mixed, blood.

units.la: ERA.
units.tr: ERA.

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Οὕτως ὠνόμασεν.
units.tr: ERA. So he named it [Οὕτως ὠνόμασεν].

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Ἀλλὰ ἢ καὶ κατὰ τὴν φύσιν τὸ σῶμα, σῶμα ἂν εἰκότως κληθείη ἡ καὶ τὸ αἷμα.
units.tr: ORTH. But if the body is also body according to nature, the blood too could rightly be called blood [Ἀλλὰ ἢ καὶ κατὰ τὴν φύσιν τὸ σῶμα, σῶμα ἂν εἰκότως κληθείη ἡ καὶ τὸ αἷμα].

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Ὁμολογῶ.
units.tr: ERA. I agree [Ὁμολογῶ].

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Ὁ δέ γε σωτὴρ ὁ ἡμέτερ[?] ἐνήλαξε τὰ ὀνόματα, ἡ τῷ μὲν σώματι, τὸ τῆς συμβόλου τέθεικεν ὄνομα· τῷ δὲ συμβόλῳ τὸ τῆς σώματος. ἔτως ἀμπελον ἑαυτὸν ὀνομάσας, αἷμα τὸ σύμβολον προσηγόρευσεν.
units.tr: ORTH. Our Saviour, however, exchanged the names: to the body he gave the name of the symbol, and to the symbol the name of the body. So, calling himself a vine, he named the symbol blood.

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Τοῦτο μὲν ἀληθῶς εἰρηκας, ἐξελόμεθ᾽ ἢ ERA. Sic nominavit.
units.tr: ERA. You have spoken truly in this [Τοῦτο μὲν ἀληθῶς εἰρηκας, ἐξελόμεθα]. So he named it.

units.la: ORTHO. Etiam secundum naturam, ipsum corpus, recte appellatur corpus & sanguis.
units.tr: ORTH. Even according to nature, the body itself is rightly called body and blood.

units.la: ERA. Ita feres habet.
units.tr: ERA. So it seems.

units.la: ORTHO. Ipse igitur Salvator noster permutavit nomina, & corpori quidem symboli nomen impolluit, symbolo vero corporis nomen. Sic vitem seipsum nominans, sanguinis nomen symbolo tribuit.
units.tr: ORTH. Our Saviour himself, then, exchanged the names: he gave the name of the symbol to the body, and the name of the body to the symbol. Thus, calling himself a vine, he gave the name of blood to the symbol.

units.la: ERA. Hoc quidem vere dixisti. Volo autem discere causam permutationis nominum.
units.tr: ERA. You have certainly said something true there. But I want to learn the reason for the exchange of names.

units.la: ORTHO. Manifestus est scopus iis, qui sacris initiati sunt. Voluit enim Sacramentis utentes non intentos esse
units.tr: ORTHO. The aim is plain to those who have been initiated into the sacred rites. For he wished that those who partake of the sacraments should not be intent

units.la: τὴν αἰτίαν μαθεῖν τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐναλλαγῆς.
units.tr: on learning the cause of the exchange of names [τὴν αἰτίαν μαθεῖν τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐναλλαγῆς].

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Δῆλον ὅ σκοπὸς τοῖς τὰ θεῖα μεμυημένοις· ἠβούλήθη γὰρ τὰς τῶν θείων μυστηρίων μεταλαγχάνοντας, μὴ τῇ φύσει τ̃ ἐλεπομένων προσέχειν, ἀλλὰ ΔΙᾺ τῆς τ̃ ὀνομάτων ἐναλλαγῆς, πιστεύειν τῇ ἐκ τ̃ χάριτ̃ γεγεννημένῃ μεταβολῇ. Ὁ γὰρ δὴ τὸ φύσει σῶμα εἶπον καὶ ἄρτον προσαγορεύσας, καὶ αὖ πάλιν ἑαυτὸν ἀμπελον ὀνομάσας, ὅτ̃ τὰ ὁρώμενα σύμβολα τῆς τ̃ σώματ̃ καὶ αἵματ̃ προσηγορίᾳ πεπίμνηκεν, ἀπὸ τὴν φύσιν μεταβαλὼν, ἀλλὰ τὴν χάριν τῇ φύσει προσεθεικώς.
units.tr: ORTH. Clearly the purpose is for those initiated into divine things; for he wished those partaking of the divine mysteries not to attend to the nature of the things seen, but, through the exchange of names, to believe in the change brought about by grace. For he who called the natural body bread, and again called himself a vine, showed that the visible symbols have taken on the names of the body and blood, not changed in nature, but having added grace to nature [Δῆλον ὁ σκοπὸς τοῖς τὰ θεῖα μεμυημένοις· ἠβούλήθη γὰρ τὰς τῶν θείων μυστηρίων μεταλαγχάνοντας, μὴ τῇ φύσει τῶν ὁρωμένων προσέχειν, ἀλλὰ διὰ τῆς τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐναλλαγῆς, πιστεύειν τῇ ἐκ τῆς χάριτος γεγεννημένῃ μεταβολῇ. Ὁ γὰρ τὸ φύσει σῶμα εἰπὼν καὶ ἄρτον προσαγορεύσας, καὶ αὖ πάλιν ἑαυτὸν ἄμπελον ὀνομάσας, ὅτι τὰ ὁρώμενα σύμβολα τῆς τοῦ σώματος καὶ αἵματος προσηγορίᾳ πεπίμνηκεν, οὐ τὴν φύσιν μεταβαλών, ἀλλὰ τὴν χάριν τῇ φύσει προσθεὶς].

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Καὶ μυστικῶς ἐρρήθη τὰ μυστικά, καὶ σαφῶς ἐδηλώθη τὰ πᾶσιν γνώεμα.
units.tr: ERA. The mysteries were spoken mystically, and what is known to all was made plainly clear [Καὶ μυστικῶς ἐρρήθη τὰ μυστικά, καὶ σαφῶς ἐδηλώθη τὰ πᾶσιν γνώριμα].

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Ἐπειδὴ τοίνυν σωσωμολόγηπω, ἡ σωλὴν ἡ προβολὴν ὑπὸ τῆς πατριάρχης τὸ δεσποτικὸν ὠνωμάσθη σῶμα, εἰς ἣν ἐκ τῶν θείων μυστηρίων εἰσελήλυθαμεν λόγον, εἰπέ
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Since, then, we agree that the Patriarch calls the stole and the pall the Lord's body, and since we have entered into a discussion of the divine mysteries, tell me: what is the thing of which this is a symbol, or the type of the most holy food? Is it the divinity of the Lord Christ, or his body and blood?

units.la: esse in naturam eorum, quæ cernuntur, sed per nominum permutationem, credere ei, quæ ex gratia facta est mutationi. Qui enim naturale corpus triticum & panem appellavit, & rursus seipsum vitem nominavit, is visibilia symbola corporis & sanguinis appellatione honoravit, non naturam mutans, sed gratiam naturæ adjiciens.
units.tr: ...not in the nature of the things that are seen, but by a change of names; we must believe in the change that grace has made. For he who called the natural body "wheat" and "bread," and again called himself "the vine," honoured the visible symbols with the name of body and blood, not changing their nature, but adding grace to nature.

units.la: ERA. Et mystice dicta sunt mystica, & perspicuè explicata sunt, quæ non ab omnibus intelliguntur.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Things said mystically were said mystically, and things that are not understood by everyone have been clearly explained.

units.la: ORTHO. Cùm igitur constet, & stolam & pallium à Patriarcha Dominicum appellari corpus, & in sermonem de divinis mysteriis ingressi simus, dic per veritatem, cujus putas
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Since, then, it is agreed that the Patriarch calls both the stole and the pall the Lord's body, and since we have entered into discussion of the divine mysteries, tell me truthfully: of what do you think the symbol is, and the type of the most holy food?

units.la: ὧν ἐς ἀληθείας, τὴν
units.tr: Of which, truly, is it the symbol?

units.la: ἡγῆ σύμβολόν π ἡ τὺ- πον τὴν παναγίαν τροφὴν; ὁ Θεότης τῆς δεσπότης Χριστὸς; ἢ τὸ σῶμα τῆς αἵματος;
units.tr: Is it the symbol or the type of the all-holy food? Is it the divinity of the Lord Christ, or his body and blood?

units.la: EPA. Δῆλον ὡς ἐκεί-νων, ὧν ἡ τὰς παρθένου ἐδέξαντο.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Clearly it is of those things which the Virgin received.

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Τοῦ σώματος ἡ τῆς αἵματος λέγεις.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. You mean of the body and blood?

units.la: EPA. Οὕτω λέγω.
units.tr: ERANISTES. So I say.

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Φιλαλήθως ἐρῆκας· ἡ ὁ κύριος τὸ σύμβολον λαβὼν, ἐκεῖνο ἔστιν ἡ θεότης μου, αὐτὸ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου· καὶ πάλιν, τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου, καὶ ἑτέρως. Ὁ ἄρτος ὃν ἐγὼ δώσω, ἡ σάρξ μού ἐστιν, ἣν ἐγὼ δώσω ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου ζωῆς.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. You have answered candidly. For the Lord, taking the symbol, did not say, "That is my divinity," but "[This is my body]." And again, "[This is my blood]," and in another place: "The bread which I shall give is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of the world."

units.la: tas symbolum & cy-pum esse sanctissimum cibum? Divinitatis ne Domini Christi, an corporis & sanguinis?
units.tr: ...the symbol and type of the most holy food? Of the divinity of the Lord Christ, or of his body and blood?

units.la: ERA. Non dubium est, quin illorum sym-bola & rypi sint, quo-rum & nomina acce-perunt.
units.tr: ERANISTES. There is no doubt that they are the symbols and types of those things whose names they have received.

units.la: ORTHO. Cor-poris & sanguinis dicis?
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. You mean of the body and blood?

units.la: ERA. Sic loquor.
units.tr: ERANISTES. So I speak.

units.la: ORTHO. Oratio-ne usus es, quae amo-rem veritatis prae se fert. Nam Dominus symbolum accipiens, non dixit: Haec est di-vinitas mea, sed: Hoc est corpus meum. Et rursus: Hic est sanguis meus. Et alibi (Joh. 6.) Panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. You have used language that shows a love of truth. For the Lord, taking the symbol, did not say, "This is my divinity," but, "This is my body." And again, "This is my blood." And elsewhere (John 6): "The bread that I shall give is my flesh, which I shall give for the life of the world."

units.la: Alter vero locu… ita ha…
units.tr: "The other passage ... thus it reads ..."

units.la: ΟΡΘ.Εἰπὲ τοίνυν τὰ μυστικὰ σύμβολα τῶν ἱερωμένων τῷ Θεῷ προσφερόμενα τίνων ἐστὶ σύμβολα;
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Tell me, then, of what things are the mystical symbols offered to God by the consecrated ministers?

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Τὰ δεσποτικὰ σώματός τε, ἢ αἵματος.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Those of the Lord's body and blood.

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Τὰ ὄντως σώματα, ἢ ἀνόντως;
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Are they truly body, or not truly?

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Τὰ ὄντως.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Truly.

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Ἀεὶ γάρ. Χρὴ εἶναι τὸ τῆς εἰκόνος ἀρχέτυπον. Καὶ γὰρ οἱ ζωγράφοι τὴν Φύσιν μιμῶνται, καὶ τὰ ὁρωμένων ζωγραφοῦσι τὰς εἰκόνας.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Always. The archetype must be of the image. For painters imitate nature, and paint images of visible things.

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Ἀληθές.
units.tr: ERANISTES. True.

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Εἰ τόινυν τὰ ὄντως σώματα ἀντίτυπά ἐστι τὰ θεῖα μυστήρια, σῶμα ἄρα ἐστὶ, καὶ νῦν τὰ δεσπότης τὸ σῶμα, οὐκ εἰς θεότητος Φύσιν μεταβληθὲν, ἀλλὰ θείας δόξης ἀναπληθέν[?].
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. If, then, the true bodies are the antitypes of the divine mysteries, the Lord's body is also a body now, not changed into the nature of divinity, but filled with divine glory.

units.la: us ex Dial. II. abet.
units.tr: ...from Dialogue II, as it has.

units.la: ORTH. Dic igitur, mystica symbola à Sacerdotibus Deo oblata, quarum rerum sunt symbola?
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Tell me, then, of what things are the mystical symbols offered to God by the priests the symbols?

units.la: ERA. Dominici corporis, & sanguinis.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Of the Lord's body and blood.

units.la: ORTH. Verne corporis, an non veri?
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Of the true body, or not of the true?

units.la: ERA. Veri.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Of the true.

units.la: ORTH. Optime. Oportet enim imaginis esse archetypum. Nam & pictores naturam imitantur, & rerum visibilium pingunt imagines.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Excellent. For the image must have an archetype. Painters imitate nature, and paint images of visible things.

units.la: ERA. Verum est.
units.tr: ERANISTES. True.

units.la: ORTH. Si igitur veri corporis exemplaria sunt divina mysteria, corpus Domini nunc quoq; corpus est, non in divinitatis naturam mutatum, sed divinae gloriae plenum.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. If, then, the divine mysteries are copies of the true body, the Lord's body is also now a body, not changed into the nature of divinity, but full of divine glory.

units.la: ERA.
units.tr: ERANISTES.

units.la: EPA. Εἰς καιρὸν τ᾽ πε- ἒ τ᾽ θείων μυστηρίων ἐκί- νησας λόγον. Εντεῦθέν σοι ῥᾷδ δείξω τὰς δεσποτικὰς σώ- ματ@ τὴν εἰς ἑτέρην φύ- σιν μεταβολήν. Απόκρισις τοίνυν περὶς τὰς ἡμὰς ἐ- ρωτήσεις.
units.tr: ERANISTES. You have raised the discussion of the divine mysteries at the right moment. From this I shall easily show you the change of the Lord's body into another nature. Now answer my questions.

units.la: OPΘ. Απόκρισις.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. I will answer.

units.la: EPA. Τί καλεῖς τὸ προσφερόμενον δῶρον, πρὸ τῆς ἱερατικῆς ἀναγνώσεως.
units.tr: ERANISTES. What do you call the offered gift before the priestly reading?

units.la: OPΘ. Οὐχ ἡ σαφῶς εἰπεῖν. Εἰκὸς γάρ τινας ἀ- μυήτως παρεῖναι.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. It is not right to say it plainly, for some uninitiated people are likely to be present.

units.la: EPA. Αἰνιγματῶδῶς ἡ ἀπόκρισις ἔχω.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Then my answer will be in riddles.

units.la: OPΘ. Τὴν ἐκ τῶν ἀσερμάτων τροφήν.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Food from such seeds.

units.la: EPA. Τὸ ἕτερον σύμ- βολον, πῶς ὀνομάζομεν;
units.tr: ERANISTES. How do we name the other symbol?

units.la: ERA. Opportune de divinis mysteriis intu- listi sermonem. Inde e- nim tibi demonstrabo, Dominici corporis in aliam naturam muta- tionem. Responde er- go ad meas interroga- tiones.
units.tr: ERANISTES. You have raised the discussion of the divine mysteries at the right moment. From this I shall show you the change of the Lord's body into another nature. Answer my questions, then.

units.la: ORT. Respon- debo.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. I will answer.

units.la: ERA. Quid vocat oblatum donum ante Sacerdotis pronuncia- tionem?
units.tr: ERANISTES. What does he call the offered gift before the priest's pronouncement?

units.la: ORTH. Non est aperto sermone utem- dum. Fieri enim po- test, ut adsint aliqui nondum mysteriis ini- tiati.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. It must not be said in plain speech, for some present may not yet be initiated into the mysteries.

units.la: ERA. Proponatur ergo informa aenigma- tis responsio.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Let the answer, then, be given in the form of a riddle.

units.la: ORTHO. Cibum ex talibus feminibus.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. Food from such seeds.

units.la: ERA. Quomodo al- terum symbolum no- minamus?
units.tr: ERANISTES. How do we name the other symbol?

units.la: ORTH.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS.

units.la: ΟΡΘ. Κοινὸν καὶ τὸ ὄνομα, πῶμα τῶ εἴδῳ σημαίνον.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. The name is also a common one, signifying the appearance of the cup.

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Μετὰ δέγε τὸν ἁγιασμὸν, πῶς τῶν ζῷα προσαγορεύεις; ΟΡΘΟ. Σῶμα Χεσοῦ, καὶ αἷμα Χεσοῦ.
units.tr: ERANISTES. After the sanctification, how do you call these? ORTHODOXUS. The body of Christ and the blood of Christ.

units.la: ΕΡΑ. Καὶ πιστεύεις γε σώματι Χεσοῦ μεταλαμβάνειν καὶ αἵματι; ΟΡΘ. Οὕτω πιστεύω.
units.tr: ERANISTES. And do you believe that you partake of the body of Christ and of the blood? ORTHODOXUS. I believe so.

units.la: ΕΡΑΝ. Ὥσπερ τόινυν τὰ σύμβολα τοῦ δεσποτικῆς σώματός τε, καὶ αἵματος, ἀλλὰ μὴ εἰσὶν ἐπὶ τῆς ἐεχαριστίας ἀπὸκλήσεως, μὴ δέγε τὴν ἀπόκλησιν μεταβάλλεται, καὶ ἔπεσχ γίνεται. ὅτω τὸ δεσποτο-ORTH. Commu-ne & hoc nomen est, poculi speciem significans.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Just as the symbols of the Lord's body and blood, before the invocation of the thanksgiving, are one thing, but after the invocation are changed and become another, so the Lord's body... ORTHODOXUS. The name is also a common one, signifying the appearance of the cup.

units.la: ERA. Post sanctificationem vero quomodo hæc appellas.
units.tr: ERANISTES. But how do you call these after the sanctification?

units.la: ORTH. Corpus Christi, & sanguinem Christi.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. The body of Christ and the blood of Christ.

units.la: ERA. Credisne te percipere corpus Christi & sanguinem?
units.tr: ERANISTES. Do you believe that you receive the body of Christ and the blood?

units.la: ORTH. Sic credo.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. So I believe.

units.la: ERA. Quemadmodum igitur symbola Dominici corporis & sanguinis alia sunt ante Sacerdotis pronunciationem, post pronunciationem vero mutantur, & alia fiunt: Ita Dominicum corpus post ascensionem in divinam essentiam mutatum est.
units.tr: ERANISTES. Just as the symbols of the Lord's body and blood are one thing before the priest's invocation, but after the invocation are changed and become another, so the Lord's body, after the ascension, was changed into the divine essence.

units.la: ORTH. Implicatus es laqueis quos con-
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. You have become entangled in the snares you yourself set.

units.la: πινὸν σῶμα μὴ τὴν αἰσθη-τὴν ψιν, εἰς τὴν οὐσίαν μετεβλη-θῆ τε θείαν.
units.tr: ...some body was changed, not in its perceptible appearance, but in its essence, into a divine one.

units.la: ΟΡΘΟ. Εἰλως αἷς ὑφίωας ἀρχυσιν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ...
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. You have fallen into the snare you set. For...

units.la: μὴ τὰ ἀγλαςμὸν τὰ μυςικὰ σύμβολα τ̃ οἰκείας ἐξίςα-τω φύςεως. Μένει γὰρ τῆς ϖροτέρας ὑςίας, κ̀ τῆς χρήματος, ὡς τὰ εἴδους, καὶ ὁρᾶται ἐςι, καὶ ἀπλᾶ, οἷα καὶ ϖρότερον ἦν. Νοεῖ-τω ἃ ἅπερ ἐγίνετο, καὶ ϖε-ςέυετω, καὶ ϖρόσκιμεῖ-τω, ὡς ἐκεῖνα ὄντα ἅπερ ϖςέυετω. Παρα-δὲς τοῖ-νυν τῷ ἀρχετύπῳ τὴν εἰ-κόνα, καὶ ὄψῃ τ̀ ὁμοιότητα. Χρὴ γὰρ ἐοικέναι τῇ ἀλη-θείᾳ τὸν τύπον. Καὶ ἐ-κεῖνο τὸ σῶμα, τὸ μὲν ϖρό-τερον εἶδος ἔχει, καὶ χρῶ-μα, καὶ ϖεριγραφήν. Καὶ ἀϖαξιωτ̀ ὡς εἰπεῖν, τὴν τ̃ σώματος ὑςίαν. Ἀθάνα-τον δὲ μὴ τὴν ἀνάςασιν γένο-ντε ̀ κρεῖττον φθορᾶς, καὶ τ̃ ἐκ δεξιῶν ἡξιώθη καθέδρας, καὶ ϖρὸς ϖάν-τος ϖροσκυνεῖτω τ̃ κλί-ςεως, ἅτε δὴ σῶμα χρη-coniexuisti. Nequa- quam enim post sanctificationem mystica symbola propriam amittunt naturam. Manent enim in priore substantia, & figura & specie, & cerni ac tangi possunt, sicut antea. Intelliguntur autem quae facta sunt & creduntur, & adorantur, quasi essent illa, quae creduntur. Confer igitur archetypum cum imagine, & videbis similitudinem. Oportet enim typum similem esse veritati: illud enim corpus priorem habet formam, & figuram, & circumscriptionem, & ut summatim dicam, corporis essentiam. Etiamsi post resurrectionem immortale & immune a corruptione factum est, & ad dexteram Dei collocatum ab omni ματἰζον τὸ δεσποτικὸς τῆς φύσεως. omni creatura adoratur, quia corpus appellatur naturæ Domini. ΕΡΑ. Καὶ μὴν τὸ μυστικὸν σύμβολον, τὴν τρεπέραν ἀμείβει ἀποσημαίνει. Οὐκέτι γὰρ ὀνομάζετε τοῦ ὅπερ τρέπέρου ἐκαλεῖτο, ἀλλὰ σῶμα ἀπορρέπει. Χρὴ τοίνυν καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, Θεὸν, ἀλλὰ μὴ σῶμα καλεῖσθαι. ER A. Imò mysti- ΟΡΘΟ. Ἀγνοεῖν μοι δοκεῖς. Οὐ γὰρ σῶμα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄρτ ζωῆς ὀνομάζετε. Οὕτως αὐτὸς ὁ κύριος ἀποσημαίνει. Καὶ αὐτὸ ἦ τὸ σῶμα, θεῖον ὀνομάζομεν σῶμα, καὶ ζωοποιὸν, καὶ δεσποτικὸν, καὶ κυριακὸν, διδάσκοντες, ὡς ἡ κοινοῦ τινός ἐστιν ἀνθρώπου, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ζῳοῦ ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρι- cum fymbolum priorem mutat appellationem. Non enim amplius nuncupatur, quod antea vocabatur, sed corpus nominatur. Oportet igitur etiam veritatem, Deum, & non corpus vocari.
units.tr: ORTHODOXUS. For after the sanctification the mystical symbols do not lose their own nature. For they remain in their former substance, and in their figure and appearance, and can be seen and touched as before. Think of them as what they have become, and believe in them, and worship them, as being what they are believed to be. Set, then, the archetype beside the image and you will see the likeness, for the type must resemble the truth. That body has its former form, colour and outline, and, to put it briefly, the essence of a body. Even though after the resurrection it became immortal and superior to corruption, and was deemed worthy of the seat at the right hand of God, and is to be worshipped by every creature, it is still called body, because it is the body of the Lord's nature. ERANISTES. Indeed, the mystical symbol signifies the other change, for it is no longer called what it was called before, but is called body. Therefore the truth too ought to be called God, and not body. ORTHODOXUS. You seem to be ignorant. For the Lord calls it not only body but also [bread of life]. And we call this same body divine, life-giving, of the Lord, and Dominical, teaching that it belongs not to some common man, but to our Lord Jesus Christ...

units.la: ORTH. Videris in maximarum rerum ignoratione versari. Non enim corpus tantùm, sed etiam panis vitæ nominatur. Hâc enim appellatione Dominus usus est (Joh. 6.) Idem porrò corpus, divinum, & vivificum, & Dominicum appellamus, docentes, quòd non communis alicujus hominis sit, sed Domini nostri Jesu Christi,
units.tr: ORTH. You seem to be ignorant of very important matters. For he is named not only "body" but also "bread of life." The Lord himself used this name (John 6). Again, we call that same body divine, life-giving, and the Lord's, teaching that it belongs not to some ordinary man but to our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God and man

units.la: {ΘΕΟΣ ΕΝ ΧΡΙΣΤΩ ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΘΕΣ, ΧΘΕΣ ΚΑΙ ΣΗΜΕΡΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΙΩΝΑΣ.}
units.tr: [Jesus Christ, God in Christ, yesterday and today, and for ever] [ΘΕΟΣ ΕΝ ΧΡΙΣΤΩ ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΘΕΣ, ΧΘΕΣ ΚΑΙ ΣΗΜΕΡΟΝ, ΚΑΙ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΑΙΩΝΑΣ.]

units.la: sti, qui Deus est, & homo (Hebr. 13.) Jesus enim Christus heri & hodie, idem etiam in secula.
units.tr: (Hebr. 13.) "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, and today, and for ever."

units.la: Quid amabo, à Theodoreto proponitur, quod suum esse Reformati nolint? Conveniunt re, sive causa, quam Theodoretus defendendam suscepit, primaria. Nullam nempe in Sacramento Cœnæ Dominicæ Elementorum fieri conversionem substantialem; sed nominum tantum mutationem, & τὴν ἀντιτύπου χάριν, additamentum gratiæ. Sed neque fieri eam posse, cum eadem illius sit ratio, quæ incarnationis; hanc enim ad illam se habere, ut πρωτότυπον ad suum τύπον, vel ἀντίτυπον; Incarnationem autem ab Ecclesia adorari ἀπερίσπαστον, ἀδιαίρετον, ἀσύγχυτον, ἀχώριστον, sine mutatione, divulsione, confusione aut separatione. Aut ergo Eutychianismum adversarii incauti imbibent, aut Transsubstantiationis commento, ex Theodoreti argumentatione, repudium mittent. Conveniunt modus loquendi. Nam & Reformati easdem cum Theodoreto amant loquendi formulas: Mystica symbola, veri, non imaginarii aut phantastici, Domini corporis esse symbola: Panem post consecrationem vocari corpus Christi; neque tamen propterea mystica symbola propriam nanaturam amittere: Manere enim in priori substantia, & figura & specie, & videri tangique posse, qualia etiam prius erant. Placuisse autem Salvatori nomina permutare, & corpori quidem symboli nomen imponere; symbolo vero corporis nomen; ut ne nempe intenti essemus in naturam eorum, quae cernuntur; sed per nominum mutationem credere mus ei, quae ex gratia facta est, mutationi. Quid desiderari a quoquam quea ad mutuum monstrandum consensum? Res nostra est, verba nostra sunt; neutrum, Vir doctissime, vestrum. Vel annon citius ex pumice aquam, quam ex prolixa & erudita Theodoreti disputatione Transsubstantiationis elicias dogma? An Viri doctissimi, ad tam claram lucem, exceptionibus, quae purae putae sunt petitiones Principii, locus superesse possit, ipse viderit. Si contradicere, excipere, negare satis sit, mox nivem habebimus atram; diem noctem; lucem tenebras, Aethiopem album.
units.tr: To give an example, dear sir, what is put forward by Theodoret that the Reformed refuse to acknowledge as their own? They agree on the chief matter, or the cause, which Theodoret undertook to defend: that in the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper no substantial conversion of the elements takes place, but only a change of names, and "the grace of the antitype" [τὴν ἀντιτύπου χάριν], an addition of grace. Nor can it take place, since the reasoning is the same as for the incarnation. For the one stands to the other as the archetype [πρωτότυπον] to its type [τύπον] or antitype [ἀντίτυπον]. The Church adores the incarnation as unconfused [ἀπερίσπαστον], indivisible [ἀδιαίρετον], unmixed [ἀσύγχυτον], inseparable [ἀχώριστον], without change, division, confusion or separation. So either your opponents will imbibe Eutychianism unwittingly, or, by Theodoret's own argument, they will repudiate the fiction of transubstantiation. They also agree in their way of speaking. For the Reformed too love the same formulas as Theodoret: the mystical symbols are true, not imaginary or fantastic, symbols of the Lord's body; after consecration the bread is called the body of Christ, yet the mystical symbols do not on that account lose their own nature. For they remain in their former substance, shape and appearance, and can be seen and touched as they were before. The Saviour was pleased to exchange names, giving the name of the symbol to the body and the name of the body to the symbol, so that we should not fix our attention on the nature of the things that are seen, but through the change of names believe in the change that has been made by grace. What more could anyone want to show agreement? The matter is ours, the words are ours; neither of them, most learned sir, is yours. Or would you sooner squeeze transubstantiation out of pumice-stone than out of Theodoret's long and learned discussion? Whether the most learned men have any room left for exceptions, which are thought pure petitions of principle, in the face of so clear a light, they must judge for themselves. If it is enough to contradict, except and deny, we shall soon have black snow, day as night, light as darkness, an Ethiopian white.

units.la: B. Theodoreto locupletissimum illud totius antiquitatis eruditae compendium & cornucopiae Epiphanium, Salaminae Episcopum, in Anchorato ita loquentem, adjungimus: Καὶ εὐχα- ριστήσας εἶπε τοῦτό μου ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα, ... [Greek text continues.]
units.tr: To Theodoret's very rich compendium of all learned antiquity, and horn of plenty, we also add Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, speaking thus in the Anchoratus: "And having given thanks, he said, 'This is my body' ..." [Greek text continues.]

units.la: Καὶ εὐχαριστήσας εἶπε τοῦτό μού ἐστι τὸ σῶμα, ὁ ὁρῶμεν ὅλως ἔχειν σύμ- βολον, ἀδὲ ὅμοιον, ἐν τῇ ἐνσάρκῳ εἰκόνι, ἐν τῇ ἀορατῷ θεί- ᾳ, ἐν τοῖς χαρακτῆρσιν τῶν μελῶν. τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐς προ- γυμνασίας καὶ ἀναλύτων. ὡς τῶν τὴν δύναμιν, καὶ ἡ θέλησι χάρις εἴωθεν, τοῦτό μου ἐστι τόδε, καὶ ἀδεῖς ἀποςῆ τῷ λόγῳ. Et cum benedixisset, dixit: Hoc meum ist ud est (corpus) & videmus, quod nec par est, nec simile, aut corporea figura, aut invisibili divinitati, nec lineamentis membrorum. Hoc enim rotundum & sensus expers. Quantum ad virtutem, gratia dicere voluit, hoc est meum istud, & nemo huic sermoni fidem derogat. Vix, in tota antiquitate, locus brevior, qui tamen maiori successu jugulum Transsubstantiationi petat. Opponit inter se Epiphanius panem, & verum corpus Christi. Illum exprimit corpus rotundum, sensus expers, adeoque assumtae carnis figurae non similie, nec ullo modo aequale, neque invisibili divinitati, nec membrorum lineamentis. Omnes similitudinis species removet, ut panem in Eucharistia manere panem, id est, ut loquitur Iremius, rem terrestrem, probet doctissimus Pater. Et tamen de hoc pane, toto coelo a Christi vel humanitate vel divinitate diverso, δυνάμει, χάριτι, sive, ut loquitur Theodoretus, dixit: Hoc est corpus meum. Quae vero illa δυνάμεις, quae χάρις, de qua Epiphanius? Est virtus illa, quam veteres Latini appellarunt, Sacramenti, quâ (sic loqui iterum placeat cum Augustino ex Tract. 80. in Joh.) accedente verbo ad Elementum, institutione & ordinatione divina fit Sacramentum. Est χάρις illa, quâ panis fit corpus Christi pro nobis traditum; non mutat tatione substantiæ; sed additione usus, ἵνα ἡ χ ἄρ- τῳ ἡμῖν γίνηται δύναμις, ἀλλὰ δύναμις ἄρτυ ut non panis sit nobis virtus, sed virtus, quæ in pane est; ut idem Epiph. loquitur in Expofit. fi-dei. Prorsus ut Ambrosius de baptismo scripsit, si quæ in aqua gratia sit, non ex natura eam a- quæ, sed ex præsentia Sp. S. procedere. Nihil hic de Speciebus, aut Accidentibus panis, nihil de pane conversō, nihil de fanatica recentiorum concomitantia: Clare omnia & perspicue tra-dunt, Christum panem vocâsse corpus, neque tamen illum cum hoc, quoad substantiam, aut externa etiam lineamenta, quicquam habere commune.
units.tr: "And having given thanks, he said, 'This is my body,' which we see has no symbol or likeness, either in the fleshly image, or in the invisible divinity, or in the features of the members. For that is round and devoid of sense. As to its power, it was pleased to say by grace, 'This is my body,' and no one derogates from this saying." [Greek: Καὶ εὐχαριστήσας εἶπε τοῦτό μού ἐστι τὸ σῶμα, ὁ ὁρῶμεν ὅλως ἔχειν σύμβολον, ἀδὲ ὅμοιον, ἐν τῇ ἐνσάρκῳ εἰκόνι, ἐν τῇ ἀορατῷ θείᾳ, ἐν τοῖς χαρακτῆρσιν τῶν μελῶν. τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐς προγυμνασίας καὶ ἀναλύτων. ὡς τῶν τὴν δύναμιν, καὶ ἡ θέλησι χάρις εἴωθεν, τοῦτό μου ἐστι τόδε, καὶ ἀδεῖς ἀποςῆ τῷ λόγῳ.] Hardly anywhere in all antiquity is there a shorter passage that nevertheless strikes at the throat of transubstantiation with greater success. Epiphanius sets bread against the true body of Christ. Illum, the one, he describes as a round thing, devoid of sense, and therefore not like the shape of the assumed flesh, nor in any way equal to it, nor to the invisible divinity, nor to the features of the members. He removes every kind of likeness, so that the most learned Father proves that the bread remains bread in the Eucharist, that is, as Iremius puts it, an earthly thing. And yet of this bread, which is wholly different from Christ, whether in his humanity or his divinity, he said by power, by grace, or, as Theodoret puts it, "This is my body." But what is that power, and what is that grace, of which Epiphanius speaks? It is that virtue which the ancient Latins called that of the Sacrament, by which (to speak again with Augustine, Tract. 80 on John) the word being added to the element, the Sacrament comes into being through divine institution and ordinance. It is that grace by which the bread becomes the body of Christ given for us. It does not change the substance, but by the addition of use, "so that the grace is not the bread's power for us, but the power that is in the bread," as the same Epiphanius says in the Exposition of the Faith. Just as Ambrosius wrote about baptism, "if there is grace in the water, it proceeds not from the nature of the water, but from the presence of the Holy Spirit." Nothing here about the species or accidents of the bread, nothing about the converted bread, nothing about the fanatical concomitance of recent writers. They hand down everything clearly and plainly: that Christ called the bread his body, and yet that the bread has nothing in common with that body, either in substance or even in external features.

units.la: C. Unum adhuc addimus, Macarium, Ægyptium, cujus ex Homilia 27. verba satis sunt emphatica. "Οτι, inquit, ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ προσφέρε- ται ἄρτῳ καὶ οἶνῳ, ἀντίτυπον τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ ἢ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ. καὶ οἱ μεταλαμβάνοντες ἐκ τὸ φανόμενον ἄρτα, πνευματικῶς τὴν σάρκα τὸ κυρίου ἐσθίουσι. Quod in Ecclesia offertur panis & vinum, antitypum carnis & sanguinis ejus. Et qui participant de visibili pane, Spiritualiter carnem Domini comedunt. Nos quoq; & dicimus, & docemus, panem atq; vinum offerenda, Symbola esse & elementa; non Accidentia: esse antitypa, carnis & sanguinis Christi: eos, qui de visibili pane, non speciebus lusoriis, digne participant, Spiritualiter carnem Domini edere. An idem RoRoma vel sentit, vel loquitur? Cur ergò, quòd in antiquitate ipsi mirantur, colunt, venerantur, in nobis, propterea quòd & nostrum sit, & cum veteribus commune, flagitium censeatur, aut scelus? Parùm abest, quin veterum nobis reperenda veniat querela: Bonus vir Cajus Sejus, sed malus tantùm, quòd Christianus; Tertull. Apol.cap.3.
units.tr: C. We add one more, Macarius the Egyptian, whose words from Homily 27 are quite emphatic. "For," he says, "bread and wine are offered in the Church, the antitype of his flesh and blood. And those who partake of the visible bread eat the flesh of the Lord spiritually." [Greek: Ὅτι, inquit, ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ προσφέρεται ἄρτῳ καὶ οἶνῳ, ἀντίτυπον τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ ἢ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ. καὶ οἱ μεταλαμβάνοντες ἐκ τὸ φανόμενον ἄρτα, πνευματικῶς τὴν σάρκα τὸ κυρίου ἐσθίουσι.] Quod in Ecclesia offertur panis & vinum, antitypum carnis & sanguinis ejus. Et qui participant de visibili pane, Spiritualiter carnem Domini comedunt. We too both say and teach that the bread and wine offered are symbols and elements, not accidents; that they are antitypes of the flesh and blood of Christ; and that those who worthily partake of the visible bread, not of playful species, spiritually eat the flesh of the Lord. Does Rome think or speak the same? Why then, what they admire, cherish and venerate in antiquity, should be counted a shameful crime or a sin in us, merely because it is ours too and common with the ancients?
