It is hardly far off that the ancients' complaint should come upon us: "A good man, Gaius Seius, but bad only because he is a Christian" (Tertullian, Apology, ch. 3).

units.la: III. In Syriam si transfretare lubeat, in ipso statim portu præstò erit magnus ille Syrorum Propheta, (hoc enim ei axioma Ecclesia Syriaca tribuit) Ephræmus, Magister alias orbis appellatus, cujus tanta apud Veteres fuit authoritas, ut post lectionem Scripturarum, publicè, in quibusdam Ecclesiis, ejus scripta fuerint recitata. Hic etiam adeò feliciter controversiam Sacramentariam dirimit, ut & prælium & bellum Eucharisticum tribusferè expediat periodis. Ita enim apud Photium C. 229. Τὸ ... (Greek) ... Corpus Christi, quod àfidelibus accipitur, substantiam sensibilem (panis videlicet) non amittit, & à gratia sub intelligentiam cadente, in separatum manet: Baptismus quin etiam, etsi totus Spiritualis sit factus, & unus tantantum existat, proprietatem substantiæ sensibilis, aquæ nimirum, servat, & id quod fuit, esse non definit. Nihil evidentius ad nostræ sententiæ explicationem. Si manducationem adhuc Spiritualem (ut per omnia habeamus consentientem Ecclesiam Syriacam) desideres, en locum Symbolicum, ex Syrorum Gazophylacio (hoc libri nomen est) depromtum: Corpus tuum, quod accepimus, & sanguis tuus vitæ, quem bibimus per fidem, sit pons & vadum, quo liberati ab igni & gehenna, hæreditatem consequamur vitæ.
units.tr: III. If you wish to cross over into Syria, right at the harbour there will be to hand that great Prophet of the Syrians (for the Syrian Church ascribes this title to him), Ephraem, called by others "Teacher of the world" [Magister orbis], whose authority among the ancients was so great that after the reading of Scripture his writings were publicly recited in certain churches. He too settles the sacramentarian controversy so happily that he dispatches the Eucharistic battle and war in almost three sentences. For so in Photius, Cod. 229: the body of Christ, which is received by the faithful, does not lose its sensible substance (that is, the bread), but remains separate, while by grace it falls under understanding. Even baptism, though it has been made wholly spiritual and exists as one thing only, keeps the property of its sensible substance, namely water, and does not cease to be what it was. Nothing is more evident for explaining our opinion. If you still desire a spiritual eating (so that we may have the Syrian Church in full agreement), see a symbolic passage taken from the Treasury of the Syrians (this is the name of the book): "Your body, which we have received, and your blood of life, which we drink through faith, may it be a bridge and a ford, by which, freed from fire and Gehenna, we may obtain the inheritance of life."

units.la: IV. Latina Ecclesia non exempla nobis tantum suppeditat; sed & regulas de Sacramentalibus locutionibus præscribit, per quas Sacramenta, visibilia esse signa, invisibilis gratiæ colligimus.
units.tr: IV. The Latin Church gives us not only examples but also rules for sacramental expressions, by which we gather that sacraments are visible signs of invisible grace.

units.la: Proinde cujuslibet Sacramenti materiam esse geminam, externam signi; internam rei significatæ. Sacramenta necessario quandam habere similitudinem earum rerum, quarum sunt Sacramenta. Panem in Cœna, quoad substantiam, manere panem; & vinum, ut similitudinem gerere possint corporis & sanguinis Christi, cujus sunt Sacramentum, manere vinum.
units.tr: Accordingly, every sacrament has a twofold matter: an external matter of the sign and an internal matter of the thing signified. Sacraments necessarily bear some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments. In the Supper, the bread remains bread in its substance, and the wine remains wine, so that they may bear a likeness of the body and blood of Christ, of which they are the sacrament.

units.la: Latina Ecclesia disertis nobiscum proponit verbis: Sacramentum corporis (sunt ipsissima. Facundi, Episcopi Hermianensis, verba lib. 9.) & sanguinis ejus, quod est in pane & poculo con-sesecrato, corpus ejus & sanguinem dici, non quod proprie corpus ejus sit panis, & poculum sanguis, sed quod in se mysterium corporis sanguinisque contineant. Hinc factum, ut & ipse Dominus benedictum panem & calicem, quem discipulis tradidit, corpus & sanguinem suum vocaverit.
units.tr: The Latin Church sets this before us in clear words: the sacrament of the body (these are the very words of Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, book 9) and of his blood, which is in the consecrated bread and cup, is called his body and blood, not because the bread is properly his body and the cup his blood, but because they contain in themselves the mystery of the body and blood. Hence it came about that the Lord himself called the blessed bread and cup, which he gave to the disciples, his body and blood.

units.la: V. Num quid hic vel violentum, vel tortum, vel mutilatum, praecipitatum, obscurum, flexiloquum? Adversarii contra, ubi vel umbram eminus vident, fugientem etiam in obsequium causae cogere allaborant. Loca reperias, quae Transsubstantiationem penitus evertunt, & tamen propter aegre blandientem ἀκυρολογίαν, ea suae ὑπονοήσεως δηλώσεων cogunt. Gelasius, (ut vel unico agamus exemplo) quem Episcopum Romanum fuisse non nostri modo observant; sed & Romanae Ecclesiae Theologi libenter concedunt, quod, suo loco, contra Virum doctissimum, commodius monebimus; Tract. adversus Eutych. & Nestorium ita scribit. Sapientia aedificavit sibi domum, septiformis Spiritus soliditate subnixam, qua incarnationis Christi, per quam efficimur divinae consortes naturae, ministraret alimoniam. Certe Sacramenta, quae sumimus, corporis & sanguinis Christi, divinares est, propter quod, & per eadem divinae efficimur consortes naturae, (alii, propterea, quod per eadem divinae consortes efficimur naturae) & tamen tamen esse non definit substantia, vel natura panis, vel vini. Et certè imago, & similitudo corporis & sanguinis Christi in actione mysteriorum celebrantur. Satis ergo nobis evidenter ostenditur, hoc nobis in ipso Christo Domino sentiendum, quod in ejus imagine profitemur, celebramus, et sumus (alii, sumimus) ut sicut in hanc, scilicet in divinam transeunt, sancto Spiritu perficiente, substantiam, permanent tamen in sua proprietate natura (alii, eodem sensu, legunt: ut sicut hæc scilicet in divinam transeunt, Spiritu perficiente, substantiam, permanente tamen in sua proprietate natura) sic illud ipsum mysterium Principale, cujus nobis efficientiam, virtutemque veraciter representant, ex quibus constat, proprie permanentibus, unum Christum, quia integrum verumque permanere demonstrant. Hic verò universus textus, tum quoad sensum, tum quoad verba, pro Reformatis mittit: sensum etiam & verba Reformati admittunt. Agnoscunt, cum Gelasio, duas in Christo Naturas: Negant verò, illas vel confundi, vel converti, vel mutari substantias: Exemplo, ἀ-τςὶ incarnationis, mysterium utrinque illustrant Symbolorum Cœna Dominica: quæ, etsi divina fiant res, per consecrationem, eandem tamen constanter Naturam retineant, vel substantiam: Hoc verò exemplum propterea rejici non posse, quia Symbola Sacramentalia, Panis & & vinum, imago sint & similitudo, qua prototypi virtutem & efficaciam veraciter repraesentent. Et tamen, quia Gelasius dixit, transfire Sacramenta in divinam substantiam, & scopum Gelasii, & vim argumenti, & phraseologiae apertam Emphasin invertere, enervare, atque obscurare Adversarii malunt, quam triumphanti hic veritati palmam concedere. Dixit Gelasius, Sacramenta transfire in divinam substantiam: Non negamus. Sed an per μετασιωσιν sive μεταποιησιν, Transsubstantiationem? Atqui hoc expresse Gelasius non modo negat; sed firmissimis rationibus refutat. Postquam enim prolixe jam ante disputasset, Verbum, Λογον assumsisse carnem ἀτρέπτως, i.e. ut veteres loquebantur Graeci, τὸ πὴν ὑπόστασιν, ἄλλὰ τὴν μετάβολον ... ἐαυτῷ θεότητα, ὡς ἀνθρώπου τύπον, neque substantem mutationem, neque convertentem suam ipsius Deitatem in humanitatem; efficacissimum argumentum tandem ex natura & conditione Symbolorum Sacramentalium; Orthodoxus author struit. Quod vero argumenti robur, quae medii termini vis illativa, si realem Substantiae mutationem, quam omnibus destruere viribus curae habuit, quamque Orthodoxa semper Ecclesia anathemate damnavit, in Coena Domini asseruisset? Certe, in tyronibus Dialecticae inepti ejusmodi & insulsi Paralogismi, absque Orbilii censura, vix tolerarentur;
units.tr: V. Is there anything here forced, twisted, mutilated, hasty, obscure, or ambiguous? Our opponents, on the other hand, when they see even a shadow from afar, labour to compel even a fleeing one into the service of their cause. You may find passages that utterly overthrow transubstantiation, and yet, by means of a catachresis [ἀκυρολογία] that barely flatters them, they force these passages into their own [ὑπονοήσεως δηλώσεων] sense. Take Gelasius as a single example. Our people observe that he was bishop of Rome, and the theologians of the Roman Church gladly grant it, as I shall point out more fully in its place against a most learned man. In his tract against Eutyches and Nestorius he writes thus: Wisdom built itself a house, supported by the firmness of the sevenfold Spirit, which would supply the food of the incarnation of Christ, through which we are made partakers of the divine nature. Surely the sacraments we receive, of the body and blood of Christ, are divine, and for this reason we are made partakers of the divine nature through them (others read: because through them we are made partakers of the divine nature), and yet the substance or nature of bread or wine does not cease to be. And certainly the image and likeness of the body and blood of Christ are celebrated in the action of the mysteries. It is therefore sufficiently and evidently shown to us that we ought to think in the same way about Christ the Lord himself as we profess, celebrate, and receive in his image, so that just as these pass into the divine substance, the Spirit working, yet remain in their own natural properties (others read in the same sense: just as these pass into the divine substance, the Spirit working, yet remaining in their own natural properties), so that principal mystery itself, whose efficacy and power they truly represent, of which the one Christ consists, properly remaining, they show to be whole and true. Yet this whole text, both as to sense and as to words, speaks for the Reformed: the Reformed also admit the sense and the words. With Gelasius they acknowledge two natures in Christ, but they deny that the substances are either confused, or converted, or changed. By way of example, they illustrate the mystery on both sides by the symbols of the Lord's Supper, which, although they become a divine thing through consecration, nevertheless constantly retain their nature or substance. Nor can this example be rejected, because the sacramental symbols, bread and wine, are an image and likeness by which they truly represent the power and efficacy of the archetype. And yet, because Gelasius said that the sacraments pass into the divine substance, our opponents prefer to overturn, weaken, and obscure both the purpose of Gelasius, the force of his argument, and the plain emphasis of his phraseology, rather than concede the palm here to triumphant truth. Gelasius said that the sacraments pass into the divine substance: we do not deny it. But does he mean by μετασίωσις or μεταποίησις, that is, transubstantiation? Yet Gelasius not only expressly denies this but refutes it with the firmest reasons. For after he had already disputed at length that the Word, the Λόγος, assumed flesh [ἀτρέπτως], that is, as the ancient Greeks put it, not changing his hypostasis but ... taking to himself divinity as a type of humanity, neither undergoing a substantial change nor converting his own Deity into humanity, the orthodox author at last builds his most effective argument from the nature and condition of the sacramental symbols. But what strength would the argument have, what inferential force would the middle term have, if he had asserted in the Lord's Supper the real change of substance which he took such pains to destroy with all his powers, and which the orthodox Church has always condemned with anathema? Surely such inept and silly paralogisms in the students of dialectic would hardly be tolerated, even without the rebuke of Orbilius.

units.la: K & & nos tanti viri in dubium vocemus vel mediocrem argumentandi dexteritatem? Haec verba, hic sensus, haec meta est Gelasii: Quemadmodum in mysterio principali natura divina non est conversa in humanam, sed Verbi divinitas assumsit humanitatem; sic in Sacramento corporis, panis Substantia non mutata est, nec conversa in divinam subsistentiam corporis Christi. Hoc est quod Gelasius vult, quod docte probat, quod Ecclesiae Orthodoxae nomine Eutychianis feliciter opponit. Manent tamen semper verba: Transfire Sacramenta in divinam substantiam. Ita est, manent verba; sed facili, commodo, & eo quidem sensu, qui Authoris scopum non pervertat explicanda. Transfire ergo dicuntur in substantiam divinam, non mutatione substantiae in substantiam, qualem Poetae olim in suis Metamorphosibus fabulabantur; sed μεταβολή additione rei coelestis. Aliud enim, per consecrationem & institutionem divinam, fiunt Elementa, quam erant per naturam; substantiamque divinam accipiunt, quatenus res coelestis, corpus Christi, modo Sacramentali, adjungitur terrestri. Haec est illa μετα-βολή, hic transitus, quem veteres in sola adjunctione gratiae, ad utramque substantiam, panis & vini, agnoscebant. Nec substantia vocabulum hoc loco quicquam aliud infert, quam veritatem, & realitatem praesentiae; opinioni & exis\-timationi opoppositam. Etsi enim panis in Sacramento sic signum corporis; suo tamen modo ipsum etiam est corpus: Non per mutationem substantiae, sed per denominationem, & divinam operationem, per quam fit, ut re ipsa & in veritate sumamus in legitimo Eucharistiae usu, corpus & sanguinem Christi, quae propterea substantia divina vocatur, quod, ceu res divina, veraciter existit, non in opinione subsistit; quae καὶ ὑπόστασιν extat, non καὶ ἐμφασιν apparet.
units.tr: Shall we, then, call into doubt the argumentative skill, even moderate, of so great a man? These are Gelasius's words, this is his sense, this is his goal: just as in the principal mystery the divine nature was not converted into the human, but the divinity of the Word assumed humanity, so in the sacrament of the body the substance of the bread is not changed, nor converted into the divine subsistence of the body of Christ. This is what Gelasius wishes, what he learnedly proves, what he happily sets against the Eutychians in the name of the orthodox Church. The words remain always: the sacraments pass into the divine substance. Yes, the words remain, but they must be explained easily, conveniently, and in that sense which does not pervert the author's purpose. They pass, therefore, are said into a divine substance, not by a change of one substance into another, such as the poets once fabled in their Metamorphoses, but by μεταβολή [metabolē], through the addition of a heavenly thing. For by consecration and divine institution the elements become something other than they were by nature; and they receive a divine substance, insofar as the heavenly thing, the body of Christ, is joined to the earthly in a sacramental manner. This is that μεταβολή, this passing over, which the ancients recognised solely in the addition of grace, to each substance, of bread and of wine. Nor does the word substance in this place introduce anything else than truth and reality of presence, opposed to opinion and mere estimation. For although the bread in the sacrament is thus a sign of the body, yet in its own way it is also itself the body: not by a change of substance, but by a denomination and divine operation, through which it comes about that, in the lawful use of the Eucharist, we really and in truth receive the body and blood of Christ. These are therefore called divine substance because, as a divine thing, they truly exist and do not subsist in opinion; they exist in reality [ὑπόστασιν], they do not appear in appearance only [ἐμφασιν].

units.la: VI. Si plura expectaverit, Vir doctissimus, Antiquitatis suffragia, per omnia nobis ὁμοούσια, non denegaremus, modo praestituti brevitatis cancelli in amplissimum excurrendi campum veniam darent. Videt spero, non ita copias nostras esse contractas, ut unius atque alterius Patris mutilatum, truncatum, fidiculis extortum, adeoque invitum emendicare calculum, necesse habuerimus: Sponte se offerunt, magnoque conatu, conferto quasi agmine Transubstantiationem impugnant illi, quorum authoritas in Ecclesia & magna semper fuit, & merito esse debet.
units.tr: VI. If the most learned man had expected more, we would not deny him the testimonies of antiquity, in every respect consubstantial with us [ὁμοούσια], provided that the limit of brevity set for us did not give us leave to run out into a very wide field. I hope he sees that our forces are not so cramped that we must beg for the vote of one or another Father, mutilated, truncated, tortured on the rack, and therefore unwilling. Rather, they offer themselves of their own accord, and with great effort, as if in a closely packed column, they attack transubstantiation: those whose authority has always been great in the Church, and rightly ought to be.

units.la: VII. Vidimus, antiquitatem; in iis locis, ubi de Sacramento S. Coenae illa agit ex professo; totam esse nostram: cominus jam congressu instructas argumentorum acies ex Antiquitate, Transubstantiationis opponere possumus novitati; sed quando receptui paulatim canendum est, ad classes hac vice tantum argumentorum rum; textibus, ex quibus illa petita, obiter indicatis; digitum intendemus, eorumq; defensionem, qualibet data occasione suscipere, pleniusq; ea exponere parati sumus. Ergo, ut videat doctissimus Vir, quantum de Antiquitate sobrie intellecta nobis in antithesi polliceamur, negamus constanter, Transsubstantiationem illi placuisse. Qui enim docent,
units.tr: VII. We have seen that antiquity is wholly ours in those passages where it treats professedly of this sacrament of the Holy Supper. Now that we have met face to face, we could oppose to the novelty of transubstantiation the battle lines of arguments drawn up from antiquity. But since we must gradually sound the retreat, for this time we will only briefly indicate, by classes of arguments, the texts from which they are drawn, and point our finger at them; and we are ready to defend them on any occasion that offers and to set them out more fully. So, that the most learned man may see how much of antiquity, soberly understood, we promise in the antithesis, we constantly deny that transubstantiation pleased them. For those who teach that

units.la: 1. Christum de pane, non vero individuo vago dixisse, Hoc est corpus meum; illi Transsubstantiationem nullam statuunt. Atqui Patres, a Irenaeus, b Tertullianus, c Origenes, d Hieronymus, e Chrysostomus, f Augustinus, g Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, h Theodoretus, &c.
units.tr: 1. Those who hold that Christ said of the bread, not of some vague individual thing, "This is my body," admit no transubstantiation. But the Fathers: (a) Irenaeus, (b) Tertullian, (c) Origen, (d) Jerome, (e) Chrysostom, (f) Augustine, (g) Cyril of Jerusalem, (h) Theodoret, etc.

units.la: a. Lib. 4. adv. haer. c. 34. & lib. 5. b. Lib. 4 adv. Marc. c. 40. c. In Matth. tract. five Homil. 12. d. Lib. 17. in Jes c 62. & ad Hedib. e. In Matth. hom. 81. & Psalm. 22. f. Serm. ad Infant. g. Catech. Myst. 3. &c. h. Dial. 1. c. 8. & Dial. 2. c. 24.
units.tr: a. Lib. 4. adv. haer. c. 34. & lib. 5. b. Lib. 4 adv. Marc. c. 40. c. In Matth. tract. five Homil. 12. d. Lib. 17. in Jes c 62. & ad Hedib. e. In Matth. hom. 81. & Psalm. 22. f. Serm. ad Infant. g. Catech. Myst. 3. &c. h. Dial. 1. c. 8. & Dial. 2. c. 24.

units.la: 2. Qui tradunt, Tropum vel esse in Copula; quam proinde per significat, repraesentat, memorat; interpretantur; vel in Praedicato; dum panem & vinum vocant corporis & sanguinis Christi signa, Sacramenta, Figuras, Symbola, typos, Antitypa, Mysteria, Exemplaria, similitudines, imagines, memorias; illi nullam potunt Transsubstantiationem. Atqui illud placuit a Tertulliano, b Basilio,c Eusebio,d Hieronymo, e Augustino f Cyrillo Alexand: Hoc g Origeni, h Gregorio Nazianzeno,i Chrysostomo, k Hieronymo,l Theodoreto,&c.
units.tr: 2. Those who teach that the trope lies in the copula, which they therefore interpret as signifies, represents, calls to mind; or that it lies in the predicate, while they call the bread and wine the signs, sacraments, figures, symbols, types, antitypes, mysteries, examples, likenesses, images, memorials of the body and blood of Christ: those cannot hold any transubstantiation. But this view pleased Tertullian, b Basil, c Eusebius, d Jerome, e Augustine, f Cyril of Alexandria; Origen, g Gregory Nazianzen, h Chrysostom, i Jerome, k Theodoret, etc.

units.tr: 10. Those who establish two distinct things in the Lord's Supper, an earthly thing, the element (for who would dare to assert that the ancients understood by the earthly thing taste and colour without substance, and that it takes the place of a part integral or essential, since it is the bread itself?), and a heavenly thing, the body of the Lord: those depart far from transubstantiation. But Irenaeus, Augustine, etc.

units.la: 11. Qui docent, eandem esse rationem aquæ in Baptismo, olei in chrismate, quæ panis & vini in Cœna Domini, illi negant Transsubstantiationem. Atqui Patres, &c. Consequentia manifesta est. Quis enim unquam Patrum dixit aut sensit, Aquam Baptismi in sanguinem Christi substantialiter mutari? Assumtum probatur authoritate Augustini, Ephræm, Cypriani, &c.
units.tr: 11. Those who teach that the case of the water in baptism, and of the oil in chrism, is the same as that of the bread and wine in the Lord's Supper: those deny transubstantiation. But the Fathers, etc. The inference is plain. For which of the Fathers ever said or thought that the water of baptism is substantially changed into the blood of Christ? The premise is proved by the authority of Augustine, Ephraem, Cyprian, etc.

units.la: VIII. Habes, Vir doctissime, Patrum consen- sum.
units.tr: VIII. You have, most learned sir, the consensus of the Fathers.

units.la: Si quid forte, vestræ causæ in Antiquitate favere videatur, ereptum illud pridem vobis est atque vindicatum, tum ab aliis, tum verò & cumprimis ab Hospiniano nostro, postea etiam Chamiero, Riveto; nuper Davide Blondello, Thoma Mortono de Eucharist. & Forbes. Instruct. Hist. Theol. Habeatis igitur hinc inde Patres, qui dum aliud agunt; Mutationis, immutationis vocabula adhibent, nunquam tamen habebitis, vel vocem Transsubstantiationis, vel rem, panem in corpus, substantiam in substantiam mumutatam. Videatur alicubi Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, videantur alii pro Transsubstantiatione rem dare confectam, cum dixerint panem, qui apparet, non esse panem, quamvis ex gustu ita videatur; sed esse corpus Christi; mox tamen ad se redibunt, & luculentissimis Epithetis, phrasibus apertissimis condocefacient, neque panem substantialiter se velle mutatum, neque vinum; devotionem autem excitaturus voces istas placuisse, ut discerent religiosi communicantes, non esse ἄρτον, λιτὸν, panem communem; sed πνευματικὸν ἄρτον, panem Spiritualem, ut idem ille loquitur Cyrillus. Loquantur alicubi de suo, ut homines; mox tamen, ut Doctores Evangelici ad originem Dominicam nos rejiciunt. His observatis regulis, repetimus, nostros esse Patres, non ex laciniis, sed ex integris disputationibus, textuum collationibus, benigniori phrasium duriorum explicatione, secundum Scripturæ Canonem, quem nobis religiose commendant, intellectos. Atque hoc est tantopere jactatum, & ad nauseam ab Adversariis inculcatum Antiquitatis præsidium.
units.tr: If anything in antiquity seems to favour your cause, it was long ago snatched from you and vindicated, both by others and above all by our Hospinian, and afterwards by Chamier and Rivet, and recently by David Blondel, Thomas Morton on the Eucharist, and Forbes in his Instructio Historico-Theologica. So you may have Fathers here and there who, while they are saying something else, use the words "change" and "alteration"; yet you will never have either the word transubstantiation or the thing itself, bread changed into body and substance changed into substance. Somewhere Cyril of Jerusalem may be found, and others, seeming to give a finished matter for transubstantiation, when they say that the bread which appears is not bread, though it seems so to the taste, but is the body of Christ. Soon, however, they come back to themselves and teach, in the most splendid epithets and the plainest phrases, that neither bread nor wine is substantially changed. Wishing to stir up devotion, they chose those words so that the pious communicants might learn that it is not ordinary bread [ἄρτον, λιτὸν], common bread, but spiritual bread [πνευματικὸν ἄρτον], spiritual bread, as that same Cyril puts it. They sometimes speak of their own accord, like men; but soon, like evangelical teachers, they call us back to the Lord's origin. Having observed these rules, we repeat that the Fathers are ours, understood not from scraps but from whole discussions, from comparison of texts, from a kinder explanation of harsher phrases, and according to the canon of Scripture, which they religiously commend to us. This is the much-boasted defence of antiquity, drummed into us by our adversaries to the point of nausea.

units.la: SECTIO XII.
units.tr: SECTION XII.

units.la: Transsubstantiatio Principia Natu- ræ evertit.
units.tr: Transubstantiation overturns the principles of Nature.

units.la: I. Scio, laterem lavari, quoties Adversariis Naturæ ordinem objicimus in Gratiæ mysterio. Sed in se descendere deberent, serióque cogitare, hæc potissimum arma in suis cudi officinis. Pridem certè, in Schola Pontificia, conclusio ex principio revelato & naturali indubitatæ fuit fidei. Nec inter locos in Theologia, unde solida deduci possunt argumenta, locum à ratione Naturali loco motum, à quoquam ipsorum, Vir doctissimus facile inveniet. Mitto obscura veterum, qui de usu rationis etiam in Theologicis scripserunt, nomina, Rodolphi Strodi, Richardi de Ferebrid, Henrici Tisberg. Recentiores, Canus, Salmeron, Vasquez, Valentia, Pesantius, Rippa, Bannes, &c. & nostri sunt, & ferventiores. Et ne longè abeamus, aut universum campum Theologicum percurramus, cur non vident boni viri manticæ quod in tergo est? Cur non observant, Theologos suos de Eucharistia differentes, neque amare phraseologiam Dominicam, neque simplicitatem Apostolicam; sed portentosa verborum monstra, perversa & absurda novæ Philosophiæ obtrudere prodigia? AuAudiamus, specíminis loco, vel unum, sed non de sece Scholasticum. Consecrationis verba (recito textum ex Thom. opusc. 4. & Augustin. Barb. Concil. Trident. pag. 72.) cum debita intentione à Sacerdotibus prolata, panem & vinum in corpus & sanguinem transsubstantialiter convertunt, & Christus Deus, & homo persectus, & in tanta quantitate, quanta fuit in cruce, & est in cælo, sub modici panis specie taliter continetur, ut manducetur à fidelibus & minimè laceretur, taliter continetur, ut dividantur Species; Christus verò integer perseveret: quia nec augetur ex augmento, vel pluralitate specierum, nec exipsarum parvitate, aut paucitate minuitur. Taliter continetur, ut divisis speciebus sub quavis divisionis particula totus Christus Dominus integer perseveret. Taliter continetur, ut Accidentia etiam sine subjecto eodem existant, & absq; panis & vini substantia eundem effectum habeant ac prius satiando & inebriando. Taliter continetur, ut fides locum habeat, dum visibile invisibiliter sumitur sub aliena specie occultatum, & sensus à deceptione reddunturimmunes, qui de Accidentibus judicant sibi notis. Hoccine est, quod Paulus flagitat, cum simplicitate & sinceritate Dei, non cum sapientia carnali versari in Mundo? 2. Cor. 1. 12. Hoccine est in captivitatem redigere omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo?
units.tr: I know that a brick is washed whenever we throw the order of Nature against our opponents in the mystery of Grace. But they ought to look into themselves and think seriously about it, since these are chiefly the weapons forged in their own workshops. Long ago, certainly, in the Papist school, a conclusion drawn from a revealed principle and a natural one was held as an indubitable article of faith. Nor will a learned man easily find, among the theological topics from which solid arguments can be drawn, a topic drawn from natural reason that has been shifted from its place by any of them. I pass over the names of the older writers who wrote about the use of reason even in theological matters: Rodolphus Strodus, Richard of Ferebrid, Henry of Tisberg, obscure names. The more recent ones, Canus, Salmeron, Vasquez, Valentia, Pesantius, Rippa, Bannes, etc., are ours too, and more zealous. And, not to go far afield or run over the whole theological field, why do these good men not see what is on their own back? Why do they not notice that their theologians, when discussing the Eucharist, love neither the Lord's own phrasing nor apostolic simplicity, but thrust upon us monstrous word-coinages and portentous prodigies of a perverse and absurd new philosophy? Let us hear, as a specimen, at least one, and one not from the Scholastic dregs. The words of consecration (I quote the text from Thomas, opusc. 4, and Augustine Barbosa, Council of Trent, p. 72): when they are uttered by priests with due intention, they transubstantiate the bread and wine into the body and blood; and Christ, God and perfect man, and in as great a quantity as he was on the cross and is in heaven, is so contained under the appearance of a small piece of bread that he is eaten by the faithful and is in no way torn; he is so contained that the species are divided, yet Christ entire remains; for he is neither increased by the addition or plurality of the species, nor diminished by their smallness or fewness. He is so contained that, when the species are divided, whole Christ the Lord remains entire under every particle of the division. He is so contained that the accidents exist even without the same subject, and without the substance of bread and wine they have the same effect as before, of satisfying and inebriating. He is so contained that faith has its place, while the visible is received invisibly, hidden under an alien species, and the senses are made immune to deception, which judge of the accidents known to them. Is this what Paul demands, to live in the world with the simplicity and sincerity of God, not with carnal wisdom? 2 Cor. 1.12. Is this to bring every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ?

units.la: 2. Cor. 10. v. 5. Hoccine est ratiocinio humamano, principiis Naturæ, in mysteriis gratiæ mittere repudium? Num Christus, num Apostoli, num Patres istis cothurnis incesserunt? Falsissimis Pseudophilosophiæ paradoxis Theologica mysteria illi incrustant; nobis verum, ad normam Dei verbi examinatum rationis usum extorquere conantur. Oracula esse volunt, ubi, contra & præter rationem, novæ Scholæ Pontificiæ clamant: Quoddam corpus non tantum posse; sed etiam revera simul & actu esse in plurimis locis: quoddam objectum sua natura visibile, palpabile, &c. cum alio corpore, vel illius speciebus præsens exhibitum, nullo sensu apprehendi posse: quoddam accidens, non tantum posse; sed etiam revera existere absque Subjecto inhærentia. Sed ubi cum, & ex ipsa ratione nos afferimus, omne corpus certo terminari spatio; omne corpus visibile esse, &c. Sacrilegi fumus, qui abstrusissima salutis mysteria rationis nostræ modulo metiamur. Plumbeos, quos ex corruptæ rationis armamentario depromtos mucrones stringunt, Herculis clavam esse volunt; amentacas sobriæ rationis hastas, ubi pro nobis cæsim & punctim feriunt, longam arundinem. Classicum Scholastici canunt, ut vel invitaNatura laboranti Ecclesiæ Romanæ suppetias ferat: Sed si nobis vel ultro dederit nomen, mox tanquam inepta, exauctoratur. Ita nempe adversariis non Antiquitatis modò, sed etiam Rationis argumenta sunt calculi suppucatorii: Valent, si favent; si contradicunt, vix teruncii loco habentur. Hanc vero qui tyrannidem in Ecclesiam Christianam volunt invectam, & vel rationem in nasum cereum, suae tantum libidini servire eam coacturi, flectunt, vel legitimum ejus usum e pomoeriis Theologicis plane proscribunt, quid quaesio, aliud illi moliuntur, nisi ut (quod Philistaei olim Simsoni) Studiosis veritatis eruant oculos, vel unico saltem privent rationis lumine, quam obsessis propositi foederis conditionem tyrannus ille Ammonita, quo contumeliosius omnes exponant omnium sannis & ludibriis? Nam & hoc revelatae veritatis indubiae atque immotae principium est, Deum Naturae non Authorem modo esse sapientissimum, sed & conservatorem constantissimum. Non minus Naturae sui limites sunt, sui termini certi, & fixi; quam Gratiae; qui, nisi aliter summo rerum Moderatori placuerit, exceptionem nullam admittunt. At quicquam contra ordinarium naturae cursum, in mutatione symbolorum Sacramentalium, agere illi placere, ex iis, quae dicta sunt, nondum observavimus. Nolumus committere μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος, & decempeda nostrae rationis ea metiri, quae infinitis modis supra nos sunt. Nec confundemus mysteria Gratiae, cum beneficiis Naturae; illius exceptiones, cum hujus regulis. Hoc interim urgemus, quaecunque Naturae Author in Scriptura, de Natura, naturaliter proponit; illa ex Natura, tanquam principio, esse aestimanda. Id ipsum enim in sacris Literis identidem inculcari, animadvertimus. Servator profecto nolter, de veritate corporis sui acturus, ad corporis proprietates, ipsamque adeo sanam nos rejicit rationem. Nemo hoc naturae negabit axioma universale esse: Omne corpus humanum suam habet extensionem; partes extra partes. Excipis corpus Christi? At Christus excipi non vult. Neque enim Christus praestigiator est, qui Marcionitarum patrocinetur errori, quasi corpus ipsius aliud esset, aliud appareret: Ipse & veritatem corporis sui, & resurrectionis evidentiam, & localem in coelum translationem physico argumento probavit: Cur ergo nos exceptionem fingamus? Cum dubitarent discipuli Luc. 24. vers. 37. 38. 39. 40. de veritate corporis Christi, post resurrectionem, adeo ut territi & expavefacti putarint se Spiritum conspicere; dixit eis Servator: Quid turbati estis, & quare disceptationes subeunt corda vestra? Videte manus meas, & pedes meos, nam ego ipse sum; contrectate me & videte, nam Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, prout me conspicitis habere. Et quum haec dixisset, ostendit eis manus & pedes. Ex Scriptura didicimus, Christum Abrahae semen assumsisse, Heb. 2. v. 16. natum esse ex muliere, Gal.4.4. genitum ex femine Davidis, Rom.1.3. similem nobis factum per omnia, excepto peccato, Heb.2.17 cap.4.15. Phil.2.7.8. Cur ergo, extam claris & perspicuis Scripturae praemissis, concludere jam non liceat, corpus Christi omnes corporis naturalis habere proprietates, adeoque & Quantitatem extensivam?
units.tr: 2 Cor. 10.5. Is this to repudiate, in the mysteries of grace, human reasoning and the principles of Nature? Did Christ, did the Apostles, did the Fathers walk in such buskins? They encrust the theological mysteries with the most false paradoxes of a pseudo-philosophy; they try to wrest from us, to the rule of the Word of God, the use of reason as it has been tested. They want their own oracles, where, against and beyond reason, the new Papist school cries out: that a body can not only be, but really is, at once and actually in many places at the same time; that an object which by its nature is visible and palpable, etc., when present with another body or its species, cannot be apprehended by any sense; that an accident can not only be, but really exists without a subject of inherence. But when we, from reason itself, assert that every body is bounded by a definite space; every visible body is visible, etc., we are sacrilegious if we measure the most abstruse mysteries of salvation by the measure of our reason. The leaden blades they draw from the armoury of corrupted reason they want to be Hercules' club; the flimsy spears of sober reason, where they strike us with cuts and thrusts, they call a long reed. The Scholastics sound the trumpet so that Nature, even if unwilling, may bring aid to the labouring Church of Rome; but if Nature gives them her name of her own accord, she is at once dismissed as useless. So, to our opponents, the arguments not only of antiquity but also of reason are reckoned as counters for the reckoning-board: they count if they favour them; if they contradict, they are scarcely held worth a farthing. Those who want this tyranny to have been introduced into the Christian Church, and who either bend reason, as if to a wax nose, so that it serves only their own lust, or utterly banish its lawful use from the theological boundaries, what else are they devising, I ask, than what the Philistines once did to Samson: to tear out the eyes of the students of truth, or at least to deprive them of the single light of reason, as that tyrant of the Ammonites demanded as the condition of a besieged covenant, so that they may be exposed to the mockery and ridicule of all, the more shamefully? For this too is a principle of revealed truth, indubitable and unshaken: that God is not only the most wise Author of Nature but also its most constant preserver. Nature has its limits and its fixed and certain boundaries no less than Grace, and these admit no exception unless the supreme Ruler of things has been pleased otherwise. But from what has been said we have not yet observed that he is pleased to do anything contrary to the ordinary course of nature in the change of the sacramental signs. We do not wish to commit a passing over into another genus [μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος], nor to measure with the rod of our reason those things which are infinitely above us. Nor will we confuse the mysteries of Grace with the benefits of Nature, or its exceptions with its rules. Meanwhile we press this: whatever the Author of Nature sets forth in Scripture naturally, about Nature, those things must be judged from Nature as from a principle. For we notice that this is repeatedly inculcated in the sacred Letters. Our Saviour, certainly, when about to speak of the truth of his body, refers us to the properties of the body, and thus to sound reason itself. No one will deny that this is a universal axiom of nature: every human body has its extension; parts outside parts. Do you except the body of Christ? But Christ does not want to be excepted. For Christ is no conjurer, to favour the error of the Marcionites, as if his body were one thing and appeared another; he himself proved both the truth of his body and the evidence of his resurrection, and his local translation into heaven, by a physical argument. Why then should we invent an exception? When the disciples doubted, Luke 24.37, 38, 39, 40, about the truth of Christ's body after the resurrection, so that, terrified and alarmed, they thought they saw a spirit, the Saviour said to them: Why are you troubled, and why do doubts rise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, for I myself am here; handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. From Scripture we have learned that Christ assumed the seed of Abraham, Heb. 2.16; was born of a woman, Gal. 4.4; was begotten of the seed of David, Rom. 1.3; was made like us in all things, apart from sin, Heb. 2.17; 4.15; Phil. 2.7, 8. Why then, with such clear and plain premises of Scripture, may we not now conclude that the body of Christ has all the properties of a natural body, and therefore also extensive quantity?

units.la: II. Frustra proinde Vir doctissimus haec nobis, ex ipsa sacra Scriptura submministrata, arma Physica, in Themate Physico, eripere, conatur, quando ait: Adferre, absurda ex Physica, sicuti, Corpus idem non posse esse in pluribus locis eodem tempore; Accidentia non posse subsistere sine Subjecto, atque alia hujuscemodi, quis dicat haec satis firma ac valida esse, ad destruendam verborum Christi, Hoc est corpus meum, divinam veritatem. Cur, amabo, toties cum umbra sua & figmentis luctari libeat Adversariis? Quis Reformatorum unquam per somnium cogitavit, divinam verborum Christi veritatem vel vocare in dubium, nedum argumentis Physicis destruere? Si ita Vir doctissimus suum formaverit argumentum: Quicquid Christus dicit, illud verum est: divinam venerabundi adoramus veritatem. Sin autem ita processerit: Quicquid Christus dixit, illud secundum literam debet intelligi; utrum & haec jam Propositio eandem habeat universalitatem, ipse Vir doctissimus judicer. Non ergo de veritate Propositionis; sed modo modo ejus, proprius sit, an improprius, mediatus an immediatus, quaestio est? Et quia Praedicatum propositionis, Corpus, ex Physica depromptum, Physicè à Spiritu sancto in Scriptura & ponitur, & exponitur, nullaque prorsus exceptionis vel vola vel vestigium in universo Codice sacro apparet, annon, quisquè, cui non pro cerebro fungus est, ad demonstrandam Propositionis Dominicae improprietatem, Physicam, quae corporis Naturalis nativa est sedes, in subsidium posse vocari, ubi exactius secum rationem subduxerit, facile concludet?
units.tr: II. Therefore the learned man tries in vain to snatch from us, in a physical theme, these physical arms, which are supplied by Scripture itself, when he says: To bring forward absurdities from Physics, such as that the same body cannot be in several places at the same time; that accidents cannot subsist without a subject; and others of this kind: who would say these are firm and strong enough to destroy the divine truth of the words of Christ, "This is my body"? Why, I ask, do our opponents take pleasure in struggling so often with their own shadow and fancies? Which of the Reformed ever dreamed of calling into doubt the divine truth of the words of Christ, let alone destroying it with physical arguments? If the learned man were to frame his argument thus: Whatever Christ says is true; we reverently adore divine truth, we agree. But if he were to proceed thus: Whatever Christ said must be understood according to the letter, let the learned man himself judge whether this proposition has the same universality. Is the question, then, not about the truth of the proposition, but about its mode: whether it is proper or improper, mediate or immediate? And since the predicate of the proposition, body, is taken from Physics, and is both posed and explained by the Holy Spirit in Scripture in a physical way, and since not even the faintest trace or shadow of an exception appears in the whole sacred Code, will not anyone, who is not a mushroom for a brain, easily conclude, once he has reckoned more carefully with himself, that to demonstrate the impropriety of the Lord's proposition one can call in physics, which is the natural seat of the natural body, as an aid?

units.la: III. Rem presius urgeamus.
units.tr: III. Let us press the matter more closely.

units.la: Tritum Naturae Principium esse, omne corpus Physicum esse quantum, Quantitate propria, quae & molis & extensionis dici debet, quaeq; congenita est materiae, & naturae corporeae, supra jam diximus. Quod verò hoc modo quantum est, illud simul & semel actu in pluribus locis esse non potest. Si pluribus in locis actu esse non potest; frustra Christi corpus naturale quotidie ostenditur in iis per orbem angulis, ubi consecratio, ex ordine Liturgiae Romanae, peragitur. Non negarent adversarii axiomatis universalitatem, modo hanc unam de corpore Christi iis largiremur exceptionem. Sed quis arbitros nos constituit aut judices, ut, quod Deus & Natura fixum, ratum, immotum esse voluntate nostro illud arbitrio aut libidine mutaremus? Sacra Scriptura corpori pori Christi tribuit Quantum, illud certo loco alligat, & nos illi πολυπτωτίας affingamus? Frustra Deum colimus, docentes doctrinas, quae sunt mandata hominum; Matth. 15. verf. 9. Πολυπτωτίας certe privilegium corpori Christi neque in statu Exinanitionis convenit, neque Exaltationis. Non in illo, quia sic unum occupavit locum, ut ab altero abesset, Joh. 6. 24. cap. 11. verf. 15. Marc. 6. verf. 56. Neque in hoc: Si enim in Exaltationis statu ei concessa fuisset πολυπτωτία, aut communicata fuisset ambulanti in terra, aut evecto in coelum. Non prius: Proprietates enim naturae humanae, adeoque certi & determinati spatii occupationem sibi ipsi tribuit; Matth. 28. 5. 6. Luc. 24. 39. 40. Act. 1. verf. 3. Neque posterius, tum quia praedixit, se ex hoc Mundo migraturum, atque ita non amplius in terris fore praesentem corporaliter, Matth. 26. verf. 11. Joh. 16. 28. c. 17. verf. 11. tum quia revera ex hoc mundo migrans eum reliquit, Luc. 24. 51. tum quia nunc localiter in coelo degit, Act. 3. 21. Heb. 8. verf. 4. tum denique, quia novissimo die e Coelo demum est rediturus: Matth. 24. 30. 1. Thess. 4. 16. 17. Ita Scriptura de corpore Christi, eoque adaequato occupationis & collocationis spatio loquitur ubique: Nullius usquam exceptionis meminit.
units.tr: It is a commonplace principle of nature that every physical body is extended, having its own quantity, which must be called both bulk and extension, and which is innate to matter and to corporeal nature, as we have already said above. But what is extended in this way cannot be actually in several places at once and at the same time. If it cannot be actually in several places, then in vain is Christ's natural body displayed every day in all those corners of the world where consecration is performed according to the order of the Roman liturgy. Our opponents would not deny the universality of the axiom if we were to grant them this one exception for the body of Christ. But who has appointed us arbiters or judges, so that we should change by our own will or whim what God and Nature have fixed, settled and unchanging? Does Holy Scripture ascribe quantity to Christ's body, bind it to a certain place, and shall we attach ubiquity [πολυτοπία] to it? In vain do we worship God, teaching doctrines that are the commandments of men (Matt. 15:9). Certainly the privilege of ubiquity agrees with the body of Christ neither in the state of humiliation nor in that of exaltation. Not in the former, because it so occupied one place that it was absent from another (John 6:24; 11:15; Mark 6:56). Nor in the latter: for if ubiquity had been granted to him in the state of exaltation, it would have been shared either with him walking on earth or with him carried up to heaven. Not the former: for he ascribes to himself the properties of human nature, and so the occupation of a certain and determinate space (Matt. 28:5–6; Luke 24:39–40; Acts 1:3). Nor the latter: first, because he foretold that he would depart from this world and so would no longer be bodily present on earth (Matt. 26:11; John 16:28; 17:11); second, because in fact, departing from this world, he left it (Luke 24:51); third, because he now dwells locally in heaven (Acts 3:21; Heb. 8:4); and finally, because on the last day he is to return from heaven (Matt. 24:30; 1 Thess. 4:16–17). Thus Scripture everywhere speaks of the body of Christ and of its occupation and location of space, which is exactly commensurate, and nowhere mentions any exception.

units.la: IV. Neque aliter universa sensit Antiquitas, quae constanter docuit, Corpus Christi non esse in terris, quia sit in cœlis. Vigil. lib. 4. cont. Eutych. Si verbi & carnis una Natura est, quomodo, cum verbum ubique sit, non ubique inveniatur & caro? Nam quando in terra fuit (caro Christi) non erat utique in cœlis; & nunc, quia in cœlo est, non est utique in terra. Et Augustinus apud Gratian. de consecrat. D. II. cap. 44. Donec seculum finiatur, sursum est Dominus; sed tamen hic etiam nobiscum est veritas Domini. Corpus enim, in quo resurrexit, in uno loco esse oportet: Veritas autem ejus ubique dissusa est. Excerpta haec sunt ex Tractat. XXX. in Johannem. Et quanquam varietas hic aliqua occurrat lectionis; certum tamen est, non modo Scholasticos & Canonistas, Ivonem Carnotensem, Petrum Lombardum, Algerum, Alexandrum de Ales, Thomam, Durandum, Gabrielem, ita citâsse; sed & hoc Συμπεφωνημα collegisse: Christi corpus in uno loco esse oportet. Nempe universalis augusti Patris erat conclusio: Nullum corpus posse esse ubique totum: Quoniam per innumerabiles partes aliud alibi habeat necesse est, & quantumcunque sit corpus, seu quantulumcunq; corpusculum, loci occupet spatium, eum denique locum sic impleat, ut in nulla ejus parte sit totum, Ep. 3. Fulgent. lib. 2. ad Thrasymund. Dominus ut localem ostenderet humanitatem suam, dixit discipulis suis: Ascendo ad Patrem meum, & ad Patrem vestrum. Immensitatem vero sua divinitatis offendens discipulis, dicit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem seculi. Ambrosius Serm. 56. de Tempore: Ergo jam non super terram, nec in terra, nec secundum carnem debemus quaerere Salvatorem, si volumus eum invenire atque contingere, sed secundum Divina majestatis gloriam. Cyrill. Alexandrin. lib. 11. in Joh. cap. 3. In coelum ascendens Spiritum immisit: Non enim conversari cum Apostolis carne poterat, cum ad Patrem ascenderit. Etsi a beato corpore, Patri pro nobis apparens, ac a dextris ejus sedens, habitat tamen in sanctis per Spiritum. Ita Scriptura, ita Patres contra exceptionem corporis Christi, quam defendunt Pontificii, loquuntur, & nobis contradicendi pruritus magis placeat?
units.tr: IV. Nor did all antiquity think otherwise, for it constantly taught that the body of Christ is not on earth because it is in heaven. Vigilius, book 4 against Eutyches: "If the Word and the flesh have one nature, how is the flesh not found everywhere, since the Word is everywhere? For when the flesh of Christ was on earth it was surely not in heaven; and now, because it is in heaven, it is surely not on earth." And Augustine, cited in Gratian, de consecratione, D. II, cap. 44: "Until the world ends the Lord is above; yet the truth of the Lord is here also with us. For the body in which he rose must be in one place; but his truth is spread everywhere." These excerpts come from Tractate 30 on John. Although some variation of reading occurs here, it is certain that not only the Scholastics and canonists, Ivo of Chartres, Peter Lombard, Algerus, Alexander of Hales, Thomas, Durandus and Gabriel, cited it in this way, but also drew from it this agreed conclusion: "The body of Christ must be in one place." Indeed the universal conclusion of that great Father was: "No body can be wholly everywhere, since it must have one part here and another part there through its innumerable parts; and however great the body, or however small the little body, it occupies a space of place and fills that place so that it is wholly in no part of it" (Ep. 3; Fulgentius, book 2 to Thrasamund). "The Lord, to show that his humanity is local, said to his disciples: 'I ascend to my Father and to your Father.' But to show the immensity of his divinity to the disciples, he says: 'Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age.'" Ambrose, Sermon 56 on the Time: "Therefore we must now seek the Saviour neither upon the earth, nor in the earth, nor according to the flesh, if we wish to find him and touch him, but according to the glory of the divine majesty." Cyril of Alexandria, book 11 on John, chapter 3: "Ascending into heaven, he sent the Spirit; for he could not converse with the Apostles in the flesh, since he had ascended to the Father. Although, appearing to the Father for us from his blessed body and sitting at his right hand, he nevertheless dwells in the saints through the Spirit." Thus Scripture and thus the Fathers speak against the exception of Christ's body which the Papists defend. Does the itch to contradict please us more?

units.la: V. Sed unum adhuc, & alterum examinemus axioma Physicum. A. Natura universaliter dicit: Omne corpus esse visibile. Est & hoc principium ab ultima retro antiquitate extra controversiae aleam positum. Neque Aristotelis (quem tamen, Schola Pontificia maximi semper fecit) tantum axioma est: Ἀναλογίαν ... Consequuntur se invicem color & magnitudo; lib. 3. de anim. cap. 1. Et lib. 2. cap. 7. Τὸ χρῶμα ἀναγκαῖον ἐν φωτὶ ὁρᾶσθαι, necesse est, colorem in lumine videri. Etiam Ecclesiae vox est, corpus ararcanum, invisibil, ísum nullum dari. Corpus hominis non aiunt illigam, quàm omnem istam struem carni ... quod videtur, quod tenetur, quod denique à nobis occiditur. Sic & parietis corpus nu madmittam, quàm cementa, quàm saxa qmiteres. Si quis arcanum aliquod coruacit, ostendat, revelet, Tertull. lib. de surect. cap. 35. Et Gregor. Nazianzenus: Greek text: ἀπότε ἐνωλήψη τὸ θεῖον; πότερον σῶμα; ... Greek text ... σώματα; Quid enim tdè Deum esse censebis? Utrum corpus? Ut ordo immensus, infinitus, sine figura, inorganibilis, & invisibilis erit? An vero hæc ocę in numero corporum sunt habenda? In ptervam vocat licentiam, quandoquidem corporum natura abhorreat, ut sine ... immensa, invisibilia. Orat. 2. Theolo. Ostiunt adversarii de reliquis corporibus cùm corpus transsubstantiatum iterum exinscio excipere; sed non probare. Ostendat, cum Tertulliano libere loquar, revelet suum corpus. Non excipit certè Christus, ut supra audivimus. Non excipiunt as. Nisi corporaliter abiret Dominus à oculis, eper ejus corpus carnaliter viderēmus vaunt Augustinus. Serm. 60. de verb. Domin. rm Christi his conditionibus subjacere ut carnata, & invisibilis sit, si-
units.tr: V. But let us examine one more physical axiom, and then another. A. Nature says universally: "Every body is visible." This principle too has stood beyond all dispute from the most ancient times. It is not merely an axiom of Aristotle, whom the Papist school has always held in the highest esteem: "Colour and magnitude follow one another" (On the Soul, book 3, ch. 1). And in book 2, ch. 7: "Colour must necessarily be seen in light." The voice of the Church too is that no body is hidden and invisible at all. Tertullian, in his book on the resurrection, ch. 35: "I do not admit that the body of a man is hidden, any more than all that structure of flesh which is seen, which is touched, which is finally killed by us. Nor do I admit that the body of a wall is hidden, any more than its cement or its stones. If anyone shows some hidden thing, let him display it, let him reveal it." And Gregory Nazianzen: "[πότερον σῶμα;] For what will you think God to be? A body? Then he will be immense, infinite, without figure, incomprehensible and invisible? Or are these things to be counted among bodies?" He calls it a wanton licence, since the nature of bodies shrinks from things that are immense and invisible (Oration 2, Theological). The opponents claim that in the case of other bodies, when a body is transubstantiated, they except it again from the rule, but they do not prove it. Let them show, to speak freely with Tertullian, "reveal their body." Certainly Christ makes no exception, as we heard above, and the Fathers make none either. "Unless the Lord had departed bodily from our eyes, we should have seen his body carnally," says Augustine (Sermon 60 on the words of the Lord). ...that the body of Christ is subject to these conditions, that it be fleshly and invisible, if-

units.la: cuc cut verbum) impossibile sit Vigil. lib. 4. contra Eutych. Et Ehn. Syrus apud Phot. Cod. 229. Οὐδεὶς ἀνεὶν ὑνατα̃ι νῦν ἔχων, ὡς ἡ αὐτὴ φύσις ψηλαφητὴ ἀψηλαφήτε, καὶ ὁρᾶτε καὶ ἀόρατε. Nemo, ut a mentis sit, dicere potest, quod eadem tu ejus, quod palpari potest, & quod palpari non potest; ejus, quod videri potest, & quod videri non potest. Quid difertius & evidentius cur Corpus Christi invisibile?
units.tr: ...(as the Word) is impossible, says Vigilius, book 4 against Eutyches. And Ephraem the Syrian, in Photius, Cod. 229: [Οὐδεὶς ... ἀόρατε] No one, being in his right mind, can say that the same thing is both palpable and impalpable, both visible and invisible. What could be more plain and evident as to why the body of Christ is invisible?

units.la: B. Naturae axiomas Omne corpus solidum est ψηλαφητόν. Omnes assensum habet & haec regula. Excipi Sol Pontificia corpus Christi. Sed Christus in xcipit: Contrectate me, inquit Luc. 24. Ecclesia non excipit, ut Vigilii modo, & pari condocefecimus verbis. Cur ergo nouvefali iterum regulae vim faciamus?
units.tr: B. Another axiom of nature: "Every solid body is tangible" [ψηλαφητόν]. This rule too has the assent of all. The Papists are wont to except the body of Christ. But Christ does not except it: "Handle me," he says, in Luke 24. The Church does not except it either, as we have just shown from the words of Vigilius and Ephraem. Why, then, should we again do violence to the force of the rule?

units.la: C. Naturae axiora: Jullum signum proprie ipsam esse rem, ujusignum est, nec signatum de signo proprie praedicari. Haec, ex natura relatorum opcic ad νοιvὰς ἐννοίας, communes, homini nti isitas, pertinet notiones. Sacramenta ecies At Deus non excipit, qui vel aperte colcite signum a re signata distinguit, Gen. 7.1 vel tecte & implicite, disparatum de di praffirmative praedicando. Patres non exipiquibus Sacramenta aliud sunt, aliud significant, vel intelligun- tur.
units.tr: C. Axiom of nature: No sign is properly the very thing of which it is the sign, and the thing signified is not properly predicated of the sign. This follows from the nature of relatives and belongs to the common notions [κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι] that are naturally implanted in human beings. The sacraments... God makes no exception to this, who distinguishes the sign from the thing signified either openly, Gen. 7.1, or covertly and implicitly, so that one must not affirm of the one what belongs to the other. The Fathers did not make an exception for those [sacraments] that are one thing and signify another, or are understood in that way.

units.la: D. Catholicum cumprimis, & universalissimum Naturæ principium est, Accidentis esse, est inesse. Ut Ens, si per se non subsistat, Substantia vocari nequit; ita nec, nisi actu insit, Accidens vel est, vel vocari potest. Ausint negare Adversarii? Reclamabit Scriptura, repugnabit Natura, refragabitur omnium Gentium consensus. Sed distinctionem confinxerunt, quæ se ipsam plane destruit & evertit. Inter Accidens distinguunt modificatum & absolutum. Illud, ex mente Scholasticorum, ne virtute quidem divina conservari sine subjecto potest: Cum ejus Essentia & Natura in hoc sita sit, ut Subjectum actu afficiat. Absolutum, habere esse perfectum in sua specie. Hoc autem a Deo conservari posse sine subjecto. Sed λόγοι sunt καὶ λόγοι. Accidentis enim proprium est, non posse inhærere; sed, actu inhærere. Ut enim perfeitas; ut loquuntur; omni convenit Substantiæ, ita Ineitas ab Accidente separari non potest. Sed quid verbis, aut argumentis in materia Physica opus est, ubi evidentissima sensuum testimonia adsunt? Quid in idea tantum philosophari, & de possibilibus disputare hic juvat? Expendatur id, quod post consecrationem in Eucharistia superest, & vel communis dictabit sensus, proprietates, virtutes, adeóque substantiam re-mamanere. Realitas hujus Accidentis (liceat adversariorum loqui verbis) adeo est manifesta, ut, vel subtilissimo Philosopho Cartesio teste, absque Substantia concipi non possit. Cum forte primi, qui hanc quaestionem Philosophico more explicare conati sunt, tam firmiter sibi persuaderent, Accidentia illa, quae sensus movent, esse quid reale a substantia diversum, ut ne adverterent quidem, ea de re posse unquam dubitari: Sine ullo examine, ac line justa ratione suppofuerant, species panis esse Accidentia ejusmodi realia, totique denique in eo fuerunt, ut explicarent, quomodo ipsa sine subjecto esse possint. Qua in re tot difficultates invenerunt, ut vel ex uno hoc (quemadmodum viatores, cum forte ad salebras, & loca nullo modo pervia, devenerunt) se a vero itinere deflexisse judicare debuissent. Deinde, non potest humana mens cogitare, Accidentia panis esse realia, & tamen absque ejus substantia existere, quin simul illa per modum substantiae concipiat. Adeo ut implicare videatur, ut tota panis substantia mutetur, quemadmodum credit Ecclesia: Et interim, ut aliquid reale, quod prius erat in pane, remaneat, quia nihil reale potest intelligi remanere, nisi quod subsistat: Et quamvis verbo vocetur Accidens, concipiatur tamen ut substantia. Ideoque in re idem est, ac si diceretur, totam quidem panis substantiam mutari, sed tamen illam ejus substantia partem, quae vocatur Accidens reale, remanere: quod si non verbis, certe in conceptu contradictionem involvit. Atque haec praecipua ratio esse videtur, ob quam nonnulli hac in parte ab Ecclesia Romana dissenserunt. Deprim. Philosoph. pag.290. Sunt haec, Vir doctissime, verba hominis non illiterati, aut obscuri Philosophi, aut Theologi Reformati, sed Cartesii ingenii; quod negari non potest; acerrimi, in castris vestris nati, educati & mortui. Votum etiam fecit, sípémque concepit acutissimus Philosophus, venturum tempus aliquando, quo illa optimo, quae ponit accidentia realia (quae revera aliud nihil sunt, quàm substantiae) ut a ratione aliena, & incomprehensibilis, & parum tuta in fide, à Theologis explodatur. Moner quidem Facultatis Theologicae Parisiensis Doctor non postremus, quòd, secundum Viri Clarissimi dogmata, salva & integra remanere non posse videantur; quae de Sacro-Sancti Altaris mysteriis, docet Ecclesia; difficultates interim, ob quas receptam Ecclesiae suae sententiam Cartesius reiecit, quaeque revera magni sunt momenti, nequidem tangit. Sed & tuo, Vir doctissime, relinquo judicio, num realia illa Accidentia revera aliud quid esse possint, quàm substantia? Nisi solomniare velimus, Accidentia sola producere substantiam, panem e.g. aut vinum vermes; sola Accidentia famem pellere, & sitim compescere: re: Adeo ut, si vel dolium vini, vel hostiæ magno numero consecrata fuerint, hæ in cibum conversæ, illud ad potum adhibitum, possint saturare, famem depellere, sitim sedare. Hæc vero virtus fuerit Accidentium. Ingens certè acquirendi compendium, si Accidentia sola consecratione vim nutriendi consequerentur, quod magno multi redimerent; illis maxime usui suturum, quorum conatibus obstat res angusta domi.
units.tr: D. The most universal and foremost principle of Nature is this: The being of an accident is to inhere. Just as a being that does not subsist of itself cannot be called a substance, so an accident, unless it actually inheres, neither is nor can be called an accident. Will the opponents dare to deny this? Scripture will cry out against them, Nature will resist them, and the agreement of all nations will contradict them. But they have devised a distinction that plainly destroys and overturns itself. Among accidents they distinguish the modified from the absolute. The former, according to the mind of the Scholastics, cannot be preserved without a subject, not even by divine power, since its essence and nature consist in affecting a subject actually. The absolute, to have perfect being in its own kind, can, they say, be preserved by God without a subject. But λόγοι are one thing and λόγοι another [the word is used in two senses]. For it is proper to an accident not to be able to inhere, but to inhere in actuality. For as perfection, as they put it, belongs to every substance, so inherence cannot be separated from an accident. But why do we need words or arguments in a physical matter where the most evident testimony of the senses is present? Why is it useful to philosophise here only in the abstract and to dispute about possibilities? Let us consider what remains after consecration in the Eucharist. Common sense itself will tell us that the properties, powers and, consequently, the substance remain. The reality of this accident (let me use the adversaries' own words) is so manifest that, by the testimony of the most subtle philosopher Descartes, it cannot be conceived without a substance. Perhaps the first men who tried to explain this question in a philosophical manner were so firmly persuaded that those accidents which move the senses are something real and different from substance, that they did not even notice that this could ever be doubted. Without any examination and without good reason they had assumed that the appearances of bread are such real accidents, and their whole effort was devoted to explaining how they can exist without a subject. In this matter they encountered so many difficulties that from this alone (as travellers who by chance arrive at rough and impassable places) they ought to have judged that they had turned aside from the true road. Then, the human mind cannot think that the accidents of bread are real and yet exist without its substance, without at the same time conceiving them in the manner of a substance. So it seems to involve a contradiction that the whole substance of the bread should be changed, as the Church believes, and yet that something real which was previously in the bread should remain, because nothing real can be understood to remain unless it subsists. And although it is called by the word accident, it is nevertheless conceived as a substance. Therefore, in fact, it is the same as saying that the whole substance of the bread is changed, but that that part of its substance which is called the real accident remains; if not in words, certainly in conception this involves a contradiction. And this seems to be the principal reason why some have dissented from the Roman Church on this point. De prim. Philosoph. p. 290 [as printed: Deprim. Philosoph. pag. 290]. These are the words, most learned sir, not of an unlettered or obscure philosopher, nor of a Reformed theologian, but of a man of the genius of Descartes, who cannot be denied to have been most keen, born, educated and died in your camp. This most acute philosopher also expressed and conceived a wish: that a time will come at some point when those doctrines which posit real accidents (which in truth are nothing other than substances) will be rejected by theologians as foreign to reason, incomprehensible, and scarcely safe for faith. Certainly a not unimportant Doctor of the Theological Faculty of Paris has warned that, according to the teachings of this most distinguished man, those things which the Church teaches about the mysteries of the most holy altar do not seem able to remain safe and whole; yet he does not even touch the difficulties, which are truly of great weight, on account of which Descartes rejected the opinion of his Church that was received. But I leave it also to your judgement, most learned sir, whether those real accidents can really be anything other than substance. Unless we want to dream that accidents alone produce a substance, for example bread or wine, worms; that accidents alone drive away hunger and quench thirst. So that, if a cask of wine or a large number of hosts had been consecrated, and these were converted into food, and the wine were taken as drink, they could satisfy, drive off hunger, and allay thirst. Yet this would be the power of the accidents. It would indeed be a great saving to acquire, if accidents alone by consecration obtained the power of nourishing, which many would buy at a high price, and which would be especially useful to those whose efforts are hindered by straitened circumstances at home.

units.la: SECTIO XIII.
units.tr: Section 13.

units.la: Transubstantiatio est dogma no- vum, incertum, ac proinde profunda- mentali fidei articulo non ob- trudendum.
units.tr: Transubstantiation is a new dogma, uncertain, and therefore not to be forced upon anyone as a fundamental article of faith.

units.la: I. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter id, quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus, verba sunt Pauli 1. Cor. 3. 11. Fundamentum Ecclesiæ, Christus, vocatur non tantum, quòd, ceu lapis ab ædificantibus pro nihilo habitus, factus est caput anguli; & quòd in nullo alio salus, nec aliud nomen sub cœlo, quod datum sit inter homines, per quod oporteat nos servari, Act. 4. verf. 12. Sed quòd per eum gratia & veritas extitit, quòd unus ille, in sinu Patris, voluntatem ejus, adeoque, quæ ad salutem sunt necessaria, nobis expolUit, Joh. c. 1. 17. coll. c. 20. 31. Omnis enim planta, quam non plantavit Pater cœlestis, eradicabitur, Matth. 15, verf. 13. Evangelium, etsi ab Angelo nunciatum, diversum ab eo, quod abApoftolis nunciatum est, anathemate feritur Galat. 1. verf. 8. Quicquid igitur præter, extra, & contra hoc fundamentum, hominum introductum est libidine, tyrannide φιλοπεωτόντων intrusum, inter ἐξελοθρησκείας, & humanas referri debet traditiones. Novum illud est, eoque ipso non Catholicum. Illud enim Catholicum esse proprie, quod ubique, quod semper, quod omnibus creditum; ex Vincentii Lirinensis, cujus magna apud eos est authoritas, discere potuissent, Commonit. cap. 3. Hoc vero Characters Transsubstantiationem destitui, ipsa nos Schola Pontificia docet. Certè subtilis eorum Doctor, Johannes Duns, Scotus, palam profitetur, nonnisi post periculosum Lateranense Decretum, sub Innocentio III. conditum, anno demum 1215. obstetricante ubique barbarie, editum, substantialem istam conversionem; sive Transsubstantiationem inter necessarios fidei articulos fuisse relatam. Nullam S. Scripturæ sententiam reperiri, nullam, ante Lateranense illud Concilium, determinationem Ecclesiasticam, quæ vel expressè doceat, vel ex qua evidenter inferri possit, non manere in Eu-
units.tr: I. "No one can lay any other foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ," as Paul says, 1 Cor. 3:11. Christ is called the foundation of the Church not only because, "as the stone rejected by the builders, he has become the head of the corner," and because there is salvation in no other, nor any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12); but also because "grace and truth came through him" (John 1:17), since he alone, who is in the bosom of the Father, has revealed to us his will, and therefore what is necessary for salvation (compare John 20:31). For every plant that the heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted (Matt. 15:13). Even if the gospel were announced by an angel, if it differs from what was announced by the Apostles, it is struck with anathema (Gal. 1:8). Whatever, therefore, has been introduced beside, outside of, and against this foundation, by the wantonness of men and forced in by the tyranny of those who love to be first [φιλοπρωτευόντων], must be reckoned among self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκείαι] and human traditions. That doctrine is new, and for that very reason not Catholic. For what is properly Catholic is "what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all"; they could have learned this from Vincent of Lérins, whose authority is so great among them (Commonitorium, ch. 3). That transubstantiation lacks this mark, their own Papist school teaches us. Certainly their subtle doctor, John Duns Scotus, openly professes that this substantial conversion, or transubstantiation, was placed among the necessary articles of faith only after the dangerous Lateran Decree, established under Innocent III and published in the year 1215, when barbarism was everywhere midwife to it. No sentence of Holy Scripture can be found, and no ecclesiastical determination before that Lateran Council, which either expressly teaches, or from which it can evidently be inferred, that the substance of bread and wine does not remain in the Eu-

units.la: charistia substantiam panis et vini. charistia, post consecratione, panis substantiam: in 4. Sententiarum dist. 11. quæst. 3. num. 3. 5. 13. 14. 15. Novum ergo est, χθὲς ἡ σήμερον natum Transsubstantiationis dogma, nec proinde Catholicum.
units.tr: charist. After the consecration, the substance of bread remains in the Eucharist (Sentences, book 4, dist. 11, quaest. 3, nn. 3, 5, 13, 14, 15). The dogma of transubstantiation is therefore new, born "yesterday or today" [χθὲς ἢ σήμερον], and consequently not Catholic.

units.la: II. Neque verò nova tantùm, adeóque non Catholica; sed & ita obscura, perplexa, intricata, Scholasticorum disputationibus impedita est Pyrrhonica de Transsubstantiatione ἐποχὴ, ut ubique feré quod negent, aut nesciant; raró quod affirment, aut sciant, reperias. Certum est, Decretum Lateranense, ex quo semel elapsum ἐργῶν ὀδόντων, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Doctores ita occupâsse, ut quid vel sentirent ipsi, vel commendarent aliis, vix occurrat.
units.tr: II. And it is not only new, and so not Catholic; it is also so obscure, perplexed, and entangled, and so hindered by the disputations of the Schoolmen, that a Pyrrhonian suspension of judgement [ἐποχὴ] about transubstantiation prevails everywhere, so that you will almost everywhere find what they deny or do not know, and rarely what they affirm or know. It is certain that the Lateran Decree, once it had slipped out from between their teeth [ἐργῶν ὀδόντων], so occupied the teachers of the Roman Church that scarcely anything can be found of what they themselves thought or recommended to others.

units.la: III. Ituri in rem præsentem, ab ipsa voce faciamus initium. Quàm tritum apud ipsos ubique est, omniúmque ore jactitatum Missa vocabulum, quod loco Cœnæ Dominicæ, Ecclesia Latina serius admisit, Romana, tanquam antiquissimum, obtrusit? Et Gallus, & Germanus, & Italus, & cæteræ etiam occidentales Ecclesiæ, imò abjectissimi in iis cerdones nomen illud venerantur, & adorant. Rogati tamen doctissimi quique eorum, quid sit? quid proprie denoter? unde originem habeat? cæspitant, ut plurimùm, & suaviludiis suis plus indulgent, quàm tantæ rei ferat momentum. Hebraicam vocem libenter vellent, ne novitate sorderet. Audent hoc asserere (post Reuchlinum, qui hunc, vir cæteroquin verè aureus, & in his literis magnus, seculi adhuc consuetudini inserviens, primus vendidit fumum) Baronius, Cottonus, Meursius, quod tamen in Philosopho magis erat excusandum, quàm Professore Linguæ sanctæ Regio, Genebrardo. Sed puduit alios adeò ineptæ, ipsíque, quod Matthæus Galenus dissimulare non poterat, Ecclesiæ Romanæ probrosæ Etymologiæ: quam proinde solidis everterunt rationibus, Picherellus, in Explic. verb. Dom. pag. 67. 87. Vasquezius In 3. t. 2. dif. 221. c. 1. Matthæus Galenus, in Catech. à Croquet. citat. Catech. 91. Alii ex Gracia eadem felicitate, vel verius eodem ludibrio Missam accersunt. Ignotum enim Ecclesiæ Græcæ hoc fuit vocabulum; &c. quod paulatim irrepsit, ei utcumque simile, μίσα, non Eucharistiam, sive Cœnam Domini; sed preces matutinas & vespertinas significat, ut ex Rigaltio, & Lexico Mixobarb. Meursii patet. Latinam tandem vocem esse, plerique DoctoresPontificii concedunt quidem; sed tot ambagibus quid efficiunt, quæso, tandem, quàm quòd Reformatorum nomenclaturam, tanquam certiorem & antiquiorem (appellare autem illi solent Cœnam Domini) magis probant? Nam, qui authoritate & exemplo Scripturæ sacræ, sanctissimum illud mysterium Domini Cœnam appellant, tot mæandris & laby-rinrinthis Etymologicis non implicantur. Eucharistia nomen, vetustissimis Patribus usitatum, Ecclesia Romana non quidem ignorat, male tamen explicat: neque felicius Grammatice, quàm Theologice. Bonam gratiam vertunt Lombardus, Thomas, Angelus de Clavasio, alii. Isidorum secuti: cùm tamen, ex consuetudine veteris Synagogæ, consecrationem, gratiarum actionem, laudationem Dei denotet. Ut enim εὐλογίαν & εὐχαριστίαν Synonyma sunt, & pro varietate circumstantiarum, significant laudare, gratias agere, consecrare; ita εὐλογία & εὐχαριστία pro cœna Domini apud veteres sumitur, vel, quia Symbolum est gratiarum actionis adversus Deum, ut Orig. cont. Celsum Tom. 8. loquitur, vel, quia Symbola εὐχαριστηθέντα, precibus Deo consecrata, accipiunt χάριν ... gratia additionem. Ex ignorantia autem verae vocis Etymologiae crassa, crassior natus est error in definitione rei. Ideo enim Cœnam D. Eucharistiam vocari ait Angelus de Clavasio, quòd contineat realiter Christum, qui est plenus gratia.
units.tr: III. Let me begin with the word itself, since it is the matter at hand. How common is the word Missa among them, and how often is it on everyone's lips? The Latin Church admitted it later, in place of Cœnæ Dominicæ, and the Roman Church thrust it on the rest as though it were the oldest term. Yet Frenchmen, Germans, Italians, and the other Western churches, even the most worthless cobblers among them, revere and worship that name. When the most learned of them are asked what it means, what it properly denotes, and where it comes from, they mostly stumble and indulge their playful trifling more than such a weighty matter deserves. They would gladly have a Hebrew word, so that it would not seem tawdry from being new. Following Reuchlin, who, though otherwise a truly golden man and great in these studies, served the custom of his age and was the first to sell this smoke, Baronius, Cottonus, Meursius dare to assert this. That was more excusable in a philosopher than in Genebrardo, a royal professor of the holy tongue. But others were ashamed of such a foolish etymology, and Matthew Galen could not hide his own shame at the Roman Church's disgraceful etymology. Accordingly, Picherellus, in his Explic. verb. Dom. pp. 67 and 87, Vasquez, in In 3. t. 2. dif. 221, c. 1, and Matthew Galen, cited in Croquet's Catechism, p. 91, overturned it with solid arguments. Others summon Missa from Greek with the same good fortune, or rather the same mockery. For this word was unknown to the Greek Church. What crept in gradually is a word somewhat like it, misa [μίσα], which signifies not the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper, but morning and evening prayers, as is clear from Rigaltius and from the Mixobarb. lexicon of Meursii. Most Papist teachers do concede that the word is at last Latin. But after so many detours, what, I ask, do they achieve except to make the Reformed nomenclature, which they usually call the Lord's Supper, seem more certain and more ancient? For those who call that most holy mystery Domini Cœnam on the authority and example of Holy Scripture are not entangled in so many etymological mazes and labyrinths. The Roman Church does not indeed ignore the name Eucharistia, which was used by the most ancient Fathers, but it explains it badly, and it fares no better grammatically than theologically. Lombard, Thomas, Angelus de Clavasio and others translate it bonam gratiam ("good grace"), following Isidore, though it denotes, according to the custom of the ancient synagogue, consecration, thanksgiving, praise of God. For just as blessing [εὐλογίαν] and thanksgiving [εὐχαριστίαν] are synonyms, and according to the variety of circumstances signify to praise, to give thanks, to consecrate, so among the ancients εὐλογία and εὐχαριστία are used for the Lord's Supper, either because it is a symbol of thanksgiving toward God, as Origen speaks against Celsus, Tome 8, or because the elements, having been given thanks for [εὐχαριστηθέντα], that is, consecrated to God by prayers, receive grace [χάριν] ... an addition of grace. From ignorance of the true etymology of the word arises a gross error, and a grosser one about the definition of the thing. Thus Angelus de Clavasio says that the Lord's Supper is called the Holy Eucharist because it really contains Christ, who is full of grace.

units.la: IV. Quòd si, missa Missae ὀνοματολογία, ad rem
units.tr: IV. But if, setting aside the verbal quibbles over the Mass, we come down to the thing itself,
