units.la: ipsam descendere placeat, quanta tricarum & ambiguitatum sèges? De Sacramento Eucharistia in se consideratio quaerunt Scholastici; An consecratio sit Eucharistia Sacramentum? Et Gabriel quidem in IV. sententiarum dist. 8. q. 1. art.
units.tr: how great a crop of thorns and ambiguities appears! The Scholastics inquire into the Eucharist as a sacrament considered in itself: Whether the consecration is a sacrament of the Eucharist? Gabriel, indeed, in the fourth book of the Sentences, dist. 8, q. 1, art.

units.la: 3. 3. dub. 2. asserit, consecrationem per fe sumtam habere rationem Sacramenti. Cajetanus Eucharistiae Sacramentum nihil aliud esse vult, quam actionem Sacramentalem, consistentem in consecratione materiae. Alexander Pesantius, Romanus, viam potius ad Sacramentum quam Sacramentum ipsum esse, decidit; in Addit.ad Tho. Q. 3. art. 1. difp. 1. Quaerunt: An corpus & sanguis Christi, qui est terminus consecrationis, sit Sacramentum Eucharistiae? Valdensis Tom. 2. de Sacram. cap. 21. Corpus & sanguinem Christi facit vere & proprie Sacramentum. Marsil. in IV. Sent. q. 1. artic. 1. & q. 6. art. 2. Sot. d. 1. art. 4. quos & ex recentioribus quidam sequuntur, non modo negant, corpus & sanguinem Christi esse Sacramentum Eucharistiae; sed neque esse de ejus constitutione, tanquam partem Essentialem; sed tantum connotatum quoddam & annexum, voluerunt. Pesan-tius, media incessurus via, corpus & sanguinem Christi non esse Sacramentum Eucharistiae; esse tamen de compositione & essentia illius Sacramenti, asserit. Quaerunt: Vtrum usus & manducatio sive sumtio Eucharistiae sit Sacramentum? Gabriel, dist. 1. artic. 3. dub. 2. sumptionem, docet, esse partiale Sacramentum Eucharistiae. Ita Aureol. apud Capreo. 6. d. 8. q. 1. art. 2. arg. 3. At contrarium statuit Tridentina Synodus, quae quidem concedit, reliqua Sacramen-ta ta consistere in usu; negat tamen de Eucharistia, quæ & receptior, priori licet è diametro opposita, imò communis est sententia. Qua tamen revera nihil est absurdius. Instantiam enim dare, in sola re controversa, concessis reliquis omnibus inductionis partibus, est veluti negatio conclusionis, post concessas præmissas; Nisi evidens ostendatur ratio exceptionis. Quærunt: Vtrum species Sacramentales sint Sacramentum Eucharistiæ: Aureol. apud Capreol. d. 8. confidenter satis negat, species esse Sacramenti materiam, adeóque consequenter Essentialiter pertinere ad rationem hujus Sacramenti: negat, species esse de constitutione illius Sacramenti. Reliqui verò Scholastici species panis & vini non esse quidem totum Eucharistiæ Sacramentum communiter tradunt, esse tamen de ejus intrinseca & Essentiali constitutione. Et quia tota de ordine Sacerdotū, modo item administrandæ Eucharistiæ doctrina, aliis atque aliis partim fuit intricata novis hypothesibus, ut varam vibia, sic superstitio fuit secuta Scripturæ neglectum. Unde fertilissima casuum, circa causam administram hujus Sacramenti messis: An solus Presbyter posset consecrare corpus & sanguinem Domini nostri Iesu Christi? Quid si quis credat, se Presbyterum esse, cum non sit, & celebret? Hanc consecrationem alii ratam habent, alii non item. Certè non habent quod dubitent, si, quæ referunt Durandus & Innocentius, vera sint, quosdam Pastores, cùm Canonem alta voce in agro cantàssent, & panem super lapidem posuissent, ad verborum prolationem, panem in carnem convertisse; Ration. Durand. lib. 4. pag. 73. Vtrum, quilibet Sacerdos hoc possit Sacramentum conficere, etiam irregularis, interdictus, suspensus, Simoniacus, Schismaticus, excommunicatus, depositus, vel quilibet publicus & notorius peccator? quod de jure non admittunt, factum vero irritum habendum negant. Vtrum plures Presbyteri possint eandem hostiam consecrare? Quid expediat Presbytero, qui, postquam indutus, & ad sacra obeunda paratus est, in memoriam revocet peccatum aliquod mortale? Quid si celebrando recoleret, se comeditse vel bibisse? Quid de eo, cui, incepta Missa, occurrit, quòd non sit Presbyter? Quid faciendum Sacerdoti, ubi non esse in calice aquam observârit? Vtrum Sacerdoti omnino a consecratione Eucharistia abstinere liceat? Vtrum ab excommunicatis, vel hæreticis seu peccatoribus communionem reciperet, & eorum Missam licitum sit audire? Vtrum Sacerdos consecrans ipse quoque teneatur sumere sacramentum &c. Hæc, & si quæ sunt alia, à Theologis Scholasticis, & Casuistis de causa hujus Sacramenti administra proposita, nostram de incertitudine totius materiæ acuere possent querelam ; sed nolumus rigidius agere, & minutissima quæque persequi: De materia Eucharistiæ plures paulatim pullulárunt quæstiones, quàm quæ cum simplicitate institutionis Dominicæ possint consistere. De pane & vino, genimine vitis, loquitur Christus: Utrumque quid sit, notius est, quàm quod tot impertinentibus quæstionibus vexari debeat, cujusmodi sunt, de Pane: Utrum panis ex qualibet frumenti specie sit materia Eucharistia, an verò solum ex tritico? Et sunt quidem, qui statuunt, quemlibet panem usualem esse illius materiam; ita Bonav. in IV. d. 12. ar. 1. q. 4. Alber. Ar. 6. Cajetanus, &c. Alii solum triticeum panem Sacramenti hujus materiam admittunt. Ita plerique tam Scholastici, quàm Canonistæ, Thom. Scot. Alens. Durand. Richard. Marsil. Paludan. Angel. de Clavas, sentiunt. Sic in specie tipha, segala removetur ab Alexand. Rosell. Palat. Non removetur ab Alb. Thom. Palud. Speltam probant Alber. Gabri. Durand. Palud. Cajetan. Rejiciunt Thom. Richar. Marsil. Sed quæruntur utrum in pasta, facta ex tritico possint confici? Utrum in pane corrupto? Utrum in acido? Utrum in pane fermentato? Utrum, in pane facto de aqua rosea, vel endiviæ? Utrum sigrana alterius generis admisceantur cum tritico, possint confici? De vino verò quærere solent, utrum possit confici de alio vino, quàm de vino vitis? quasi aliud detur. Vtrum possit confici in M acaceto? Vtrum in agresto possit confici? Vtrum in musto? Vtrum in pufca, seu aqua vinata, sive in aqua, quæ, postquam vinum est expressum, superfunditur acervis uvarum, aut in aqua rubea, in qua lotus est pannus, vino rubeo t nstus? Quid si aqua aqualiter misceatur vino? Vtrum aqua debeat admisceri in vino calicis? Quid si omittatur? Qua aqua debeat apponi? In quanta quantitate &c.
units.tr: 3, dub. 2, asserts that consecration taken by itself has the nature of a sacrament. Cajetan wants the sacrament of the Eucharist to be nothing other than the sacramental action, consisting in the consecration of the matter. Alexander Pesantius of Rome decided that the consecration is rather the way to the sacrament than the sacrament itself, in Addit. ad Tho., q. 3, art. 1, disp. 1. They ask: Whether the body and blood of Christ, which is the term of consecration, is the sacrament of the Eucharist? Valdensis, vol. 2, de Sacram., chap. 21, says that the body and blood of Christ truly and properly make the sacrament. Marsil. on the Fourth Book of the Sentences, q. 1, art. 1, and q. 6, art. 2; Soto, dist. 1, art. 4, whom some of the more recent writers also follow, not only deny that the body and blood of Christ is the sacrament of the Eucharist, but have held that it is not even a part of its constitution, as an essential part, but only something connoted and attached. Pesantius, about to walk a middle way, asserts that the body and blood of Christ is not the sacrament of the Eucharist, yet that it belongs to the composition and essence of that sacrament. They ask: Whether the use, and the eating or taking of the Eucharist, is the sacrament? Gabriel, dist. 1, art. 3, dub. 2, teaches that the taking is a partial sacrament of the Eucharist. So too Aureol. in Capreolus, dist. 8, q. 1, art. 2, arg. 3. But the Tridentine Synod holds the contrary: it concedes that the other sacraments consist in use, but denies this of the Eucharist. Yet this view, though it is the opposite of the first, is more widely received, indeed it is the common opinion. Nothing, however, is really more absurd. For to raise an objection, when all the parts of the induction are conceded save the one in dispute, is like denying the conclusion after the premises have been granted, unless a clear reason for the exception is shown. They ask: Whether the sacramental species are the sacrament of the Eucharist? Aureolus, in Capreolus, dist. 8, quite confidently denies that the species are the matter of the sacrament, and consequently that they belong essentially to the nature of this sacrament; he denies that the species are part of the constitution of that sacrament. The other Scholastics, however, commonly teach that the species of bread and wine are not indeed the whole sacrament of the Eucharist, but are part of its intrinsic and essential constitution. And since the whole doctrine of the order of priests, and likewise the doctrine of the manner of administering the Eucharist, has been entangled partly in one new hypothesis after another, like the twigs of a wicker basket, superstition has followed upon the neglect of Scripture. Hence there is a most fertile harvest of cases concerning the administering cause of this sacrament: Whether a priest alone can consecrate the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ? What if someone believes that he is a priest when he is not, and celebrates? Some hold this consecration valid, others not. Certainly they have no reason for doubt, if what Durandus and Innocent report is true, that certain ministers, when they had sung the Canon aloud in a field and had placed bread upon a stone, converted the bread into flesh at the utterance of the words (Durandus, Rationale, bk. 4, p. 73). Whether any priest whatever can consecrate this sacrament, even if he is irregular, interdicted, suspended, a simoniac, a schismatic, excommunicated, deposed, or any public and notorious sinner? By law they do not admit this, but they deny that the deed is to be held void. Whether several priests can consecrate the same host? What is expedient for a priest who, after he has put on his vestments and is ready to perform the sacred rites, recalls some mortal sin to memory? What if, while celebrating, he recollects that he has eaten or drunk? What of the one who, the Mass having begun, realises that he is not a priest? What must be done by a priest who has observed that there is no water in the chalice? Is it lawful for a priest to abstain altogether from consecrating the Eucharist? Should he receive communion from the excommunicated, or heretics, or sinners, and is it lawful to hear their Mass? Whether the priest who consecrates is himself also bound to take the sacrament, etc.* These and any other such questions, proposed by the Scholastic theologians and casuists about the administering cause of this sacrament, could sharpen our complaint about the uncertainty of the whole matter; but we do not wish to proceed too rigidly, and to pursue every smallest detail. Concerning the matter of the Eucharist, many questions have gradually sprung up which cannot be reconciled with the simplicity of the Lord's institution. Christ speaks of bread and wine, the fruit of the vine. What these are is better known than that they should be troubled by so many irrelevant questions, such as these about the bread: Whether the bread of any kind of wheat is the matter of the Eucharist, or only that of wheat? And there are indeed some who hold that any ordinary bread is its matter; so Bonaventure, in the Fourth Book, dist. 12, art. 1, q. 4; Albert, art. 6; Cajetan, etc. Others admit only wheaten bread as the matter of this sacrament. So most Scholastics as well as canonists, Aquinas, Scotus, Alexander of Hales, Durandus, Richard, Marsilius, Paludanus, Angelus de Clavasio, think. Thus in the particular case of spelt, rye, is excluded by Alexander, Rosellus, Palatinus. It is not excluded by Albert, Thomas, Paludanus. Albert, Gabriel, Durandus, Paludanus, Cajetan approve spelt. Thomas, Richard, Marsilius reject it. But they ask whether it can be consecrated in paste made from wheat? In corrupted bread? In sour bread? In leavened bread? In bread made of rose water or endive? Whether, if grain of another kind is mixed with wheat, it can be consecrated? Concerning wine, they are accustomed to ask whether it can be consecrated from any wine other than the wine of the vine, as if there were something else. Whether it can be consecrated in vinegar? In verjuice? In must? In pufca, or watered wine, or in the water which is poured over heaps of grapes after the wine has been pressed out, or in red water in which a cloth dyed with red wine has been washed? What if water is mixed with the wine in equal measure? Whether water ought to be mixed into the wine of the chalice? What if it is omitted? What water ought to be added? In what quantity, etc.?

units.la: IV. Hæc tamen omnia, ex augmento adventitii elementi, aquæ, pleraque orta, levia sunt, si cum iis conferantur, quæ in Forma hujus Sacramenti, Mutatione præsertim Symbolorum in ipsam substantiam corporis Christi, in Scholis Pontificiis, & olim, & nunc controverluntur. Et circa verba quidem consecrationis, tam conjunctim, quàm sigillatim sumpta, primùm; postea etiam circa verborum usum & effectum acriter digladiari Scholasticos, breviter indicabimus. De verbis quæritur: Qua verba sint Essentialia consecrationis panis & vini? Panis consecrationem pleriq; fieri volunt verbis: Hoc est corpus meum. Particula enim negant quidem esse Essentialem; nec aliter necessariam, quàm ad connexionem continuationis verborum, scienter tamen omittendam non esse: imò credit mortaliter peccaturum Angelus, qui in consecratione tam panis, quàm vini scienter omitteret. In vini autem consecratione Doctores Scholastici ægrè se exexpediunt. Alens. Bonavent. Durandus, cum Magistro, docent, formam sufficientem consecrationis vini, esse sola illa verba: Hic est calix sanguinis mei; vel Hic est sanguis meus. At Richard: & Argent. sententia est, omnia verba, quae habentur in forma Romana, consecrationi calicis ita esse necessaria, ut vel uno demto, non conficeretur sanguis Christi. Scoti opinione duo non sunt certa, primum, an ad formam consecrationis sanguinis pertineant aliqua verba, post illud sanguinis mei; deinde: anillud: Hoc facite? &c. Ideóque periculo carere non existimat, de utroque, in hac materia, asserrere, cùm sufficiens authoritas non habeatur; q. 2. ff. de isto. Ita etiam Marsilius, & pauci ex Thomistis. Ipsemet Thomas à suis asseclis diversimodè intelligitur. Capreolus & Palud. putant, ipsum cum Richardo sentire & Argent. omnia nempe verba, quae sunt in forma Romana, esse de essentia formae consecrationis calicis. Sotus verò d. 11. q. 1. ar. 3. negat, ejusmodi opinionem sustineri posse. Unde Cajetanus & Pesantius, Thomam ita explicant, quòd; cùm in corpore dicit, omnia verba, quibus Romana Ecclesia utitur, in calicis consecratione, esse de substantia formae (quia sunt quaedam determinationes Praedicati, hoc est, sanguinis Christi) non sic intelligere, quasi essent de essentia, ita ut sine illis non sit forma; sed quòd sint de integritate, tate, adeò ut sine illis non sit forma perfecta. Sed pergunt quærere: An prædicta forma consecrationis à Christo sint instituta, i. e. an Christus in Cœna, cum panem consecravit, usus sit hac ipsa eorundem verborum forma, qua Pontifici utuntur, &c. ut pane azymo usus est? Et alii quidem sentiunt, Christum solo actu voluntatis effecisse Transsubstantiationem, panis & vini in suum corpus & sanguinem. Ita Aliac, in 4. q. 5. ar. 1. Alii volunt, Christum effecisse Transsubstantiationem verbis nobis ignotis; non tamen iisdem, quibus Ecclesia Romana utitur. Ita Catharinus. Plerorumque tamen sententia est, Christum consecrâsse iisdem verbis, quibus hodie consecrant Sacerdotes; cujus mox sententiæ explicandæ iterum varii sunt modi, quorum conciliationem illis relinquimus. Nos pergimus quærendo: Quomodo consecrationis verba pronuncientur à Sacerdotibus? Innocentius, Durandus, Scotus, Major, Ocham, Gabriel, Catharinus dicunt, Sacerdotem non uti verbis formarum enunciativè, & materialiter, veluti si quis legeret verba: Ego sum vitis: Ego sum lux mundi; sed recitativè. Thom. verò, Cajet. & communiter Thomistæ statuunt, verba formarum proferri à Sacerdote recitativè & significativè simul, ita ut Sacerdos illis verbis, & quod Christus pridie suæ passionis fecit, & quod tunc ipse facit, significet. Sed &c; An verba consecrationis prius sint vera, vera, quàm efficiant, quod significant, quærunt? Et ne hîc quidem conveniunt. Scotus asserit, formas Sacramentales Eucharistiæ conversivas panis & vini in corpus & sanguinem Christi, esse priores naturâ, & forte etiam tempore, sua veritate. In illo autem priori, etsi non sint veræ, non tamen esse eas falsas, sed neutras, id est, neque veras, neque falsas, d.8.q.2. At Thomas, & cum eo plerique Scholastici docent, Propositiones, quæ sunt Formæ consecrationis, prius natura esse significativas, & veras, quàm effectivas. At difficultas est in hac sententia, inquit Pesantius, quomodo in illo priori, in quo nondum intelligitur corpus & sanguis Christi per conversionem ex pane & vino factum, vera sit Propositio, enuncians, contentum sub speciebus, esse corpus & sanguinem Christi? Vult proinde, Propositiones Practicas & effectivas, ejus, quod significant, simul & tempore esse cum suo esse & conceptione. In 3.P.Thom.Q.78.d.2.
units.tr: IV. Most of these matters, arising from the addition of the extraneous element of water, are trivial if they are set beside those disputed in the Papist schools, both formerly and now, concerning the form of this sacrament, above all the change of the symbols into the very substance of the body of Christ. I will briefly indicate how the Scholastics fight fiercely, first about the words of consecration, taken both together and separately, and then also about the use and effect of the words. As to the words, the question is: Which words are essential to the consecration of bread and wine? Most want the consecration of the bread to be effected by the words This is my body. They indeed deny that the particle enim is essential, and say it is necessary only to connect the continuity of the words, yet that it must not be knowingly omitted. Indeed, they believe that a priest who knowingly omitted it in the consecration of either bread or wine would sin mortally. In the consecration of the wine, however, the Scholastic doctors extricate themselves with difficulty. Alensis, Bonaventure and Durandus, with the Master, teach that the sufficient form for consecrating the wine is only these words: This is the cup of my blood, or This is my blood. But Richard and Argentine hold that all the words found in the Roman form are so necessary to the consecration of the cup that if even one were removed, the blood of Christ would not be consecrated. According to Scotus, two things are uncertain: first, whether any words after of my blood pertain to the form of consecration of the blood; second, whether Do this etc. does. He therefore does not think it free from danger to assert either about either in this matter, since sufficient authority is lacking; q. 2 ff. de isto. So also Marsilius and a few of the Thomists. Thomas himself is understood in different ways by his followers. Capreolus and Palud. think that he agrees with Richard and Argentine, namely that all the words which are in the Roman form belong to the essence of the form of consecration of the cup. Soto, however, in d. 11 q. 1 art. 3, denies that such an opinion can be maintained. Hence Cajetan and Pesantius explain Thomas thus: when in the body of the article he says that all the words the Roman Church uses in the consecration of the cup belong to the substance of the form (because they are certain determinations of the predicate, that is, of the blood of Christ), one must not understand that they are of the essence, so that without them there is no form; rather, they belong to the integrity, so that without them the form is not perfect. But they go on to ask: Were the aforesaid forms of consecration instituted by Christ, that is, did Christ at the supper, when he consecrated the bread, use this very form of words which priests use, etc., just as he used unleavened bread? Some indeed think that Christ effected the transubstantiation of bread and wine into his body and blood by the act of his will alone. So Aliaco, in 4 q. 5 art. 1. Others hold that Christ effected transubstantiation by words unknown to us, yet not the same as those the Roman Church uses. So Catharinus. But the opinion of most is that Christ consecrated with the same words with which priests now consecrate; and of this opinion there are again various ways of explanation, whose reconciliation we leave to others. We proceed to ask: How are the words of consecration pronounced by the priests? Innocent, Durandus, Scotus, Major, Ockham, Gabriel and Catharinus say that the priest does not use the words of the forms enunciatively and materially, as if someone were reading the words I am the vine; I am the light of the world, but recitatively. Thomas, however, Cajetan and the Thomists commonly hold that the words of the forms are uttered by the priest recitatively and significatively at once, so that by those words the priest signifies both what Christ did on the day before his passion and what he himself now does. But they ask further: Are the words of consecration true before they effect what they signify? And here too they do not agree. Scotus asserts that the sacramental forms of the Eucharist which convert bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ are prior in nature, and perhaps also in time, to their truth. In that prior moment, although they are not true, they are not false either, but neither, that is, neither true nor false; d. 8 q. 2. But Thomas, and with him most Scholastics, teach that the propositions which are the forms of consecration are significative and true by nature before they are effective. Yet, says Pesantius, the difficulty with this view is how, in that prior moment, when the body and blood of Christ are not yet understood to have been made from bread and wine by conversion, the proposition stating that what is contained under the species is the body and blood of Christ can be true. He therefore wishes that practical and effective propositions be simultaneous in time with what they signify, together with their being and conception. In 3 P. Thom. Q. 78 d. 2.

units.la: V. Sed & singulæ propemodum voces pomum contentionis in Scholis Pontificiis objiciunt. Incertitudine hîc nihil certius. Sit, exempli loco, pronomen demonstrativum Hoc, in verbis: Hoc est corpus meum. Tres de eo sunt sententiæ generales, suis iterum subdistinctæ explicandi modis diversis, qui tamen se ipsos penè destruunt. Ipsos juvat spectare in sua sævientes viscera adversarios. Prima sententia, inquit Ale-
units.tr: V. But almost every single word, too, is an object of contention in the Papist schools. Nothing here is more uncertain. Take, for example, the demonstrative pronoun this in the words This is my body. There are three general opinions about it, each further subdivided into different ways of explaining, which nevertheless almost destroy one another. It pleases them to watch their adversaries raging in their own entrails. The first opinion, says Alex-

units.la: Alexand. Pesantius, est, cùm dicitur: Hoc est corpus meum, per illud Pronomen Hoc, demonstrari panem: Et similiter, cùm dicitur, Hic est calix, demonstrari vinum, quæ sententia diversimodè explicatur. Bonavent. in 4. d. 8. 2. p. distinctionis ar. 1. q. 1. ut exponat, quomodo per pronomen Hoc, fiat panis demonstratio, pervertit significationem verbi: Vult enim, Est idem sonare, quod, fit, ut sit sensus: Hoc, quod est panis, fit corpus meum: Sed hoc, ut ait Sot. est nimium formam invertere aliter, quàm ea Christus ulus est. Juxta Marsil. in 4. q. 6. ar. 1. explicationem, sensus formæ est: Id, in quod hoc, i.e. panis convertitur, est corpus meum; Sed hoc est immutare formam à Chrilto traditam, ut Sot. excipit. Secunda sententia est, cùm dicitur, Hoc est corpus meum, indicari corpus ipsum Christi: Quod etiam variis modis explicatur. Ocham quodl. 2. q. ult. mavult, indicari corpus, sub conceptis corporis, & verbum est supponere, pro, erit, ut sensus sit: Hoc corpus meum erit. Sed nec hoc placet. Scotus putat, indicari singulariter corpus; sed sub conceptu transcendenti Entis, ut sensus formæ sit: Hoc est corpus meum. Cajetanus, simul cum Scoto exististimat, pronomine Hoc indicari singulariter corpus Christi, non tamen sub conceptu transcendenti Entis, sed sub conceptu particulariori subsistentia, ut sensus sit: Hæc subsistentia est corpus meum: Neque hi modi Scoto &c. & Cajet. satisfaciunt, Tertia sententia est Thoma, cùm dicit: Hoc est corpus meum; illo pronomine Hoc indicari singulariter; sed indeterminate & vage contentum sub Speciebus; quod erat panis, sit corpus Christi. Ita etiam Richar. d. 8. art. 3. q. 1. Durand. & communiter Scotista. Ita Pesant in 3. Par, Thom. Quæst. 78. disput. 3. Hæcne est aperta illa simplicitas, quam Transsubstantiationis patroni tantopere commendant? Hoccine est retinere literam, & religiosè Christi venerari verba? Imò verò, hoc est cœlum terræ, & suprema miscere imis. Novam fingere hypotyposin, quam vix Gentium Apostolus, qui & in tertio cœlo cœlestem, & in terris humanam ad pedes Gamaliel didicit sapientiam, si jam rediret, cum sua componere posseт tum verborum perspicuitate, tum mysteriorum convenienti tractatione. Ergòne illi verbis Servatoris inhærent, qui ex pane, quem Christus accepit, fregit, distribuit, individuum exsculpunt vagum? Ergòne illi, qui tam longis à se invicem recedunt spatiis, & quibus nec illud, quod multis aliis, iisque doctissimis probatur, placet; consensum suum adeò thrasonicè crepent? Sed quid si utraque sententia contradictoria vera sit? Id sibi persuadent subtiles Scholastici. Si enim laicus dixerit, contentum sub speciebus, esse corpus Christi, falsa est ejus propositio: quia contentum sub speciebus, quatenus dicit panem.
units.tr: Alexander Pesantius, is that when it is said, This is my body, the pronoun this demonstrates the bread; and similarly, when it is said, This is the cup, the wine is demonstrated. This opinion is explained in various ways. Bonaventure, in 4 d. 8, part 2, art. 1 q. 1, in order to explain how the bread is demonstrated by the pronoun this, perverts the meaning of the verb. For he wants is to mean the same as becomes, so that the sense is: This, which is bread, becomes my body. But, as Soto says, this is to invert the form too much, in a way other than Christ used it. According to Marsilius' explanation in 4 q. 6 art. 1, the sense of the form is: That into which this, that is the bread, is converted, is my body; but, as Soto objects, this is to change the form handed down by Christ. The second opinion is that when it is said, This is my body, the body of Christ itself is indicated; this too is explained in various ways. Ockham, Quodl. 2 q. ult., prefers that the body is indicated under the concept of body, and that the verb is stands for will be, so that the sense is: This body will be mine. But this does not please either. Scotus thinks that the body is indicated singularly, but under the transcendent concept of Being, so that the sense of the form is: This is my body. Cajetan, together with Scotus, thinks that the pronoun this singularly indicates the body of Christ, not under the transcendent concept of Being, but under the more particular concept of subsistence, so that the sense is: This subsistence is my body. Neither of these modes satisfies Scotus etc. or Cajetan. The third opinion is Thomas', when he says, This is my body: by that pronoun this is singularly indicated what is contained under the species, but indeterminately and vaguely, namely that what was bread is the body of Christ. So also Richard, d. 8 art. 3 q. 1, Durandus, and commonly the Scotists; so Pesantius on 3 Part Thom. Q. 78 disp. 3. Is this that plain simplicity which the advocates of transubstantiation commend so highly? Is this keeping to the letter and reverently honouring the words of Christ? Indeed, this is to bring heaven down to earth and mix the highest with the lowest. It is to invent a new hypotyposis, which the Apostle of the Gentiles, who in the third heaven learned heavenly wisdom and at the feet of Gamaliel learned human wisdom on earth, could scarcely match with his own clarity of words and fitting handling of the mysteries if he returned now. Do those adhere to the words of the Saviour who carve out a vague individual from the bread which Christ took, broke and distributed? Do those, who stand so far apart from one another, and whom even that opinion which is approved by many others, and those most learned, does not please, so boastfully proclaim their agreement? But what if each contradictory opinion is true? Subtle Scholastics persuade themselves of this. For if a layman says that what is contained under the species is the body of Christ, his proposition is false, because what is contained under the species, as far as it signifies bread,

units.la: M 4 prapræscindendo à conversione, quam laicus facere non potest; non est corpus Christi: Si vero, qui dicit, contentum sub speciebus esse corpus Christi, sit Sacerdos, habens intentionem consecrandi, Propositio ejus vera est; quia contentum sub speciebus, quod includit panem per conversionem in instanti ejus Propositionis terminativo, est corpus Christi; Hæc Pelant l.c. Itáne, qui veritas ipsa est, in Apollinem mutetur λογίῳ, flexiloquum Prometheum? Verba ejus in Cothurnum versatilem, utriq; pedi aptum? Eadem verba prout vel laicus ea expresserit, vel clericus aut vera sint, aut falsa; etsi nulla legitimæ oppositionis ostendi possit exceptio? Possemus intestina hæc dissidia speciosius exaggerare. Sed nolumus esse θεομάχοι. Dolemus potius triste eorum fatum, quibus, sub prætextu thesauri cœlestium mysteriorum, tot Scholasticorum venduntur fumi. Verè cum Servatore dicere nobis licebit: Vos adoratis, quod nescitis, nos adoramus quod scimus, Joh.4.verf.22. Deo certè ignoto oras extruunt, qui tot discrepantium sententiarum ventis circumferuntur.
units.tr: Abstracting from the conversion, which a layman cannot effect, what he says is not the body of Christ. But if the one who says that what is contained under the species is the body of Christ is a priest intending to consecrate, his proposition is true, because what is contained under the species, which includes the bread through conversion at the instant that his proposition terminates, is the body of Christ. These are Pelant's words, loc. cit. Can he who is Truth itself be turned into an oracular [λογίῳ] Apollo, a Prometheus of many words? Can his words be turned into a buskin that fits either foot? Are the same words true or false depending on whether a layman or a cleric utters them, even though no lawful exception to them can be shown? We could magnify these internal quarrels more splendidly, but we do not wish to be fighters against God [θεομάχοι]. We rather lament the sad lot of those who, under the pretext of the treasure of heavenly mysteries, are sold so much smoke by so many Schoolmen. We may truly say with the Saviour: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know" (John 4.22). Those people build altars to an unknown God who are tossed about by the winds of so many conflicting opinions.

units.la: VI. Cæteris jam, de verbis consecrationis, Scholasticorum quæstionibus (utrum Presbyter, dicens solum prafata verba super panē, consecret? ubi etiam sententiarum occurrunt divortia: Utrum Sacerdos verborum prædictorum possit unam partem ipsius hostiæ consecrare. re, sine alia hostia continua remanente? Quid si Sacerdos acceptis pluribus hostiis consecrandis, quando venit ad actum consecrationis, non advertit, nisi ad eam, quam habet in manu Casuisticis magis, quàm dogmaticis praetermissis, ad virtutem verborum consecrantium accedamus. Et hic quidem aenigmata iterum ubique obvia sunt, & Sibyllina folia. Agnoscit enim Concilium Tridentinum, post panis & vini consecrationem, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum verum Deum atque hominem vere, realiter, ac substantialiter sub specie illarum rerum sensibilium contineri. Id quod veteres Scholastici ita expresserunt: Conversionem fieri in Sacramento, per virtutem verborum praefatorum, de qua firmiter tenendum, quod substantia panis, secundum totam suam materiam & formam existens, actu transubstantiatur in totum corpus Christi actu existens, ita quod materia in materiam, & forma in formam, scilicet corpoream, transubstantiatur, solis accidentibus remanentibus. Ita ex Bonavent. Richardo, &c. Angelus. Ex quo jam novo, planeque absurdo dogmate, novae iterum emergunt quaestiones, quibus δὶς ἀλῶ πτωσῶν a se differunt. Et primo, ne in ipso quidem hujus dogmatis fundamento conveniunt. Quaerit 1. Pesantius, an ex sacris literis certo haberi possit, quod in Eucharistia non maneat panis? Non audet affirmare Scotus,qui solius Ecclesiæ authoritati illud tribuit. Quin existimat, manente pane, Propositionem illam, Hoc est corpus meum, veram esse. Cui & Durandus accedit. Cæteri, qui affirmant, fundamentum quæruntin ipsis verbis controversis: quod, quàm sit inconveniens, supra indicavimus. Differunt 2. in eo, utrum in Eucharistia remaneat materia panis & vini, sub forma corporis Christi ? Durandus ea manere defendit, in 4.d. 11.q.3. num. 5. Thomas, Bonaventura, Alensis, Scholastici communiter docent, non substantiam modò panis & vini, id est, totum completum; sed neque materiam ipsorum in hoc Sacramento manere; imò totum panem & vinum in corpus & sanguinem Christi transsubstantiari. Discrepant 3. in eo, an substantia panis, quæ in hoc Sacramento non manet, annihiletur ? Hic iterum tribus diversis inceditur viis. Et Scotus quidem vi Transsubstantiationis panem solum in illo loco, scil. sub illis speciebus, sub quibus incepit esse corpus Christi, vult esse desinere. Ita d. 11. q. 4. st. Potest ergo teneri. Durandus vero statuit, terminum à quo, secundum materiam sub forma corporis Christi, non manere, adeóque necessariò panem & vinum annihilari dici debere. Tertia Thomæ opinio est, & Thomistarum, Bonavent. Paludan. Capreol. Alens. Mars. Ferrar. Cajet. Sot. Ledes. qui omnes, desitionem panis in hoc Sacramento non esse annihilationem tenent. Hæc verò adeò recentioribus placet sententia, ut, Pesantii judicio, neganda sit in hoc Sacramento conversio, quam ponunt Concilia, si detur, panem desinere per annihilationem; in 3. P. Thom. q. 75. ar. 3. d. 1.
units.tr: VI. Now let us come to the other questions of the Schoolmen about the words of consecration: whether a priest who says only the aforesaid words over the bread consecrates; here too the opinions diverge. Whether a priest, using the aforesaid words, can consecrate one part of the host itself, while another host remains unconsecrated? What if a priest, having taken several hosts to be consecrated, when he comes to the act of consecration, attends only to the one he holds in his hand? Leaving aside these casuistical matters rather than dogmatic ones, let us come to the power of the consecrating words. Here too riddles and Sibylline leaves are everywhere to be met. For the Council of Trent acknowledges that, after the consecration of the bread and wine, our Lord Jesus Christ, true God and man, is truly, really and substantially contained under the species of those sensible things. The older Schoolmen expressed this as follows: The conversion takes place in the sacrament through the power of the aforesaid words; and concerning this it must firmly be held that the substance of bread, existing according to its whole matter and form, is actually transubstantiated into the whole body of Christ actually existing, so that matter is transubstantiated into matter and form into form, namely corporeal form, the accidents alone remaining. So Bonaventure, Richard, &c., Angelus. From this new and plainly absurd dogma, new questions again arise, on which they differ in two ways [δὶς ἀλῶ πτωσῶν] from one another. And first, they do not agree even on the foundation of this dogma itself. Pesantius asks first: can it be held with certainty from Holy Scripture that the bread does not remain in the Eucharist? Scotus does not dare to affirm this, and he attributes it to the authority of the Church alone. Indeed he thinks that the bread remaining, that proposition, This is my body, is true. Durandus agrees with him. The others who affirm it seek their foundation in the disputed words themselves, which, how unsuitable this is, we have shown above. They differ, second, on this point: whether the matter of bread and wine remains in the Eucharist under the form of the body of Christ? Durandus defends that it remains, in 4 d. 11 q. 3 n. 5. Thomas, Bonaventure, Alexander of Hales and the Schoolmen commonly teach that not only the substance of bread and wine, that is, the whole complete thing, but also their matter does not remain in this sacrament; rather the whole bread and wine are transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ. They differ, third, on this point: whether the substance of the bread, which does not remain in this sacrament, is annihilated? Here again they proceed by three different ways. Scotus, by the power of transubstantiation, wills that the bread simply ceases to be in that place, that is, under those species under which it has begun to be the body of Christ. So in d. 11 q. 4 st.: It can therefore be held. Durandus, however, holds that the terminus from which, according to its matter, does not remain under the form of the body of Christ, and that therefore the bread and wine must necessarily be said to be annihilated. The third opinion is that of Thomas and of the Thomists: Bonaventure, Paludanus, Capreolus, Alensis, Marsilius, Ferrariensis, Cajetan, Soto, Ledesma, who all hold that the ceasing of the bread in this sacrament is not annihilation. This opinion, however, is so pleasing to more recent writers that, in Pesantius's judgement, the conversion which the Councils posit must be denied in this sacrament, if it is granted that the bread ceases to be by annihilation; in 3 P. Thom. q. 75 a. 3 d. 1.

units.la: VII. Ipse Transsubstantiationis modus, quàm longè variantibus sententiis, abstrusis & obscuris proponitur terminis, ambiguis traditur Scholasticorum definitionibus? Et quanquam ita perplexa & intricata sit tota hæc Transsubstantiationis materia, ut Scholæ Pontificiæ consensus tantopere ubique jactatus, vel ex hoc tantum conflictu gravissimè vulneretur, brevitatis tamen, & modestiæ, quàm ubertatis materiæ, majorem habituri rationem, ea tantùm, quæ ipsi subministrant Adversarii, dissensionum capita tangemus. Illa primaria est: Quòd nam substantiale illud sit, quod in hac Transsubstantiatione, tanquam terminus ad quem, producatur? Scotus videtur ἀνάκρισις, & in termino Transsubstantiationis assignando fluctuare; portu tamen tandem reperto, definit: Transsubstantiationem terminari ad successionem substantialem corporis Christi: Unde Transsubstantiationem ita terminare in corpus Christi, censet, ut illud, sub speciebus, successione quadam substantiali ad substantiam panis, quæ suberat accidentibus, adducat; non tamen det illi esse, quia illud in suo esse reperit. Non video autem, inquit Pesantius, in quo poni possit hujusmodi successionis substantialitas, nisi in hoc, quod subsistentia adducitur, & succedit substantia. Eandem sententiam, Ocham, Major, aliique Nominales; qui terminum hujus Transsubstantiationis esse volunt corpus Christi, ut in loco & officio speciem succedit; defendunt. Sed hic dicendi modus aperte falsus est, inquit Pesantius. Secunda sententia eorum est, qui Transsubstantiationem in hoc Sacramento terminari ad modum aliquem substantialem docent. Si enim generatio hominis, inquiunt, omnium voce, sit substantialis, quanquam immediate terminetur in unione animae cum corpore : sufficere etiam videtur, ad Transsubstantiationem, ut ea terminetur ad modum aliquem substantialem. Varios jam modos substantiales diversi proponunt; qui tamen omnes, inquit Pesantius, facile confutantur. Tertia classis nihil assignat pro termino Transsubstantiationis: Neque substantiam, neque successionem, neque modum ullum substantialem, per hoc tamen conatur explicare, quod hoc Sacramentum conversione substantiali fiat, quo actio, qua corpus Christi adducitur sub speciebus ex se, & natura sua, est productiva; licet illud in hoc Sacramento, per Accidens, non producat, quia scil. productum jam invenit. Ita Gab.d. 11.q.1.ar. 3.dub.2. Sot. d. 9.q.2.artic.4. Sed hoc est dicere, conversionem hanc non esse actu in hoc sacramento, contra Tridentinum, inquit Pesantius.
units.tr: VII. How far, with varying opinions, is the very mode of transubstantiation put forward in abstruse and obscure terms, and handed down in the ambiguous definitions of the Schoolmen? And although this whole matter of transubstantiation is so perplexed and intricate that the consensus of the Papist schools, so much boasted of everywhere, is seriously wounded by this conflict alone, nevertheless, having regard to brevity and modesty rather than to the abundance of the matter, we shall touch only on those heads of disagreement which our adversaries themselves supply. The first is this: what substantial thing is it that is produced in this transubstantiation as the terminus to which it tends? Scotus seems to be undecided and to waver in assigning the terminus of transubstantiation; at last, however, having found a harbour, he defines: transubstantiation terminates in the substantial succession of the body of Christ. Hence he thinks that transubstantiation terminates in the body of Christ in such a way that it brings that body, under the species, by a certain substantial succession to the substance of bread which underlay the accidents, yet does not give it being, because it finds it already in its being. But I do not see, says Pesantius, in what this substantiality of such succession can consist, except in this, that a subsistence is brought in and a substance succeeds. Ockham, Major and the other Nominalists, who wish the terminus of this transubstantiation to be the body of Christ, as a species succeeds in place and office, defend the same opinion. But this manner of speaking is plainly false, says Pesantius. The second opinion is of those who teach that transubstantiation in this sacrament terminates in some substantial mode. For if the generation of a man, they say, is by everyone's voice substantial, although it terminates immediately in the union of the soul with the body, it seems also sufficient for transubstantiation that it terminate in some substantial mode. Various substantial modes are now proposed by different men; yet all of these, says Pesantius, are easily refuted. The third class assigns nothing as the terminus of transubstantiation: neither substance, nor succession, nor any substantial mode; yet it tries to explain by this alone that this sacrament is made by substantial conversion, in which the action by which the body of Christ is brought under the species is by its own nature and essence productive; although in this sacrament it does not produce it, by accident, because, namely, it finds it already produced. So Gabriel, d. 11 q. 1 a. 3 dub. 2; Soto, d. 9 q. 2 art. 4. But this amounts to saying that this conversion is not actually in this sacrament, contrary to Trent, says Pesantius.

units.la: Quarta sententia, Transsubstantiationem terminari in substantiam corporis & sanguinis Christi, statuit. Quorum quidam sic corpus Transsubstantiationis terminum constituunt, non tanquam per illam accipiat de novo suum esse, sed tanquam per illam conservetur in esse, accepto per incarnationem. Itaque nullam novitatem in termino ponunt; sed, ad definitionem panis, intelligunt, Deum velle Christum adductum sub speciebus conservare, Sot. Quodl. q. 10. ar. 2. Gab. Sed neq; hic probatur modus Pesantio, quia panis desitio ponitur esse annihilatio, quod absurdum ille vocat. Quinta sententia eorum est, qui sic corporis Christi substantiam constituunt esse terminum Transsubstantiationis, ut ea per Transsubstantiationem fiat, & de novo accipiat idem esse, quod per incarnationem habebat, & consequenter, sicut vi novæ productionis accepit esse; sic etiam ratione talis productionis incipiat de novo conservari. Ita ex Scholasticis veteribus Thom. Hug. Altiscod. Richar. Marsil. Cajet. Post concilium Tridentinum (quod aperte definivit, per consecrationem, conversionem fieri totius substantiæ panis in substantiam corporis Christi, & totius substantiæ vini in substantiam sanguinis) recentiores communiter. Nónne, Vir doctissime, hoc est regnum divisum? Si ipsi eruditi, si Doctores vel non exprimere facis perspicuè; vel confirmare mentem suam possunt solide, quomodo alios in sua perrahent castra, aut Catechumenos instruent?
units.tr: The fourth opinion holds that transubstantiation terminates in the substance of the body and blood of Christ. Some of these so constitute the body as the terminus of transubstantiation, not as if it received its being anew through it, but as if it were preserved in being through it, having received being through the incarnation. Thus they place no novelty in the terminus, but understand, with regard to the definition of bread, that God wills that Christ, brought under the species, be preserved; Soto, Quodl. q. 10 a. 2; Gabriel. But this mode too is not approved by Pesantius, because the ceasing of the bread is posited to be annihilation, which he calls absurd. The fifth opinion is of those who so constitute the substance of the body of Christ as the terminus of transubstantiation that it is made by transubstantiation and anew receives the same being which it had through the incarnation; and consequently, just as by virtue of a new production it received being, so also by reason of such production it begins to be preserved anew. So from the older Schoolmen: Thomas, Hugh, Altisiodorensis, Richard, Marsilius, Cajetan. After the Council of Trent (which plainly defined that by consecration there is conversion of the whole substance of bread into the substance of the body of Christ, and of the whole substance of wine into the substance of the blood), the more recent writers commonly so hold. Is this not, most learned sir, a kingdom divided against itself? If the learned themselves, if the Doctors, either cannot express it clearly, or cannot solidly confirm their own mind, how will they draw others into their camp, or instruct the catechumens?

units.la: VIII. Sed Transubstantiatione posita magis, quàm exposita; aliæ; ut uno dato absurdo, cætera sequi necesse est; subnascuntur de modo præsentiæ, quæstiones. Cùm enim verum & reale Christi corpus, ex pane transubstantiatum, præsens agnoscant, quærendi campum Scholastici ingrediuntur patentissimum; respondendi vero exitum ut quærunt diversissimum; ita inveniunt nullum : Id quod est λαζεὶν ... κεφαλὴν κακῶς.
units.tr: VIII. But once transubstantiation is laid down rather than explained, further questions arise about the mode of presence, as they must, since one absurdity granted brings the rest with it. For since they acknowledge the true and real body of Christ, transubstantiated from the bread, to be present, the Scholastics enter a very wide field of questions, yet the ways out of answering them are most divergent, so they find none. This is "to grasp the head badly" [λαζεὶν ... κεφαλὴν κακῶς].

units.la: Quærunt, Vtrum præsentia corporis Christi, ex natura rei sequatur Transsubstantiationem? Et hic, inter Scholasticos, dividias reperias, quas recensét Pesantius. Acriter disceptatur, Vtrum sine conversione ulla, acquiri possit præsentia corporis Christi sub Speciebus? Hic iterum in quatuor itur sententias. Et primò quidem, statur quæstionis à nonnullis ita formatur, An hoc fieri possit de potentia ordinata, ex qua corpus Christi, vi verborum formæ consecrationis, succedit substantia panis & vini sub speciebus eorum? Quo sensu Scotus & Durandus, veram esse consecrationis formam, etiam manente panis substantia, dummodò cum illa incipiat etiam esse corpus Christi, existimant. Alitèt tamen sentiunt Nominales, aliíque, quibus ratum est, desinitionem panis, esse annihilationis mutationem, omnino distinctam ab inceptione corporis Christi. Sed utramque sententiam aperta falsitatis ream agit Pesantius, tum, quòd definitum sit à Concilio Tridentino, vi forma consecrationis, panem & vinum converti & transsubstantiari in corpus & sanguinem Christi; tum quòd certum esse debeat, de potentia ordinata, præsentiam Christi, sine conversione, in hoc Sacramento, esse non posse. Ab aliis verò quæstio ita concipitur; An simpliciter, & ex potentia absoluta, Deus possit Christi corpus collocare sub speciebus, absque eo, quod panis in illud convertatur? Thomista, simpliciter sieri non posse, ut corpus Christi eandem præsentiam habeat sub speciebus, remanente substantia panis in conversione asserunt. Scholastici verò communiter tradunt, potentiâ absolutâ, sine ulla panis conversione, simul posse poni sub speciebus substantiam corporis Christi; cujus contrarium non sine temeritate possit asseri. Ubi ad definitionem præsentiæ Sacramentalis corporis Christi fuerit deventum, quot hic amabo iterum fluctus? Durandi sententia est, præsentiam Sacramentalem corporis Christi ad species, esse præsentiam ordinis, atque ita consistere solùm in quadam relatione rarationis, per quam ipsum intelligitur in iis, aut per illas, ubicunque fuerint, operari posse. Hoc, ceu evidenter falsum, & realis praesentiae destructivum, alii Theologi rejiciunt. Scotus ait, praesentiam, relationem esse extrinsecus advenientem, sed & hoc aperte falsum est, inquit Pesfantius. Cajet. & Cap. statuunt, hanc praesentiam Sacramentalem, esse relationem praedicamentalem; cujus tamen nullum assignant fundamentum aliud, quam conventionem: quae tamen, aliorum judicio, talem praesentiam fundare non potest. Thomista nonnulli, quibus recentiores quidam accedunt, praesentiam illam in actuali operatione corporis Christi circa species constituunt, ad modum, quo praesentia Angeli ad locum est, per operationem transeuntem. Quinta Scoti, Palud. Gab. Maj. Aliac. Pesant. sententia est, rationem, qua corpus Christi Sacramentaliter exitit in Eucharistia, esse modum absolutum, in quo fundatur relatio praesentiae.
units.tr: They ask: Does the presence of the body of Christ follow from the nature of the thing, that is, from transubstantiation? Here among the Scholastics you will find many divisions, which Pesantius recounts. It is hotly disputed whether any presence of the body of Christ under the species can be obtained without conversion. Here again there are four opinions. First, some frame the question thus: Can this happen by ordained power, by which the body of Christ, through the force of the words of the form of consecration, takes the place of the substance of bread and wine under their species? In this sense Scotus and Durandus hold that the form of consecration is true even while the substance of bread remains, provided that the body of Christ also begins to be present with it. The Nominalists and others, however, hold that the ceasing of the bread is an annihilating change, wholly distinct from the beginning of the body of Christ. Pesantius charges both opinions with manifest falsehood: first, because the Council of Trent defined that by the force of the form of consecration the bread and wine are converted and transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ; and second, because it must be certain that by ordained power the presence of Christ in this sacrament cannot be without conversion. Others frame the question differently: Can God, simply and by absolute power, place the body of Christ under the species without the bread being converted into it? The Thomists assert that it cannot simply happen that the body of Christ has the same presence under the species while the substance of the bread remains unconverted. The Scholastics, however, commonly teach that by absolute power the substance of Christ's body can be placed under the species at the same time, without any conversion of the bread; the contrary, they say, cannot be asserted without rashness. When we come to the definition of the sacramental presence of the body of Christ, how many waves, I ask, break over us again? Durandus holds that the sacramental presence of the body of Christ to the species is a presence of order, and so consists only in a certain relation of reason, by which he is understood to be able to act in them, or through them, wherever they may be. Other theologians reject this as plainly false and destructive of real presence. Scotus says the presence is a relation coming from outside, but this too is manifestly false, says Pesantius. Cajetan and Capreolus hold that this sacramental presence is a predicamental relation, yet they assign no foundation for it other than agreement, which, in the judgment of others, cannot ground such a presence. Some Thomists, joined by certain more recent writers, place that presence in the actual operation of the body of Christ upon the species, in the way that the presence of an angel is to a place, through transient operation. The fifth opinion, of Scotus, Paludanus, Gabriel, Major, Aliacus and Pesantius, is that the manner in which the body of Christ exists sacramentally in the Eucharist is an absolute mode, in which the relation of presence is grounded.

units.la: IX. Quantitatem Christi, in hoc Sacramento, ratione naturalis concomitantiae, quam habet cum propria substantia, in qua per se, primo ex vi verborum, sit conversio panis & vini communis fere Scholasticorum; qui Scotum ea in re sequuntur; est sententia: nisi quod Durandus, ut effugiat difficultates, quae ex Christi quantitate in hoc Sacramento oriuntur, neget corcorpus Christi, ut existens in Eucharistia suam habere quantitatem (quod alii erroneum, alii erroris proximum, quidam temerarium & periculosum appellant:) Rogati vero, quomodo Quantitas Christi in Eucharistia sit indivisibiliter, mirum se in modum torquent, & extricando intricant. Nominales finxerunt, corpus Christi sub speciebus esse quantum realiter, non formaliter, cum habeat totum id, quod realiter est quantitas, seu suas partes omnes substantiales; non autem habeat ordinem illum ad locum. Hæc vero sententia cur nobis placeat? Ne Pontificiis quidem satisfacit. Hac sententia non placet; magni sunt Theologi Romani verba; quia formalitas Quantitatis non est posita in ordine aliquo ad alterum, sed ex intensione intrinseca partium. Altera vero, & communis quidem, sententia ponit rationem formalem Quantitatis in extensione intrinseca, quâ partes substantiæ extenduntur in ordine ad se, ita ut una sit extra aliam. Hi vero; loquor cum ipsis Theologis Pontificiis; valde laborant, ut declarent, quomodo huiusmodi extensio fiat in hoc Sacramento indivisibilis in ordine ad locum, ita ut pars, quæ est extra partem, in ordine ad se, in ordine tamen ad locum non sit extra illam, sed cum illa & in illa. Arctius nodum constringunt ipsi Scholastici, novisque instantiis dissensum augent. Et quia tutius est ex specula prospicere, quomodo ipsi mutuis adversarii cadant mucronibus, quàm nostris eos lacessere armis, eorum etiam, etsi forte Scholastica potiùs, quàm Theologica, recitabimus verba. Huic indivisibili Quantitati duo obstare observant: Primum, quòd non tantùm extensio, & ratio illa partium intrinseca, sed etiam extrinseca, in ordine ad locum, videatur esse de Quantitatis Essentia; & consequenter impossibile videatur, quòd duo hæc in hoc Sacramento salvari possint, scilicet, quòd in eo sit quantitas Christi, & quòd sit in ordine ad locum indivisibilis. Antecedens Durandus probat, quòd, quemadmodum quantitas Essentialiter sit divisibilis; Ita Essentialiter habeat partes positione distinctas: In hoc enim non posse esse indivisibilem. Alterum, quod eos urget, est: Quantitatem, posse esse sub ubi indivisibili, repugnare: Dato enim, quod extensio extrinseca, in ordine ad locum, sit quoddam Essentiam Quantitatis consequens; ita tamen cum illa connexum, & conjunctum esse, ut neque supernaturaliter Quantitas illo possit privari. Id quod Gabriel & Ocham argumento probatum eunt evidentissimo: omnem nempe Quantitatem finitam necessariò sequi figuram; figuram autem sine ordine partium ad locum non dari. Quantitatem proinde finitam, ordine suarum partium ad locum, privari non posse. Idem valere de raritate & densitate. Hic nodus est. Quæ vero solutio? Albertus in eo rimam quærit, quòd corpus Christi, Quantitate sua, in Eucharistia esse existimet tanquam in signo, non tanquam loco. Hæc vero ratio difficultatem non tollit, inquit Pesantius. Henriq. Quodlib. 1. q. 5. ideo vult Quantitatem in hoc Sacramento esse inextensam, in ordine ad locum, quòd sub speciebus, ratione substantiæ, sit, ac proinde per modum Substantiæ tota in toto, & iterū tota in qualibet parte. Hanc n. rationem esse Substantiæ. Eandem Scotistæ ferè sequuntur sententiā, vel ideò, quod Patriarcham suum, Scotum, non aliter sensisse habeant persuasum. Sed negant alii, hanc Scoti fuisse opinionem; negant, eam tantam tollere difficultatem: Cùm illa non assignet, per quod Quantitas amittat divisibilitatem in ordine ad locum, quem naturaliter petit; sed tantùm ex ea, quod concomitanter ad Substantiam ponitur, sub speciebus, colligit, quòd ponatur indivisibiliter.
units.tr: IX. As for the quantity of Christ in this sacrament, the view of almost all the Scholastics, who follow Scotus in this matter, is that it is present by reason of the natural concomitance it has with its own substance, into which the conversion of bread and wine takes place first and directly by the force of the words. The exception is Durandus, who, to escape the difficulties arising from Christ's quantity in this sacrament, denies that the body of Christ, as it exists in the Eucharist, has its own quantity. Some call this erroneous, others near to error, and some rash and dangerous. When asked, however, how the quantity of Christ in the Eucharist is indivisible, they twist themselves in wondrous ways and, in untying the knot, tie it tighter. The Nominalists devised that the body of Christ under the species is quantified really but not formally, since it has everything that is really quantity, that is, all its substantial parts, but does not have that order to place. Why should this opinion please us? It does not even satisfy the Papists. "This opinion does not please," say the great Roman theologians, "because the formality of quantity is not placed in any order to another, but in the intrinsic intension of the parts." The other opinion, which is indeed the common one, places the formal reason of quantity in intrinsic extension, by which the parts of a substance are extended in order to one another, so that one is outside another. "But these men," I speak with the Papist theologians themselves, "labour hard to explain how such extension is made in this sacrament indivisible in relation to place, so that a part which is outside another part in relation to itself is not outside it in relation to place, but is with it and in it." The Scholastics themselves tighten the knot further and increase the disagreement with new objections. And since it is safer to watch from a lookout how the adversaries fall upon one another's swords than to provoke them with our own weapons, I will recite their words, though they are perhaps more Scholastic than theological. Two obstacles to this indivisible quantity are noted. First, extrinsic extension in relation to place, as well as that intrinsic extension of the parts, seems to belong to the essence of quantity; and consequently it seems impossible that both can be preserved in this sacrament, namely that Christ's quantity is in it and that it is indivisible in relation to place. Durandus proves the antecedent: just as quantity is essentially divisible, so it essentially has parts distinct in position, for in this it cannot be indivisible. The second objection that presses them is that quantity cannot be under an indivisible place. For granted that extrinsic extension in relation to place is something following from the essence of quantity, it is so connected and conjoined with quantity that quantity cannot be deprived of it even supernaturally. Gabriel and Ockham prove this by a most evident argument: every finite quantity necessarily follows a shape, and a shape is not found without an order of parts to place; therefore finite quantity cannot be deprived of the order of its parts to place. The same holds of rarity and density. This is the knot. What is the solution? Albert seeks a loophole in it, since he thinks the body of Christ is in the Eucharist by its quantity as in a sign, not as in a place. But this explanation, says Pesantius, does not remove the difficulty. Henry, Quodlibet 1, q. 5, therefore wants the quantity in this sacrament to be unextended in relation to place, because under the species it is, by reason of the substance, and so by the mode of substance is whole in the whole and again whole in every part; for this is the reason of substance. The Scotists largely follow this same opinion, either because they are persuaded that their patriarch Scotus thought no differently. Others deny that this was Scotus's opinion, and deny that it removes so great a difficulty, since it does not show by what means quantity loses its divisibility in relation to place, which it naturally seeks; it only infers from the fact that quantity is posited under the species concomitantly with the substance that it is posited indivisibly.

units.la: Nuper demum Conciliator accessit Pesantius, qui, prolixo discursu rem quidem confectam daturus, inepta petitione Principii peccat. De essentia Quantitatis esse, concedit, ut habeat partes radicaliter, & quasi in actu primo divisibiles, & sic pariter positione distinctas; non formaliter & in actu secundo; sed hoc consequens quid esse à Deo, separabile ab Essentia Quantitatis. Verùm, ut dixi, hoc est τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαβεῖν. Aliter de quantitate extensiva corporum, eorumque proprietatibus Essentialibus loqui sobriam Philosophiam, aliter de corpore Christi Scripturam, supra probavimus. Et quia simul & semel Missæ propemodum habentur innumeræ, adeóq; idem corpus, plurimis locis simul præsens esse, necesse est, aliud emergit dubium: An ergo corpus Christi a Deo in pluribus locis, modo extenso & reali, ponipossit? Thomistæ certe plerique statuunt, neque per miraculum fieri posse, utidem corpus situaliter, & extensum in duobus sit locis, & connaturaliter implicare contradictionem. Quando vero negatio πολυτοπίας praesentiam corporalem plane evertit, Scotus, ejusque discipuli Scotistæ, & Nominales, Deum corpus Christi, & quodcunque aliud in duobus locis extendere posse, affirmant. Et quoniam Entia sua sunt Accidentia, pergunt rimari: Utrum ergo corpori existenti, per Dei potentiam, in duobus locis, eadem prædicata utrobique conveniant? Utque suam satis exprimere videantur mentem, cardinem controversiæ in Qualitatibus, non necessario requisitis ad corpus, absolutis, intrinsecè inhærentibus in corpore, a quibus forma corporis necessario non dependet, actione productiva in illo positis, ostendunt: An scilicet, præexistente corpore in duobus locis, applicato vero agente in uno tantum, terminus actionis in utroque loco simul cum corpore esse debeat? Amplus, sed periculosissimus ingenii exercendi campus, in quo alius aliud latibulum quaerit. Et sunt quidem, qui volunt, suppositio miraculo constitutionis in duobus locis, ex natura rei, & de lege ordinaria, habere ipsum posse aliquot Accidentia, & Praedicata absoluta in uno loco, quae non habet in alio: Imo opus esse novo miraculo, ut Accidentia, quae corpus habeat in uno loco, eadem recipiat in alio. Ita, verbi gratia, si idem corpus, quod simul Romae est & Mediolani, Romae frigefiat, non sine novo miraculo idem frigus posse utrobique poni. Ita Ocham, Major, Richard. Ledes. Alii contra, ne de potentia quidem absoluta, corpori in pluribus existenti locis; Accidentia aliqua absoluta in uno loco posse tribui, quae non habeat in alio. Ita Thomas, Scotus, quos recentiores nonnulli sequuntur. Alii itaque duo affirmant: Et de potentia absoluta fieri posse, ut corpus in duobus locis constitutum in uno habeat Accidentia quaedam absoluta, in alio vero non habeat. Et de lege ordinaria, & ex natura rei, omnia Accidentia absoluta, quae hujusmodi corpus habet in uno loco, debere pariter habere in alio. Hic tamen iterum excipiunt actus vitales contrarios, plenos, perfectos; si intelligantur esse dependenter a virtute effectiva potentiae &c. Quid si vero (adeo hic tam quaestionum, quam dissensionum ferax ager est) idem corpus, postquam positum est in duobus locis, sive Sacramentaliter, sive extense; anne in uno manere, in altero vero potest corrumpi? In hoc quidem Theologi Romani conveniunt, quòd, de lege ordinaria, corpus in uno loco vere & subftantialiter corruptum, non possit in alio manere incorruptum; de potentia vero absoluta communiter receptum est, pariter impossibile esse, idem corrumpi & manere: quandoquidem corpus, si annihilatur, vel corrumpitur, revera in rerum natura esse desinat; adeóque consequenter, nullibi realiter manet. Plerisque tamen oppositum in hoc placet, de potentia absoluta idem corpus in uno loco integrum, in altero corrumpi, vel annihilari posse. Unde & Alensis asserit, corpus Christi in Eucharistia esse impassibile, etiam dato, quòd extra sit passibile & mortale. Creditne doctissimus Vir, vel Apostolos redivivos, aptos novæ hujus Scholæ fore Auditores? Sed nondum finis insolitarum, totiq; antiquitati (unde ne quidem talium apud Veteres mentio) ignotarum quæstionum. Pergunt igitur dubitare: An habitudo corporis Christi ad species, sit habitudo præsentiæ tantum, vel etiam alicujus unionis? Et Scotus quidem, Gabriel, Aliac. cæterique Nominales, inter corpus Christi, & species nihil videntur agnoscere, nisi habitudinem præsentiæ Sacramentalis, quæ ex sola Dei voluntate, & Christi institutione permaneat & duret, quoad durant & permanent spe-cies. cies. Hanc tamen sententiam prolixè refellit Sot.dist. 9. q.2. dist. 10. q. ar. 5. Rejiciunt eam cum veteres Scholastici, Thom. Palud. cum recentiores, Cajet. Sot. Ledes. qui præsentiam in corpore Christi, aliquam ponunt, habitudinem unionis ad species, ratione cujus simul cum illis esse debeat, & in quiete & in motu; illisque desinentibus, desinere, aliásque denominationes accipere. Rogati verò posteriores, qualis illa sit unio, hærent iterum & cespitant ubique. Cajetanus simpliciter dicit & docet, esse ineffabilem. Sotus & Claudius in hoc consistere volunt; quòd corpus Christi vices panis circa species, supplear, seclusa tamen inhærentia. Quomodo verò illud fiat, non explicant. Pesant. unionem inter corpus Christi & species, negat esse unionem formalem; per quam species formaliter substantiæ corporis uniantur (ita enim Accidentia non essent sine Subjecto) sed effectivam, consistentem in duplici actione, immediatione suppositi, scilicet corporis Christi, consevantis species; & specierum, per divinam elevationem producentium ubi Sacramentale; quod est fundamentum inseparabilis præsentiæ, quam species & corpus Christi mutuò habent.
units.tr: Lately Pesantius has also come forward as a mediator, but in his long discourse, which purports to finish off the matter, he commits the fallacy of begging the question. He concedes that it belongs to the essence of quantity to have parts that are divisible radicaliter, and as it were in actu primo, and so likewise distinct by position; but not formaliter and in actu secundo. That, he says, is a consequence that God can effect, separable from the essence of quantity. But, as I have said, this is to assume the very point at issue (τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ λαβεῖν). We have already shown above that sober philosophy speaks one way about the extended quantity of bodies and their essential properties, and Scripture speaks another way about the body of Christ. And because countless Masses are celebrated more or less at the same time, it necessarily follows that the same body is present in very many places at once. Here another question arises: Can God therefore make the body of Christ exist in several places at once, in an extended and real mode? Most Thomists certainly hold that it cannot be done even by miracle, that the same body should be located and extended in two places, and that this implies a contradiction in its very nature. But when the denial of πολυτοπία utterly overturns bodily presence, Scotus and his disciples, the Scotists, and the Nominalists affirm that God can extend the body of Christ, or any other body, into two places. And since their entities are accidents, they go on to inquire: Then, if a body exists in two places by the power of God, do the same predicates belong to it in both places? And so that they may seem to express their mind adequately, they show the crux of the controversy to lie in qualities that are not necessarily required for the body, that are absolute and inhere intrinsically in the body, on which the form of the body does not necessarily depend, and that are placed in it by a productive action: namely, if a body already exists in two places, but the active agent is applied in only one, ought the term of the action to exist in both places at once with the body? This is a broad but very dangerous field for exercising the intellect, in which each man seeks a different hiding place. Some indeed hold that, granted the miracle by which a body is constituted in two places, the body can by the nature of the thing and by the ordinary law have some absolute accidents and predicates in one place which it does not have in the other; indeed that a new miracle is needed for the accidents which the body has in one place to be received in the other as well. So, for example, if the same body which is at Rome and at Milan at once were to grow cold at Rome, the same cold could not be present in both places without a new miracle. So hold Ockham, Major, and Richard of Lediesma. Others, on the contrary, hold that even by God's absolute power a body existing in several places cannot be given some absolute accidents in one place which it does not have in another. So hold Thomas and Scotus, whom some more recent writers follow. Thus some affirm two things: that by God's absolute power it can happen that a body constituted in two places has certain absolute accidents in one and not in the other; and that by the ordinary law and the nature of the thing, all absolute accidents which such a body has in one place ought equally to be had in the other. Here, however, they again except contrary vital acts, which are full and perfect, if they are understood to depend on the effective power of the faculty, and so on. But what if (so fertile is this field of questions as well as of disputes) the same body, once it is placed in two places, whether sacramentally or by extension, can remain whole in one and be corrupted in the other? On this the Roman theologians agree, that by the ordinary law a body corrupted substantially and truly in one place cannot remain incorrupt in another; but by absolute power it is commonly held to be equally impossible for the same thing to be corrupted and to remain, since a body, if it is annihilated or corrupted, truly ceases to be in the nature of things and consequently remains nowhere really. Most, however, prefer the opposite view in this matter: that by absolute power the same body can remain whole in one place and be corrupted or annihilated in another. Hence Alensis also asserts that the body of Christ in the Eucharist is impassible, even granting that outside it is passible and mortal. Does that most learned man believe that the Apostles, if restored to life, would be fit hearers of this new school? But there is still no end to these unusual questions, unknown to all antiquity (among the ancients there is not even mention of such things). So they go on to doubt: Is the relation of the body of Christ to the species a relation of presence only, or also of some union? Scotus indeed, Gabriel, Ailly, and the other Nominalists seem to recognise between the body of Christ and the species nothing but the relation of sacramental presence, which remains and lasts from the sole will of God and Christ's institution, for as long as the species last and remain. Yet Soto refutes this opinion at length (dist. 9, q. 2; dist. 10, q. art. 5). The earlier Scholastics reject it, Thomas and Paludanus, and the more recent ones, Cajetan, Soto, and Ledesma, who posit some presence in the body of Christ, a relation of union to the species, by reason of which it must exist together with them both in rest and in motion, and cease when they cease and take on other denominations. But when asked later on what sort of union this is, they stick and stumble everywhere. Cajetan simply says and teaches that it is ineffable. Soto and Claudius want it to consist in this: that the body of Christ, apart from inherence, supplies the place of bread around the species. But how this happens they do not explain. Pesantius denies that the union between the body of Christ and the species is a formal union, by which the species are formally united to the substance of the body (for then the accidents would not be without a subject), but an effective union, consisting in a twofold action: the immediate sustaining of the supposit, namely the body of Christ, which sustains the species; and the producing by divine elevation of the species' sacramental ubi, which is the foundation of the inseparable presence that the species and the body of Christ have mutually.

units.la: X. Videte manus meas & pedes meos; Luc. 24. Ita de suo corpore Christus; sed, quod in Missa creatur à Sacerdote, corpus, Characterem hunc non habet. Ad quæstionem enim, an corpus existens indivsibiliter in ordine ad locum ;sit visibile? Pridem responsum fuit; Corpus Christi in Sacramento videri non posse,nec per naturam,nec per gloriam,nec per miraculum.Sententia etiam,quòd corpusChristi,sub ubiSacramentali, non sit visibile, placet Thoma, Scoto, Richardo, Paludano, Durando, Cajetano, Capreolo; cæterîsque, qui Nominalium sectæ non sunt adscripti. Hi enim aperte docent,quòd,nisi Deus ad meritum fidei (quasi fidei esset mereri,non verò meritum apprehendere) impediret concursum causarum; naturaliter,non tantùm à beatis,sed etiam à nobis corpusChristi in Eucharîstia videretur.Rationes tamen eorum Pesantius non probat. Quid si verò neque Pesantii exceptiones placerent Ochamo? Nihil ergo hic veri, nihil solidi. Sed an oculus Christi videt corpus suum in Eucharistia existens? Affirmativa Thoma tribuitur,qui oculum corporalem Christi videre se ipsum,sub Sacramento existentem, quidem concedit; non posse tamen ipsum essendi modum,quo est sub Sacramento, quod ad solum pertinet intellectum, videri. Hoc autem Thoma dictum,sicut communiter intelligitur; non esse verum,alii ingenuè fatentur.
units.tr: X. See my hands and my feet, Luke 24. So Christ said of his own body. But the body that is created in the Mass by the priest does not bear this mark. For to the question whether a body that exists indivisibly with respect to place is visible, an answer was given earlier: the body of Christ cannot be seen in the Sacrament, neither by nature, nor by glory, nor by miracle. The opinion also that the body of Christ, under sacramental ubi, is not visible pleases Thomas, Scotus, Richard, Paludanus, Durandus, Cajetan, Capreolus, and the others who are not enrolled in the Nominalist sect. For these openly teach that, unless God by withholding the concurrence of causes impeded it on account of the merit of faith (as if faith merited, and did not rather apprehend merit), the body of Christ in the Eucharist would naturally be seen not only by the blessed but also by us. Yet Pesantius does not prove their reasons. But what if Pesantius's exceptions did not please Ockham either? So there is nothing true here, nothing solid. But does the eye of Christ see his own body existing in the Eucharist? Thomas is credited with the affirmative answer: he concedes that Christ's bodily eye sees himself existing under the Sacrament, but that the mode of his being under the Sacrament, which pertains to the intellect alone, cannot be seen. But that this saying of Thomas, as it is commonly understood, is not true, others openly confess.

units.la: XI. Illud cumprimis omnia Naturæ principia evertit: Sola,in Eucharistia,superesse Acciden- tia, destructo Subjecto.
units.tr: XI. Above all, it overturns all the principles of nature: in the Eucharist only the accidents remain once the substance has been destroyed.

units.la: Et quia vident Doctores Scholastici, elementa illa nutrire, saturare, in cinerem redigi, generare vermes &c. anxiè quaerunt: Quod, & undesit Subjectum generationis illius? Ubi incertitudine iterum nihil certius. Thomam, nonnulli asserunt subjectum in hujusmodi generatione quantitatem per se subsistentem, statuisse. Ita etiam Richard Henrici Quidam, sicut in omni alia generatione, ita etiam in hac materia, per quam ex Eucharistia fit vermis, vel ignis, certum subjectum & necessarium esse existimant. Unde verò illa provenit? Hic vel quinque distinctas reperias classium sententias. Prima credit, materiam ex ambiente sumi. Hanc verò sententiam ipse confutat Thomas. Secunda materiam ex corpore Christi desumit. Quibus Alensis resistit, Bonaventura, hoc potissimum argumento, quòd ita corpus Christi esset corruptibile. Tertia tradit, in corruptione specierum redire totam substantiam panis & vini, & sic ex substantia panis & vini redeunte, generari cineres. Sed et his dicam scribit Thomas, quòd inde sequeretur, corpus Christi desinere. Quarta vult, redire solam materiam, & quidem, ut nonnulli docent, partim supernaturaliter creatam à Deo (sed nec in his acquiescit Thomas, quòd non sit necesse miracula multiplicari: Quamvis alii hunc metum frustra obtendi velint) partim verò naturaliter, quod tamen ipsum eodem modo non explicant. Quinta, Thoma, asserit
units.tr: And because the Scholastic Doctors see that those elements nourish and satisfy, are reduced to ash, and generate worms, etc., they anxiously ask: What, and where, is the subject of that generation? Here, from uncertainty, nothing is more certain. Some assert that Thomas posited as the subject of this kind of generation a quantity subsisting in itself. So too Richard Henrici Quidam thinks that, as in every other generation, so in this matter, from which a worm or fire arises out of the Eucharist, there is a certain and necessary subject. Whence then does it come? Here you may find five distinct opinions of the schools. The first believes that the matter is taken from the surroundings. Thomas himself refutes this opinion. The second draws the matter from the body of Christ. Alensis opposes this, and Bonaventura chiefly on the argument that the body of Christ would thus be corruptible. The third teaches that in the corruption of the species the whole substance of bread and wine returns, and that from the returning substance of bread and wine the ashes are generated. But Thomas writes against this too, that from it would follow the ceasing of the body of Christ. The fourth holds that only matter returns, and indeed, as some teach, partly created supernaturally by God (yet Thomas does not rest even in these, since it is not necessary for miracles to be multiplied; although others wish this fear to be put forward in vain), and partly naturally, which, however, they do not explain in the same way. The fifth, Thomas, asserts
