units.la: N in hac generatione, ex conversione, quæ fit à Deo, vi conditionis, in eodem instanti temporis, quo fit naturaliter generatio, venire, sed in priori naturæ & rationis. Quam sententiam recentiores etiam recipiunt, fuíeque eam Pesantius explicat.
units.tr: that in this generation, from the conversion effected by God by virtue of the condition, the matter comes in the same instant of time in which the natural generation takes place, but in priority of nature and of reason. Recent writers also accept this opinion, and Pesantius explains it.

units.la: XII. Atque hæc quidem de verbis institutionis, earúmque ficta virtute: ex actionibus Sacramentalibus fractio non postrema est. Fractione enim panis (ita vocat Spiritus Sanctus) non fractionem Accidentium) Synecdochice ipsa Domini Cœna exprimitur. Sed ignorat Ecclesia Romana veterem Apostolicum stylum. Rogati enim, quid in Sacramento frangatur? Hæsitant iterum. Alii, teste sententiarum Magistro, ipsam corporis Christi substantiam frangi dixerunt. Sed negat Lombardus, negant recentiores, propterea, quòd Christi corpus fractionis jam, omnisque passionis sit expers. Alii proinde non veram, sed apparentem tantum & phantasticam somniant fractionem: quod eadem rejicitur, qua affertur, facilitate. Ita enim perpetuam illusionem in abstrusissima mysteria inferremus. Accidentia igitur tandem frangi volunt: quod absurdissimum est. Mathematicam ei quodammodo tribuunt quantitatem, à materia separatam, quæ divisa, vi tantum mentis, & intellectus fit facultate: cum tamen constet, symbolum fractum ita dividi, ut partes quàm mani-fefestissimè videantur separatæ. Unde Pesantius: Illud quidem, quod manducatur in propria specie, ipsum & frangitur & masticatur in sua specie. Corpus autem Christi non manducatur in sua specie; sed in specie Sacramentali, nec etiam aliter frangitur, nisi secundum speciem Sacramentalem.
units.tr: XII. These things are said concerning the words of institution and their supposed power; among the sacramental actions the breaking is not the least. For by the breaking of bread (so the Holy Spirit calls it), the Lord's Supper itself is expressed by synecdoche, not the breaking of the accidents. But the Roman Church is ignorant of the ancient apostolic usage. For when asked what is broken in the sacrament, they hesitate again. Others, as the Master of the Sentences attests, have said that the very substance of Christ's body is broken. But Lombardus denies it, and recent writers deny it, because the body of Christ is now free of all breaking and all suffering. Others therefore dream of a breaking that is not real but only apparent and fantastic; this is rejected with the same ease with which it is advanced, for in that way we would introduce perpetual illusion into the most abstruse mysteries. So at last they want the accidents to be broken, which is most absurd. They attribute to them a kind of mathematical quantity, separated from matter, which is divided only by the power of the mind and the understanding; yet it is plain that the broken element is divided so that its parts are seen to be separated most manifestly. Hence Pesantius: That which is eaten in its own species is both broken and chewed in its own species. But the body of Christ is not eaten in its own species, but in the sacramental species, nor is it broken in any other way than according to the sacramental species.

units.la: XIII. Causam finalem Eucharistiæ & ipse Servator ponit, ut fiat sacra hæc actio, εἰς ἀνάμνησιν, in recordationem passionis Dominicæ, & Paulus exponit, quando communionem corporis Christi tam naturalis, quàm mystici appellat.
units.tr: XIII. The Saviour himself states the final cause of the Eucharist, that this sacred action be done in remembrance [εἰς ἀνάμνησιν] of the Lord's passion, and Paul sets it out when he calls it the communion of the body of Christ, both natural and mystical.

units.la: Quæ quidem plana omnia sunt & perspicua, tyronibus etiam & Catechumenis perceptu facilia. Nulla hic certamina, nullæ collisiones, nulli dissensus. Sed postquam Ecclesia Romana ex hoc Sacrificii Christi in cruce semel peracti memoraculo, aliud iterum sacrificium reale & expiatorium extruxisset, in quo tamen nulla nec materia ejus, nec forma apparet, nova disputandi materia nata, & ea quidem, quæ etiamnum Scholas Pontificias acerrimè exercet.
units.tr: All these things are indeed plain and clear, easy to grasp even for novices and catechumens. Here there are no contests, no collisions, no disagreements. But after the Roman Church, from this memorial of Christ's sacrifice once offered on the cross, had built another, real and expiatory, sacrifice, in which however neither its matter nor its form appears, a new matter for dispute arose, and indeed one that still keeps the Papist schools in fierce exercise.

units.la: Ad quæstionem enim: Quid in Missa offeratur? Respondet Casalius, duplex in Missa esse sacrificium, unum panis & vini; alterum corporis & sanguinis Domini. Bellarminus duo dicit, primo, panem & vinum verè & proprie sacrificari: negat deinde, panem & corpus Domini, vinum & sanguinem ejus, duo esse sacrificia, sed unum integrum. Pesantius vero non credit, concedendum esse, quod panis & vini substantia sacrificetur. Dato enim, inquit, quod panis & vinum fiat sacrificium, vix aut ne vix quidem salvari poterit, quod non sint plura Ecclesiae sacrificia. Mavult igitur, panem esse remotam materiam unici sacrificii, quod est in Ecclesia, ejúsque substantiam desinere, dum consecratur, & fieri proximam atque optimam materiam sacrificii; id vero, quod in Missa consecratur, offertur, & sumitur, adeóque sacrificatur, esse Eucharistiam, id est, speciesque, cum corpore & sanguine Christi. Ad quaestionem, in qua parte Missae sit Essentialis ratio sacrificii? Quidam respondent: Sacrificium Missae essentialiter consistere in sola actione consecrationis: quam sententiam Thomas tribuunt. Alii statuunt, oblationem esse totam sacrificii essentiam; propterea, quod offerre & sacrificare Scripturae & Patribus sint aequipollentia. Alii tamen, solam consumtionem essentialiter facere sacrificium, dum fit a Sacerdote, ex officio Sacerdotii, malunt. Sed excipiunt iterum alii, consecrationem illam non habere rationem sacrificii, nisi lata significatione. Sotus, Bellarminus, Henriquez, recentiores plerique, asserunt, Missae sacrificium essentialiter tribus actionibus contineri, consecratione, oblatione & consumtione, ita ut his sacrificium non modo integretur; sed etiam constituatur. De valore denique hujus sacrificii non magis inter ipsos convenit. Alii enim docent, Missam esse simpliciter valoris infiniti, ita ut oblatio pro pluribus, aeque illis prosit, ac si pro singulis separatim offerretur. Sed ipse, hanc sententiam, Thomas confutavit. Alii proinde, recentiores praesertim, dicunt, Missae valorem, secundum se sumtum, esse infinitum; sumtum vero, ut applicatur ex intentione, & devotione offerentium, esse finitum. Sed neque hanc sententiam probant alii, quod non videantur intelligere rationem & Essentiam sacrificii, cum non distinguant sacrificium a re, quae sacrificatur. Alii proinde tradunt, valorem Missae simpliciter esse finitum, ita ut applicatus plurimis minuatur pro rata; quae sententia, ante Cajetanum, fuit communiter recepta. Atque horum mentem Thomas ita exprimit: Quamvis virtus Christi, quae continetur sub Eucharistia, Sacramento sit infinita, tamen determinatur et effectus, ad quem illud Sacramentum ordinatur: Unde non oportet, quod per unum sacrificium altaris tota poena eorum, qui sunt in purgatorio, expietur, sicut etiam nec per unum sacrificium, quod homo offert, liberatur a tota satisfactione, debita pro peccatis: unde etiam quandoque plures Missae in satisfactionem unius peccati injunguntur; in 4. d. 45. q. 2 ar. 4. q. ult. Sed alia hinc difficultas. Quae causa sint hujus hujus Christi voluntatis ? Et fatetur quidem Pesantius, investigationem ejus esse difficillimam. Cum enim Christus idem, qui se obtulit in cruce per sacrificium cruentum, pariter se offert in altari per sacrificium incruentum, parem videtur dare debere utrique satisfactionis valorem, & cum eadem sit victima, idemque Sacerdos, non apparere rationem, quare infinitus valor oblationis Christi ad finitam quantitatem in Missa restringatur. Plerorumque ratio ex parte Hostiae est defumta. Cum enim in sacrificio cruento, in Dei honorem, ipsum esse Naturale Christi in forma humana destructum sit: In sacrificio vero Missae tantum esse Sacramentale destruatur; nobilius utique, magisque pretiosum videri esse Christi naturale, quam Sacramentale. Ita plerique. Sed nihil valet haec ratio, inquit gravis Ecclesiae Romanae Theologus, quia omnino idem est esse existentia creata, & esse subsistentia increata in Christo, sub speciebus Eucharistiae posito. Altera ergo magis placet ratio, quae a priori, ex Natura ipsius sacrificii impetratorii & satisfactorii desumitur, ubi non rei tantum oblatae, sed & personae offerentis ratio habetur. Etsi ergo Sacerdos persona sit digna, & Minister Christi, sed finitae dignitatis: Is autem, cui sit oblatio, sit Deus infinitus, respectu tamen infinitatis hujus omnem oblationem creaturae potius minui, quam valore accipere. At ne haec quidem dem sententia ab exceptione est libera. Id quod monere, quàm persequi jam malumus.
units.tr: For to the question What is offered in the Mass? Casalius answers that there are two sacrifices in the Mass: one of bread and wine, the other of the body and blood of the Lord. Bellarminus says there are two things: first, that bread and wine are truly and properly sacrificed; he denies then that the bread and the body of the Lord, the wine and his blood, are two sacrifices, but one whole sacrifice. Pesantius, however, does not believe that it must be conceded that the substance of bread and wine is sacrificed. For granting, he says, that bread and wine become a sacrifice, it can scarcely, or not even scarcely, be preserved that they are not several sacrifices of the Church. He prefers, therefore, that the bread be the remote matter of the one sacrifice which is in the Church, and that its substance cease while it is consecrated, and become the proximate and best matter of the sacrifice; and that what is consecrated in the Mass, offered, and taken, and so sacrificed, is the Eucharist, that is, the species together with the body and blood of Christ. On the question in which part of the Mass lies the essential nature of the sacrifice? some answer: the sacrifice of the Mass consists essentially in the sole action of consecration, an opinion they attribute to Thomas. Others hold that the oblation is the whole essence of the sacrifice, because to offer and to sacrifice are equivalent in Scripture and the Fathers. Others, however, prefer that the consumption alone makes the sacrifice essentially, when it is done by the priest in virtue of the priestly office. But others again object that that consecration has the character of a sacrifice only in a broad sense. Soto, Bellarminus, Henriquez, and most recent writers, assert that the sacrifice of the Mass is essentially contained in three actions, consecration, oblation and consumption, so that by these the sacrifice is not only completed but also constituted. Finally, about the value of this sacrifice they do not agree any more among themselves. Some teach that the Mass is simply of infinite value, so that an oblation for many profits them just as much as if it were offered separately for each. But Thomas himself refuted this opinion. Others, therefore, especially recent writers, say that the value of the Mass, taken in itself, is infinite; but taken as it is applied by the intention and devotion of those offering, it is finite. Others do not approve this opinion either, because they do not seem to understand the nature and essence of a sacrifice, since they do not distinguish the sacrifice from the thing that is sacrificed. Others, therefore, hold that the value of the Mass is simply finite, so that when applied to many it is diminished in proportion; this opinion was commonly received before Cajetanus. Thomas expresses the mind of these men thus: Although the power of Christ, which is contained under the Eucharist, is infinite as a sacrament, yet it is determined to the effect to which that sacrament is ordained. Hence it is not necessary that by one sacrifice of the altar the whole punishment of those who are in purgatory be expiated, just as neither by one sacrifice which a man offers is he freed from the whole satisfaction owed for sins; hence also sometimes several Masses are enjoined in satisfaction for one sin; in 4 d. 45 q. 2 a. 4 q. ult. But there is another difficulty here: What are the causes of this will of Christ? And Pesantius indeed confesses that the investigation of it is most difficult. For since Christ himself, who offered himself on the cross by a bloody sacrifice, likewise offers himself on the altar by an unbloody sacrifice, he seems to have to give equal value of satisfaction to each; and since the victim is the same and the priest the same, no reason appears why the infinite value of Christ's oblation should be restricted to a finite quantity in the Mass. The reason of most men is drawn from the side of the victim: since in the bloody sacrifice, for the honour of God, Christ's natural being in human form was destroyed; but in the sacrifice of the Mass only his sacramental being is destroyed; it seems plainly more noble and more precious that Christ's natural being should be given than his sacramental being. Thus most men. But this reason is worth nothing, says a grave theologian of the Roman Church, because the created existence and the uncreated subsistence in Christ, placed under the species of the Eucharist, are altogether the same. Another reason, therefore, pleases more, which is drawn a priori from the nature of an impetratory and satisfactory sacrifice, where account is taken not only of the thing offered but also of the person offering. Although, then, the priest is a worthy person and a minister of Christ, yet of finite dignity; but he to whom the oblation is made is the infinite God, and in respect of this infinity every oblation of a creature is rather diminished than takes on value. But not even this opinion is free of objection. Which we would rather point out than pursue now.

units.la: XIV. Pergamus igitur ad Subjectum tum remotum, tum proximum. Et de illo etiam variæ in Scholis Theologorum Pontificiorum sunt quæstiones: Utrum solius hominis sit hoc Sacramentum spiritualiter sumere? Utrum solus homo justus possit Christum Sacramentaliter manducare? Utrum peccator sumens corpus Christi Sacramentaliter, peccet? &c. quas vel indicasse sufficiat: de hoc verò, ventre scilicet & stomacho, præstaret religiose silere, quàm profanè quærere. Quærere tamen solet Schola Pontificia: Utrum corpus Christi etiam trajiciatur in ventrem bestiæ? Et respondet Alensis: Corpus Christi contineri in illis speciebus inseparabiliter, quamdiu salva est forma panis, & ubicunque ponuntur species, sive in loco mundo, sive immundo, sive in ventre muris, ibi esse corpus Christi. Atque, si canis vel porcus deglutiat hostiam consecratam integram, corpus Domini una cum specie trajici in ventrem canis & porci. P. 4. q. 11. memb. 2. art. 2. ff. 1. Sed & Thomas respondet, manere Christum sub speciebus Sacramentalibus, donec talis & tanta mutatio contingat speciebus, per quam corrupta fuisset, & esse sub eis desiisset substantia panis & vini, si non facta esset Transubstantiatio:
units.tr: XIV. Let us go on, then, to the subject, both remote and proximate. On this too the schools of the Papist theologians raise various questions: Is it for the man alone to receive this sacrament spiritually? Can only a righteous man eat Christ sacramentally? Does a sinner who receives the body of Christ sacramentally sin? etc. It is enough merely to indicate these. As for the question of the belly and the stomach, it would be better to keep a reverent silence than to inquire into it irreverently. Yet the Papist school is accustomed to ask: Is the body of Christ also carried into the belly of a beast? And Alensis answers: the body of Christ is contained inseparably in those species as long as the form of bread remains, and wherever the species are placed, whether in a clean or an unclean place, or in the belly of a mouse, there the body of Christ is. And if a dog or a pig swallows a consecrated host whole, the body of the Lord, together with the species, is carried into the belly of the dog or pig. Part 4, question 11, member 2, article 2, folio 1. But Thomas also answers that Christ remains under the sacramental species until such a great change comes upon the species that, had it not been for the transubstantiation, they would have been corrupted and the substance of bread and wine would have ceased to be under them. 3 P., question 77, article 4.

units.la: 3. P.q. 77. ar. 4. Eadem sententia est Gabrielis in 4. sentent. dist. 12. q. 1. art. 3. Bonaventura quidem etiam concedit, non solum specierum; sed et corporis Christi veri, quod ibi est, quamdiu est species panis, in ventrem trajectionem; in 4. Sentent. d. 12. Par. 1. ar. 3. q. 1. eam tamen opinionem rejiciendam putat, ut intolerabilem piis auribus, quae non sustinent audire, quod in ventre muris & in cloaca sit corpus Christi. Alteram tamen, ceu communiorem, praevaluisse, supra jam a nobis indicatum est. De mora corporis Christi sub speciebus Sacramentalibus quaeras? Respondet Hugo de S. Victore, tamdiu Christum communicanti esse corporaliter praesentem, quamdiu manducantis sensus corporaliter afficitur, non ulterius: Specul. Eccles. c. 7. Thomas & Gabriel descendere in stomachum, ibique manere, donec eo usque alterentur species, ut non subsisteret amplius sub illis natura panis & vini, non facta Transubstantiatione. Alii dicunt, Christum descendere in ventrem hominis, ibi{*}e morari, quousque refectionis operatio compleatur. Alii Christum ad ventrem pervenire, quousque incipiant species consumi, & amplius non morari. His quatuor opinionibus commemoratis Bonaventura subjicit, difficile esse judicare, quid in tanta diversitate tenendum sit: In 4. Sent. d. 13. art. 2. q. 2. Glossa autem, in Canon. Tribus gradibus &c. Dist. 2. de Consecratione, negat iplas speciesSacramentales tales in stomachum descendere; addita tamen mox correctione, descendere in stomachum. De Christi autem corpore idé Glossa illa negat: Certum est, inquit, quod species, quàm cito dentibus teruntur, tam cito in cœlum rapitur corpus Christi. Rossensis autem: Sin, inquit, eandem carnem, quæ pro nobis in cruce fuerat immolata, taneges in os nostrum sumi realiter, & edi, atque transglutiri, sicut est in Sacramento citra transformationem in corpus nostrum, perperam cogitas & sentis, & plane contra ipsius Christi verba, qui dixit; Accipite & edite, hoc est corpus meum; lib. 3. cont. Oecolamp. c. 13.
units.tr: The same view is held by Gabriel, in book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 12, question 1, article 3. Bonaventure indeed also concedes that not only the species but also the true body of Christ, which is there as long as the species of bread remain, is carried into the belly; in book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 12, part 1, article 3, question 1. Yet he thinks this opinion should be rejected, as intolerable to pious ears, which cannot bear to hear that the body of Christ should be in the belly of a mouse or in a sewer. The other opinion, however, as the more common one, has prevailed, as we have already indicated above. Would you ask about how long the body of Christ remains under the sacramental species? Hugh of St. Victor answers that Christ is bodily present to the communicant only as long as the sense of the one eating is bodily affected, and no longer: Speculum Ecclesiae, chapter 7. Thomas and Gabriel hold that he descends into the stomach and remains there until the species are so altered that the nature of bread and wine no longer subsists under them, without transubstantiation having taken place. Others say that Christ descends into the belly of the man and remains there until the work of nourishment is completed. Others say that Christ comes as far as the belly and remains only until the species begin to be consumed, and then does not stay. Having recalled these four opinions, Bonaventure adds that it is hard to judge what is to be held amid such great diversity: in book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 13, article 2, question 2. The Gloss, however, on the canon Tribus gradibus etc., distinction 2, On Consecration, denies that the sacramental species themselves descend into the stomach; yet it immediately adds a correction: they descend into the stomach. About the body of Christ, the same Gloss denies it: It is certain, it says, that as soon as the species are ground by the teeth, the body of Christ is at once caught up into heaven. Rossensis, however, says: But if, he says, you think and feel that the same flesh which was sacrificed for us on the cross is really taken into our mouth, and eaten, and swallowed down, just as it is in the sacrament without being transformed into our body, you think and feel wrongly, and plainly against the very words of Christ, who said: Take, eat; this is my body; book 3 against Oecolampadius, chapter 13.

units.la: XII. Hæc cine est harmonia & consensus in doctrina, quam inter notas Ecclesiæ Catholicæ referunt Scriptores Pontificii? Heic, heic vere, si uspiam alibi, viis erroribus implicitis, implicita succurrat fides necesse est.
units.tr: XII. Is this the harmony and agreement in doctrine which the Papist writers present as one of the marks of the Catholic Church? Here, here truly, if anywhere else, faith must be implicit, entangled in its own errors and implicit in them.

units.la: Non disseram prolixius de momento capitis, in quo controvertitur: Certum est, esse ex primariis Ecclesiæ Romanæ dogmatibus, pro quo hactenus Scholastici acerrimè dimicârunt: Esse Articulum, meo judicio, stantis & cadentis Papatus. Unde etiam factum, ut superiori seculo in hoc maximè retinendo & defendendo Transsubstantiationis dogmate Doctores Pontificii aprârint lacerros. Nihil dicam, de gradibus dissensus, ejus vehementia, animorumque exacerbatione, quæ tanta sæpe est, ut apertam hæreseos notam alterutra contradicentium pars evitare non possit. Illud vero expendere velim Virum doctissimum, an vel Christus, vel Apostoli salutarem nobis Sacramentorum usum & administrationem tot obscuris, ambiguis & sinuosis anfractibus proposuerint? An in Ecclesia primitiva vel umbra umbratilis hujus disputationis de Accidentibus (elementa enim symbola, signa &c. illa vocat; Accidentium certe nunquam & nufpiam, Tridentino sensu meminit) occurrat? An haec ratio fit mysteriorum, ut quae credere simpliciter debemus & religiose mirari; adeo curiose rimari vel conveniat, vel expediat? Si mysterium est, Coena Domini, ut revera μυστήριον ἀπορρήτον, teste Epiphanio, mysterium ineffabile est, cur omnes, minutiffimae etiam ejus circumftantiae, abstrusissimi illius modi, in Scholis Pontificiis excutiuntur, ventilantur, ad digitos numerantur? Mysteria non sunt, quae non latent; nec quod humano aflequi licet ratiocinio, divinorum annumerari debet mysteriorum catalogo. Id certe, cujus τὸ ὄν pariter atque ποιον, cujus substantiam & circumstantiam ex causis suis cognoscimus, inter mysteria referri nec poteft, nec debet. Sed placuit divinae providentiae, ut illi, qui expressa forma faniorum sermonum retinere noluerunt, incerti & vagabundi viis suis irent; cogitationibusque suis confusi & perplexi, exemplum aliis praeberent, quam fit pepericulosum à simplicitate Apostolica recedere adeóque plus sapere, quàm oportet. An igitur dogma novum, adeò incertum, variè in Scholis traditum, & nec dum ad certæ & constantis Methodi leges revocatum, pro fundamentali fidei articulo possit obtrudi, ipse V.d.judicet?
units.tr: I shall not go on at length about the weight of the question in dispute. It is certain that this is one of the chief dogmas of the Roman Church, and the Schoolmen have fought most fiercely for it until now. In my judgement it is the article on which the Papacy stands or falls. For this reason, in the last century the Papist doctors tore themselves to pieces in retaining and defending chiefly the dogma of transubstantiation. I say nothing of the degrees of disagreement, of its vehemence and the exasperation of minds, which is often so great that either side of the contradiction cannot avoid the plain mark of heresy. But I would like the most learned gentleman to consider this: did Christ or the Apostles set forth the saving use and administration of the sacraments in so many obscure, ambiguous and tortuous windings? Does even the shadow of this shadowy dispute about accidents appear in the primitive Church? (They call the sacramental things elements, symbols, signs and so on; they certainly never, and nowhere, mention accidents in the Tridentine sense.) Or is it fitting or expedient to pry so curiously into the nature of mysteries, which we ought simply to believe and religiously wonder at? If the Lord's Supper is a mystery, indeed an unspeakable mystery [μυστήριον ἀπορρήτον], as Epiphanius witnesses, a mystery ineffable, why are all its most minute circumstances, of that most abstruse kind, examined, debated and counted off on the fingers in the Papist schools? Things that are not hidden are not mysteries, and what human reasoning can grasp ought not to be numbered in the catalogue of divine mysteries. That thing certainly, whose being [τὸ ὄν] and quality [ποιον] alike, whose substance and circumstance we know from their causes, can be referred neither to mysteries nor should be. But it has pleased divine providence that those who would not keep to the fixed form of sound words should go their own uncertain and wandering ways; confused and perplexed in their own thoughts, they provide an example to others of how dangerous it is to depart from apostolic simplicity and so to be wiser than one should be. Let your judgement decide: can a new dogma, so uncertain, variously handed down in the schools, and not yet brought back to the laws of a fixed and constant method, be thrust upon us as a fundamental article of faith?

units.la: XIII. Addimus, coronidis loco, Idololatriæ periculum, quod ex Intentione, àSchola Pontificia præcipè in celebratione Sacramentorum requisita, emergit præsentissimum. Ubi tamen iterum monemus, ne hanc quidem de Intentione doctrinam in Scholis Pontificiis eadem Methodo tradi. Primò enim Thomas ait requiri, ut Minister intendat facere, quod facit Christus & Ecclesia, 3.P. q. 64. ar. 8. Bonaventura asserit, necessariam esse Ministri intentionem, quà intendit saltem facere, quod Ecclesia facit, in 4. Sent. d. 6. P. 1 1. ar. 2. q. 1. Ambrosius Catharinus Episcopus Minoriensis, in Concilio Tridentino palam asseruit, Deum constituisse, ut illud sit verum Sacramentum, quod ritu ab ipso instituto celebratur, etiamsi Minister aliam habeat intentionem internam: Quam suam sententiam ita confirmat, ut contrariam refutet. Ipsum verò Concilium anathema denunciat dicenti: In Ministris Ecclesiæ, dum Sacramenta conficiunt, & conferunt, non requiri intentionem saltem faciendi, quod facit Ecclesia, sess. 7. can. 11. Et quanquam virulentam in sententiam
units.tr: XIII. As a crowning point, we add the danger of idolatry, which arises most acutely from the intention, which the Papist School requires especially in the celebration of the sacraments. Here, however, we again warn that this doctrine of intention is not taught in the Papist Schools by a uniform method either. For first, Thomas says that it is required that the minister intend to do what Christ and the Church do, 3 P. q. 64, art. 8. Bonaventura asserts that the minister's intention is necessary, by which he intends at least to do what the Church does, in 4 Sent. d. 6, P. 1, art. 2, q. 1. Ambrosius Catharinus, Bishop of Minori, openly asserted at the Council of Trent that God has so ordained that that is the true sacrament which is celebrated with the rite instituted by himself, even if the minister has another internal intention, and he confirms this opinion of his in such a way that he refutes the contrary. But the Council itself pronounces anathema on anyone who says that in the ministers of the Church, while they confect and confer the sacraments, an intention at least of doing what the Church does is not required, sess. 7, can. 11. And although against this virulent opinion

units.la: Cathárini Bellarminus strinxerit censuram, lib. 1. de Sacram. cap. 27. expressa tamen illa nititur authoritate Innocentii IV. apud Angel. de Clavaf. voce Baptismus d. 5. Variant deinde Doctores in intentionis extensione. Thomas sufficit intentio Ecclesiae, si nihil contrarium ex parte Ministri, vel recipientis, exterius exprimatur. Scotus vero negare videtur, Sacramenti veritatem, si interveniat in Ministro motus voluntatis contrarius, licet exterius non expressus. Caetera sicco jam pede transfibimus. Vel breviter dicta, abunde satis probant, decumanam certe Ecclesiae Romanae esse miseriam, quae tot nexatur scrupulis, tot urgetur difficultatibus; dum quotidie prosternere se, in genua procidere, cultum adorationis deferre illi jubetur, de quo nihil certi (est enim cor hominis fraudulentum supra omnia, & morbiferum, & quis cognoscat ipsum, ut Jeremias loquitur, cap. 17. vers. 9.) polliceri sibi possint. Aut, unde communicaturus exploratum habebit, Sacerdotem confecturum (Scholae Pontificiae terminum retineo) intentione accedere, id faciendi, quod facit Ecclesia Romana? Si eam non affert, ut non semper afferre illum extra controversiam est, jam id, quod adoratur, Idolum est, & creatura, ex propria adversariorum hypothesi. Hinc Bonaventura: In quodam Decretali dicitur, quod plus peccat malus Sacerdos, qui non conficit, & simulat se conconficere, quam ille, qui conficit: pro eo, quod facit populum Idololatrare: In 3. sententt. d. 19. art. 1. q. 6. Ergo ne adeo malitiosos & perversos Ecclesia Romana alat Sacerdotes, qui, cum impiis & dissolutis vivant moribus, sceleribus manifestissimis cooperti, scientes etiam & destinato animo ad altare accedant, studio imperitam plebem Idololatriae nexibus implicandi? Ita est; Contigisse hoc, superiorum seculorum fides dubitare nos non finit. Quod autem contigit semel, id ipsum, maximo cum animarum discrimine, evenire potest saepius. Memorabile, in Historia suorum temporum, exemplum refert Johannes Vitoduranus, Monachus Franciscanus, Sacrificuli cujusdam. Quidam, inquit, Sacerdos ut percepi viva voce, fide digna relationis cujusdam Baronis, Parochianus (utinam fuisset inofficians!) quandam Parochialem Ecclesiam territorii Diœcesis Constantiensis, in Pago Turgaviensi, lubricam valde duxit vitam, in tantum, quod, licet tabernarius, lusor, corruptor, perjurus, usurarius, ebrius & fornicarius frequenter existeret, non minus tamen intrepide quotidie Missam celebravit: Quod dum sibi objiceretur, & duris & invectivis verbis redargueretur, & diceretur sibi, qua fronte toties praesumeret celebrare, cum sciret, se absque contritione tam multis enormibus vitiis continue implicatum, respondit: Quod nunquam confi-
units.tr: Bellarmine has briefly touched on the censure of Catharinus (bk. 1 on the Sacraments, ch. 27), yet that opinion rests on the express authority of Innocent IV, as cited in Angelus de Clavasio, s.v. Baptism, d. 5. The Doctors then differ on how far the intention extends. Thomas holds that the intention of the Church suffices, provided nothing contrary is expressed externally on the part of the minister or the recipient. Scotus, however, seems to deny the truth of the sacrament if a contrary movement of the will is present in the minister, even though it is not expressed externally. The rest we shall cross with dry feet. Even these brief remarks amply prove that the lot of the Roman Church is surely a wretched one, beset by so many scruples and pressed by so many difficulties. Every day its people are ordered to prostrate themselves, fall on their knees, and offer the worship of adoration to that about which they can promise themselves nothing certain (for the heart of man is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked, and who can know it, as Jeremiah says, ch. 17, v. 9). Or, from whom will the one who is about to communicate know for certain that the priest, whom the Papists' schools call the one who "confects" (I keep their term), approaches with the intention of doing what the Roman Church does? If he does not bring that intention (and it is not beyond controversy that he always brings it), then what is adored is an idol and a creature, by the adversaries' own hypothesis. Hence Bonaventure: "In a certain Decretal it is said that a bad priest who does not consecrate, but pretends to consecrate, sins more than one who does consecrate, because he causes the people to commit idolatry" (In 3 Sent., d. 19, art. 1, q. 6). Is the Roman Church, then, to nourish priests so malicious and perverse, who live with impious and dissolute morals, covered in the most manifest crimes, and who knowingly and with settled purpose approach the altar, so that they may eagerly entangle the untaught common people in the snares of idolatry? So it is. The faith of earlier centuries does not let us doubt that this has happened. But what has happened once can happen again, and more often, with the greatest peril to souls. John of Winterthur, a Franciscan monk, relates a memorable example from the history of his own times, concerning a certain little priest. "A certain priest, he says, as I heard by word of mouth from the trustworthy account of a certain baron, a parishioner (would that he had not been a parishioner!), led a very slippery life in a certain parish church in the territory of the diocese of Constance, in the Thurgau district. He was so given over to vice that, although he was often a tavern-keeper, gambler, corrupter, perjurer, usurer, drunkard and fornicator, he nonetheless celebrated Mass every day no less fearlessly. When this was objected to him, and he was rebuked with harsh and abusive words, and asked with what face he dared to celebrate so often, knowing that he was continually entangled in so many enormous vices without contrition, he answered that he never consecrated, but only showed a white wafer, shaped like a host, at the hour of elevation. He kept this in a most secret place and drew it out, because the necessity and the opportunity of celebrating Mass at the due time were close at hand."

units.la: ceret, sed tantum albam regulam, in modum hostiæ formatam, horâ elevationis, demonstraret; quam & loco secretissimo conservaret, & extraheret, quia necessitas & opportunitas celebrandi Missam, tempore debito, immineret. Ex his patet, quod ille maleficus Sacerdos, ex instinctu Diabolico concitatus, immanissimum scelus commisit. Nam more etiam Ieroboam populum peccare fecit, eum ad Idololatriam pertrahendo. Nam lignum pro corpore Christi vero adorabant. O quanta dementia, error & iniquitas in illo perversissimo, cæcissimo Presbytero, filio Diaboli, cujus opera fecit, ebullivit: Nam volens effugere grande peccatum, incidit in enormissimum. Nam Idololatria causam scienter dedit, sicut prius dixi, quæ est flagitium perniciosissimum, & execrabilissimum, ut patet in multis sacra Pagina locis. Patet etiam per hoc, quia omnis celebrans ex institutione Christi & Ecclesiæ tenetur conficere integrè. Sed sit hoc adeo enorme & rude, profligatæ nequitiæ, specimen, ut rarius contingat; num præstabit doctissimus Vir, Sacerdotes ad obeunda sacra Missatica sic semper vel paratos, vel devotos accedere, ut de Intentione serio cogitent? An ipsa de Transsubstantiatione doctrina ita coparata est, ut cujuslibet sacrificuli memoria exactè satis omnia capiat, quæ in officio Missatico Intentione celebrando requiruntur? Cur ex unus nius hominis vel scientiæ, vel conscientiæ defectu ipsa periclitetur unitas, & integra Ecclesia? An hæc talia Evangelio congrua sint, an magis Theologi isti secundùm Evangelium sentiant, ut doctissimi Viri verba repetam, quàm Protestantes, qui tot controversiarum nodos uno felicissimè solvunt verbo, ipse viderit. Nos prosecto ad tam horridam & hispidam Scholasticarum contentionum sylvam prorsus contremiscimus. Deóque, quòd infantibus mysteria sua, simplicitate sermonis, revelârit, gratias agimus, eandem facilitatem & felicitatem ex animo aliis apprecantes
units.tr: to the eyes of the people, but only a white wafer, shaped like a host, at the moment of elevation; and he would keep it in a most secret place and bring it out, since the need and the opportunity of celebrating Mass, at the appointed time, were at hand. From these things it is plain that that wicked priest, stirred up by the devil's prompting, committed a most monstrous crime. For, in the manner of Jeroboam, he also made the people sin, drawing them into idolatry; for they adored wood as if it were the true body of Christ. O what great madness, error and iniquity boiled up in that most perverse and blindest priest, a son of the devil, whose works he performed! For, wishing to escape a great sin, he fell into a most enormous one. For he knowingly gave occasion for idolatry, as I said before, which is a most pernicious and execrable crime, as is shown in many places of Sacred Scripture. It is also shown by this: every celebrant, by the institution of Christ and of the Church, is bound to consecrate completely. But let this be so monstrous and gross an example of flagrant wickedness that it rarely happens. Will the most learned man show that priests come to perform the sacred Mass always so prepared or devout that they seriously think about the intention? Or is the very doctrine of transubstantiation so arranged that the memory of any little sacrificer grasps exactly all the things required in the Mass to be celebrated with intention? Why should the very unity and the whole Church be endangered by the lack of knowledge or conscience of one single man? Whether such things are in agreement with the Gospel, or whether those theologians think more according to the Gospel (to repeat the words of that most learned man) than the Protestants, who with a single very happy word resolve so many knots of controversy, let him see for himself. We indeed tremble utterly at that horrid and bristly forest of Scholastic contentions. And we give thanks to God that He has revealed His mysteries to infants by the simplicity of His speech, and from our heart we wish the same ease and happiness for others.

units.la: SECTIO XIV.
units.tr: SECTIO XIV.

units.la: Transsubstantiatio est dogma scan- dalosum, quo non tantùm infideles, Gentes, Judæi & Muhammedani graviter offendun- tur; sed & ad blasphemas, contra Christum & Christianos, voces irri- tantur.
units.tr: Transubstantiation is a scandalous dogma, which not only gravely offends unbelievers, Gentiles, Jews and Muhammadans, but also provokes them to blasphemous words against Christ and the Christians.

units.la: I. Non adderem hanc mantissam (cur enim canes & porcos mysteriorum sacrorum Antistites, vel etiam Censores Christiani constituant?) nisi & Ecclesia Romana hostium testimonio multum deferret, imò inter Ecclesiæ notas numeraret, & ipsum hoc scandalum esse datum, non acceptum. Et mittam quidem, quod Cicero de Deo panaceo in genere dixit: Ecquem tem amentem esse putas, qui id, quo vescatur, Deum esse credat? Loco suo relinquam, quod Averroi tribuitur, de Christianismo judicium: Omnes regiones peragravi, nec Christiana gente deteriorem ullam reperi: Quia, quem Deum adorant, hunc dentibus devorant. Non solicitabo responsum Legati cujusdam Muhammedici, qui in aula quadam Principis Christiani interrogatus, cur adeo infensis animis Turcae Christianos persequerentur, & non potius in Christianorum castra transirent, dixisse fertur: Nemini, vel ex sensuum judicio, eam placere posse religionem, quae Numina colat, ipsis cultoribus inseriora. Imagines potissimum & Artolatriam intellexit, quae Genti barbarae sudes hactenus fuerunt in oculis, & periculosus lapis offendiculi. Referam; non urgebo tamen hac vice; quae de Friderico Imperatore tradunt Scriptores Pontificii: Eum; postquam cum exercitu ingenti feliciter contra Soldanum pugnasset, & magna potitus victoria, Hierosolymis Eucharistica Deo persolvere paratus esset; Templariorum & Hospitaliorum avaritia & contentionibus sic offensum fuisse & perturbatum, ut de religione sua, Missae praesertim sacrificio, dubitare caeperit. Unde (verba sunt Iohannis, Monachi Vitodurani in Historia sua Msc.) agens in in partibus forte, ut suspicor, transmarinis, triumpho jam potito, secundum opinionem istorum ac relationem astruitur, quadam dierum ipsum in pompa praecellenti, stipatum undique corona Procerum, Missarum solenniis interfuisse, & ibidem a Soldano vel Principe quodam alio infideli inquisitum ab eo, fuisse, quid in manibus Sacerdotis elevaretur, & cum adoratione tam reverenda ab eo & cunctis Christicolis tam diligenter conspiceretur? Tale dicitur ei dedisse responsum: Sacerdotes nostri fabulantur, id quod sursum erigitur, fore Deum. Ad quod ille: Si fuisset Deus ille tantae magnitudinis, ut mons maximus, dudum a Presbyteris vestris ipsum quotidie in Missa manducantibus, consumtus fore potuisset. Quidam tamen de eo referunt, quod totis vellet niti viribus, ut ritus salutares Hostia seu Eucharistiae e medio tollerentur, & huic cogitatui malitiosissimo, meo judicio, incitamentum praestitit praedicti Principis Pagani venenosum verbum. De eodem refert Friderico Imperatore, quod aliquando, cum exercitu prope Rhenum in uberrimo plenae messis campo transiens, exclamarit: O quot autem suo tempore ex hoc frumento conficientur! His, ut dixi, non immorabor, tum quod ab aliis etiam sint notata, tum quod ex nostratibus tantum petita.
units.tr: I would not add this appendix (for why should dogs and swine be entrusted to the keepers of sacred mysteries, or even to Christian censors?) were it not that the Roman Church sets great store by the testimony of its enemies, and even counts among the marks of the Church this very scandal, which it gave rather than received. I will pass over what Cicero said in general about the god Panaceus: Do you think anyone so mad as to believe that the god is the very thing he eats? I will leave for its proper place the judgement ascribed to Averroes about Christianity: I have travelled through all regions and found no people worse than the Christians, for the god they worship, they devour with their teeth. I will not press the reply of a certain Muslim envoy who, when asked at the court of a Christian prince why the Turks persecuted the Christians with such hostile minds and did not rather cross over into the Christian camp, is said to have answered: No one, even by the judgement of the senses, can be pleased with a religion that worships gods inferior to its own worshippers. He meant chiefly images and artolatry, which have hitherto been stakes in the eyes of a barbarous people and a dangerous stone of offence. I will relate, but I will not press this time, what the Papist writers hand down about the Emperor Frederick: that after he had fought successfully against the Sultan with a huge army and gained a great victory, and was preparing to offer thanksgiving to God at Jerusalem, he was so offended and troubled by the greed and quarrels of the Templars and Hospitallers that he began to doubt his religion, especially the sacrifice of the Mass. Hence (these are the words of John, monk of Vitoduran, in his manuscript History), while he was acting perhaps, as I suppose, in those transmarine parts, with the triumph now won, it is asserted, according to their opinion and report, that on a certain day, in most splendid pomp and surrounded on all sides by a crowd of nobles, he was present at the solemn Masses, and there, being questioned by the Sultan or some other infidel prince as to what was being raised in the priest's hands and why it was so carefully gazed upon with such reverent adoration by him and all Christians, he is said to have given this answer: "Our priests fable that what is lifted up is God." To which the other replied: "If that God were of such magnitude as a very great mountain, he could long ago have been consumed by your priests, who eat him every day in the Mass." Some, however, report of him that he wished with all his strength to have the saving rites of the Host or Eucharist abolished, and to this most malicious design, in my judgement, the venomous word of the said pagan prince gave the incitement. Of the same Emperor Frederick they report that once, when passing with his army near the Rhine across a most fertile field of ripe harvest, he cried out: O how many [loaves] will be made from this grain in its season! I will not dwell on these, as I have said, both because others have noted them too, and because they are drawn only from our own people.

units.la: II. Sed & veterum argumenta contra Gen- tium
units.tr: II. But also the arguments of the ancients against the Gentile idols

units.la: tium Idola, aras, delubra folicitare possemus, quæ certè causæ nostræ non obscurè favent. Annon enim per Paganismi latus ipse quoque μετασχηματίζως Pontificius transfigitur? Tertullianus audiatur ex Apologet. Igitur, fistatuas & imagines frigidas, mortuorum suorum similimas, non adoramus, quas milvi, & mures, & aranea intelligunt, nonne laudem magis, quàm pœnam merebatur repudium agniti erroris? Audiatur Minucius Felix: Quanta verò de Diis vestris, animalia muta naturaliter judicant, mures, hirundines, milvi? Non sentire eos sciunt, nōrunt, inculcant, insidênt, ac nisi abigatis, in ipso Dei vestri ore nidificant. Audiatur Lactant. Firmian. ex lib. 2. divin. Instit. cap. 2. Adorant ergò insensibilia qui sentiunt; irrationabilia qui sapiunt; ex anima, qui vivunt, terrena, qui oriuntur è cœlo. Audiatur Athanasius cont. Gent. pag. 17. Postea, adorantes lapides & ligna, non vident, quod alia iis similia, pedibus conculcant, & comburunt, partem verò eorum Deos nuncupant, & quæ paulò ante ad usum (communem adhibuerunt) jam per insaniam sculptum colunt. Item: Quomodo quis vel hoc nomine eos non miseretur, quod videntes illi ea, quæ non vident, adorant, audientes ea, quæ non audiunt, invocant? &c. Audiatur Arnob. lib. 6. adv. Gentes: Insimularchis Diihabitant, singuli ne in singulis toti, an partiliter atque in membra divisi. Nam neque unus Deus (Gentium puta & corporeus, ut Vulcanus) in compluribus potis est uno tempore inesse simulachris, neque rursus in partes sectione interveniente divisus. Constituamus enim decem millia simulacrorum toto in orbe esse Vulcani. Numquid esse, ut dixi, decem omnibus in millibus potis est uno in tempore? Non opinor. Qua causa? quia qua sunt privata, singulariaque natura, multa fieri nequeunt, simplicitatis sua integritate servata (id est, si non dividuntur) Et hoc amplius nequeunt, si hominum formam Dii habent, opinatio ut vestra declarat. Neque enim manus a capite separata, aut pes divisus a corpore, summam possunt praestare totius. Aut dicendum est, portiones idem posse, quod totum cum consistere nequeat, nisi fuerit partium congregatione conflatum. Si autem in cunctis idem esse dicetur, perit omnis ratio atque integritas veritati, si hoc fuerit sumtum, posse unum in omnibus uno tempore permanere. At Deorum unusquisque dicendus, ita ipsum semet ab ipso se dividere, ut & ipse sit & alter, non aliquo discrimine separatus; sed ipse idem & alius. Quod quoniam recusat, & respicit, aspernatúrque Natura, aut innumeros dicendum est, confitendumque, esse Vulcanos, si in cunctis volumus eum degere, atque inesse simulacris: aut erit in nullo, quia esse divisus natura prohibetur in in plurimis, Egerit differtiffimus Scriptor contra Gentes, ex eo principio, quòd unum corpus non possit esse in pluribus locis, & crediderit ipse corpus Christi in Eucharistia tot simul locis esse præfens? An existimat Vir doctissimus, hæc etiam argumenta ab iis opponi infrunito & infano posse Idolorum cultui, qui Transfubstantiationem admittunt? Quin potius ex ipsis Patrum verbis evidentissime colligimus, laudem magis, quàm pœnam mereri eos, qui ea ignorent numina, quæ milvi mures (supra enim jam probavimus, & murium arrofionibus corpus transfubstantiatum esse expositum) araneæ intelligunt? Quidvel Minucius Felix, vel Lactantius vel Athanafius, vel cæteri Patres, Gentilium objecerunt stupori, in cultu arte factorum Numinum, quod Deo Panaceo Christianorum, fi tam absurda cum hominum animis infedifiet sententia, non potuisset regeri? Aut, quid vel jam legimus in antiquissimorum Doctorum Elencho contra cultum Idolorum, cujus reatum subterfugere possint Transfubstantiatores? Ubi Vir doctissimus partium studio valere jusso; rem cum re, argumentum cum argumento contulerit, nobiscum, spero, scapham appellabit fcapham. Quid juvat Patrum in ore habere nomen, & tamen eorum monita, argumenta, etiam ubi recte sentiunt, contemnere? Annon pudeat, aliorum five malitiâ, five ignorantiâ, five ve conniventia factum, ut veterrimorum Doctorum arma, crassissimo olim opposit_a Gentilismo, jam Christianorum superstitioni jugulum petant? Neque vero mirum, cum nec ovum ovo, nec lac lacti, quàm Veteris Romae Idololatria, hodiernae Artolatriae propius accedat. Sed nos istis diutius inhaerere nolumus. Paganos mox ipsos audiemus, Patrum ore & more loquentes, Transsubstantiationisque absurditatem iisdem argumentis, quibus Gentilium olim in cultu Idolorum insaniam perstrinxerunt, arietantes.
units.tr: We could also press the arguments of the ancients against the idols, altars and shrines of the Gentiles, which certainly favour our cause not obscurely. For does not the Papist also get transfigured, by a metaschematism, into the side of paganism itself? Let Tertullian be heard in the Apologeticus: Therefore, we do not worship statues and cold images, most like their dead originals, which kites, and mice, and spiders understand; does not renouncing a recognised error deserve praise rather than punishment? Let Minucius Felix be heard: How much do dumb animals naturally judge about your gods: mice, swallows, kites? They know that they do not feel, they gnaw, they trample, they sit upon them, and unless you drive them away, they build their nests in the very mouth of your god. Let Lactantius Firmianus be heard, from book 2 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 2: Therefore they worship insensible things, those who have sense; irrational things, those who have reason; earthly things born of the soil, those who live by a soul, though it comes from heaven. Let Athanasius be heard against the Gentiles, page 17: Afterwards, worshipping stones and wood, they do not see that they trample underfoot and burn other things like them, and they call some part of them gods, and they worship, through madness, what they had a little before used for common purposes once carved. Likewise: How could anyone not pity them, since they worship things that they see not, and call upon things that they do not hear? etc. Let Arnobius be heard, book 6 against the Gentiles: Let us ask whether the gods dwell in each image wholly, or divided partly, as into limbs. For neither can one god, a corporeal one such as Vulcan, be present at one time in many statues, nor again, if divided by a cutting into parts. For let us suppose that there are ten thousand statues of Vulcan in the whole world. Can ten thousand, as I said, exist in all of them at one time? I think not. Why? Because, being private and singular in nature, they cannot be many things while keeping the integrity of their simplicity (that is, if they are not divided). And they cannot do this further, if the gods have human form, as your opinion declares. For a hand separated from the head, or a foot divided from the body, cannot render the sum of the whole. Or it must be said that the parts can do what the whole cannot, unless it is made up of a gathering of parts. But if it is said that the same is in all, all reason and integrity of truth perishes, if it is granted that one can remain in all at one time. Rather each one of the gods must be said to divide himself from himself so that he is both himself and another, separated by no distinction, yet the same and other. Since nature refuses and rejects this, and turns away, we must say either that there are countless Vulcans, and confess it, if we want him to dwell in all and be present in the statues, or he will be in none, since nature forbids that he be divided among many. That most learned writer argued against the Gentiles on the principle that one body cannot be in many places, and did he himself believe that the body of Christ is present in the Eucharist in so many places at once? Does the most learned man think that these arguments too can be opposed by those who admit Transubstantiation to the foolish and mindless worship of idols? Rather, from the very words of the Fathers we most clearly gather that those who fail to recognise as divinities what the kites, mice and spiders understand deserve praise rather than punishment (for we have already shown above that the corrosions of mice are set forth as affecting the transubstantiated body). Did Minucius Felix, or Lactantius, or Athanasius, or the other Fathers, object to the Gentiles' wonder at gods made by art anything that could not have been turned back against the Christians' god Panaceus, if so absurd an opinion had taken hold of men's minds? Or what do we read even now in the ancient teachers' refutation of idol worship from which the Transubstantiationists could escape the charge? Let the most learned man, having laid aside the zeal of his party, compare thing with thing and argument with argument; with us, I hope, he will call a boat a boat. What good is it to have the names of the Fathers on the tongue, and yet to despise their warnings and arguments, even where they judge rightly? Should it not be a shame that, through the malice, ignorance or connivance of others, the weapons of the most ancient teachers, once opposed to crass paganism, now aim at the throat of Christian superstition? Nor is it any wonder, since egg is no more like egg, nor milk like milk, than the idolatry of ancient Rome is like the present-day artolatry. But we do not want to dwell on these any longer. We shall next hear the pagans themselves, speaking in the voice and manner of the Fathers, battering the absurdity of Transubstantiation with the same arguments with which they once censured the madness of the Gentiles in the worship of idols.

units.la: III. Unum ergo atque alterum afferemus locum, à paucis hactenus observatum, & ex Scriptis adversariorum vel publicis, vel fide dignis eruderatum: An forte iustissimis infidelium flecti Transsubstantiationis Patroni mallent querelis, quàm modestis nostratium ad saniorem revocari mentem Apologiis. Caveant ne ab iis, qui vel ex solo lumine Naturae animadvertunt tot absurditatum ternam atque sententias, converti debeant in rubórem. Regina Austri, inquit Servator Matth. 12.42. surget in judicio cum Gente ista, & condemnabit eam: venerat a terminis terrae, ut audiret sapientiam Solomonis, & ecce plus quam Solomon est in hoc loco. Surgent populi Aljamen, Australes, Arabes Muhammedani cum Gente ista, & condemnabunt eam, quod per id, quod de Deo cognosci potest, quódque manifestum est iniis, Rom. 1, 19.
units.tr: III. I will therefore set out one or two passages, observed by few until now and dug out of the writings of our opponents, both published and reliable. Perhaps the Patrons of Transubstantiation would rather be moved by the most just complaints of unbelievers than be brought back to a saner mind by our modest Apologies. Let them beware lest those who perceive from the light of Nature alone so many absurdities in it be turned to blushing. The Queen of the South, said the Saviour, Matth. 12.42, shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it: for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, a greater than Solomon is here. The peoples of Aljamen, the southern Arabs and Muhammadans, shall rise with this generation and condemn it, because of what may be known of God, and what is manifest among them, Rom. 1.19.

units.la: rœ rectius de Deo naturaque tam divina, quam humana sentiunt, quam ut vel gloriam incorruptibilis Dei, mutent in efformatam imaginem, non mortalis hominis, aut animalis; sed buccellae: vel naturam humanam in spectrum & phantasma; vel benefactorem suum tam indigne excipiant. Abhorrent ergo Muhummedani a Transsubstantiatione & orali manducatione, & ita quidem, ut aperte fateantur, per eam crudeliores hodie reddi Christianos, quam olim fuerint Judaei. Ahmed ben Edris, doctissimus quidam in Mauritania ante quingentos annos, Scriptor, in Tractatu suo contra Christianos, & Judaeos ita inter alia scribit: Verba autem Isa (sic Arabes Servatorem nostrum vocant) super quo pax: Qui edit carnem meam & bibit sanguinem meum, ille in me est & ego in ipso: sum enim panis ille, qui descendi de coelo, Christiani literaliter intelligunt. Atque sic Christiani atrociores sunt in Christum, quam Judaei. Illi enim Christum occisum reliquerunt; hi carnem ejus edunt, & sanguinem bibunt, quod, ipsa teste experientia, truculentius est. Ita Muhammedanus loquitur. Sed annon fere ad mentem Apostoli? Si judaei sapientiam Dei latentem in mysterio cognovissent, nequaquam Dominum Gloriae crucifixissent; 1. Cor. 2.8. Judaei Christum, quem non noverant, cruci affixerunt, Christiani eum, quem Mundi Servatorem, Domiminum Gloriae agnoscunt, quotidianæ tamen manducationi subjiciunt : eóque ( liceat Muhammedani insistere, argumentatione) truculentiores sunt judæis.
units.tr: they think more rightly of God and of nature, both divine and human, than to change the glory of the incorruptible God into the image of a mortal man or of an animal, or into a little morsel of bread, or to reduce human nature to an appearance and a phantom, or to receive their benefactor so unworthily. Muhammadans therefore shrink from transubstantiation and oral manducation, and so much so that they openly admit that Christians have been made more cruel by it today than the Jews ever were. Ahmed ben Edris, a certain very learned writer of Mauritania about five hundred years ago, in his treatise against Christians and Jews, writes among other things as follows: But the words of Isa (so the Arabs call our Saviour), upon whom be peace: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him: for I am that bread which came down from heaven," the Christians understand literally. And so Christians are more savage towards Christ than the Jews. For the Jews left Christ slain; these eat his flesh and drink his blood, which, as experience itself testifies, is more brutal. So speaks the Muhammadan. But is this not almost the mind of the Apostle? If the Jews had known the wisdom of God hidden in the mystery, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. 2.8. The Jews fixed to the cross the Christ whom they did not know; the Christians acknowledge him as the Saviour of the world and the Lord of glory, yet subject him to daily manducation. Therefore (let me insist on the Muhammadan's argument) they are more cruel than the Jews.

units.la: IV. Sed & Judæi ipsi sacra illa, quibus Naturæ ordo prorsus invertitur, neque tamen miraculi ulla ratio reddi potest, abominantur. R. Joseph Albo, de Ikkarim, lib. 3. cap. 25. plus quàm trecentis post Berengarium annis de Transfubstantiationis paradoxis ita scripsit : Præterea, quod dicunt de sacrificio panis & vini, quod fit sacrificium, res non ita habet. Nam panis est corpus Dei ipsorum. Ajunt enim, corpus Iesu, quod est in cœlis, venire in altare, & vestiri pane & vino, post pronuntiata verba (Hoc enim est corpus meum) à sacrificulo, qualiscunque ille demum fuerit, sive pius, sive impius, & omnia fieri corpus unum cum corpore Messiæ, descendentis è cœlo in instanti, & post comestionem & bibitionem reverti in cœlum, in locum suum. Et hæc fieri in omnibus altaribus. Hæc est ipsorum sententia de sacrificio isto. Talis verò ista res est, quam intellectus humanus capere nequit, neque sibi imaginari. Repugnant enim hic omnia Intelligibilibus primis, & ipsis etiam sensibus. Necesse enim est, ut credatur, sic motum fieri absque tempore, ab ultima cœlorum distantia, & a folio gloriæ Dei in terram usque. Deinde corpus unum simul esse in pluribus locis. corpus enim Messiæ juxta ipsos, existit in altaribus pluribus diversis, uno & eodem tempore. Tertiò ascendere & descendere corpus Messiæ, quin tamen dilacerentur cœli, quia cœli non admittunt ejusmodi dilacerationem. Quartò, quia dicunt carnem & sanguinem, qui nunc fit ex substantia panis & vini, quæ finita sunt & determinata, esse illud ipsum corpus Christi, quod olim fuit, neque tamen illud vel augeri vel diminui à quantitate sua; ex quo consequitur penetratio corporum hujus in illud. Omnia hæc & intellectui & sensui repugnant. Dicunt enim, panem & vinum, quæ videntur oculis, non esse cibum, neque nutrire vivens aliquod, vel hominem comedentem illud. Nos verò videmus, panem illum & vinum, si in magna quantitate efsent, omnino nutritura hominem comedentem, & in membrorum nutrimentum cessura, sicut alius panis & vinum. Præterea dicunt, substantiam panis & vini converti in corpus Christi, & remanere tantum accidentia, in seipsis subsistentia, non in subjecto, neque saporem, colorem, tactu, gravitatem, mollitiem, duritiem, quæ adhuc in pane deprehendimus, esse in pane. Corpus enim transire in corpus Christi. Omnia ista talia sunt, quæ mens non potest concipere, neque os eloqui, neque auris audire. Judæi verba sunt, fateor, adeóque jurati & infensissimi Christianorum hostis; vera tamen sunt, non quia judæi, sed sed quia hominis, rationabiliter ex Natura, de Naturalibus, judicantis. Non heic; quis dicat, sed quid dicatur, ex trito Orientis proverbio, attendendum est. Qui fidem rationi opponit; fidei fundamentum ostendat, revelationem divinam, qua sine frustra creditur, quod credere nemo jubetur. Non deerunt fidei sua exercitia, etsi sponte natæ, & rancidæ, male informatæ rationis, non accedant. Neque ratione caret, quòd rationi, in examine corporis sui Naturalis, locum etiam dulcissimus Servator reliquit. Præviderat malitiam hominum, qui, in carnem venisse Eum, perverse essent negaturi, in carne passum, præsentè inficiaturi (sicut etiam num Muhammedismus pro veterum Cerinthianorum, Basilidianorum delirio Iesum non passum, tanquam pro aris & focis certant) in conclavia, Ciboria, sine quantitate & mole revocaturi; qui certe errores omnes etiamnum felicius & facilius dilui à nobis non poterunt, quàm si iis utamur argumentis, quibus Christum usum esse, jam diximus. Ne sit discipulus supra Magistrum: neque ubi summus Doctor præscribit regulas generales, discipulorum est fingere exceptiones. Aut quod, quæso, hic excipiamus corpus Christi? An illud, quod resurrexit? Nec eos audiamus, inquit Augustin. lib. de agon. Christiano, cap. 24. qui negant tale corpus Domini resurrexisse, quale positum est in monumento: Si enim tale non fuisset, non ipse dixisset post resurrectionem discipulis: Palpate & videte, quoniam Spiritus carnem &ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere. An illud, quod ascenditin cœlos? Nec eos audiamus, qui negant ipsum corpus secum levâsse in cœlum, Dominum nostrum, ut cum eodem loquamur cap. 2 s. Si ergò nullum, ne gloridosum quidem Christi corpus excipi debet à veris veri corporis proprietatibus, ecquod tandem restat, quod Adversariorum corpori transsubstantiato invisibili respondeat? Aut quid periculosis ejusmodi suffugiis & exceptionibus obtinebunt? Materiam præbebunt infidelibus, Christo & Christianorum sacris impiè insultandi, profano ea ludibrio exponendi. Cum mœrore referimus, in omnes occasiones intentos Judæos, novo hoc Transsubstantiationis dogmate ita irritari, ut Christum, convitiis gravioribus lacessant, imò ad cruciandum eum, torquendum, transfodiendum, quantum in ipsi est, blasphemis consiliis conspirent. Transsubstantiationis, hæc insolentia maledicta, frustus est. Cùm enim Hostias consecratas, Judæorúmque ære redemtas corpus Christi & vocent, & esse velint, cur miremur, gentem reprobam nec dum Messiæ sanguine satiatam? Nolumus hic de nostro quicquam largiri, eos audiemus, qui ante restauratum bellum Sacramentarium rium vixerunt, devotissima Pontificis Romani mancipia. Exempla quædam enarrat Johannes, Monachus Vitoduranus. Unum, ex Scriptore hactenus nunquam edito, referam, quod (pag. m. 47.) ita habet: Posthac quidam, solo nomine Christicola, re autem hareticus pessimus, imo Judæ mercatoris maligniffimi verissimus imitator, corpus Dominicum, ab eo de Ecclesia sancti Pauli Civitatis Constantiensis sublatum, Judæis ille vendidit, ut ludibrio, quo velent, haberent, quod dum sub multis hostiis junctum, pasta in frixorio confrixum esset, & adhuc continuè in eo adureretur (ita de corpore Ghristi loquitur coremptibiliter, & Ancilla Judæorum Christiana et appropinquaret, mox in ea siliens suo brachio adhæsit, quod videns quidam ex Judæis astantibus, illico abstraxit, & in locum pristinum rejecit. Ancilla vero rem tacita animadvertens, & in vicum & plateas exiens, importunis vocibus lamentabiliter valenterque acclamavit dicens: Corpus Christi horribiliter à Judæis torquetur. Eadem hora Plebanus Ecclesiæ sancti Pauli, cui hostiæ consecratæ ablatæ & suratæ fuerant, horribilius succlamabat, dicens: Heu mihi! quia plures oblatæ Corporis Christi consecratæ de altari sublatæ sunt! Quod audientes cives Constantienses turmatim concurrerunt, & ulciscI Dei sui injuriam, & contumeliam illatam à Judæis conantes, plures Judæos in insania, & furore magno deprehendentes in scelere necaverunt.
units.tr: IV. But the Jews too abhor those sacred rites in which the order of nature is entirely inverted, and no account of a miracle can be given. R. Joseph Albo, in his Ikkarim, book 3, chapter 25, more than three hundred years after Berengarius, wrote thus of the paradoxes of transubstantiation: Moreover, what they say about the sacrifice of bread and wine, that it becomes a sacrifice, is not the case. For the bread is the body of their God. For they say that the body of Jesus, which is in heaven, comes into the altar and is clothed in bread and wine, after the words (For this is my body) have been pronounced by the priest, whatever he may be, whether pious or impious, and that everything becomes one body with the body of the Messiah, descending from heaven in an instant, and after eating and drinking returns to heaven, to its place. And these things happen on all altars. This is their opinion about that sacrifice. Such a thing is one which the human intellect cannot grasp nor imagine. For here everything contradicts the first intelligibles and the very senses. For it must be believed that such motion takes place without time, from the farthest distance of the heavens and from the throne of God's glory down to earth. Next, that one body is at the same time in several places: for the body of the Messiah, according to them, exists on many different altars at one and the same time. Thirdly, that the body of the Messiah ascends and descends without the heavens being torn, since the heavens do not admit such a tearing. Fourthly, because they say that the flesh and blood which now comes from the substance of bread and wine, which are finite and determined, is that very body of Christ which once was, and yet is neither increased nor diminished in its quantity; from which follows the penetration of bodies into that one. All these things contradict both intellect and sense. For they say that the bread and wine, which are seen by the eyes, are not food, nor nourish any living thing, or the man eating them. But we see that this bread and wine, if they were in great quantity, would certainly nourish the man eating them, and would turn into the nourishment of the limbs, just like other bread and wine. Moreover, they say that the substance of bread and wine is converted into the body of Christ, and only the accidents remain, subsisting in themselves, not in a subject, and that the taste, colour, touch, weight, softness and hardness which we still perceive in bread are not in the bread. For body passes into the body of Christ. All these things are such that the mind cannot conceive them, the mouth cannot express them, nor the ear hear them. These are the words of Jews, I admit, and so of the sworn and most hostile enemies of the Christians; yet they are true, not because they are Jews, but because they are the judgments of a man who reasons rationally from nature about natural things. Here we must attend not to who says it, but to what is said, as the common Eastern proverb has it. Whoever sets faith against reason must show the foundation of faith, the divine revelation, by which alone it is believed, since no one is bidden to believe what is absurd. Nor will there be lack of exercises of faith, even though they are not in accord with the spontaneous, rancid and ill-formed reason. Nor is it without reason that the most sweet Saviour left a place also for reason in the examination of his natural body. He foresaw the malice of men, who would perversely deny that he had come in the flesh, deny that he suffered in the flesh, now in the present, (just as even now Muhammadanism fights for the notion that Jesus did not suffer, as for altars and hearths, following the delirium of the old Cerinthians and Basilidians), and would call him back into cupboards and pyxes, without quantity and bulk. Indeed, all these errors cannot be refuted by us more happily and more easily than if we use the arguments by which we have said Christ himself used. The disciple is not above the master; nor, where the highest Teacher lays down general rules, is it for the disciples to invent exceptions. Or what exception, I ask, shall we make here for the body of Christ? That which rose again? Nor let us listen, says Augustine, in the book On the Christian Struggle, chapter 24, to those who deny that the body of the Lord rose such as it had been laid in the tomb: for if it had not been such, he himself would not have said to the disciples after the resurrection: "Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having." Or that which ascended into heaven? Nor let us listen to those who deny that our Lord carried the same body up into heaven, so that we may speak with that same body, chapter 2 sq. If, then, not even the glorified body of Christ is to be excluded from the true properties of a true body, what in the end remains that could answer to the transubstantiated, invisible body of our opponents? Or what will such dangerous evasions and exceptions achieve? They will provide material to unbelievers to insult Christ and the sacred things of the Christians impiously, and to expose them to profane ridicule. With sorrow we report that the Jews, always on the watch for every occasion, are so provoked by this new dogma of transubstantiation that they assail Christ with more grievous insults, and even, so far as in them lies, conspire with blasphemous plans to torment, torture and pierce him. This insolence of the Jews is the fruit of transubstantiation. For since they both call the consecrated hosts, redeemed with the money of the Jews, the body of Christ, and wish them to be so, why should we be surprised that a reprobate nation, not yet sated with the blood of the Messiah, does so? We will not here concede anything of our own; we will listen to those who lived before the Sacramentarian war was renewed, most devoted slaves of the Roman Pontiff. John, the monk of Vitoduran, relates some examples. I will report one from a writer never yet published, which (p. 47) reads as follows: Afterwards a certain man, a Christian in name only but in reality the worst of heretics, indeed the most true imitator of the most malicious merchant Judas, took the body of the Lord from the church of St Paul in the city of Constance, and sold it to the Jews, so that they might have it as a mockery to do with as they wished; and when it had been joined under many hosts, fried in a pan, and was still continually being burnt in it (he speaks thus contemptibly of the body of Christ), and a Christian maidservant of the Jews came near, she at once leapt and clung to her arm; which seeing, a certain one of the Jews standing by immediately pulled it away and threw it back into its former place. But the maidservant, noticing the matter in silence and going out into the village and the streets, cried out in a lamentable and loud voice with importunate cries, saying: The body of Christ is horribly tortured by the Jews. At the same hour the parish priest of the church of St Paul, from whom the consecrated hosts had been taken and stolen, cried out even more horribly, saying: Alas for me! for many consecrated hosts, the offerings of the body of Christ, have been taken from the altar! When the citizens of Constance heard this, they ran together in crowds, and trying to avenge the injury and insult done to their God by the Jews, they found many Jews in madness and great fury, and killed them for their crime.

units.la: V. Irritantur & Gentes ad idem designandum facinus, prout ex eodë (p. 45.) constat Vitodurano, Rhutenos, quos Paganos vocat, Marchionatum Brandenburgicum invasisse, Ecclesias diruisse, altaria destruxisse, & (retineo authoris verba) quod execrabile dictu, corpus Christi in scriniis super aris reconditum sustulisse, eique lanceas suas infixisse, blasphemando dicentes : Ecce Deus Christianorum, in nullo se defendere valens! Quod Deus dissimulavit. Si autem eos plaga crudeli percussisset, ipsos & suos posteros forsitan convertisset, & judicio meo disciplina & fidei Catholicæ non modicum profuisset. Crevit & opprobrium in Christianos, & desiderium vindicandæ injuriæ, occasione Elementorum Sacramentalium veneno infectorum. Horrendum fuit facinus Monachi illius, qui hoc supplicio e medio sustulit Henricum VII. Imperatorem Romanorum, cui Tragœdiæ a se (pag. 33.) commemoratæ Scriptor noster domesticus sequentia subjicit. Hic (Imperator) erat regula justitiæ, summa Legis, Lux Ecclesiæ, fidei immobilis columna, insolentium silentium, lima correctionis, Zelator præcipuus veritatis, fidelis in commissis, constans in promissis, amator sedulus latriæ, norma temperantiæ, castitatis speculum, liberalitatis exemplum, forma justitiæ, de-senfensor & patronus pauperum, imitator egregius Evangelica doctrina. Hic talis & tantus, quod cum maxima cordis mei amaritudine loquor, veneno necatur ; quod heu Christiana disciplina ruina & plaga perniciosissima fuit! Nam maxime ei derogavit, quod in altissimo Sacramento religionis Catholica homo tanta supereminentia interemtus est. Nam ubi in nostris temporibus affluentissime vernat fides credentium, & in Sacramento, in quo maxime dependet devotio modernorum, ibi nefandissimum scelus perpetratum est, scandalum etiam perpetuo duraturum, quod infidelibus nauseam & displicentiam generavit nostrae professionis, imo insultant nobis per hoc, dicentes: Si illa species, quam sumunt, & reverentur Christiani, Deus esset, tam horribile & execrabile facinus sua in specie & participatione fieri nullatenus permisisset. Quantum Christianismus a se mutatus! Solebant veteres Christiani; poterant etiam, ab Artolatria liberi; Gentilibus exprobrare stuporem, quod, ceu Numina colerent, quae & a muribus laederentur, & ab avibus calcarentur: jam, verso stylo, Christiani a Gentilibus eandem expectent reprehensionem? Hoccine est Antiquitatis religiose insistere vestigiis? Pergit author & deplorat sortem Christianismi. Et quia, inquit, taliter nobis insultant, judicio humano, & sensuum meorum, compellor dicere,
units.tr: V. Nations too are stirred up to the same crime. As the same author (p. 45) reports of Vitoduranus, the Ruthenians, whom he calls Pagans, invaded the margraviate of Brandenburg, overthrew the churches, destroyed the altars, and (I keep the author's own words, which are horrible to say) took away the body of Christ kept in boxes above the altars, ran their lances through it, saying blasphemously: Behold the God of the Christians, who cannot defend himself in anything! God overlooked this. But if he had struck them with a cruel blow, perhaps he would have converted them and their descendants, and in my judgment it would have done no little good to discipline and the Catholic faith. Reproach against the Christians grew, and so did the desire to avenge the injury, because of the sacramental elements poisoned with venom. Horrible was the deed of that monk who by this punishment removed Henry VII, Emperor of the Romans. To the tragedy I mentioned (p. 33) our own domestic writer adds the following. He (the Emperor) was the rule of justice, the highest law, the light of the Church, the unshakeable pillar of faith, the silencer of the insolent, the file of correction, the chief zealot for truth, faithful in what was entrusted to him, steadfast in his promises, a diligent lover of worship, the standard of moderation, the mirror of chastity, the example of generosity, the model of justice, the defender and patron of the poor, an outstanding imitator of the Gospel teaching. He, so great and so good, as I speak with the greatest bitterness of heart, was killed by poison; alas, this was a most destructive blow and wound to Christian discipline! For it especially detracts from the fact that a man of such eminence was slain in the most high sacrament of the Catholic religion. For where in our times the faith of believers flourishes most abundantly, and in the sacrament on which the devotion of the moderns chiefly depends, there the most abominable crime was committed, a scandal that will last for ever, which has produced nausea and displeasure at our profession among unbelievers. Indeed they mock us for it, saying: If that appearance which Christians take and revere were God, such a horrible and execrable deed would never have been permitted to be done in its very appearance and by its very reception. How far Christianity has changed! The ancient Christians used to be able, free from bread-worship, to reproach the Gentiles for their stupidity in worshipping as deities things that mice gnaw and birds tread on. Now, the tables turned, will Christians expect the same rebuke from the Gentiles? Is this to follow the footsteps of religious antiquity? The author goes on and laments the fate of Christianity. And because, he says, they insult us in this way, I am compelled by human judgment and my own senses to say,

units.la: P 3 & & exclamare, dicens: O Domine, quare si non justè, vel si ob aliquam causam, Tibi soli notam, sinere voluisti, quod est in tam grande judicium & detrimentum fidei? Quare ergo, secundum verbum sapientis, non innovasti signa tua, & immutasti Tua mirabilia, ad demonstrandum potentiam dextera Tua, & adfirmandam plebis fidem, sicut caecum a nativitate illuminare voluisti, ad manifestandam gloriam Tuam &c.
units.tr: and to cry out, saying: O Lord, why, if not justly, or if for some cause known to you alone, did you allow this to happen to such great judgment and loss for the faith? Why then, according to the word of the wise man, have you not renewed your signs and changed your wonders, to show the power of your right hand and to confirm the faith of the people, as you wished to give sight to the man blind from birth, to make known your glory, etc.

units.la: Sed frustra a Deo exigitur, quod ab eo nunquam fuit promissum. Non rejicit nos Spiritus sanctus ad miracula; sed ad voluntatem revelatam, ad Scripturam. Qui alio incedunt Canone, qui miracula quotidiana expetunt, tentant Deum, digni proinde, quibus respondeat Moses: Quid contenditis mecum, quid tentatis Iehovam? Exod. 17.2. Et Deut.6.16.
