Ne tentate Iehovam Deum vestrum, (in Massa) quemadmodum tentarunt Israelita in Massa. Camaraeorum, Baalitarum est, ejulando, lancinando, sauciando pulsare caelum ferreum, & ea fatigare Numina, quibus nec vox est, nec responsio, 1.Reg.18.26.28. Sed de his alibi. Quid, quod Magorum & maleficarum etiam libidini inservire debuisse corpus Dominicum, diffiteri non audent? Id quod tum ex eodem Authore (p.m.48.a,) tum aliis etiam documentis probatu esset proclive, nisi brevitatis majorem, quam prolixae demonstrationis habere rationem constituissemus.
units.tr: But it is in vain that one demands from God what he never promised. The Holy Spirit does not send us to miracles but to the revealed will, to Scripture. Those who proceed by another rule, who seek daily miracles, tempt God, and so deserve the answer of Moses: Why do you contend with me, why do you tempt Jehovah? Exod. 17.2. And Deut. 6.16: Do not tempt Jehovah your God (at Massah), as the Israelites tempted him at Massah. It is the way of the Canaanites and Baalites to beat the iron heaven with wailing, cutting and wounding, and to weary those deities who have neither voice nor answer, 1 Kings 18.26, 28. But of these things elsewhere. As for the fact that they dare not deny that the Lord's body was obliged to serve even the lust of magicians and sorceresses: this could easily be proved both from the same author (p. 48) and from other evidence, were it not that we decided to give more weight to brevity than to a long demonstration.

units.la: V.Ri-
units.tr: V. Ri-

units.la: VI. Rimam, quærunt, scio: Sed vix elabentur. Ab omni decore; inquiunt; incommodo, vi & violentia Christi corpus in Eucharistia esse liberum, immortale esse: & in gloria. Nihil proinde vel somniandum, quod lædere illud quocunque modo posset. Sic illi quidem excipiunt; sed magno suo dispendio. Sacra Scriptura nobis in Cæna nullum aliud proponit corpus, quàm fractum; nullum alium sanguinem effundit, quàm effusum. Hoc; inquit Christus; est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur; (de frangendo & passibili loquitur corpore) hic sanguis meus, qui pro vobis effunditur. Aliud igitur corpus suæ destinant Missæ Pontificii, aliud discipulis tradidit Christus. Hoc mortale fuit, & πνευματικόν; illud immortale & ἀπαθές. Sed & obcæsi·orum narium fumus, crassiore sub aëre nati, quàm qui capiamus, in corpus Christi agi, non tamen illud pati; corpus frangi, nec tamen minui; carnem verè comedi, in ventrem trajici, in stomacho morari; sed fine ulla mutatione, passione, diminutione. Hæc, & si quæ sunt alia, summo Deo indigna, doctissimi Viri solicitæ subjicimus censuræ, an vel pia cogitatione possint comprehendi, vel devota religiosáque fide credi, vel denique cum verbo Dei conciliari?
units.tr: VI. They seek a loophole, I know, but they will hardly slip out of it. They say that the body of Christ in the Eucharist is free from every indignity, harm and violence, that it is immortal and in glory. Therefore nothing is to be imagined that could injure it in any way. So they answer, but at great cost to themselves. Holy Scripture presents us at the supper with no other body than a broken one, and sheds no other blood than blood that has been poured out. This, says Christ, is my body, which is broken for you (he speaks of a body that is broken and capable of suffering); this is my blood, which is poured out for you. The Papists therefore assign one body to their Mass, and Christ gave another to his disciples. The one was mortal and spiritual [πνευματικόν]; the other is immortal and impassible [ἀπαθές]. Yet also the smoke that stings the nostrils, born in a thicker air than we can breathe, is said to be acted upon in the body of Christ without itself suffering; the body is broken yet not diminished; flesh is truly eaten, carried into the belly, and remains in the stomach, yet without any change, suffering or diminution. We set these and any other things, unworthy of the supreme God, before the careful judgment of learned men: can they be grasped even by a pious thought, or believed with a devout and religious faith, or finally reconciled with the Word of God?

units.la: VII. Promissis, ut spero, pro virili stetimus: ostendimus, doctrinam, quam Reformatæ per HelHelveriam Ecclesiæ, adeóque & Tigurina, profitentur, Verbo Dei, traditioni Dominicæ, & authoritati Evangelicæ non modò esse congruam; sed & Antiquitatis suffragio, sanæque rationis calculo approbatam: Eam contrà, quæ, de Transsubstantiatione, paulatim in Ecclesiam irrepsit, sententiam e diametro & Scripturæ repugnare, & Analogiæ, fidei, & sanæ rationi; adeò denique incertam, perplexam, esse dubiam (dubia certè ultra trecenta de Eucharistia proponit author expositionis Evangeliorum, editæ à F. Antonio de Gislandis, de Laveno Inquisitore, Lugd a. ch. 158. Dominica Palmar. pag. 133.
units.tr: VII. We have, I hope, kept our promises as far as we could: we have shown that the doctrine which the churches of Helvetia, and so the Tigurine church, profess is not only in agreement with the Word of God, the Lord's tradition and the authority of the Gospel, but is also approved by the testimony of antiquity and the reckoning of sound reason. The opinion, on the other hand, which has crept gradually into the Church concerning transubstantiation, is entirely opposed to Scripture, to the analogy of faith and to sound reason; indeed it is so uncertain, perplexed and doubtful (the author of the exposition of the Gospels, published by Father Antonio de Gislandis, of Laveno, Inquisitor, at Lyon in the year 158, on Palm Sunday, p. 133, puts forward more than three hundred doubts about the Eucharist) that

units.la: Nec Pesantius in dubiorum five propositione, five solutione alio, quàm putandi verbo utitur) scandalíque plenam, ut nomen etiam Christi & Christianismi ab infidelibus propterea indignissimè traducatur & blasphemetur. Ordo jam ad reliqua, quæ ad totius Sacramenti Cœnæ Dominicæ mysterium pertinent, nos ferret; sed malumus, hoc congressu infirmitatem causæ, quam vir doctissimus suscepit defendendam, ostendere, quàm novam ordiri telam. Non existimo, ignotum V. d. esse Apologum, de malo irritatione aucto. Solebant in oppidoquodam de certis catibus excludi omnes vitiati, quacunque corporis parte, erantque constituti, qui de illorum (si qui forte obrepsisse comperirentur) singulis vitiis singulos nummos exigerent. Hi a-liliquando, claudo conspecto, cum exigerent ab eo nummum, & renitentem invaderent, scabiem etiam in eo deprehendunt. Ergo postulant jam nummos duos. Etiam tunc illo refragante, apparet, lippitudo oculorum. Tum isti, jam tres dabis nummos, inquiunt. Ego ne? inquit ille. Pugnabo potius. In lucta igitur ea apparet hernia quoque. Tum exegere tandem nummos quatuor ab eo, qui se uno liberare potuisset. De verbis Institutionis primaria inter Tigurinos & doctissimum Virum erat controversia: ne hanc quidem Adversarii nostris dare volunt aut largiri.
units.tr: Pesantius, in proposing or solving these doubts, uses no word other than to think; and it is so full of scandal that the very name of Christ and of Christianity is for this reason most shamefully disparaged and blasphemed by unbelievers. The order of our argument would now carry us on to the rest, which pertains to the whole mystery of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; but we prefer, in this encounter, to show the weakness of the cause which the most learned man has taken up to defend, rather than to begin a new web. I do not think the most learned gentleman is unaware of the fable about an evil made worse by irritation. In a certain town it was the custom to exclude from certain cats all who were afflicted, in whatever part of the body, and there were officials who demanded a coin from each of them for each fault (if any were found to have crept in). Once, when a lame man was seen, they demanded a coin from him, and when he resisted and attacked them, they also found scabies on him. So they now demand two coins. When he still resisted, a sore eye appeared. Then they said: now you must give three coins. Me? said he. I will rather fight. In the struggle a hernia also appeared. At last they extracted four coins from a man who could have freed himself with one. The main dispute between the Tigurines and the most learned man was about the words of institution. Our opponents do not even want to grant us this.

units.la: Quid si, quod evidenter hactenus ex Scriptura potissimum, Fidei Analogia, & Antiquitate de explicatione verborum probavimus, eosdem in tota etiam actione Eucharistica, ab exemplo Christi, & Praxi Apostolica recedere, diceremus: nihil diceremus quod vel probatu esset operosum, vel ab instituto nostro alienum. Unius morbi nolunt agnoscere malum, & ecce totum corpus a calce ad caput laborat. Nos, Servatoris exemplo, in celebratione Coenae retinemus usum Linguae vernaculae, non illi. Nos, Christi authoritate porrigimus communicantibus utrumque elementum, panem & vinum; non illi, &c. Verum, quod pollicitii sumus, nolumus hac vice prolixitate nimia Lectori afferre taedium. Satis sit, luce meridiana clarius patere, nostrae sententiae nihil non patrocinari. Et Scripturam, & fidei analogiam, & Antiquitatem &c. nobiscum facere. Viri contrà doctissimi fupelleEtilem ita esse curtam, ut ne unum quidem, ex universo Codice sacro, proferre possit locum, nullum producere argumentum, quo vel verba institutionis Cœnæ Dominicæ proprie, crudè, & fecundum literam, vel Caput Johannis 6. de manducatione corporis Transfubstantiati, esse intelligenda, solidè demonstret. Hæc aureola nostra est; hæc palma, quam tam diu fartam tectam retinebimus, donec & contrarium authoritate Scripturæ fuerit assertum, & argumenta nostra, ea maximè, quæ ex natura Sacramentorum sunt petita, fuerint refutata. Si quid, hinc inde tantùm, Vir doctissimus deinceps vellicârit, & non, quod nos in examine articuli primi, adeóque primariæ controversiæ, religiosè præstitimus, vestigia nostra legerit, ne nostram quidem causam agi existimabimus: bonas horas, melius, quàm continuæ ferræ huius reciprocationi impensuri, aliis destinabimus meditationibus.
units.tr: What if we were to say that, having proved clearly so far from Scripture above all, from the analogy of faith and from antiquity, the right explanation of the words, they also depart from the example of Christ and the apostolic practice in the whole eucharistic action? We would say nothing that would be hard to prove or foreign to our plan. They refuse to recognise the evil of one disease, and behold, the whole body is sick from heel to head. We, following the example of the Saviour, retain the use of the vernacular tongue in celebrating the Supper; they do not. We, by the authority of Christ, offer both elements, bread and wine, to those who communicate; they do not, etc. But, as we promised, we do not wish at this time to burden the reader with excessive length. It is enough to make plain, clearer than the midday light, that nothing of our position is left unsupported, and that Scripture, the analogy of faith, antiquity, etc. all agree with us. But the most learned man's stock of arguments is so scanty that he cannot produce even a single passage from the whole sacred Code, nor any argument by which he could solidly demonstrate that the words of the Lord's Supper are to be understood properly, plainly and according to the letter, or that John 6 concerns the eating of a transubstantiated body. This is our little golden prize, this is the palm which we shall keep hidden and guarded for so long, until the contrary has been asserted by the authority of Scripture and our arguments, especially those drawn from the nature of the sacraments, have been refuted. If the most learned man henceforth merely nibbles here and there, and does not follow our footsteps, as we have faithfully done in examining the first article, and so the primary controversy, we shall not think our cause is being argued at all: we shall devote the good hours, better spent than on this continual back-and-forth of the saw, to other meditations.

units.la: VIII. Cæteri jam ordine articuli excutiendi restarent: Sed quando consultius longè visum fuit, primarium de sensu verborum Domini Thema à cæteris (quæ adventitia sunt, & de circumstantiis potius quibusdam agunt, quàm de substantia rei; vindicias quorundam allegatorum, concernunt, fundamentum controversiae Sacramentariae non concutiunt; secernere, pedem hic sistemus. Ita enim & doctissimi Viri, & cujuslibet Lectoris occupationibus gratificaturi, moderata & mediocria examinis, censurae, praemittimus pensa; caeterorum, suo tempore, curam non abjecturi. Si nihil superfit doctissimo Disceptatori, quod dogma ei Transsubstantiationis commendet, quam quod sequentibus adhuc aliquot propositum articulis, bene sperat; hunc, sine magno negotio, obicem, bono cum Deo, removebimus, perspicue monstraturi, non plus in recessu difficultates illas omnes habere, quam frontispicium prae se ferat. Nihil enim doctissimi Viri ostendunt exceptiones, quod non vel ex Bellarmino, aliisque mutuatum Theologis, sexcentes jam a nostris refutatum sit; vel quod nostram sententiam vel leviter stringat; vel quod Transsubstantiationi laboranti opem ferre possit. Saepe noster est doctissimus Vir, cum maxime repugnare videtur; saepe Tigurinorum mentem vel non assequitur, vel incommode exprimit; saepe Patribus, Patrumque luculentissimis verbis insolitum affingit sensum: Saepissime, de Patrum explicatione solicitus, plane extra oleas vagatur, & ne tum quidem, cum, quod intendit obtinet, nocet. Nuspiam in tota disceptatione id video agi, ut causae hinc Reformatorum periculum imineat: Nolumus esse polli-cicitis, divites; ex unius tamen adhuc articuli cursoria censura, vel ipse argumentorum suorum aut exceptionum æstimet robur. Frustra certe initio Artic. 2. Vir doctissimus timet, Reformatis verba Johannis 6. a vers. 48. valde esse contraria. Fuse enim contrarium supra oftendimus. Imprudenter, Tigurinorum, qui, ex Augustino & Gratiano, perspicuis docuerunt verbis, Credere & manducare esse æquipollentia, sententiam, refutaturus, eandem per multas ambagis tandem confirmat potius, quàm elevat. Evidentissimè enim, quod & nos volumus, Christi & Augustini verbis condocefacit, Credere esse edere. Verba Viri doctissimi clara sunt, nullius proinde plenioris deductionis indiga. Sed prorsus ἀδεόλογον est, quòd, concedo, credere, ex mente Christi, idem esse, quod edere, negat tamen, illud quicquam pertinere ad manducationem Spiritualem corporis Christi; sed ad fidem solam in Christum: Quasi vel ulla detur alia manducatio Spiritualis, quàm quæ fit per fidem; aut organum illud, quo Christum ita edimus, aliud sit, quàm fides. Ignoscat Vir doctissimus, si suspicer, hæc ex officina Theologica non prodiisse. Ex Aenea Sylvio supra palàm fecimus, Spiritualem manducationem esse, qua salvandi utuntur, incarnationem, passionemque Domini pia & assidua meditatione recolentes. Hæc verò nonne est fidei? Quid est manducare Spiritualiter tuatualiter (quæritAngel.deClavas.in Summ.voce Eucharistiæ) & respondet, secundum Bonaventuram in 4. dist. 9. quòd manducatio Spiritualiter translata sit à corporalibus; adeò ut quemadmodum in manducatione corporali sint duo principaliter, scilicet masticatio & incorporatio; sic & in Spirituali duo sint, recogitatio per fidem, sed carnis Christi pro nobis exposita in precium, in cruce, ad redimendum, & Spiritualis incorporatio per Charitatem. Quomodo Christi corpus Spiritualiter est accipiendum, ex Dec. P. III. de Consec. dist. 2. C. 59. quærere possumus? & ex textu respondere: Credere in Iesum Christum, hoc est manducare panem vivum. Qui credit in eum, manducat. Hanc manducationem & nos quoque Spiritualem vocamus; hanc fidei tribuimus, non verò, quod novo plane & ipsis Theologis Scholasticis inusitato exemplo, molitur Vir doctissimus fidei opponimus. Quemadmodum ergo Vir doctissimus totus in eo est, articulo secundo; quod & operosè probat; ut credere & edere carnem Christi aliquando esse æquipollentia, ostendat; ita ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ hypothesi longè recedit; quando ea, quæ à vers. 27. Johannis 6. ad vers. 48. extant, non negat pertinere ad fidem in Christum, inficiatur tamen, pertinere ad manducationem Spiritualem corporis Christi, aut in Sacramento, aut extra Sacramentum. Quod re-vera vera aliud nihil est, quàm dicere, hominem esse animal rationale, rationem tamen ad hominem non pertinere.
units.tr: VIII. The remaining articles would now have to be examined in their order. But since it seemed far more advisable to set aside the primary theme, the sense of the Lord's words, from the others (which are incidental, deal with certain circumstances rather than the substance of the matter, defend some of the cited authorities, and do not shake the foundation of the Sacramentarian controversy), we shall stop here. In this way we shall both accommodate the occupations of the most learned man and of any reader, by first setting out moderate and middling weighings of examination and censure, and we shall not abandon care for the others in their due time. If the most learned disputant has nothing left that recommends the dogma of transubstantiation to him, except what he hopes for from the several articles still proposed, we shall, with God's blessing, remove this obstacle without great effort, clearly showing that those difficulties hold no more within than their façade displays. For the objections of the most learned man show nothing that has not either been borrowed from Bellarmine and other theologians and refuted by our side a hundred times already, or that either barely touches our opinion or can bring help to transubstantiation in its distress. Often our most learned man seems to be most opposed to us when he is in fact on our side; often he either does not grasp the mind of the Tigurines or expresses it awkwardly; often he attaches to the Fathers, and to the Fathers' own most lucid words, a sense they never had; and most often, anxious about the Fathers' explanation, he wanders completely off the olive-paths, and even when he does attain what he aims at, he does harm. Nowhere in the whole dispute do I see any effort to place the cause of the Reformed in danger. We do not want to be boastful, rich men; yet from a cursory censure of this one article, let him judge for himself the strength of his own arguments and objections. Certainly the most learned man fears in vain at the beginning of Article 2 that the words of John 6 from verse 48 are "very contrary to the Reformed." For we have shown at length that the opposite is true. Carelessly, he undertakes to refute the opinion of the Tigurines, who from Augustine and Gratian taught in plain words that to believe and to eat are equivalent; yet after many circumlocutions he ends by confirming the same opinion rather than overturning it. For he most clearly teaches, with the words of Christ and of Augustine, what we also want: that to believe is to eat. The words of the most learned man are clear and need no fuller deduction. But it is wholly ἀδιάλογον [absurd] that, while he concedes that to believe means, in the mind of Christ, the same as to eat, he nevertheless denies that this has anything to do with the spiritual eating of the body of Christ, but only with faith in Christ alone. As if there were any spiritual eating other than that which is done through faith, or as if the organ by which we thus eat Christ were anything other than faith. Let the most learned man forgive me if I suspect that these ideas did not come out of the theological workshop. From Aeneas Sylvius we have openly shown above that spiritual eating is that by which the saved use the incarnation and passion of the Lord, recalling them by pious and constant meditation. But is this not of faith? What is it to eat spiritually (Angelus de Clavasio asks in the Summa under the word "Eucharist"), and he answers, following Bonaventure on the Fourth Book, distinction 9, that eating spiritually has been transferred from bodily eating; so that just as in bodily eating there are two things principally, namely chewing and incorporation, so in spiritual eating there are two: recollection through faith of the flesh of Christ set forth for us as the price on the cross, to redeem us, and spiritual incorporation through charity. How can we ask in what manner the body of Christ is to be received spiritually, from Decretum, part III, On Consecration, distinction 2, chapter 59? And from the text we can answer: To believe in Jesus Christ, this is to eat the living bread. He who believes in him eats. We too call this eating spiritual; we attribute it to faith, and not, as the most learned man does through a wholly new example, unusual even to the Scholastic theologians themselves, set it against faith. Therefore, just as the most learned man in the second article is wholly intent on showing, and laboriously proves, that to believe and to eat the flesh of Christ are sometimes equivalent, so he departs far from the hypothesis of the Roman Church, when, although he does not deny that those things which stand from verse 27 to verse 48 of John 6 pertain to faith in Christ, he nevertheless denies that they pertain to the spiritual eating of the body of Christ, whether in the sacrament or outside the sacrament. Which, in truth, is nothing other than to say that man is a rational animal, yet that reason does not pertain to man.

units.la: IX. Neque felicius disputat Articulo III. Demus, Augustinum verba, Joh.6.verf. 42. explicare de justitia Dei, sive de justitia divina, ex gratia nobis imputata; num propterea ex loco illo Tigurini vitiosè concludunt: Credere in Christum, & manducare panem vivum æquipollere? Imò difertissima sunt Augustini verba Tractat. 26. in Johannem: Daturus ergo Dominus Spiritum sanctum dixit, se panem, qui de cœlo descendit, hortans, ut credamus in eum. Credere enim in eum, hoc est manducare panem vivum. Sive jam de Eucharistia ex professo agat, sive non agat, Augustinus nihil refert: Satis est, Tigurinos evidenti ejus assensu probâsse, Credere in Christum, esse manducare panem vivum, cœlestem. Consentiunt optimæ & recentissimæ Decretorum editiones, Dec. P.2.II.de Confec.d.2.C.47.rubrica est: Credere in Christum, est manducare & bibere Christum: Textus verò: Ut quid paras dentem &c. De cæteris nos disputare non est necesse. De Baptismo hoc loco agi, plane impertinens est. Ne apex quidem insolitæ hujus explicationis occurrit, quam proinde Ecclesiæ Romanæ Theologi, qui de Spirituali manducatione locum explicant, non viderunt, etsi ἐξοχοι ἀληθῶν. Qui Augustini verba de Baptismo accipiunt, gravissimum authorem imperitè torquent. Qui credit in eum, inquit, manducat, invisibiliter saginatur, quia invisibiliter renascitur: Infans intus est, novus intus est; ubi novellatur, ibi satiatur. Comparat Augustinus inter se Spiritualem manducationem, cum Spirituali generatione. Utramque ait fieri invisibiliter; utramque eadem numero Subjectum posse referri. Illum, qui intus, qui regeneratus, qui invisibiliter novellatus est; invisibiliter etiam satiari. Verbo, utriusque Sacramenti legitimum usum in Spirituali consistere participatione. Hæc sponte fluunt, illa obtorto rapiuntur collo. Gratianum (qui in vulgatis exemplaribus, pro panem vivum, legit, panem & vinum; illa tamen lectio, emendata ex plerisque vetustis codicibus, in nostra habetur editione Lugdunensi, 1606.) vapulare Viro doctissimo, nostrâ nihil interest. Ipsi operam dent, ut maximæ in Scholis Pontificiis authoritatis Scriptorem ita deinceps effingant, ne tot, quæ ubique in Scriptis adversariorum sunt obviæ, vel negligentiæ vel malæ fidei objici illi debeant næwi. Si verò locus, prout apud Gratianum extat, Credere in eum, esse manducare panem & vinum, clarissimè pertineat ad Eucharistiam; cur ergo in Eucharistia sua atque Synaxi utrumque Elementum, panem & vinum Pontificii non retinent?
units.tr: IX. Nor does he argue more happily in Article 3. Grant that Augustine explains the words of John 6, verse 42, of the righteousness of God, or divine righteousness, imputed to us by grace; does the Tigurine therefore wrongly conclude from that passage that to believe in Christ and to eat the living bread are equivalent? Indeed, Augustine's words in Tractate 26 on John are most express: The Lord, therefore, about to give the Holy Spirit, said that he himself is the bread which came down from heaven, exhorting us to believe in him. For to believe in him, this is to eat the living bread. Whether Augustine treats the Eucharist professedly or not, it makes no difference to him: it is enough that the Tigurines have proved, by his evident assent, that to believe in Christ is to eat the living, heavenly bread. The best and most recent editions of the Decretum agree: Decretum, part II, On Consecration, distinction 2, chapter 47, has the heading: To believe in Christ is to eat and drink Christ. The text itself reads: Why do you prepare your tooth, etc. As for the rest, we need not dispute. That baptism is treated in this place is plainly irrelevant. Not even a trace of this unusual explanation appears, which therefore the theologians of the Roman Church, who explain the passage about spiritual eating, did not see, although they are ἐξοχοι ἀληθῶν [eminent in the truth]. Those who take Augustine's words about baptism badly twist the most weighty author. He who believes in him, he says, eats; he is invisibly fed, because he is invisibly reborn. The infant is within; the new man is within; where he is renewed there he is also satisfied. Augustine compares spiritual eating with spiritual generation. He says that both happen invisibly; and that the same subject can be referred to both: he who is within, who is regenerated, who has been invisibly renewed, is also invisibly satisfied. In a word, the lawful use of each sacrament consists in spiritual participation. These things flow naturally; those are dragged along by the neck. As for Gratian (who, in the printed copies, reads bread and wine instead of living bread; yet that reading, corrected from most of the old manuscripts, is found in our Lyons edition of 1606), whether he is roughly handled by the most learned man is no concern of ours. Let them take pains to shape so great an authority among the Papist schools in such a way that they will not have to be charged with the blemishes, of carelessness or bad faith, that are found everywhere in the writings of our opponents. But if the passage, as it stands in Gratian, To believe in him is to eat bread and wine, pertains most clearly to the Eucharist, why then do the Papists not retain both elements, bread and wine, in their own Eucharist and Synaxis?

units.la: Ita vero sequeretur, (inquit Vir doctissimus) non solum manducari, per fidem, corpus & sanguinem Christi; sed & panem & vinum. Omnino sequitur. In legitimo enim Coenae usu, haec duo indivulso nexu fidelibus exhibentur, elementa externa; panis videlicet & vinum, res terrestris; & corpus Christi, res coelestis. Atque hoc ex praesenti capite necessario sequi, vestrorum supra Theologorum authoritate ostendimus. Digna sunt verba quae, mutuata ab Augusti. in lib. sententiarum Prosp. ex Decreti P. III. de Confec. d. 2. cap. 48. doctissimo Viro scrupulum eximunt: Hoc est, quod dicimus: Hoc modis omnibus adprobare contendimus, sacrificium scilicet Ecclesiae duobus confici, duobus constare, visibili elementorum specie, & invisibili Domini nostri Jesu Christi carne & sanguine, Sacramento & re Sacramenti, id est, corpore Christi: sicut Christi persona constat & conficitur Deo & homine: cum ipse Christus verus sit Deus, & verus homo: quia omnis res illarum rerum naturam, & veritatem in se continet, ex quibus conficitur. Conficitur autem Sacrificium Ecclesiae Sacramento, & re Sacramenti, id est, corpore Christi. Est igitur Sacramentum, & res Sacramenti, id est corpus Christi. Item (addam caetera, quia hic unicus textus totam de Coeno Domini sententiam ex mente Reformatorum commodè explicat) Caro ejus est, quam forma panis opertam, in Sacramento accipimus, & sanguis ejus, quem sub vini specie, & sapore potamus. Caro videlicet carnis, & sanguis Sacramentum est sanguinis: carne & sanguine, utroque invisibili, intelligibili, Spirituali significatur visibile Domini nostri Iesu Christi corpus palpabile, plenum gratia omnium virtutum, & divina majestate. Item: Sicut ergo caelestis panis, qui vere Christi caro est, suo modo vocatur corpus Christi; cum revera sit Sacramentum corporis Christi, illius videlicet, quod visibile, palpabile, mortale, in cruce est suspensum; vocaturque ipsa immolatio carnis, quae Sacerdotis manibus fit, Christi passio, crucifixio, non rei veritate, sed significante mysterio; sic Sacramentum fidei, quod Baptismus intelligitur, fides est. Emphatica satis omnia sunt, claréque docent, 1. Manducationem Sacramentalem, & Sacramenta, sive elementa, requirere, & rem Sacramenti. 2. Carne & sanguine invisibili, visibile & palpabile significari Christi corpus. 3. Panem caelestem, modo suo, id est Sacramentali (quis enim alius Sacramentorum modus?) vocari Christi corpus. 4. Id, quod vocatur Christi corpus, ejus tantum esse Sacramentum, symbolum, signum. 5. Eadem ratione baptismum vocari fidem, quâ immolatio Sacerdotis repraesentativa, vocetur Christi passio &c. significante nempe mysterio. Panem autem vinum mera,id est, vacua & inania signa esse, juxta Tigurinos, supra jam, ne quisquam hac nos oneraret injuria, modeste fumus deprecati. Qui ex infirmitate haftenus vel insciria tam crassum nobis impegerunt errorem, illis ignoscat Deus: qui vero, contra scientiam & conscientiam, Ecclesias reformatas, calumniis onerare pergent, eos, dubio procul, gravissima tandem calumniatorum manebit poena, ἀκούμενοι ἐκλινῶν ἡσὶ ὀμμάτων, dormire nescius atque vindex Dei oculus. Certis, etsi tacitis vindicta Dei sequetur pedibus. Sed ita, credendo in eum simpliciter, manducaremus corpus & sanguinem ejus, & praeterea panem & vinum: quo facto nihil esset opus pane & vino. Credendo in Christum, manducari Christum, ne quidem controverti amplius debet. Habemus authorem ipsum Christum, Interpretes Patres, consentientem Ecclesiam Romanam: Quid igitur in hoc scirpo quaeramus nodum? Nec tamen propterea elementorum usus inanis est, aut superfluus. Utramque Christus manducationem urget; Mysticam, sive Spiritualem, quae sit absque symbolis, sola fide, Joh. 6. Sacramentalem vero, quae symbola requirit, & de qua Matthaeus, Marcus, Lucas, & Paulus; in Institutione Coenae Dominicae; agunt. Regeneratio opus est solius Spiritus sancti. Qui per Sp. S. non fuerit regenitus, non ingredietur regnum coelorum, Joh. 3. 5. Neque tamen propterea baptismus, lavacrum regenerationis esse definit. Non est aliquid qui rigat, nec qui plantat; sed ille tantum, qui dat incrementum: Num vero nec plantandum, nec rigandum? Summae & execrandae ingratitudinis in Deum fuligine se aspergunt, qui eximiam & plane paternam Christi pro salute nostra curam, in utriusque manducationis mandato, hoc non agnoscunt. Ne externis, quae non semper praesto sunt, symbolis salutem animarum Christus alligaret, mysticam, ubi, absque culpa contemtus, alia haberi non poterit, vera fide peractam, sufficere ostendit. Iterum, ut in ordinaria Evangelii dispensatione infirmitatem nostram juvaret, fidem nutantem corroboraret, captui se nostro accommodaret, promissionibus suis signa addidit, & sigilla, & ea quidem, quae in sensus nostros incurrunt. Haec Deus conjunxit, cur nos illa separaremus? Subordinata non pugnare, vel Dialecticae Scholae nos docent. Repetat doctissimus Vir, quae supra, de manducatione mystica & Sacramentali plenius disseruimus. Sed ita fides & Sacramentum Eucharistia res erit eadem? Inanis, hujus confusionis, est metus! Id tantum sequitur, fidem, aptum & idoneum recipiendi & manducandi corporis Christi esse organum. Esse os Spirituale, quod rem Sacramenti percipit. Manducationem dari Spiritualem sive mysticam, tam in Sacramento, quàm extra Sacramentum, constanter affirmamus; non, quòd Spiritualis & Sacramentalis, per omnia, eadem sit, sed quia hæc illam includat; & omnis quidem digna manducatio Sacramentalis necessariò etiam esse debet Spiritualis: at non vice versa. Sacramentalis enim manducationis materia duplex est, elementaris & cœlestis; mysticæ una tantum, cœlestis. Mystica necessitatem medii habet; Sacramentalis præcepti. Ergo non opus est hanc facere in Sacramento, inquit Vir doctissimus. Suo alius credat periculo: Nobis ex sacra Scriptura mandatum Dominicum non est ignotum. Hoc, quod ego feci, facite in mei recordationem Luc. 22. verf. 19: Mandatum igitur Domini geminum, ad geminam nos manducationem; tam Sacramentalem, quàm mysticam; obstringit. Quod quidem discrimem, de quo supra suius, miror doctissimum Virum non satis assequi. Breviter, hæc manducatio omnibus Christianis imperatur omni loco & tempore; illa iis tantum, qui se probare possunt in legitimo cœnæ usu: Illa & signum & rem signatam ambitu suo comprehendit; hæc rem signatam tantum. Hæc privatim fieri potest, domi, belli, ruri, in remotissimis & inhospitis tesquis; illa in cætu, & synaxi publica ordinariè peragi solet. Hanc Christus injungit Joh. cap. 6. Illa præcipit in Evangelio, in institutione Cœnæ suæ. Nulla etiam hinc metuenda contrarietas, etsi & Augustinum & Gratianum intelligamus de manducatione Spirituali, quæ in ipso quoque Sacramento alia esse non debet, symbolorum licet fulcimentis sit stipata. Lectio proinde Gratiani varia nec adversarios juvat, nec nobis incommodat. Illud utrinque in confesso est, Gratianum, ex Augustino, recte legere : Vt quid paras dentes & ventrem? Crede & manducasti. Adeoque manducationem, de qua Christus Joh. 6. recte, ex mente Augustini, & Gratiani, ad fidem referri, quæ cum orali manducatione, quam Christus penitus, disputatione sua luculenta, tollit, nihil habeat commune. Concedere, Johannis 6. agi de manducatione atque saginatione invisibili fidei, justitiæ, gratiæ, Charitatis; & negare, de ulla ibidem sermonem esse manducatione Christi; est nescire, quid sit Christum Spiritualiter, & vera fide manducare. Qui credendo, etiam in legitimo Sacramenti usu, Christum manducant, non corporis tantum ejus Sacramento tenus & symbolicè fiunt participes; sed omnium Christi meritorum, adeoque & justitiæ illius, gratiæ, Spiritus sancti, quorum Augustinus meminit; de quibus supra Sect. 9. prolixius differuimus. Qui manducat carnem meam (iterum recito verba Augustini ex Gratiano de Confec. d. 2. C. 59.) & meum bibit sanguinem, habet vitam æternam. Participatione enim filii (quod est per unitatem corporis Christi & sanguinis) homo manducans vivit, non sumens tantum in Sacramento (quod & mali faciunt) sed usque ad Spiritus participationem, ut in corpore Domini tanquam membrum maneat, & ejus Spiritu vegetetur, quod est, dum ejus mandata servat. Hanc difertius Spiritualium donorum communionem Apostolus exprimit, quando ait: Christum nobis factum sapientiam a Deo, justitiam, sanctificationem, redemtionem; 1. Cor. 1. 30. Manet ergo Tigurinorum thesis & scopus, ex Augustini Tract. 25, & 26. in Johannem, quod non, ubicunque mentio fit manducationis corporis Christi, necessario debeat intelligi oralis. Sive enim de Christo loquatur Augustinus, sive de merito & thesauris per mortem ejus acquisitis; illud semper extra controversiae aleam erit positum, edendi vocabulum improprie sumi, & Spiritualiter: manducationem notare mysticam & Spiritualem corporis Christi, quae fiat corde credendo, non dente premendo: Ὁπερ εἰδει δεῖξαι. Nonne igitur (ut doctissimo Viro sua reponamus verba,) id quod res est, profiteri praestat, & tam clara Christi, apud Johannem, verba cap. 6. intelligere, sicut per se satis intelliguntur, a v. 48. non de manducatio ne futura Eucharistia mox instituenda (cur enim illud fieri non potuit, suo loco, Sect. 9. ipsis adversariorum argumentis evicimus) sed de manducatione praesenti, nulla symbolorum fulcro subsistentia. Qui manducat meam carnem, & bibit meum sanguinem, habet vitam aeternam; in praesenti tum loquebatur Christus, non futuro. Et qui jam tum, eo modo, quem Christus exegit, Tros Rutulus fuerit, carnem ejus comedit; non demum postea transsubstantiandam ex pane, quem nec ad manus tunc habuit, nec consecravit, sed existentem jam; vitae utique candidatus erat aeternae. Nisi omnibus illis, qui in Christum, jam multis ante cum Abrahamo seculis crediderunt, neque tamen corpus ejus, in Sacramento longe post instituendo, ederūt, salutem, contra expressa Christi verba, velimus abjudicare; Christum de institutione Coenae Dominicae loquentem hoc loco introducere non debemus. Sed satis textus Johannis à nobis supra vindicatus est. Patres omnes, vel de Eucharistia locum intelligere, vel de corpore in Eucharistia transsubstantiato, nec dare possumus; nec, si daremus, causa propterea nostra periclitaretur. Rejicimus Virum doctissimum ad Sect. 9. ubi hanc antiquitatis larvam detraximus. Sed nec recentiorum, & veteratium quidem omnium, hanc esse sententiam, ibidem monstravimus. Ut turpiter se det Vir doctissimus, quòd adeò confidenter in Patrum antiquorum omnium, & recentiorum exemplo, praesidium, quod siculneum plane est, quaerat. Verba institutionis apud Matthæum, Marcum, Lucam, & Paulum lucem accipere, ex verbis Christi Joh. c. 6. non modo libenter damus, sed etiam, Sectione citata, rationibus confirmavimus. Quod verò frustra laborare Tigurinos, Articulus tertius concludit, in quibusdam locis Augustini, Athanasii, Hieronymi, Tertulliani, Origenis, & aliorum, ad suam manducationem mysticam & Spiritualem tantum in Sacramento, quam extra Sacramentum, detorquendis; illud ipsum in Virum doctissimum retorquemus. Patrum enim hypothesis, de manducatione corporis Christi Spirituali, de corpore Christi localiter in cœlum sublato, de veritate corporis gloriosi; de symbolis, Typis, antitypis &c. cum Transsubstantiatione subsistere non posse, tam est apertum, quàm quod apertissimum. Exceptionibus ad Patrum dicta, à Tigurinis allata, Vir doctissimus nihil proficit. Vas quidem vitreum allambit; sed pultem non attingit. Corticem arrodit, nucleum non lædit: Circumstantiarum varietatem magno conatu quæsierit, substantiæ diversitatem non reperit. Et quoniam; Virum doctissimum, ad loca quædam Patrum in causæ nostræ subsidium vocata, excepturum, se jam in Disceptatione publica ad ea respondisse; haud obscure augurari potuimus, minimo minus abfuit, quin hanc etiam illi unius atque alterius testimonii examine, eripuisse tergi versandi anansam. Sed veriti, ne, quod in disceptationibus ejusmodi fieri frequenter solet, scopo ad quem utrinque tendimus, neglecto; meta, ad quam currendum, posthabita, seria hæc de re magni momenti disquisitio in puram putam abiret vitilitigationem, aut conqueri jure Vir doctissimus posset, me, non collato pede congressum, carptim tantum ea, quæ placuissent, perstrinxisse, hæc jam diverticula, anfractus, & suffugia ostendere noluimus. Suo dicendum erit loco, aliter Patres à nobis citatos loqui, aliter eos interpretari doctissimum disceptatorem. Nisi, quod speramus, ex iis, quæ citata à nobis sunt, defæcatioris antiquitatis documenta, ipse, quo est candore, & judicio, sit animadversurus, luculentiora Theodoreti, verbi gratiâ, Gelasii, Augustini esse verba; argumenta, quæ, à symbolis Sacramentalibus petita, Transsubstantiatoribus Eutychianis iidem opposuerunt, solidiora & nervosiora, quàm quæ in alienû, & à nobis diversum, rapi possint sensum. Legat, quæso, cum cura & attentione (sed & absque præjudicio) totam Theodoreti disputationem, nostram ex eodem formatam analysin, expendat, cum suis exceptionibus conferat, pudebit, credo, deinceps disertis disertissimi scriptoris verbis, tanto cum veritatis dispendio, injuriam facere. Solis radiantis negare splendorem, & Theodoreti suffragium bonæ Reformatorum causæ subtrahere, perinde est. Hoc expectamus à doctissimo Viro, ut, quæ dicta à nobis sunt, æqui boníque consulat. Non ignorat, Apologeticum genus scribendi & antiquissimum esse, & innocentissimum, addo & utilissimum. Nunquam Majores nostri hæc infeliciter arripuerunt arma. Nobis etiam bene cessura, speramus. Non calumniado modò, sed & defendendo aliquid semper dicitur, aut scribitur, quod hæreat. Si quæ fortassis in Apologia nostra asseque nondum potest vitio illud ei non dabimus. Novimus enim, quòd resta eum, quo semel odore recens est imbuta, diu servet. Novimus, χαλεπὸν μεζοδιδάσκειν difficile esse ea dedisce re, quibus à puero assuevimus: Novimus, domesticum, parentum exemplum, magis in veneratione esse, quàm extraneum, opinione adversariorum. Qui oculorum usum in Evangelio recepit, non statim lynces provocare fuisset ausus. Homines ei ambulare visi fuerunt tanquam arbores, Marc. 8.25 Paulatim ad se rediit. Id nobis satis hac vice fuerit, constare doctissimo Viro, nostræ nobis de Eucharistia sententiæ rationes abundè suppetere: Constare, Tigurinam Ecclesiam magis convenienter Evangelio & Scripturæ docere, quàm Romanam. Si hoc obtinuerimus, res erit in vado: sin minus, & scrupuli adhuc obstiterint (alii tamen, quàm qui in Disceptatione sunt deresti, quibus etiam doctissimum Virum facilime, ubi nihil aliud superesse nobis innotuerit, liberrabimus) operam nostram tanto ei libentius offerimus, quanto majorem in Tigurinos amorem atque solicitudinem, ad scripti sui calcem, profitetur. Sed manum de tabula, ubi velunum adhuc addiderimus.
units.tr: "Then it would follow," says the most learned man, "that not only the body and blood of Christ are eaten through faith, but also the bread and wine." It certainly follows. In the lawful use of the Supper, these two external elements, bread and wine (an earthly thing), and the body of Christ (a heavenly thing), are given to believers in an inseparable bond. We have shown from the authority of your own theologians above that this necessarily follows from the present chapter. The words that the most learned man's scruple should be removed by are fitting. They are taken from Augustine's book of Sentences, quoted by Prosper from the Decretum, part 3, De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter 48: "This is what we say: we contend in every way to prove that the sacrifice of the Church is made up of two things and consists of two: the visible form of the elements, and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ. Just as the person of Christ consists and is made up of God and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man, because each thing contains within itself the nature and truth of those things of which it is made. The sacrifice of the Church, however, is made up of the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ. Therefore there is the sacrament, and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ." Likewise (I will add the rest, since this single text conveniently explains the whole doctrine of the Lord's Supper in the mind of the Reformers): "It is his flesh that we receive in the sacrament under the form of bread, veiled, and his blood that we drink under the appearance and taste of wine. The flesh, namely, is the sacrament of the flesh, and the blood is the sacrament of the blood: by the flesh and blood, both invisible, intelligible and spiritual, is signified the visible, palpable body of our Lord Jesus Christ, full of the grace of all virtues and of divine majesty." Again: "Just as, therefore, the heavenly bread, which is truly the flesh of Christ, is in its own way called the body of Christ, since in reality it is the sacrament of the body of Christ, namely of that which, visible, palpable and mortal, was suspended on the cross; and just as the very immolation of the flesh, which is performed by the hands of the priest, is called the passion, the crucifixion of Christ, not in the reality of the thing but in the significant mystery; so the sacrament of faith, which is understood as baptism, is faith." All these statements are emphatic enough and clearly teach: (1) that sacramental eating requires the sacraments, or elements, and the reality of the sacrament; (2) that the visible and palpable body of Christ is signified by the invisible flesh and blood; (3) that the heavenly bread is called the body of Christ in its own way, that is, sacramentally (for what other way is there for the sacraments?); (4) that what is called the body of Christ is only the sacrament, the symbol, the sign of it; (5) that for the same reason baptism is called faith, just as the priest's representative immolation is called the passion of Christ, etc., namely by a significant mystery. As for bread and wine being "mere, that is, empty and vain signs, according to the Tigurines," we have already above modestly protested against this, lest anyone burden us with this injustice. God forgive those who, out of weakness or ignorance, have so far fastened such a gross error upon us; but those who, against knowledge and conscience, shall go on burdening the reformed Churches with slanders, undoubtedly the most serious punishment of the slanderers will await them: "ever-wakeful, never sleeping, the avenging eye of God" [ἀκούμενοι ἐκλινῶν ἡσὶ ὀμμάτων]. The vengeance of God will follow them, though with silent feet. "But thus, by simply believing in him, we would eat the body and blood of him, and besides the bread and wine; and then there would be no need of bread and wine." That by believing in Christ we eat Christ ought no longer to be disputed at all. We have Christ himself as the author, the Fathers as interpreters, and the Roman Church agreeing: why then do we seek a knot in this reed? "Nevertheless, the use of the elements is not on that account empty or superfluous." Christ insists on both kinds of eating: the mystical, or spiritual, which is without symbols, by faith alone (John 6); and the sacramental, which requires symbols, and of which Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul speak in the institution of the Lord's Supper. Regeneration is the work of the Holy Spirit alone: unless a man is born again of the Spirit he will not enter the kingdom of heaven (John 3:5). Yet for all that, baptism is not thereby denied to be the washing of regeneration. "Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase" (1 Cor. 3:7). Are we then to neither plant nor water? Those who in the matter of both kinds of eating, with a command from Christ, do not acknowledge this, smear themselves with the soot of the most extreme and detestable ingratitude toward God, who ignore Christ's remarkable and plainly fatherly care for our salvation. So that Christ might not tie the salvation of souls to external symbols, which are not always at hand, he shows that the mystical eating, performed in true faith, where it cannot otherwise be had without fault of contempt, is sufficient. Again, so that in the ordinary dispensation of the gospel he might help our weakness, strengthen our wavering faith, and accommodate himself to our capacity, he added to his promises signs and seals, and indeed those which fall under our senses. God has joined these things together; why should we separate them? Even the schools of dialectic teach us that subordinate things do not fight. The most learned man repeats what we argued above at greater length about mystical and sacramental eating. But will the reality of the sacrament and faith therefore be the same thing? The fear of this confusion is empty! It follows only that faith is the fit and suitable organ for receiving and eating the body of Christ: a spiritual mouth which perceives the reality of the sacrament. "We constantly affirm that a spiritual or mystical eating is given both in the sacrament and outside the sacrament," not because the spiritual and the sacramental are in every respect the same, but because the former includes the latter; and every worthy sacramental eating must necessarily also be spiritual, but not the reverse. For the matter of sacramental eating is twofold, elemental and heavenly; the mystical has only one, the heavenly. The mystical has the necessity of a means; the sacramental that of a precept. Therefore, says the most learned man, it is not necessary to do the former in the sacrament. Let another believe at his own risk: for us the Lord's command is not unknown from holy Scripture. "This do in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19). Therefore the Lord's command binds us to a twofold eating, as much sacramental as mystical. This distinction, about which I spoke above, I wonder that the most learned man does not sufficiently grasp. Briefly: the former eating is commanded to all Christians at every place and time; the latter only to those who can prove themselves in the lawful use of the Supper. The former embraces within its compass both the sign and the thing signified; the latter only the thing signified. The latter can be done privately, at home, in war, in the country, in the most remote and inhospitable wastes; the former is ordinarily celebrated in an assembly and public synaxis. Christ enjoins the latter in John chapter 6; the former he prescribes in the gospel, in the institution of his Supper. Nor is there any contradiction to fear from this, even if we understand both Augustine and Gratian to speak of spiritual eating, which in the sacrament itself ought to be no other, though it is crowded with the props of symbols. Therefore the varied reading of Gratian neither helps our opponents nor inconveniences us. It is agreed on both sides that Gratian rightly reads, following Augustine: "Why do you prepare teeth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten." And so the eating about which Christ speaks in John 6 is rightly referred, according to the mind of Augustine and Gratian, to faith, which has nothing in common with the oral eating that Christ entirely removes by his brilliant argument. To concede that "John 6 treats of the eating and invisible feeding of faith, righteousness, grace, and charity", and yet to deny "that there is any discourse there about eating Christ," is to fail to know what it is to eat Christ spiritually and by true faith. Those who, believing, eat Christ even in the lawful use of the sacrament, become partakers not only of his body in the sacrament and symbolically, but of all the merits of Christ, and therefore of his righteousness, grace and the Holy Spirit, of which Augustine makes mention; of which we spoke more fully above in Section 9. "He who eats my flesh" (again I quote the words of Augustine from Gratian, De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter 59) "and drinks my blood, has eternal life. For by participation in the Son" (which is through the unity of the body and blood of Christ) "the man who eats lives, not merely taking in the sacrament (which the wicked also do), but even to the participation of the Spirit, so as to remain as a member in the body of the Lord, and to be quickened by his Spirit, which is done while he keeps his commandments." The Apostle expresses this communion of spiritual gifts more plainly when he says that Christ was made to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30). The thesis and aim of the Tigurines therefore remains, from Augustine's Tractates 25 and 26 on John, that wherever mention is made of eating the body of Christ, it need not necessarily be understood as oral. For whether Augustine speaks of Christ himself, or of the merit and treasures acquired by his death, it will always stand beyond the reach of controversy that the word "eat" is used improperly and spiritually, denoting the mystical and spiritual eating of the body of Christ, which is done by believing with the heart, not by pressing with the teeth: which was to be shown [Ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι]. Is it not better, then (to return the most learned man's own words), "to profess what is the case, and to understand the clear words of Christ in John chapter 6, as they are sufficiently understood of themselves, from verse 48, not of the eating of the Eucharist about to be instituted soon (for why that could not be done in its proper place, Section 9, we proved from the very arguments of our opponents), but of the present eating, which stands on no props of symbols. 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life': Christ was speaking then in the present, not the future. And whoever at that time, in the manner Christ required, was a Trojan or a Rutulian, ate his flesh, not one to be transubstantiated later from bread which he then neither had at hand nor consecrated, but already existing; he was assuredly a candidate for eternal life. Unless we wish to deny salvation to all those who believed in Christ many ages before, along with Abraham, and yet did not eat his body in the sacrament instituted long afterwards, contrary to the express words of Christ, we ought not to introduce Christ here speaking about the institution of the Lord's Supper. But the text of John has already been sufficiently vindicated by us above. "All the Fathers" we cannot grant either to "understand the passage" of the Eucharist, or of the body transubstantiated in the Eucharist; nor, if we did grant it, would our cause on that account be endangered. We refer the most learned man to Section 9, where we stripped away this mask of antiquity. But we showed there also that this is not the opinion of "all, both recent and very old" writers. So the most learned man shows himself in a shameful light, in that he seeks, so confidently, protection from the example of "all" the ancient and recent Fathers, a support which is plainly a spider's web. That "the words of institution in Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul" receive light from the words of Christ in John chapter 6, we not only gladly grant but, in the section cited, also confirmed by arguments. As for the third article's conclusion that the Tigurines "labour in vain" to twist "certain passages of Augustine, Athanasius, Jerome, Tertullian, Origen and others to their mystical and spiritual eating in the sacrament only, and not outside the sacrament," we turn this very charge back upon the most learned man. For the Fathers' hypothesis, of "spiritual eating of the body of Christ, of the body of Christ locally raised into heaven, of the truth of a glorious body; of symbols, types, antitypes, etc.", cannot stand together with transubstantiation, as plainly as anything can be plain. The most learned man achieves nothing with the objections brought by the Tigurines against the sayings of the Fathers. He licks the glass vessel, but does not touch the porridge; he gnaws the bark, but does not harm the kernel. He has made a great effort to seek variety of circumstances, but he does not find a difference of substance. And since we could foresee that the most learned man, when some passages of the Fathers were called upon in aid of our cause, would make excuses, which he had already answered in the public Disputation, we did not doubt that he would, with the examination of one or two testimonies, wriggle out of the fight with a turn of his back, and very nearly so. But fearing that, as often happens in disputations of this kind, the goal toward which we both strive might be neglected, the finish line disregarded, and this serious investigation of a matter of great importance dwindle into pure and useless wrangling, or that the most learned man might justly complain that I did not join battle on equal footing, and had only touched in passing on what pleased me, we did not wish to show these side-paths, windings and hiding-places. It will have to be said in its place that the Fathers we cited speak one way, and that the learned disputant interprets them another. Unless, as we hope, from those things we have cited, the documents of a purer antiquity, he himself, with the candour and judgement which are his, will notice that the words of Theodoret, for example, of Gelasius and of Augustine are clearer; and that the arguments which the same men set against the Eutychian transubstantiators, drawn from the sacramental symbols, are more solid and sinewy than what can be snatched into a sense alien to us and different from ours. I ask him to read with care and attention (but also without prejudice) the whole disputation of Theodoret, to weigh our analysis formed from the same, and to compare it with his own objections; I think he will be ashamed henceforth to do an injury, at such great cost to the truth, to the eloquent words of that most eloquent writer. To deny the brightness of the shining sun and to withdraw the testimony of Theodoret from the good cause of the Reformers is much the same. This we expect from the most learned man: that he take in good part what has been said by us, fairly and kindly. He is not unaware that the apologetic genre of writing is most ancient, most innocent, and, I add, most useful. Our forefathers never took up these arms unhappily. We hope they will also turn out well for us. Not only in accusing but also in defending something is always said or written which sticks. If perhaps there is anything in our Apology which he cannot yet grasp, we shall not impute the fault to him. For we know that a vessel keeps the odour with which it was once steeped for a long time. We know that "it is hard to unlearn" [χαλεπὸν μεταδιδάσκειν] "those things to which we have been accustomed from boyhood." We know that the domestic example of parents has more veneration than the opinion of outsiders, our opponents. He who has received the use of his eyes in the gospel would not have dared at once to challenge the lynxes. Men seemed to him to walk like trees (Mark 8:24); little by little he came to himself. For the present, let it be enough that it is established to the most learned man that the reasons for our opinion about the Eucharist are abundantly at hand; that the Tigurine Church teaches more agreeably to the gospel and Scripture than the Roman. If we obtain this, the matter will be on safe ground. But if not, and scruples still stand in the way (other than those which are in the Disputation, from which we will also very easily free the most learned man, when we learn that nothing else remains for us), we offer our labour to him all the more willingly, as he professes at the end of his writing a greater love and concern for the Tigurines. But I take my hand from the tablet, where I shall perhaps still add a little.

units.la: IX. Credis, Rex Agrippa, quaerit Paulus Act. 26.verf.27.28. Prophetis? Scio te credere. Agrippa vero dixit Paulo, propemodum persuades mihi, ut fiam Christianus. Ego dedoctissimo Viro illud mihi polliceor, pro explorato eum deinceps habiturum, Reformatorum de Eucharistia sententiam non ita profanam esse, irreligiosam, aut sacrilegam, ut convitia proprerea ubique mereatur & atrocissima supplicia. Non nuda abiis in CoenaDomini proponi signa, aut vacua symbola; sed ipsum Christum, ipsius corpus & sanguinem vere communicari. Surdis fere haftenus fabulam narravimus, si quando causae innocentissimae susceperimus patrocinium. Jam vero, quando Vir doctissimus publice testatur, se Tigurinis omnibus publice & privatim, in coelis & terris optime consultum velle; cur non vel hanc sperenus ab eo gratiam, ut causae nostrae vel aliqua saltem (neque enim dum omnia enarravimus) momenta legat, expendat; judicet denique, an digni simus, qui vel desertores habeamur vestigiorum Dominicorum, a quibus ne latum unguem recedimus, vel contemtores verae Ecclesiae, vel purae antiquitatis derisores, prout magna ubique licentia traducimur. Spero, non propemodum tantum, sed ἐν πολλῷ, -imo in totum, nos doctissimo Viro perspuasisse, ut clementius deinceps & aequius de nobis sentiat. Et vero nec dum videmus, ullam sive odii, sive indignationis in Tigurinis residere culpam, quod religionis non eadem vel dogmata, vel ritus, vel etiam administrationis regimem, cum Ecclesia Romana, agnoscant, Curae merito fuit Tigurinis, ut Deo darent, quod Dei est, hominibus, quod illis debetur. Amicus illis Cicero, amicus Plato, amicus Graecus, amicus Barbarus, sed magis amica veritas. Matrem Ecclesiam venerantur, reverentur; sed tum demum, ubi Patris coelestis non retrahit authoritas. Et cur, quaeso, Tigurini aliis, amicis caeteroquin & Confoederatis, propter eam invisi sint aut exosi religionem, quae solum Deum authorem suum agnoscit & veneratur? Cui nullius articuli fundamentalis objici aut exprobrari potest defectus? Quae sola fidei & vitae eam recipit cynosuram, quam Deus ipse praescripsit, Apostoli retinuerunt, tota Ecclesia primitiva reverenter coluit? Qui suo ab Ecclesia Romana discessu nihil aliud intenderunt, quam ut gloriae Dei, & saluti proximi consulerent. Num propterea, ne quid gravius dicam, vulgi fabula sint, & maleferiatorum incus? Patere, doctissime Vir, modestum destrum hoc meum, ex sinceritate animi profectum, alloquium. Repeto igitur, magnaque fretus optimae causae fiducia ingemino, religionem Reformatam solam esse, quae solius authoritatis, indubitatae divinae, suffulta stet fundamento. Soli enim sunt Reformati, qui Scriptis Prophetarum, Evangelistarum & Apostolorum, tanquam unico religionis principio, adeoque, revelatae per Scripturas, Dei voluntati inniuntur. Quam praeclare de hac Christianismi coelesti cynosura metreatur Roma, suo heic loco relinquemus. Hanc enim Camarinam movere, hujus instituti non est. Ex phrasibus impiis, disputationibus absurdis, processibus horrendis posteritas, si quae futura est, judicabit, utra Ecclesia, Pontificia an reformata de Verbo Veri & aeterni Dei, religiosius sentiat atque loquatur. Illud dolemus, non perjurium tantum, magno Christianismi damno, Christianis, a Turcis exprobrari, sed ab iisdem, nec sine ratione, inde a multis retroactis seculis, fuisse objectum, illos novos ritus, nova dogmata, novum regimen, contra expressam Dei voluntatem, contra Christi, supremi Doctoris authoritatem invexisse. Horret animus, stantque comae, quoties memini, jam ante Reformationem, magno inter Mauritanos Viro, natam occasionem, Christianis autem vellicandi, iisdemque objiciendi, sanctorum invocationem, Ἁγιολογίαν
units.tr: IX. Credis, Rex Agrippa, asks Paul (Act. 26.27,28). Prophetis? Scio te credere. Agrippa vero dixit Paulo, propemodum persuades mihi, ut fiam Christianus. I promise the most learned man this much: that he will henceforth hold it as settled that the Reformed view of the Eucharist is not so profane, irreligious or sacrilegious that it deserves insults everywhere and the most atrocious punishments. We do not propose bare signs or empty symbols in the Lord's Supper, but that Christ himself, his body and blood, are truly communicated. Hitherto we have told our tale almost to deaf ears whenever we have taken up the defence of a most innocent cause. But now that this most learned man publicly declares that he wishes all the Tigurines, publicly and privately, to be most well provided for in heaven and on earth, why should we not hope to obtain from him this favour: that he read and weigh at least some of the points of our case (for we have not yet set out everything), and finally judge whether we deserve to be regarded either as deserters of the Lord's footsteps, from which we do not depart a finger's breadth, or as despisers of the true Church, or as mockers of pure antiquity, which is how we are everywhere slandered with great licence. I hope that we have persuaded the most learned man not merely almost, but [ἐν πολλῷ] – indeed altogether – so that he will henceforth judge us more mildly and fairly. And indeed we do not yet see any fault in the Tigurines, whether of hatred or of indignation, in that they acknowledge neither the same doctrines, nor rites, nor even the same form of government of the religion as the Roman Church. It was rightly the Tigurines' concern to give to God what is God's, and to men what is owed to them. Cicero is their friend, Plato is their friend, the Greek is their friend, the barbarian is their friend, but truth is a friend still more. They venerate and revere Mother Church, but only when the authority of the heavenly Father does not call them back. And why, I ask, should the Tigurines be hated or detested by others, who are otherwise friends and confederates, on account of that religion which acknowledges and worships God alone as its author? Against which no lack of any fundamental article can be objected or reproached? Which alone takes as its guiding star that which God himself prescribed, which the Apostles held to, and which the whole primitive Church reverently observed? Those who, in departing from the Roman Church, intended nothing other than to serve the glory of God and the salvation of their neighbour. Are they therefore, to speak no more harshly, the stuff of popular fable and the anvil of wicked men? Allow me, most learned sir, to address you with this modest speech of mine, which proceeds from sincerity of mind. I repeat, therefore, and, relying on the great confidence of a most good cause, I say again: the Reformed religion alone stands supported on the foundation of sole and indubitable divine authority. For the Reformed alone rest upon the writings of the Prophets, Evangelists and Apostles as the single principle of religion, and thus upon the will of God revealed through the Scriptures. How splendidly Rome measures itself against this heavenly guiding star of Christianity we shall leave in its place here. For it is not our purpose to stir up this hornet's nest. From impious phrases, absurd disputations and horrible proceedings, posterity, if there is to be any, will judge which Church, the Papist or the Reformed, thinks and speaks more religiously concerning the Word of the true and eternal God. This we lament: that not only perjury, to the great damage of Christianity, is thrown in the teeth of Christians by the Turks, but that by the same people, and not without reason, it has been objected for many centuries past that they have introduced new rites, new dogmas and a new government, against the express will of God and against the authority of Christ, the supreme Teacher. My spirit shudders and my hair stands on end whenever I remember the occasion, arising even before the Reformation through a great man among the Moors, of plucking at and objecting to Christians the invocation of saints, [Ἁγιολογίαν] hagiology,

units.la: τεία
units.tr: -teia [τεία]

units.la: τξείαν, judicium Episcoporum ἀνυπεύθυνον, superstitiosas creaturarum consecrationes, cultum imaginum, fraudulenta in iis confirmandis miracula, Confessionem auricularem, festorum multiplicationem, aliáque, humana authoritate, stimulante vel dominandi libidine, vel novaturiendi pruritu, contra Dei verbum, contra Christi mandatum, paulatim fuisse recepta, commendata, obtrusa. Talia per Reformationem sunt abolita, quod Scripturae fundamento carerent. Haec ergo labes illa est, haec macula, quâ se Ecclesia Reformata, sponsa Christi, quod aliam, quàm Sponsi vocem audire nolit, reddit infamem. Quò abibimus; quaerit Petrus, ex Servatore; verba aeterna vitae habes? Joh.6.68. Quò nos alio abiremus? Vir doctissime? An ad Concilium Tridentinum, quò rejici solent Romanenses? Hoc, nisi me fallat opinio mea, non suadebis. An ad Pontificem Romanum, Oecumenicum, & ipsis Conciliis superiorem, Episcopum? Hoc nec ipse facies, nec aliis commendabis, qui pro authoritate Conciliorum libentius pugnabis. An ad Decreta Pontificum? Nihil hic solidi. Negat Johannes & Stephanus quod Formosus affirmavit, & nihil usitatius Romanae sedis novis Praestatis, quàm Praedecessorum refigere placita. Traditiones, quas vocant Apostolicas, consulemus? Quis vero eas, quae hoc nomine veniunt, non esse supposititi-as, præstabit? Quis exactum hactenus Catalogum earum proferre fuit ausus? An Patrum tandem stabimus simpliciter judicio? Vix author erit Vir doctissimus, cui non est obscurum, nec Romæ placere omnia, quæ illi scripserunt, qui & multa ignorârunt, & sæpe inter se sunt conflictati, interdum secum ipsi pugnârunt. Quid ergo restat, nisi ad eum tantùm recurramus, qui solus via est, vita, & veritas, Joh. 14. v. 6. Habet tamen & Ecclesia Romana verbum Dei, Biblia sacra? Habeat; sola tamen non habet, sed alia religionis, eámque curvam, imò Lei biâ Traditionum ad huc sequitur regulam: Quo certè nomine Reformati Ecclesiæ Romanæ palmam felicitatis præripiunt. Vel optimus cibus, ex levissimo veneni pulvisculo exitium afferre potest. Purum, defæcatum cum Ecclesia veteri, Reformati agnoscunt Ἰατρεῖον ψυχῆς, medicamen anima, Scripturam sacram; non mixtum. Ut tutiùs, citiùs & jucundiùs ille curat chirurgus, qui emplastrum vulneri adhibet, quod omnium consensu salutare est, & malo curando sufficiens; quàm qui, sub specie commodioris medicamenti, alia admisçet, de quibus inter artis peritos disceptatur: Ita minori cum periculo agunt, qui in examinandis, determinandis, recipiendis fidei dogmatibus, illud tantùm amplectuntur, quod omnium calculo & suffragio, ubique & semper in Ecclesia Christiana pro divino, citra controversiam, oraculo fuit habitum & cui officium cum judicis in fide, tum judicis in vita, nemo fuit aulus abjudicare; quàm qui, sub prætextu plenioris revelationis, ea etiam, quæ dubia semper fuerunt & controversa, arripiunt. Non ergò vel Angelus, si aliud annunciaverit Evangelium, quàm quòd annunciatum nobis est, tam insigni cimelio nos defraudare debet. Sed & cur ea Ecclesia vel odium, aliquo suo merito, aliorum expectet, vel convitium, quæ salutis retinet fundamentum? At retinere illud Tigurinos, Confessio Helvetica fidem abunde facit. Quòd errores, qui, paulatim dogmatibus adnati, vel periculose à scopo aberrant, vel aliàs fundamento insidiantur, emusçárunt, id verò in laude ponendum erat iis, qui Deo magis, quàm hominibus, Apostolico exemplo, obediverunt. Vel unū inapricum proferat Schola Pontificia articulum, in Ecclesia Dominica, Apostolica, primitiva fundamentalem, quem Reformatores nostri rejecerint. Si ergò salutis fundamento per Reformationem nihil decessit; cætera contrà dogmata, ritus, & regimen in Ecclesia hactenus Romana observata, alia quidem directè, alia indirectè fundamentum labefactant; alia conscientias miserè turbant; alia per infirmitatem ingenii humani non capiuntur; alia ab interna devotione plebem abstrahunt, cur non illi lubentissime accedamus religioni, quæ salvo fundamento, tot incommodis & difficultatibus, periculosis & modestis non impeditur? Quid, quaeso, hic iterum vel reatus, vel criminis? Aut num propterea, quòd negativi nobis non omnes placeant articuli; quòd nec imagines colamus, nec sanctos defunctos adoremus, neque legem cibariam ex praxi Romana admittamus, neque caelibatum cleri probemus, neque in purgatorium consentiamus, neque Pontificis infallibilitatem in judiciis, nec universalem potestatem sive intemporalibus, sive Ecclesiasticis agnoscamus, vel haereseos debeamus accusari, vel aqua & igni interdici? Scio, ita olim vísum fuisse Pontifici, Extrav. Comm. I. 1. Tit. 8. de Majoritate & obedientia, ubi ex ungue statim leonem: Omnes Christi fideles (ita argumentum capitis 1. sonat.) de necessitate salutis subsunt Romano Pontifici, qui utrumque gladium habet, & omnes judicat, & a nemine judicatur. Clausula verò ipsius capitis: Porro subesse Romano Pontifici omni humanae creaturae (tam in temporalibus, quàm Spiritualibus, huc enim tota Pontificis tendit disputatio) declaramus, dicimus, definimus & pronunciamus omnino esse de necessitate salutis. Sed non placuisse hæc vel Christianissimo Regi Galliarum, vel Facultati etiam Theologicae Parisiensi, tum ex documentis plurimis aliis, tum verò ex nupero Arresto supremæ Curiæ, d. 30. Maij 1663. edito, satis
units.tr: -teian [τξείαν], the unaccountable judgment of bishops, superstitious consecrations of creatures, the worship of images, fraudulent miracles adduced to confirm them, auricular confession, the multiplication of feasts, and other things which, by human authority, spurred either by the lust for domination or by the itch for innovation, and against the word of God and the command of Christ, were gradually received, commended and imposed. Such things were abolished through the Reformation, because they lacked the foundation of Scripture. This, therefore, is that blemish and that stain by which the Reformed Church, the bride of Christ, renders herself infamous, because she is unwilling to hear any voice other than the Bridegroom's. Where shall we go? Peter asks of the Saviour: "Thou hast the words of eternal life" (Joh. 6.68). Where else should we go, most learned sir? To the Council of Trent, to which the Romanists are wont to be referred? This, unless my opinion deceives me, you will not recommend. To the Roman Pontiff, the Ecumenical bishop who is superior even to the Councils themselves? This you will neither do yourself nor commend to others, you who would more readily fight for the authority of the Councils. To the decrees of the Popes? Nothing solid here. John denies what Formosus affirmed, and nothing is more usual for the new occupants of the Roman See than to unsay the decisions of their predecessors. Shall we consult the so-called Apostolic traditions? But who will guarantee that those which go under this name are not spurious? Who has hitherto dared to produce an exact catalogue of them? Shall we at last simply abide by the judgment of the Fathers? The most learned man will hardly vouch for this, since he is not unaware that not everything they wrote pleases Rome, for they were ignorant of many things, often clashed with one another, and sometimes contradicted themselves. What remains, then, except that we have recourse to him alone who is the way, the life and the truth (Joh. 14.6)? Yet the Church of Rome also has the Word of God, the holy Bible? Let it have it; but it does not have it alone, and it follows another religion, and that a crooked one, indeed by the arrangement of traditions it still follows a rule of its own. By which name the Reformed certainly snatch the palm of happiness from the Roman Church. Even the best food can bring destruction from the tiniest grain of poison. The Reformed, together with the ancient Church, acknowledge as the medicine of the soul [Ἰατρεῖον ψυχῆς] the holy Scripture, pure and purified, not mixed. As the surgeon who applies a plaster to a wound, which by universal consent is healing and sufficient for curing the injury, heals more safely, more quickly and more pleasantly than one who, under the appearance of a more convenient remedy, mixes in other things about which those skilled in the art dispute, so those act with less danger who, in examining, determining and receiving the dogmas of faith, embrace only that which, by the reckoning and vote of all, everywhere and always in the Christian Church, has been held as a divine oracle beyond controversy, and to which no one has dared to deny the office both of judge in faith and of judge in life; rather than those who, under the pretext of fuller revelation, seize upon even those things which have always been doubtful and controversial. Therefore not even an angel, if he should announce any other gospel than that which has been announced to us, ought to defraud us of so distinguished a treasure. But why should that Church expect hatred or reproach from others on account of any merit of its own, when it keeps the foundation of salvation? That the Tigurines do keep it, the Helvetic Confession amply attests. That they have cut away the errors which, gradually grown into the doctrines, either dangerously stray from the goal or otherwise undermine the foundation, is something to be counted to their praise, since they obeyed God rather than men, after the Apostolic example. Let the Papist school produce a single article, fundamental in the Lord's, Apostolic and primitive Church, which our Reformers have rejected. If therefore nothing has been lost of the foundation of salvation through the Reformation, while the other doctrines, rites and government observed hitherto in the Roman Church, some directly and others indirectly undermine the foundation, others miserably disturb consciences, others are not grasped by the weakness of human intellect, others draw the common people away from inner devotion, why should we not most gladly adhere to that religion which, the foundation being preserved, is not hindered by so many inconveniences and difficulties, dangerous and modest? What, I ask, is here again either guilt or crime? Or are we to be accused of heresy, or banned from water and fire, because not all the negative articles please us; because we neither worship images, nor adore the dead saints, nor admit the dietary law as practised in Rome, nor approve the celibacy of the clergy, nor assent to purgatory, nor acknowledge the infallibility of the Pontiff in judgments, nor his universal power, whether in temporal or in ecclesiastical matters? I know that this was once the view of the Pontiff, in Extrav. Comm. I. 1, Tit. 8, de Majoritate et obedientia, where from the claw one at once recognises the lion: All the faithful of Christ (so the argument of the first chapter runs) are, of necessity for salvation, subject to the Roman Pontiff, who holds both swords, and judges all, and is judged by no one. But the closing clause of the same chapter: Moreover, we declare, state, define and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation that every human creature be subject to the Roman Pontiff (in temporal as well as spiritual matters, for to this the whole of the Pontiff's disputation tends). But that these things have not pleased either the Most Christian King of France or the Faculty of Theology of Paris, is sufficiently clear both from many other documents and from the recent decree of the Supreme Court, published on 30 May 1663. The propositions of the Faculty stand verbatim thus: First, that it is not doctrine that the supreme Pontiff has any authority over the temporal affairs of the Most Christian King; indeed the Faculty has opposed even those who wished that authority to be only indirect. Second, that it is doctrine of the Faculty…

units.la: R tis est manifestum. Positiones Facultatis αὐτολεξεὶ ita habent: Primò non esse doctrinam Facultibus, summum Pontificem aliquam in temporalibus Regis Christianissimi auctoritatem habere; imò obstitisse Facultatem etiam in iis, qui indirectam tantummodo voluerunt esse illam auctoritatem. Secundò, esse doctrinam Facul tatis, quòd Rex Christianissimus nullum omnino agnoscit nec habet in temporalibus superiorem, praeterDeum, eámque esse antiquam doctrinam, a qua nunquam recessura est. Tertiò, doctrinam Facultatis esse, quòd subditi fidem & obedientiam Regi Christianissimo ita debent, ut ab iis nullo praetextu dispensari possint. Quarto eandem facultatem non probare, nec probasse unquam propositiones ullas Christianissimi Regis auctoritati, aut germanis Ecclesiae Gallicanae libertatibus & receptis in regno Canonibus contrarias: Verbi gratia, quòd summus Pontifex deponere possit Episcopos adversus eosdem Canones. Quinto, doctrinam Facultatis non esse, quòd summus Pontifex sit supra Concilium Oecumenicum. Sextò, non esse doctrinam, nec dogma Facultatis, quòd sumus Pontifex, nullo accedente Ecclesiae consensu, sit infallibilis. Haec facultas Theologica Parisiensis. Sed, num forte propterea Reformati male audient, quòd sacra sua ad normam Scripturae sacrae exactissimè voluerint reformata, aut repurgata? Caeteri, qui EcEcclesiæ Romanæ adorant culmen, si quid forte habeant ex Scriptura, traditionum mox humanarum luto permiscent; laneum lineo intexunt; ignem alienum ad aram Domini asserunt, verbum Dei καπηλεύοντ cauponum more adulterant. Reformati vero vel ideo hoc gaudent nomine, quòd ad normam & formam verbi Dei omnia voluerint repurgata. Aut num Tigurini eo displiceant nomine, quòd per Reformationem è medio sustulerint, longéq; valere jusserint, quicquid vel honorem Dei laedit, vel per quod proximi salus ad scopulos allidit & syrtes?
