Non videt Ecclesia Reformata, Verbum Dei scriptum, cum Traditionibus, ceu verbo non scripto, posse subsistere. Cur? Reclamat gloria Dei, quæ non permittit Deo tribui ita & non, 2. Cor. 1.18. At constat, duplex illud verbum è diametro sibi esse oppositum. Illud cultum imaginum prohibet, hoc eum commendat. Tollunt Ecclesiæ Reformatæ mercatum Indulgentiarum, metum Purgatorii, &c. Cur? Detrahunt hæc humanæ curiositatis inventa gloriæ justitiæ divinæ, quæ ejusdem debiti geminam solutionem non admittit. Satisfecisse Christum pro peccatis nostris, Scriptura ubique testatur. Cur ergo satisfaciendum denuo sit iis, qui si satisfacere potuissent, Christum è gremio Patris sui non elicuissent? Non probat Ecclesia Reformata immoderatum, quem Ecclesia Romana recipit & admittit cultum B. Mariæ Virginis & Sanctorum. Cur? Quia adorationis sibi honorem soli deberi, clarissimè Deus pronunciavit, Deut. 10. 20. Matth. 4. verf. 10. Unum agnoscit Ecclesia nostra Sponsum, unum Sacerdotem, unum caput, unum Mediatorem. Cur? Quia non conveniunt conjugi duo Sponsi, nec Ecclesiæ N. T. duplex Sacerdotium proprie sic dictum; nec corpori, nisi monstroso, geminum caput, nec Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ nisi unus Mediator. Cur ergo talia vel somniaremus? Non Reformati per religionis emendationem, gratiam hominum aucupantur, opum, vel authoritatis incrementum quæruntur. Gloria Dei suprema hic Lex est; cui proximè accedit salus hominum. Lectionem & Translationem Scripturæ sacræ in Linguas vernaculas strenuè defendimus. Cur? Animarum illud salus exigit. Si enim Scripturæ sacræ sint Epistola Dei ad homines, cur non debeant legi? Si legi, cur non etiam transferri? Si sint Testamentum, filiis Dei legatum, cur denegetur illarum usus hæredibus? Si ideo datæ sunt, ut credamus, Jesum esse Christum, & credentes habeamus vitam æternam, cur arceamur à legitimo earum usu? Justificationem gratuitam, Christi merito acquisitam, & vera fide apprehensam, cum Apostolo, grata mente accipimus, sequestrato bonorum operum merito, adeóque rejecto veteri Pharisaismo. Cur? Id & gloria Servatoris nostri (qui si persectè nos non redemisset, Jesus noster non esset) & salus postulat hominum, de qua actum planè esset, si suæ quisque salutis faber esse deberet. Quantò Christiani plerique Turcis & judæis essent inferiores, si vel eleemosynarum liberalitate, vel precum sive numero sive murmure, vel quibuscunque exercitiis corporis, quibus vera pietas non absolvitur, certandum esset? Sed de his alias. Videt doctissimus Vir, nullum, religionem reformatam, odium mereri, nullam invidiam. Si qui tamen optimæ causæ insultare, & quocunq; modo Gregem Domini infestare perrexerint, nôrint, vivere adhuc Eum, qui de cœlo clamavit; Saul, Saul, quid me persequeris? Difficile tibi erit contra stimulum calcitrare, Act. 9. vers. 4. 5. Beati contrà erunt, qui persecutione invaduntur justitiæ causa; quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Beati & nos erimus, quum conviciati nos fuerint & persecuti, & mentientes quidvis mali adversus nos, propter Christum, Matth. 5. 10. 11. Gaudeamus, quoniam merces nostra gratuita magna erit in cœlis!
units.tr: ...is manifest. The Faculty's propositions [αὐτολεξεί] read word for word as follows. First, it is not the Faculty's doctrine that the Roman Pontiff has any authority in the temporal affairs of the Most Christian King; indeed the Faculty has opposed even those who wished that authority to be only indirect. Second, it is the Faculty's doctrine that the Most Christian King acknowledges no superior in temporal matters at all except God, that this is an ancient doctrine, and that it will never depart from it. Third, it is the Faculty's doctrine that subjects owe faith and obedience to the Most Christian King in such a way that they cannot be released from them on any pretext. Fourth, the same Faculty does not approve, and never has approved, any propositions contrary to the authority of the Most Christian King or to the genuine liberties of the Gallican Church and the canons received in the kingdom; for example, that the supreme Pontiff can depart from those canons by deposing bishops. Fifth, it is not the Faculty's doctrine that the supreme Pontiff is above an Ecumenical Council. Sixth, it is neither the doctrine nor the dogma of the Faculty that the supreme Pontiff is infallible without the consent of the Church. So says the Parisian Theological Faculty. But do the Reformed perhaps get a bad hearing for this reason, that they wished their sacred matters to be reformed or cleansed most exactly according to the rule of Holy Scripture? Others, who adore the summit of the Roman Church, if they have anything from Scripture, straightway mix it with the mud of human traditions; they weave wool into linen; they offer strange fire on the altar of the Lord; they adulterate the Word of God [καπηλεύοντες] like tavern-keepers. The Reformed, however, rejoice in this name precisely because they wished everything to be cleansed according to the norm and form of God's Word. Or do the Zurich Reformed displease on this account, that through the Reformation they have removed from the midst and utterly renounced whatever either injures the honour of God or dashes the salvation of neighbours upon rocks and quicksands? The Reformed Church does not see how the written Word of God can stand together with traditions as with an unwritten word. Why? The glory of God protests, which does not allow God to be ascribed "yes and no" (2 Cor. 1:18). But it is clear that those two words are diametrically opposed to each other. The one forbids the worship of images, the other commends it. The Reformed Churches abolish the trade in indulgences, the fear of Purgatory, and so on. Why? These inventions of human curiosity detract from the glory of divine justice, which does not admit a double payment of the same debt. Scripture everywhere testifies that Christ made satisfaction for our sins. Why then must satisfaction be made again by those who, if they could have satisfied, would not have drawn Christ from the bosom of his Father? The Reformed Church does not approve the immoderate cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the Saints which the Roman Church receives and admits. Why? Because God has most clearly declared that honour of worship is due to him alone (Deut. 10:20; Matt. 4:10). Our Church acknowledges one Bridegroom, one Priest, one Head, one Mediator. Why? Because two bridegrooms do not suit one spouse, nor does the Church of the New Testament have a double priesthood properly so called; nor does a body, unless it be monstrous, have two heads, nor does the Apostolic Church have more than one Mediator. Why then should we even dream of such things? The Reformed do not seek the favour of men through the amendment of religion, nor do they aim at an increase of wealth or authority. The supreme law here is the glory of God; the salvation of men comes closest to it. We vigorously defend the reading and translation of Holy Scripture into the vernacular tongues. Why? The salvation of souls demands it. For if the Holy Scriptures are God's letter to mankind, why should they not be read? If they are read, why should they not also be translated? If they are a Testament bequeathed to the children of God, why should the use of them be denied to the heirs? If they were given so that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, and that believing we may have eternal life, why should we be shut out from their lawful use? We receive with a grateful mind, with the Apostle, justification freely given, acquired by the merit of Christ and grasped by true faith, the merit of good works being set aside and the old Pharisaism thereby rejected. Why? The glory of our Saviour (who, if he had not redeemed us perfectly, would not be our Jesus) and the salvation of men both require this; and salvation would be utterly undone if each person had to be the maker of his own salvation. How far inferior would most Christians be to Turks and Jews, if we had to contend for salvation by the generosity of almsgiving, or by the number or murmur of prayers, or by whatever bodily exercises, with which true piety is not fulfilled? But of these matters on another occasion. The most learned man sees that the Reformed religion deserves no hatred and no ill will. If, however, any should persist in insulting a good cause and in troubling the flock of the Lord in any way, let them know that he lives still who cried from heaven: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It will be hard for you to kick against the goad" (Acts 9:4-5). On the contrary, blessed will be those who are assailed with persecution for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. We too shall be blessed when they revile and persecute us and say all manner of evil against us falsely, for Christ's sake (Matt. 5:10-11). Let us rejoice, for our reward will be great in heaven!
